paragraphs.text: On Exhortation
First discourse, by Mar Jacob the Teacher: On Exhortation.

Stir my voice to praise you, Son of God, and let all my senses glorify you with their songs. For my tongue has been fashioned for your praise from the beginning, and if it ceases from praising you, it deserves punishment. My Lord, let me not cease from singing your songs, lest justice punish me in a righteous judgment. The human mouth is fashioned to praise the divine nature, and whoever keeps silent instead of praising is blameworthy and subject to rebuke. The Creator himself, when he created the mouth, placed voice and speech within it so that it might be moved to offer praise. Thus everyone who recognizes that there is a Creator is obliged to give praise, like tribute, to the Lord who created him.

Empty tales and these unseemly words— the human mouth is not permitted to employ them. The Creator himself, when he was creating, fashioned it this way: the mouth is for his praise, not for the use of empty things. “Cry out with your throat and raise your voice like a trumpet,” says the Lord to anyone who keeps silent instead of praising him. I am your creature, my Lord; grant that I may marvel at your works. Since you created me, grant that I may be moved to offer praise. Grant that the heart may serve you with holy thoughts, for you are awesome above all creatures. Sanctify my tongue from all worldly talk, and let it be moved to offer praise in converse with you. See, my mouth is open to you; fill it with praise, my Lord, as you promised. Let no empty speech pass through it or be uttered by it. Let my voice be stirred by your gift, so full of wonder, Son of God, as I give thanks in praise of you.
Finished.
On the Descent of the Most High upon Mount Sinai
Again, the second discourse: On the Descent of the Most High upon Mount Sinai, and the Mystery of the Church, composed by Mar Jacob.

Mighty One of the ages, whose power descended upon Mount Sinai, grant that I may sing with my voice of the strength of your might. You who hold the ends of the world, who humbled yourself so that Sinai could contain you, let my mind grasp you without limiting you, insofar as it is possible. O you who descended upon the lofty mountain without descending, descend in truth to the height of the mind that awaits you. Through you, O Fiery One, let my mind send up smoke like Mount Sinai, and let a cloud of voices proclaiming your glory rise from it. Grant that I may say that the mountain bore you figuratively: a small measure of your power overshadowed it, and the whole of it trembled. You descended to the summit of Sinai, the rocky mountain, in a borrowed form. Come to the spiritual mind, which is looking toward you. The earth does not perceive you and embrace you as the mind does, nor do the mountains receive you as thoughts do.

The mind is greater in breadth than Mount Sinai. Overshadow it, and let a voice of thanksgiving rise from it. You did not reject the one you betrothed in the region of Sinai. Come, betroth the soul that hangs upon the beauty of your songs. After you loved her, the congregation of the people committed adultery with the calf. My Lord, do not let silence enter my mind and commit adultery within it. Let the account of you become a husband to my speech, and its guardian too. Let it unite with her, so that she too may bear fruits of praise. Be zealous like Moses, and scatter silence as he scattered the calf, so that the soul may cling to conversation with you through her songs. Speaking of you is beyond all the mouths of Watchers and human beings, and spacious minds cannot encompass you with their thoughts. The account of you surpasses both speakers and listeners, and the search for you is hidden from those above and those below. Your dwelling is concealed from bodily and spiritual beings, and your abode is far beyond earthly and heavenly beings. The power that holds the ends of the world cannot be bounded, and the command swifter even than lightning cannot be overtaken. He cannot be expressed by tongues of flame.

Nor can even the fiery beings proclaim him in their utterances. The speaking mouths of Gabriel’s company cannot encompass him, and he is far beyond the trumpet of Michael’s company. He is high and exalted, remote and concealed, hidden and lifted up; mighty and veiled, secret and glorious, powerful and wondrous. He holds the depths and reaches the outer limits by the power of his being. He holds created things and nourishes the worlds through his works. All created things are filled from him, while he remains undiminished. All the ends of creation are contained in him and sustained by him. Greater than the heights, he dwells within the depths and throughout everything. He sits at the summit of the heights like a judge, and at his command the ranks of all created things move. His power also spread out the earth upon nothing by a command, and the might of his creative power carries it like a mighty warrior. Below, his command supports creation so that it does not sink; above, his decree holds the heavens fast, lest they fold up [?]. He dwells like a soul within created things and carries them. They rest upon him and are not far from his sustaining care. He is beyond them, on this side of them, and within them all. They are contained in him, for he is the boundary of all their limits.

For he is not in a location, a place, or a region. Resting and journeying can be attributed to him only figuratively. This power, for whom all places are too small, is said to have descended to Mount Sinai and dwelt there. The mind floats on the waves of discourse about his wondrous nature, and does not know with what sounds to sing of his deeds. Shall I confine my account to his descent upon Mount Sinai, or speak of this: that he never descended except in a likeness? Let us proclaim his boundlessness here in the account, and approach and speak of his descent with great wonder. Consider, discerning one, the questions at the beginning of the discourse, and prepare your hearing to receive glorious things. Reflect on this mighty one who holds the ends of the earth: what reason summoned him to descend upon Mount Sinai? His compassion drew him toward humanity to show her mercy, and in his love he came to betroth and marry the daughter of earthly beings. He desired the congregation, that daughter of the righteous, because of her ancestry, wishing to draw near to that lineage of Abraham’s house. He saw the young woman while the Egyptians were abusing her.

Yet the Holy One felt no revulsion at the prostitute. He sent after the corrupted woman to bring her back to himself, so that through union with him the daughter of the righteous might be made holy. He made Moses a matchmaker and sent him to her, to settle the terms with her as a mediator. He gave him strength and might as he went down, so that he might persuade her through wonders to come up with him. The Levite went down, performed wonders, and led her up. He placed on her hand the ring he had received from the bush. He betrothed her to the Holy Name and brought her up out of Egypt, for he was guarding her as a trust belonging to the house of God. He placed the crown of salvation on her head and went out with her. He summoned created things to honor her with their harps. Because reckless Pharaoh wanted to keep her from him, the Holy One grew jealous, overthrew him in the sea, and led her up. When she was set free, he sent [?] after her to Egypt. The waves escorted her, and she crossed the sea amid great wonder. Horeb welcomed her and brought out extraordinary gifts. The wilderness bowed before her with its offerings when she entered it. All creation knew to whom she had been betrothed, and all the forces of nature came and accompanied her to honor her.

All the elements carried offerings and went before her, crowding together to come with her to the Holy One. The great pillar of light ran ahead to illuminate her way. Like a torch accompanying a bride, it followed her and traveled with her. Every day gifts from created things accompanied her, while she reveled in the finest foods. The heights delighted her with the manna they sent her, and the depths fattened her with the quail they offered her. Blessed waters flowed for her from the flint, and all the forces of nature nourished the pampered woman. All created things agreed to go with her, so that the world might see the great wedding feast being held for her. She was escorted in honor by her companions as far as Sinai, and reached the place where her Lord had arranged to meet her. Moses, her bridal attendant, left her opposite the mountain and went up to see when the bridegroom would come to meet her. He heard the Hidden One commanding him: “Go down and tell this bride whom I redeemed and brought out of Egypt: ‘See, I carried you as though on an eagle’s wings through the air, and escorted you through the lands unharmed.

Let us live in love, and let an agreement stand between me and you. Then I will come and marry you in holiness. Before the feast, I am making all my wishes known to you. If you agree with me, come to the wedding that I desire for you. I want you to remain beside me in a pure union, without throwing yourself at another to commit sexual immorality. I will establish you forever in hope in me. Never again let yourself be drawn to another who would come in to you. I will marry you in holiness if you belong to me; but if you debase yourself with strangers, I will divorce you. Let me see in you no hateful sign of adulteresses, nor the behavior found in a woman who has secret affairs. Do not show me the shameful gestures of loose women, or practice the arts of shameless women. Do not bow down in worship before anyone but me, and from now on do not enter into another covenant. Be holy, humble, chaste, and without blemish; radiant, spotless, clear, and pure in every way. Be diligent, guarded, and pure; calm and quiet; serene and watchful; gentle, beautiful, and unstained.

If you come to me like this, with confidence, you will be mistress over everything I possess, with no one commanding you. I will give you a great crown, the adornment of kings, and cause holiness, the treasure of priests, to dwell in you. Prophets who reveal hidden things will belong to you, and priests who make atonement for sins will dwell with you. See, the Levites will go with you like officers, and ministers will accompany you like servants. Heaven will [?] its dew gently upon your land, and the earth will lavish abundant good things upon you. The air will pour out every splendor upon your camp, and the sun will ripen sweet fruits for you to eat. You will inherit the land of all the kings who fight against you, and you will not be defeated by the warriors who come out to confront you. You will set your heel upon the necks of the rulers of the earth, trampling all crowns beneath your authority. I am giving you a document written with my own hands concerning these things. If you conduct yourself toward me according to my will, they will all be yours.’” The bridegroom sent this covenant through Moses, so that he would go down and see whether the bride agreed to it with the bridegroom. The mediator, a son of the Hebrews, came down from the mountaintop.

He called the heads of Jacob’s household and its rulers. He repeated before them the bridegroom’s words exactly as they had been spoken, asking whether they agreed to the terms he had set or not. They answered him affectionately, rejoicing in him: “We agree to your mediation, Moses, our scribe. The bridegroom rightly seeks our daughter in holiness. If only we could unite that family with ours! We are too insignificant for such a bridegroom to be proposed for us! Whoever is marrying into whose family, for us—for us it is a great blessing! Here before you is the girl we raised among the Egyptians. Learn from her about the terms your Lord has set.” Moses called her to question her before the elders, and she joyfully gave her consent to go with him. The Levite heard that she had given herself willingly, and he joyfully returned to his Lord to tell him. “My Lord, the girl has agreed to our mystery, as we asked her, and she does not hold back from living in holiness. Look, the good girl has made a pledge to me, as you instructed me; and if she is faithful, as she says, she will not be stolen away.” He answered Moses again and told him, “Return to her.

Go down and adorn her, both outwardly and inwardly. Outwardly, let her wear splendid white garments in which she will shine; inwardly, thoughts of holiness through which she will be beautiful. Let her consecrate herself to me today and tomorrow in a mystical way, and on the third day I will come to her in power.” Moses went down and began to adorn the bride. He toiled and exerted himself to prepare the unruly girl. He taught the headstrong girl not to behave wantonly, and instructed her: “Do not let the hidden bridegroom loathe you. Strew holiness before him on the road along which he will come in procession, so that you may see his face in purity when you welcome him. Place a crown of holiness on your head when he sees you, so that in radiance you may enter the bridal chamber of light with him.” A great mystery met me here and detained me beside it. Because I had wronged it, it now disputes with me and reproaches me: “Why, you ignorant man, did you not honor [?] me as you passed by? Do not be ashamed of me, for I am the beauty of your songs.” The Son’s story shone forth in the midst of the discourse about his Father, demanding of me: “Unless you sing of me, you shall not pass on. Do not divide us with your inventions, you misguided fool! Our story is one; let it not be divided between your lips.”

Since the truth has constrained me and I cannot escape it, I will raise my voice about the Son of the Living One, and then move on. Do not separate the likeness of Moses from that of Christ. Let us see here in what way he resembled the Son of God. In his descent from the mountaintop to the Hebrews, the path of Jesus is visible to anyone who understands. Through his mediation, as he went down and up to the daughter of Jacob, Christ’s mediation toward humanity was prefigured. Listen, you who understand, to how closely the servant resembled his Lord, and how, in a mystery, he called him “a prophet like me.” Through him the daughter of Abraham was delivered from Egypt, and through him she was betrothed to become the bride of that Holy One. Through his hand she drew near to become the bride of the King, her Lord. He sanctified her so that she might behold the Most High in purity. He became a mediator between God and his camp, resembling his Lord, through whom his Father was reconciled to the world. In this pattern Christ came down to humanity: he redeemed her, sanctified her, purified her, bathed her, and cleansed her. In place of the white garments in which Moses clothed the daughter of Jacob, Jesus made the soul white through sanctification in the water.

For three days Moses sanctified the daughter of the people, but through the hands of our Lord holiness was established forever. The shadow of the Son of God rested there, and as it passed, it portrayed an image of the realities. Because of these mysteries accomplished through Moses’ hands, he dared to call the Son of God “a prophet like me.” If I open the door to the mysteries of my entire account, they will not let me approach its conclusion. For throngs of hidden things press upon me; I cannot bring their revelations to an end. I undertook to speak about the Most High’s descent to Sinai. My speech, hurry straight toward the point of the account! Do not become entangled among the mysteries of all my words. It is clear that they cannot be brought to an end, nor have they ever been. Let me travel swiftly along the path of this discourse toward its conclusion, leaving many things aside in the midst of the account. Moses then went down to adorn the bride he had brought, so that the bridegroom to whom she was betrothed might see her in her beauty. He instructed her, and she dressed herself; he rejoiced in her, and she grew beautiful; he adorned her, and she became lovely. He heightened her radiance, guided her, taught her wisdom, and completed her adornment. For three days Moses attended to her, teaching her,

and instructing her in how she should behold her Lord. He fashioned wise words for her and placed them in her mouth, so that she would know how to answer the glorious bridegroom if he called her. Moses, her tutor and guardian, was teaching her wisdom, so that through her he might have confidence before the Holy One. When she had learned how she should behold the bridegroom, and what appearance she should assume before him when she reached him, and when she had prepared herself for three days in holiness, then the bridegroom went out from his place to come down to her. The Mighty One arose and clothed himself in heroic strength, to come mightily in majesty. He moved without moving, to descend to earth without descending, and cast terror upon the heights and the depths: “Look, he is coming!” The command stirred the heavenly armies, and the King prepared to journey without moving. The ranks of fire stirred before him, saying, “Look, he is coming!” They moved vigorously to go ahead of his arrival. The ranks surged forward, one after another, in haste, and one company of the sons of light joined another. The companies on high were astonished at descending to earth, and the burning, flying beings sped through the air before the Mighty One.

A commotion arose among the assemblies on high, and they burned with eagerness to come, for they heard the Fiery One roaring behind them. Thousands of flaming ranks assembled to escort the living Fire as he descended to earth. The command swiftly descended to the meadows of light and quickly gathered the angels within them. The spiritual beings trembled, saying, “Look, he is coming to descend upon the mountain!” The terrifying sounds that went out with him hurried them along. The new report astonished the heavenly beings: the Hidden One had set his course to descend to earth. They gathered to see what place he was coming out of, where he had been concealed, how he was coming, and on what he was traveling. While the rational ranks were bewildered, the Power appeared, along with burning fire, the dwelling of the Hidden One—a wondrous sight. Was it not in a likeness that the Watchers saw the bodiless One? For he did not truly journey from the heights into the depths. Under a borrowed name he descended mightily upon the mountain, so that the daughter of Abraham might long for his majesty. He went out, though he came only figuratively, and set created things trembling with the triumphant shouting of his armies. He sent forth a voice at which the roots of the mountains trembled,

so that the world might become aware of the banquet he had descended to hold. The archangel’s horn sounded mightily. Its sound rose, and created things trembled in their very natures. The trumpet cried out from the summit of heaven’s height and shook the rocks with the force of its mighty sound. He set out to come in awe and great wonder. He left his place and crossed the firmament, for he was about to descend. He gathered lightning and swiftly went out into the air, to tread upon the rays of light he had poured out and pass over them. He kindled fire in the horses of fire and spurred them on, so that they might go brightly before him like torches. He flooded the region of the air with his blazing fire and dazzled the eyes so that they could not look upon him as he is. Voices cried out high in the vault of heaven, for it was most fitting that shouting should accompany the Bridegroom. The lightning bolts stretched out over creation were intertwined: threads of fire that the living Silkworm had spun. The Mighty One descended and settled upon the mountain, making all of it tremble. It smoked and melted from the flame that rested upon it. A cloud enveloped it to cool it with its chill, with the moist dew that the command sprinkled over its burning.

The smoke of the flame rose as from a furnace, while the stones burned in a fire that could not be touched. It is a wonder to recount how the rocks split apart there, and even the flints burned like sparks. The flame spread even through the cliffs; smoke rose even from the stones as from wood. The fire had loosened the mountain, and it was about to fall, but the Power that carries all creation supported it with a firm command. That mighty one who trod upon it and made it tremble all over was himself supporting the mountain by his power so that it would not collapse. The mountain of stone could not bear the Power that carries the ends of the world in his might. He himself carried the mountain that carried him when he overshadowed it, for he is the Power who, in his hidden being, sustains everything. It has indeed been heard that the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai; but how he descended is a wonder to recount among marvelous things. Let us weave together our account of how he descended and how he did not descend. Let us give the statement a double sense: I do not confine him, even while saying that he was confined. To the simple person let us say firmly that he descended; to the discerning person, however, it is clear that he did not descend at all. He whose hidden being the heavens cannot contain—

could the little space of Mount Sinai contain him? For him whose footstool is the earth beneath his feet, how could one corner of that footstool suffice for him to dwell upon? He descended upon the mountaintop figuratively, not by becoming confined, without moving from where he was to the place where he descended. He indeed inclined over Mount Sinai by [?] of his power, without traveling from there to here in that descent. While he remained on high, he dwelt on the mountain without being confined; and without moving, he made use of the image of descent. He sent forth from within the bush a manifestation full of trembling, while he himself remained where he was. The words are awe-inspiring, the subject fearful, and the discourse formidable; even the tongue falters over it in its weakness. If the mouth could recount it as it deserves, even the ear would be torn apart by the mystery. If I could express its awesomeness, I would cast astonishment upon the listeners through sheer terror. If my mind did not rebuke me, saying, “Say no more,” I would not have confined that descent within ordinary words. How shall I speak, how much shall I say, and when shall I fall silent?

By what means can I confine the limitless within an account? If Mount Sinai, though it was rock, melted because of him, will not a tongue of flesh shrink from recounting him? The Holy One held a wedding feast for the wanton woman, and he came to her so that she might be made holy through union with him. He built his pavilion out of thick darkness on the summit of Sinai, a great bridal chamber of flame in a lofty place. And because shouting is constant at a feast and there is much commotion, he made sounds ring out so that the bride would rejoice on the day of her happiness. The cloud on the mountain became a chamber for the royal bridegroom, and he dwelt there, displaying his majesty through terrifying wonders. Sounds that tore the earth came out of the thick clouds, and wondrous sights whose flashes overwhelmed the eye. Dense flashes of lightning darted swiftly, and a surge of fire flared up with burning heat. Ranks of Watchers shone with spiritual radiance, and thousands of heavenly hosts sang praise with mighty voices. The sound of the horn was exceedingly powerful and shook the mountain; it overwhelmed the ear with wonder and made it tremble. Let us listen to this too with wonder and understanding; let us attend discerningly to these marvelous things.

What was the horn that cried out there on Mount Sinai? What was it made of, and was it really a horn? Look, learned one, how forceful borrowed expressions are, and how powerful they are in the realm of hidden things. He made sounds heard without [?] anything, as though through something; and he called it the sound of a horn, although it was not a horn. He commanded the air, and all of it roared toward Sinai—a sound confined neither in horns nor in pipes. The command blew within the thick clouds as though into a horn, and thunder came out that tore the earth with its force. Even in this, the wedding custom was observed: the bridegroom enters his chamber to the sound of a horn. He had given Moses this sign before he went down to the people, while he alone knew it. He said, “When the horn falls silent, let the people go up [?] the mountain.” Its sound both rose and fell silent according to an established order. Whenever it rose so high that hearing itself would fail before it, it was softened so that it would not overwhelm its listeners. When the hidden power made it cry out, it then lowered it again, so that it would reach the ear in an orderly way. At this sight, which was terrifying to those on earth,

the people thought that the Lord in his entirety was dwelling on the mountain. Childish people think that a hollow horn produced these sounds, which the hidden command had fashioned. Because it was said that the Lord descended, the unlearned trembled, thinking that the heights had been emptied of him because he was on the mountain. Because it was heard that the sound of the horn was exceedingly powerful, they likewise imagine that he spoke as a being made up of parts. From the borrowed expressions used to help them, those who went astray thought that the one who has no parts was made up of parts. In keeping with their childishness, he also presents the demonstration in this way; he can even measure out visions to match the understanding. With the measure of the intellect he pours them out upon the mind, so that everyone may see him according to their understanding, as far as they are able. A reason called him to incline his might toward Mount Sinai: that the congregation might attach herself to him through a vision of majesty. Had he not descended, she might have said after her adultery, “Since I have not seen him, how can I still wait for him?” And although he had so carefully arranged the matter of the requests, word went out: “Look, the Lord is descending to the mountain!” He displayed a wonder, as though he dwelt in his entirety upon the mountain.

Sinai shook, for the Mighty One of strength had trodden upon its summit. Smoke rose like a furnace throughout the mountain, so that she might be assured of the fiery One who dwelt there. The heaps of rock melted in the fire that consumed them, so that it might be believed that the One wrapped in flame was there. The lightning flashed swiftly, the thunder followed repeatedly, and the sounds were terrifying, so that one might think from them that the whole divine Presence was there. He stretched out a cloud like a doubled veil and wrapped it around the mountain, as though he were there within it in his entirety. He spread thick clouds like bridal veils on every side, as though the Glory were outside them [?], for he was their bridal chamber. He kindled rays of light in the air like torches, as though his [?] truly burned in honor. Even so, he gave no grounds for questioning; indeed, he gave Abraham’s daughter no grounds for complaint. After she had invited him to stay, he came to her and dwelt beside her; a little later she fashioned a calf with which to commit adultery. It is not her adultery that we must discuss now. This is reserved for another discourse that will expose her falseness.

I have extended my discourse on the Lord’s descent to Sinai. I will not stray from this incomprehensible account. The Mighty One descended and dwelt upon the mountain in the manner of his descent, and he sent Moses down to summon the bride to come to him. She came out, stood, trembled, was bewildered, recoiled [?], grew faint, turned back, knelt, weakened, shook, tottered, and diminished. She shuddered, fell, fell silent, faded, feared, perished, choked, died, and her spirit departed while she was being courted. The sounds struck her, the lightning terrified her, and the thunder roared at her. The visions frightened her, for she could not endure them. The bridegroom began to speak to her in holiness, but she would not receive him and listen to him gladly. She cried out to Moses, “You are gentle; speak to me yourself! The Lord’s voice is casting me into the realm of death!” Was the voice pleasing [?] to that adulteress? Therefore, in her filth, she recoiled from purity. She asked Moses to speak the bridegroom’s word to her, because she found it easy to argue shamelessly with him. Because these voices from Mount Sinai gave her no relief, she cried out that if she grew stubborn, she had fire to contend with. She said to that gentle man, “You speak with me.”

For she knew that he was struck and did not complain. She wanted to strike him when he spoke to her and turn on him with the troubled cries of doubt. The voice thundering from within Sinai was not feeble, so she could neither refuse nor grumble against its might. She called Moses to put up with her insolence, for she was confident that if he grew stern, putting him to death would be easy. The cries of the lion that roared and made Sinai tremble frightened her, and she wanted Moses, the lamb, to answer her gently. The eagle’s voice had shaken the hideous kite, and she asked for the chick held between her claws. She had drawn back from that voice which shakes mountains, and she longed for Moses’ halting speech. The blaring horn high in the air had shaken her, and she longed to hear the stammerer’s speech, which pleased her. But it was not because Moses was dear to her that she wanted him to speak with her; the adulteress had drawn back from God. She heard the bridegroom warning her against strangers, and the pure word did not please the adulteress. She devised an excuse to drive the Holy One’s voice away from her. Craftily she called to Moses, “You speak with me.”

For had she not been determined to do wrong there, she would not have drawn back from the bridegroom who had come to her. Had she not been casting her eye on strangers, she would not have preferred Moses’ speech to that of the Hidden One. Had she not been disgraced in the bridegroom’s eyes, she would not have shrunk from speaking with him when she met him. Had her heart not loved her corrupter, she would have welcomed her true betrothed to speak with her. If she was pure, why was she ashamed before the Holy One? It became plain that she was disgraced, and that was why she recoiled. She saw that the hour had come when the bridegroom demanded faithfulness, and she disclosed her secret to the one who had raised her: she was debauched. She called Moses to speak to her as she wished, for she thought her adultery would remain hidden. “You speak with me, gentle one,” she said to him, “but let God restrain his cries, which make me tremble.” Moses coaxes and encourages her as though she were a little girl: “He wants to test you. Do not be frightened of the Mighty One. He will make an agreement and ascend to his lofty dwelling. Enter his covenant, and see—the thunder of his cries has fallen silent. Come and see him, for I am not ashamed of the one to whom I betrothed you.

Look at his presence, how awe-inspiring it is over his creatures!” Your betrothed has this power in his glory; do not shrink from his majesty in your terror. Establish with him the perfect covenant for which he came. Do not let me be put to shame because of you, for I have watched over you ever since Egypt. The congregation trembles, and Moses is alarmed but encourages her. The mountain smokes, the height is mighty, and Sinai burns. Sounds [?], astonishing visions, terrifying thunder; ranks arrayed, rows extended, glorious orders. Bands surround it, thousands are assembled, armies are drawn up; seraphim proclaim holiness, cherubim hover, and watchers fly. An astonishing sight, a wondrous appearance, the dwelling of the Hidden One; a cloud standing still, a fire burning, a cry rising high. Radiance spread abroad, light poured out, glory overflowing; brightness extending, a mighty voice, a tumult rising. Moses is humble, the bridegroom mighty, the bride contemptible; the bridal chamber is radiant, the pavilion adorned, the beauty splendid. The wedding attendants are reclining, the worlds rejoice, and the wedding feast is ready; and [?], as she draws back from the banquet. The scribe stands holding a pen to write down the terms, and the bridegroom waits to bestow the world as a dowry.

Then Abraham’s daughter despised this bridegroom, for she took no pleasure in his company—she was the calf’s companion. Curtains of clear air hung outside the mountain, along with crowns of fire, and Sinai was covered with thick clouds. God, the bridegroom, brought out wondrous garments of flame from that cloud which he had brought down with him. The bedchamber was warm with garments woven from flame, and within it lay a bed of fire that could not be grasped. Untouchable door curtains were wrapped around it; they had been prepared on that loom in God’s house. Outside was stretched a covering of cloud, dark in color, dense in substance, and slight in strength. The wind rolled it back a little, as one does a curtain, so that the congregation could see these beautiful things within it. Inside were thick darkness and burning fire on the mountaintop, and outside it was air massed together as though in its honor. The glory was hidden within that wall of clouds, appearing, yet not appearing as it truly was. The cloud concealed within itself the radiance of his face, while sifting a little brightness down upon the onlookers.

Blessed light poured from its edges, a small fragment of that glory which his people saw. Whenever the radiance burst forth and was about to appear, the cloud held it back. Mount Sinai smoked, and when it was about to split apart, the divine command upheld it. Whenever a little glory peered out from the thick darkness, he held it back with the cloud so that it would not pour out upon the onlookers. They saw him, yet did not see him clearly, for the glory within would have burned their minds. Even the sight that was hidden from their eyes encouraged them to learn that something great was within. A radiance was moving about within the thick clouds. They were afraid that if it poured out, it would set the world ablaze. They saw him through that covering of cloud, and because he was hidden, he astonished everyone around him all the more. For something distant and hidden is highly prized. For this reason the cloud became a veil for the mountain. Smoke rose to make it known that fire was there. He gathered thick clouds so that the flame would be tempered. Sounds came forth as though a horn were crying out beside him. The mountain trembled like someone oppressed by the weight upon him.

A dense cloud formed so that the flame would be revealed, and Sinai thundered because his presence was dwelling upon it. The mighty voices of the heavenly beings resounded there, proclaiming that the Lord of the heights was on the mountain with his host. Creation trembled at the sounds and terrifying sights, for the Lord of creation was on Sinai amid the thick clouds. Thunderclaps were hurled over the mountaintop, and with all this the cries signaled, “The King is here!” Trumpets sounded mightily on the height of Sinai, so that the earth would gather there for the appointed meeting with the voice of the Lord. The song of the Watchers rang out within the clouds, to announce to those outside that he was within. Whenever the fiery radiance moved within the thick cloud, the cloud restrained it so that it would not pour out beyond it. Whenever the flame poured out above the mountain, the cloud held it back so that it would not burst forth upon those below. Whenever waves of burning coals rose on Sinai’s summit, the trembling air received them lightly. The cloud was outside and the flame within it, so that the heat would be tempered by the cold. An awesome radiance flashed over the mountaintop,

and it was veiled so that it would not appear in its full force. The light was bound within that double fold of clouds, confined and fastened so that it would not [?] the whole earth. A multitude of Watchers could be heard from within the bush, and their praises surged like the sound of the sea. They were hidden in the mist that surrounded them on every side, and their voices rang out from the darkness beyond the mountain. They were hidden and singing praises; though near, they were far away. In two different ways, they were hidden from the eyes but revealed to the ears. The mountain bore that Mighty One, though it could not endure him. Had there been a way to escape, it would not have stayed. Sinai shook, and its stones burned in the blaze. Its smoke made it known that it was burning. The angels marveled that the limitless One had settled on the mountain, and though his height was so great, Sinai did not cease to bear him. The hosts who descended with him rejoiced greatly that they had been found worthy to accompany him on his journey to those made of dust. Those ranks that remained in the heights also took pride in having stayed there as members of his household, in his lofty dwelling. These thought that he was beside them in the heights above, while those imagined that he was there with them on Mount Sinai.

These peered toward the chariot to look at him, while those stood on the mountaintop to gaze at him. He was concealed from both groups, on either side, and hidden in his dwelling from those above and those below. Those below saw the fire burning on the mountaintop, while those above saw the radiance surrounding the chariot. His presence dwells within his hiddenness and is not seen; nor does he reveal himself in the depths except in due order. It is not possible for him to travel and settle in different places, for all created things are contained in him—where could he go? He was on the mountain, he was in the heights, and he was in everything: on the chariot, within the bush, and in every region. He displayed the appearance of blazing fire on the mountaintop, so that through a wonder he might hold a wedding feast among earthly beings. A wondrous sight [?] for Abraham’s daughter, so that through the wonder he might draw the bride’s gaze toward himself. Mount Sinai was supported by him even as it bore him, just as the cherubim hang upon his arm while carrying him in procession. All created things and their utmost limits hang upon him, and he arranged an occasion to dwell on the mountain to provide help. He displayed the appearance of blazing fire on the mountainside,

so that through wonders he might bind her to himself in a holy union. But when the lover of adultery drew near to come to him, she asked not even to hear his teaching. Moses calmed her so that she would remain quiet for a while, until the covenant with her was confirmed and the bridegroom ascended. While the divine presence hovered over the mountain in great wonder, the Lord called his chosen one, Moses, to enter his presence. A voice went out after Moses like a [?], telling him to enter and establish a covenant with him amid the thick clouds. He entered the cloud and was about to ascend to the Holy One, and the voice ran ahead, marking out for him a path of flame. He lifted before him the doors of that gateway of clouds, so that he might enter and see the bridegroom in his glory, where he dwelt. A command went out and cut a passage for him through the thick clouds, so that the lofty radiance from within Sinai would not terrify him. Moses entered the chamber of the bridegroom, the king, to learn his mysteries and bring the bride to the Holy One. He entered and learned, then went out to bring her as he had been commanded, so that she might draw near and hear the teaching of God’s household. He did not lead her into the bridal chamber, because she was not pure. She stood outside to listen and learn the bridegroom’s will.

Then a voice thundered toward her from the thick cloud, so that there might be a covenant of faithfulness for both him and her. He began pouring out instruction to her in a loud voice and speaking the truth to her openly and forcefully. He warned her earnestly about observances that were easy, for he did not place a heavy yoke on her neck. He taught her not to make carved images for herself, and admonished her not to turn away from him. He made known to her that he was jealous and would demand an accounting, and assured her that he would exact repayment through succeeding generations. He set ten milestones on the road of righteousness, so that they might lead her, from one to the next, to the kingdom. He placed one lamp at her head and ten before her, so that the splendid light in the Law might go before her. While she was being instructed how to observe the commandments and how to be pleasing, she despised and abandoned the awesome things that had been spoken. The Lord speaks, Sinai trembles, and the place is terrifying. Great is the wonder, and mighty the power on the mountaintop. The Lord uttered wondrous sounds before the people: terrifying thunderclaps that roared before the thick clouds.

With these sounds, filled with the trembling of flame, he taught her to listen to them in fear. From a speaking mouth that traced burning coals upon its lips, he poured out to her the sound of the commandments, so that she might learn them. With that tongue which flashed in the blaze, he extended to her the word of truth, so that she might be made firm in it. The pipe of flame sounded on the mountaintop, and the sound that thundered from the blaze terrified them. To the melody played by the voice of fire, he established the Law and built a fence so that she would not stray from the commandment. When she heard the speech that called to her and urged her on, she was asked also to listen to the instruction. Here the account of the Church took hold of me readily and gave me its hand, so that I might draw toward the conclusion with it. Let us today bring this awesome, boundless discourse to a close, so that the course of the account may turn toward another beginning. The mind has learned from the account of the mountain, which has no end. It seeks to rest, and then returns again to its story. Look, the tongue has raised a finger along the course of the account:

The time has come to bring the hidden things to completion. The word that flew over Mount Sinai seeks to teach me wisdom. Its wing has grown weary, and the height of the discourse cannot be bounded. The subject is mighty and the mind is weak—how can this be? It seeks a pause, so that it may rest upon another beginning. For it is not fitting that that daughter of Jacob should be compared with her. Let us address her briefly and bring her account to a close. In her pride, that one despised the Mighty One, while this pure one followed the Son in lowliness. He did not descend to her with angels as he did on Sinai, nor did he sound a fanfare for her with the horns of heavenly beings. Not through laws, nor in thick darkness, nor in clouds; not in a blazing fire, nor in flashes of flame. Not with the house groaning because of him wherever he dwelt: the mighty Son came down to earth in humility. He appeared to humanity in lowliness: in hunger and thirst, in sleep and weariness, and in need. While he was being tempted by Satan in the desolate wilderness; while he was being called the chief of demons by unbelievers.

While waves of stumbling blocks were battering him from every side; while he was being reproached for eating with sinners. While they were rebuking him because he also mingled with tax collectors; while they were demanding that he pay the poll tax to the king. While he had nowhere to lay his head; while he was being borne in procession on nothing more than an unadorned colt. While a linen cloth was wrapped around his waist like a servant; while he was washing the feet of the dust that his own hands had formed. While he was being sold by members of his own household who had accompanied him; while even the faithful who followed him were denying him. While he was being questioned by the judge like a murderer; while he was being scourged with whips like a guilty man. While he embraced a pillar in the court and drank in lashes; while madmen dressed him in clothes of mockery. While on his head was a crown of thorns that unclean men had woven; while he was being struck and asked, “Who hit you?” While he went out carrying the wooden cross on his shoulder; while his hands and feet were being nailed by those who had gone astray. While lots were being cast for his clothes to determine who would receive them; while gall and vinegar were offered to him on a sponge. While his side was being pierced with a merciless spear; while he was being embalmed, wrapped, and buried—blessed is her discernment!
In all these things the Church saw the Son of God. Blessed is he who won her away from the worship of idols!
The discourse on the descent of the Most High upon Mount Sinai is finished.
On the Dedication of the Church and on Moses the Prophet
Again, Discourse 3, on the Dedication of the Church and on Moses the Prophet, composed by Mar Jacob the Teacher.

You who are rich, give to the needy man who asks of you, for however much he receives, he does not hold back from returning to ask. Pour out your gift upon the beggar, though he is unworthy. He knocks at your door; my Lord, do not send him away in poverty. However much you give me, I ask again that you give me still more. Your gift has not satisfied me so much as it has made me hungry. Through the stream of your word that flows abundantly toward me, my thirst has grown greatly from drinking it.

With these drops that my tongue has lapped from his story, the thirst of my mind has not been quenched so much as it has increased. Moses is a spring, and the more I draw from him, the more he increases. Give me soil that will receive the water and yield fruit. May your story yield its harvest of praise from those who hear it: praise for you, help for them, and forgiveness for me. I have entered Moses’ field to reap a sheaf of your mysteries. Summon workers for me to praise you as they perform your task. I have begun to place a heap yielding tenfold in your barns. Grant that I may reach the blessed heap that yields a hundredfold. Your substance is too great for speakers and hearers alike. Therefore I have pressed forward to recount the beauty of your shadow. The mind cannot contemplate your true nature. That is why your image appears through me in all these accounts. See, Moses, your likeness, is being portrayed between my lips. Because he called you ‘a prophet like me,’ I have portrayed him entirely in terms of you. Simon’s shadow supported the sick. Support my feeble mind with your shadow in Moses. As long as he resembles you, I will not cease recounting his story. Since I have seen you in him, how could I stop speaking about him? He entices me to follow him swiftly, giving me hope that he is now bringing me close to the end.

And when I have brought the great account to its conclusion, thinking, ‘Now I shall rest,’ another beginning appears to me at its end. Let me flee now and enter the shelter of silence, so that I am not left halfway along the outstretched road of his mysteries. I shall leave much unsaid and speak a little about his wonders, so that in a few words we may receive a taste of his marvels. Through Moses the church was depicted in a mystery, and because it was a pattern, it was called the temporary tabernacle. He did not actually build the church, for he was not its Lord. He merely depicted it symbolically, then left it and passed on. For the chosen church had already been built from eternity, and Moses bears witness, having seen its likeness on Mount Sinai. My own thoughts did not hastily devise this reversal. Truth signaled to me: ‘This is the truth; let it be spoken through you.’ Moses saw the church’s prior existence on the mountain. He came down and depicted it within the camp, so that it might be established there. When he was commanded to construct the temporary tabernacle, it was truly the likeness of the church that he saw. You who have discernment, listen without resistance to the revealed truth. For it is Truth himself who speaks through me, though I am incapable. For when his Lord commanded Moses to show and make the temporary tabernacle, which served for a time through symbols of the church,

after listing all its forms for him, he concluded with this: ‘According to the likeness that I show you on the mountaintop.’ When he went up, he showed him the church already built within the thick cloud. It was the free Jerusalem above that he saw there. For an apprentice learning a craft first sees the completed work and then approaches it. A master does not impart instruction through words alone. He shows the completed work to the learner. For someone cannot make something without seeing it, since a craft cannot be learned without a demonstration. When a teacher takes pains to teach without growing weary, he brings a finished object and sets it before his pupil. This is what the Creator did for Moses his servant: he showed him the completed Church so that he could reproduce its likeness. So that its image would not slip away from him as he descended, he saw it in reality, so that he would not go wrong when depicting it. The likeness of something cannot be conceived merely by hearing about it; sight can gather and grasp every form. Had Moses not seen the Church built before his own eyes, he would not have been able to reproduce and make all its adornment. For according to the likeness that appeared to him on Mount Sinai,

he came down and completed that construction without uncertainty. He saw its structure crowned with flame, and its spaciousness, filled with delight in the lofty heights. He saw its dwelling, adorned in its very nature, and its great [?] enclosure, firmly established among the angels. He saw that it encompassed the limits of heaven, which were too small for it; its tent ropes stretched over the ends of the world and still extended farther. He saw its interior, which contained the heavenly hosts; they dwelt within it without being crowded, numerous though they were. He saw the divine Presence dwelling within it in the Holy of Holies, while the ranks of fire acclaimed it with voices of praise. He saw the companies standing within it as spirits, and the long ranks extending through it in fiery array. He saw the orders of heavenly beings dwelling there, and the Watchers praising and crying out words of holiness. He saw it filled, yet its interior could hold however many entered; it awaited bodily beings, to contain them just as it contained the Watchers. Moses saw that its adornment was made entirely of flame, and that its great house was wholly fire on every side. He saw the assemblies of those offering praise rejoicing within it, pouring forth majestic acclamations of holiness from their mouths. He saw creation made into a footstool for its feet,

while it, like a free woman, stood proudly in the heights above. He saw it above the limits of all the heavens, with only its Lord above it as its head. He saw the splendor of those proclaiming holiness, how they trembled, and how mighty were the voices of those offering blessing. He saw within it a place glorious, majestic, and indescribable, and farther within, what was hidden, beautiful, and beyond investigation. He saw within it light poured out and spreading without limit, the awesome, indescribable radiance of flame. He saw the arrangement of open gates before other gates, with radiance spread over them and the divine Presence dwelling beyond the light. In the likeness he saw an inner house like the one he made, surrounded by an outer courtyard like the one he constructed. He saw the ranks and the pillars surrounding it, a work of light, cut and carved from flame. He saw the clouds bound together within it, and in their place he made curtains for his own. He saw that it was covered with the color of fire in every form, and he dyed skins to imitate these colors. He saw the moon resembling the rainbow in the clouds, and he dyed the red leather and the blue leather to resemble it. He saw it borne upon the cherubim, on shoulders of fire.

And he made poles so that he might have his own carried in procession by the Levites. Exactly as he saw it, so he depicted it. If he had not seen it, could he have outlined all its ornaments? Here the mystery was revealed as clearly as the sun. As it flows to me, let it be expressed through me in its actual workings. Moses resembled our Lord in the things he did, for he was his likeness, his shadow, and an image of his body. In the structure that the Levite saw on the mountain, he portrayed the Church herself, acting as an image of Christ. David bears witness that the Church had already been built symbolically from that time, for he too saw it, just as Moses did. “Remember the congregation that you acquired long ago.” In these words David openly proclaimed the construction of the perfected Church. Moses saw its perfection, came down, and depicted it. He conveyed the mystery of the Church and our Lord through its construction. These things I have said are not obscure, listeners. They require understanding, and then they become known. Now I have undertaken to show you truly how Moses depicted the Church in every form. In the tabernacle he portrayed the dwelling of the crowned one, and in the Holy of Holies, the radiant altar of the mistress of mysteries. He portrayed the seventy leaders of the people as apostles,

and in the Twelve, the heads of the tribes whom he chose. He poured into these men some of the spirit that was in Moses, just as Christ poured into his apostles the breath of his mouth. Through Moses they became teachers of all the people, and he himself was honored as a god by the camp. The seventy received some of his spirit and went out among the tribes, just as Christ was proclaimed by the company of seventy. This mystery accompanied the stammerer who rose to greatness, and because of this he received authority to be a god. This order, which came into the world through our Lord, had already been handed down through Moses as a pledge. For if Moses had not portrayed him fully in every respect, he would not truly have called him “a prophet like me.” Mysteries were heaped upon him until he burned and consumed his body, and his form remained for the great radiance of the Godhead. He was intensely [?] in the image of his flames, until he shone like a fiery being in the glory he had put on. He entered into the likeness and seethed within it as though in fire; he came out of it blazing fiercely. His appearance had acquired a burning radiance from Christ, and the people regarded him as God, with great fear.

The mystery wove itself a nest of fire within his face and settled there, and he terrified those who saw him. His whole image had been fashioned after that Savior, and because of his beauty he cast terror upon everyone who saw him. He burned with colors that had been mingled in him from Christ, and the people were on the verge of thinking that he was God. He had climbed to the height of the mysteries and risen far above, almost sharing in the adored name of the Godhead. The whole earth marveled at the varied deeds he performed and was close to believing that he was its Lord. A reputation for mighty power accompanied him among the nations, and they thought that perhaps he was the ruler over created things. The camp saw him commanding the heights and the depths, and lifted its eyes to regard him as bearing the name of Creator. The people had forgotten even God, because he was hidden, while Moses, who was near, filled his Lord’s place. Moses has drawn me this far with his wonders, and I can no longer keep pace with him, for he outstrips me. For I am overwhelmed by the story of the son of the Levites: however much I say, still more remains, and there is no end to it. If my mind had not been weakened by the subject itself,

only now would I have begun to speak in detail. If the mind were not drowning in such abundance, this would be the beginning, not the end, of the discourse on Moses. Here I will set a milestone of silence as a resting place, and if there is time, I will travel again along the path of [?]. The mystery he served there is wondrous and inexpressible, and I remain silent so that the great figure may not be diminished through me. Who, indeed, is capable of describing that descent from the mountaintop to the people as it really was? Until this point he had been serving amid glorious mysteries; here he took on the King’s great image and descended. He rose like the sun upon the Hebrews and dazzled them; rays went out from his face over the camp. His light flashed, and the people marveled at its intensity. His beams descended, and the tribes trembled at the wonder they saw. A sun of flesh, wrapped in rays, descended from the mountain, and with a veil he concealed his majesty from those who looked at him. O veil wrapped in mysteries, you are a wonder to me, for your likeness is portrayed in the humanity of the Son of God. In that veil which Moses placed over his face, the bodily nature of the Son of God was visible. Because of these mysteries of truth with which Moses was clothed,

he called his Lord [?] “a prophet like me.” Within the veil, the synagogue honored Moses; and in his humanity, the Church received our Lord. [?] she fell before Moses near the camp: this is the image of the Church taking hold of our Lord in his body. These mysteries were sung by someone learned, and through someone [?] and sharp-minded they would have grown still richer. Although the story of Moses has been poorly told by me, do not, my Lord, withhold the reward for this lazy man's little labor. Receive the weakness of this discourse lovingly, and let my little coin fall upon your table, with discernment. Because I have not encompassed you, my Lord, I cannot justly be blamed. For who is capable of telling your story comprehensively? Accept the gift of little utterances that my tongue has sent, and keep a treasure of mercy for me with you until I come. In return for the short verses I have sung here feebly, may your mercies, your mercies, endure, and through them may I live for a long time. Son of God, about whom Moses your servant wrote: to you be praise, to your Church hope, and to me forgiveness.
On the bronze serpent that Moses raised in the wilderness
(By Saint Jacob. Discourse 4. On the bronze serpent that Moses raised in the wilderness.

Your words have brought me down into the sea of your mysteries, Son of God; through you may I be drawn up from the surging waters surrounding me. The waves of your stories have multiplied their assaults against me. You are the sailor: bring me into the harbor of truths. Moses, the shepherd who led the sheep through the surging waters, has led me to the sea of mysteries, that I may enter through his writings. Lord of Moses, draw me up from the sea as you did Moses, as I bring up the great cargo of his reading. Wonderful are all the things that happened through Moses' hands, for he was portraying you throughout the whole journey appointed to him. In the staff he took you from beside your Father on Mount Sinai, and he followed you and came like a shadow following a great body. He showed Egypt the cross of your humiliation when he entered it; it trembled before it and yielded to its might. He carried a great image as he passed through the wilderness, and the mountains danced when they saw your likeness over the Hebrews.

The hills saw your great Passover and leaped like lambs, so that the procession of your image might be honored throughout the lands. Moses set up your sign, our Lord, in the wilderness, and all created things were astonished when they saw it. He became a painter and mixed the colors of prophecy, and in the wasteland he painted an image full of wonder. He portrayed you in that bronze serpent and set you on high, so that your likeness might be like a healer for [?] his people. He set up your symbol against the venom of serpents, so that through you, O Life, he might heal the bites suffered by his people. Here let love be your teacher, you listeners, and learn from it all the hidden things that Moses spoke. With the eyes of your soul, behold these symbols, for they all carry the beauties of the Son in their arms. Through him the great Moses did everything he did, in Egypt, in the sea, and in the wilderness. He carried the image of the Son and went before the camp, and through it he kept every harm away from among his people. He showed the Son’s majesty to the worlds and made them tremble. Created things saw the sign of his death and shook before him. He set up the cross at every stopping place where he camped,

so that the people could camp without fear beneath its shadow. There was nowhere that he did not shelter beneath the cross. It became a wall for him, and he kept his camp within it. Moses portrayed the Son of God in many ways, and hosts of symbols surrounded him along his whole journey. Today let us leave aside the many things that cannot be comprehended, and speak of one that fills whoever beholds it with wonder. Let us now speak of the symbolism of that bronze serpent, and of the purpose for which Moses placed it within the camp. First let us recount the bites of the serpents, and the reason they were sent against the Hebrews. The people ate manna and grumbled against the Creator. In their self-indulgence, they did not praise him for their food. They withheld the gratitude owed for their feast, and amid their great abundance they did not thank the one who fed them. The bread of the angels was sent to them so that they might be well fed by it, but this provision did not please them, because they were ungrateful. Instead of the thanksgiving owed for the gift, their mouths were full of grumbling, insulting the one who fed them. Splendid bread was sent to the glutton from the cloud, but he despised it, though he was being fed without a care.

The winds served the lazy fellow his fill, yet even as he was being fed, he complained every day against the giver. He was well fed and yet grumbled, because he was ungrateful. He was nourished and yet gave no thanks, because he was not righteous. Gifts and blessings were laid before him in abundance, yet amid his enjoyment he knew nothing but blasphemy. Manna and quail were repulsive to the glutton and seemed ordinary to him. Stuffed with his food, he wailed and wailed like someone hungry, and blasphemed. He drank blessed water from the flint in the wilderness, yet he did not marvel at that astonishing miracle. Clouds and winds brought him provisions, yet he was too lazy to offer praise when he ate. He became a pupil of the great Moses, who belonged to God’s household, yet all he learned was to blaspheme against the Creator. His heart was idle, and he had no love for instruction. He was eager for food but unwilling to offer praise. His soul was dulled by food, for he was a glutton, and he refused to give praise to the one who fed him. He grumbled against Moses and blasphemed against his God every day. He showed great ingratitude for the kindness done to him. “Why did you bring us out of Egypt?” he protested angrily.

“We are sick of this paltry bread,” he complained bitterly. The ungrateful man called the bread of angels “paltry bread” and treated that food prepared in God's house with great contempt. The delicious manna sent to him seemed worthless in his eyes, and instead of praise he sent back grumbling through Moses. A sweet kind of food came to him from the whirlwind. He tasted it and brazenly blasphemed against his provider. His food was sweet, but what he belched out was very bitter. He ate honey and belched gall, for he was perverse. When his bitterness grew intense in loud grumbling, the Just One disciplined him with serpents that spewed gall. He punished that bitter man by means of bitter creatures, for his judgment is just, and he does not taint it with favoritism. He inflamed the creeping creatures with gall and sent them against the ungrateful, so that the wicked people would be tormented by loathsome creatures. Because he had not offered praise for escaping from the Egyptians, venomous serpents came to bite him bitterly. He defeated Leviathan, who is Pharaoh, and crushed his heads. Yet because the man did not give thanks, he was struck by the heads of serpents. He drowned that great serpent of Egypt in the sea; and [?] justice [?] to the place of judgment against the ungrateful man,

so that she might take vengeance on him for acting insolently against his provider. It was as though these words were being spoken by Justice to the greedy servant who blasphemed whenever he ate: “Be struck by the creeping creatures that eat dust and refrain from blasphemy, you who eat sweet manna and blaspheme! By the serpents that never [?] over the dust, see, you ungrateful people, how much you have blasphemed against your provider! The biting snakes eat dust and remain quiet, although they are bitter. But you greedy people eat the bread of angels and will not be quiet. The serpent is bitter, but not as bitter as the Hebrew. He is wicked by his own choice; his bitterness is not a matter of nature. The venomous serpent is wicked, but the Jew is more wicked than it, for his food is pleasant, while his mouth is bitter with blasphemy. Under his lips is the gall of an asp, as it is written. Although the manna that nourished him was good, he coughed up gall.” For this reason he was punished with serpents and struck down by the bites of biting snakes. He was punished with cruel scourges so that through these blows he, who was bitter, might become sweet. Ranks of biting serpents surrounded him in Jeshimon, and with their bites they poured their venom upon the rebels. Vipers swarmed from every side against the oppressor.

His spirit was distressed, and he began to seek refuge in prayer. He knew that he was being punished as a wrongdoer, and he began pleading with Moses to bring relief from the punishment. “We have sinned by grumbling against you and against the Lord,” they said to him. “Pray that we may be delivered from the vipers surrounding us.” The people suffered until they confessed that they were sinful. The biting serpents bit them, and in their distress they pleaded for mercy. When the prayer was brought before the Lord through Moses, a command went out concerning what the son of the Hebrews should do. The Lord said to him, “Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign in the camp [?] of your people.” “Whenever a serpent bites someone, let him look at it and live.” Moses did as God had commanded him. He made a viper and set it up as a sign in the camp. Whenever a serpent bit someone, he would look at it. Whenever he looked at it, he was healed through a great wonder; but if he did not look, he was struck down in great pain. Something great is revealed in this deed, and whoever looks discerningly can see it. Here the cross clearly displayed its power, and its symbol healed the people who had suffered from the serpents.

He depicted its image [?] in that viper Moses made. Pain would see it and flee from the limbs. It fought against the serpents’ venom, and when the venom saw it, it quickly lost its force. Moses the physician cut a medicinal root of crucifixion and placed it in the assembly before the Hebrews, so that they might be healed by it. He saw the daughter of Jacob, who had been torn by vipers, and set up the sign of our Lord in the wilderness so that she might be healed by it. An army of serpents had come out against the flock, and the cross came out like a captain and exposed them. The biting serpents had stirred up a great conflict with the Hebrews, and the cross of our Lord stood in their midst as their deliverer. A legion of loathsome crawling creatures came against the daughter of the people, and the symbol of Jesus, like a mighty warrior, drove it back from her. The cross fought against the serpents’ tongues, quenched their venom, and drove it away from the Hebrews. The sweet one stood up to fight the bitter ones, and its taste defeated them in a spectacle full of wonder. Whenever they poured venom upon the Hebrews, it spread its shadow over them and made them sweet. Whenever the vipers’ venom spread through their bodies,

they were made sweet by the sweetness of the crucified Light. The stag was a symbol of our Lord to the serpents; in the wilderness it cried out and drove them away. The cross was raised, and the people who had been bitten saw it; the venom fled from their battered limbs. Moses made a symbol in the wilderness before the eyes of the Hebrews, and our Lord explained it as he taught aloud. “Just as Moses raised the serpent in the wilderness for the people,” he said, “so I too am raised for the whole world, so that they may look at me.” Learn from our Lord himself about the great image Moses fashioned in the wilderness, and see that it belongs to him. “Just as Moses raised the serpent, so I am raised,” he said. “Let everyone who has been bitten come and look at me, and be healed through me.” “The great serpent bit Eve among the trees. Now I am raised; she looks, and if she looks at me, I heal her.” “Demons fell upon the world and bit it like venomous snakes, and I must be raised like that serpent Moses made.” The viper bit the mother of all peoples among the trees, and its venom spread throughout her entire race, bringing destruction. For this reason the cross was raised on Golgotha, so that people who had been killed might look at it and live.

You who have been bitten by Satan, look at Christ! For this reason he was raised [?]: so that you might look at him and be healed through him. You through whose limbs hidden venom has spread, you are restored to health by this sight of the crucified Light. You who have been killed by the bites of evil demons, lift your eyes, look, and be healed, if you are willing. You whose soul has been bitten by the evil one, do not doubt! Look at the cross, and it will quickly restore your soul to health. Sins have tormented you like the bites of serpents, and unless you look at the one who was slain, you will not be healed. Just as Moses raised the serpent, your Lord was raised. Look at him, man, and the wound inflicted on you will disappear. See, he hangs there so that all who have been bitten may look at him and be healed through him, for he is full of compassion for the wounded. Sinners, see, he looks toward you so that you may look at him, for the sight of him holds medicine that heals every wound. He hangs like a sign in the midst of the world, so that it may gaze at him and draw from him the mercy that has compassion on whoever looks at him. The sight of him has been made a remedy for the wounded, and through him the soul’s pains are healed without medicines. For this reason he was raised on Golgotha: so that you might look [?] at him, and he might heal you of the wounds you have suffered.

“Just as Moses raised the serpent,” he said, “I must be raised [?].” This is clear to anyone who needs healing. Whoever had been bitten by a visible serpent would look at that one; let anyone whom the hidden viper has stung look at this one. That one drove visible venom from the limbs; this one drives hidden sin from the thoughts. In Moses’ serpent, our Lord’s body was depicted, through which all the bodies of the [?] are healed. Apart from venom, it resembled the snakes. So it is with the Son, who became like us in everything. Apart from sin, the one who formed everything became like us; and in him he healed us, for there is no life except in him. The venom of snakes was not in that serpent, nor was sin in the body of our Lord, who became like us. As far as venom was concerned, Moses’ serpent was like something sweet, and symbolically it overcame the venom of the snakes. Our Lord’s body is without sin, as it is written, and for this reason all sinners are healed through it. Oh, how that serpent resembled the snakes! Yet it was unlike them, for it was not bitter and did not bite. Oh, the Son, who became like us in everything except sin, as Paul, the chosen one, writes!

All the mysteries shone brightly in the cross, and in it all the types were truly fulfilled. It stood in the world like that serpent in the camp, so that all who had been wounded might look at it and be healed through it. O soul whom the serpent has bitten, look at the cross! Through it the hidden wound inflicted on you is healed. Sin has stung you: here is the medicine of life from Golgotha! Apply it to the wound, and through it the wound is truly healed. If the likeness of the serpent brought relief to whoever looked at it, how much more will the image of the Son heal whoever sees him! I will repeat these very things that have been spoken through me, so that the mystery of the serpent may again become clear to the listeners. I will thoughtfully turn my discourse back to the story, for a saying becomes clear when the speaker repeats it. I will repeat my words about that serpent Moses raised, for the more the story is repeated, the more the cross is glorified through it. Whenever a viper stung someone among the Hebrews, if he despised Moses’ serpent and did not look at it, the power of the venom killed him because he had been negligent and had not believed enough to run to the serpent for refuge. There were those who despised it and died from their wounds without being healed;

and there were those who believed, approached, looked at it, and forgot their pain. The one who had been stung was free to decide what to do, for it was easy for him either to look or not to look. Looking was free, and Moses demanded no payment. The serpent stood there, and whoever looked at it was relieved of his suffering. It was up to the one who had been bitten to decide what to do: whoever looked was healed, and whoever did not look at it died from his wound. Faith triumphed there among the wounded, for whoever believed and saw the serpent lived by looking at it. But the venom of the snakes killed whoever did not believe, and he was not healed because he would not look as he had been commanded. Here too, that is, faith heals sores, and the healing of the wounded person rests upon his own will. The cross was stretched out, and it never demands a fee from you. If you look at it, it binds up your wounds and heals you free of charge. Look, Satan has made serpents throughout the whole world. You who have been bitten, look at the cross so that it may heal you. Let no one despise the sight revealed before so many, for anyone who despises it dies from the venom of the great serpent. The cross never forces anyone to come to it. Whoever wishes to be healed through it does so of his own accord.

The sinner too has freedom and has been given the power to heal his pain by his own choice, without intermediaries. Look, he has before him a healing sign: if he looks at it, he is truly healed through it. The sin of the body dies away completely through the body of the Son. Through this one who did not sin, those who sinned are now healed. Just as the serpent at Horeb overcame the serpents, the body peacefully heals the bodies that cling to it. Through that serpent the venom of the serpents was quenched, and through this body the sin of bodies disappears completely. Its appearance is ordinary, but its healing power is very great. Death is depicted on it, yet life flows from it every day. By its appearance the cross proclaims death to whoever sees it, but when examined, it gives life to whoever looks at it. That serpent too, by its appearance, terrified the person who had been bitten. Its name and its appearance frightened the one who had been struck. But when he ventured to look at it, his pain immediately departed, for its power for whoever looked at it was not ordinary like its appearance. Perhaps the person who had been bitten was afraid or trembled when they told him, “Come, look at the serpent, and you will be healed.” He would even say, “A serpent has killed me, so why indeed

should I look at a serpent, when even its appearance frightens me? Why should I look at it? Here I am, tormented by its wound! Its appearance is hateful to me. Let it go away from me; it has already killed me! What good does it do me? It carries no medicine to heal my wound, nor any medicinal root that I could put on my sore and find relief through it. Its appearance is terrifying, and if I look at it, it increases my pain. A serpent in any form reminds me of my wound.” The cross too has met with this response from many. They flee from it because they do not know what its power is. Death is depicted on it, yet it rewards those who draw near it with life. It proclaims killing, yet for those who understand, it is full of resurrection. The foolish pagan who hates his own life does not love it. He hates its very name, and who can persuade him to come to it? When the Church called the pagan to come and live, he saw within her the cross, the sign of death, and fled from her. When she urged him to come to the life found within her, he peered inside, saw a corpse, and was frightened. When she told him, “If you come to me, you will overcome death,” he entered, found a slain man within her, and began to doubt. How the pagan says these things against the Church: I tremble before death, and here a sign of death is set within you.

I have seen a corpse within you, and who will heal me, since I have been slain? I needed to come to life, yet here the image of a dead man is displayed within you. You called me to life, but how can a dead man give me life? Death has killed me, so why am I coming to death again? I expected to find bandages for my wounds within you, as you led me to hope, but here you have shown me a slain man, wounded like me. Death is a terrifying sign that makes me tremble. If I see death within you too, why should I come to you? The pagan sees the crucified one and trembles, not knowing what power flows from him to anyone who approaches him. Just as Moses’ serpent frightened the one who had been bitten, so the sight of the cross of death frightens the pagan. They urged the Hebrew whom a serpent had bitten to come and look at another serpent, and then he would be healed. It is the same with the pagan whom death has killed and who comes to the Church: she brings out and places before him a sign that is entirely death. When the Hebrew had been bitten and was in distress, all his relatives would tell him, ‘Run to the serpent!’ If he despised its unimpressive appearance and would not go, someone who had experienced it would urge him not to doubt. The first person who had looked at the serpent and been healed became like a herald among the people to all who had been bitten.

If he saw someone doubting, he would encourage him and teach him everything from his own experience. Such things as these were said to the bitten man by someone before him who had also been bitten, had looked, and had been healed: ‘Come near; do not be afraid. It is not a serpent merely because its name is “serpent.” It is like a medicinal root containing life for anyone who looks at it. It is not like the serpent that bit you. Why are you afraid?
