Look at it and see that the very sight of it helps you. A serpent bit me just as it did you, and Moses’ serpent seemed contemptible to me. But when I looked at it, my sufferings passed away. When you hear “viper,” do not be terrified. It is the physician’s handiwork. Look at it and test what its power is. It is a sweet serpent, and I know from experience that when I looked at it, the sight of it took all the venom from my limbs.’ In the same way, the Church teaches the pagan every day not to doubt when she calls him to look at the crucified one. She also tells him, ‘Look at the corpse in which death is depicted, and you will also find that resurrection flows from it. Come in and test the power of the slain man laid within me. Then you will learn that he himself killed ravenous death. You have seen the crucified one, and you can discover that he is also God,

who, through the sign of his death, abolished death for many. When you hear of a man who has been slain, do not be terrified. Examine the slain man, and you will discover that he is not mortal.’ An image of death is depicted on the cross for anyone who looks at it, yet life wells up for anyone who approaches and clings to it. See that the report of the dead man does not disturb you when you hear it, for you can discover in him that death died in him, while he himself was not defeated. Look at him who is crucified, and consider him who gives life. Put his deeds to the test, and do not doubt because of the name of his disgrace. Take faith along with you when you look, and then disgrace and suffering will not disturb you when you encounter them. Do not consider him only by his outward appearance. Look into what is hidden, and you will find him mighty. Do not doubt when you see a corpse lying there: a man slain, a crucified man stripped naked, a dead man embalmed. Approach him, and you will find him to be the Lord and the Son, the mighty one of the ages, the bearer of created things, the giver of life, the reviver of the dead, the raiser of the departed, the binder of death, the liberator of Adam, and also God, who suffers no diminishment. The designation “crucified” disturbs the pagan, keeping him from worshiping him.

But when he entered and saw what his work was, he took refuge in him. While he was far away, he was frightened by the report of the killing. But when he approached him, his soul shone with the life he found. Just as that Hebrew whom the serpent bit was healed, so too the sinner whom death has killed is healed. [?] the venomous serpent, and here the crucified one is triumphant. In both the New and the Old, he is made a medicine of life. For this reason our Lord said as he taught, “Look, I am being lifted up like that serpent which Moses lifted up.” Moses set forth a great riddle among the Hebrews, and Christ came and explained it clearly to the nations. The Hebrew depicted a wonder of mysteries in that venomous serpent, and in the crucified one light dawned upon the hidden things that had been concealed. It was our Lord himself who healed by his power both here and there: there through his symbol, and here truly in his own person. Today and yesterday he is the same and does not change. Blessed is the crucified one who gave life to the world that had been stricken.
The discourse on the bronze serpent is concluded.
On Aaron the Priest
Discourse 5. On Aaron the Priest.

From the beginning, when the Lord created Adam, he made him a priest to stand in his service. The Lord firmly established a boundary for Adam: “Eat, Adam, from all the fruits that are in Paradise. But do not approach the tree that is in the middle, for when you approach it, you will taste death.” The evil one envied Adam, who was made in the image of God. He counseled Eve, and she picked and ate from the tree. She gave it to Adam, and he ate and transgressed the commandment. Death gained power over Adam, just as had been said. Adam was dead, carried along through every generation. Death came and reached Moses like a captor. He brought a document and showed it to Moses, as one who takes everyone captive. Death called out and spoke to Moses, the son of Amram: “I have a legal claim against you,” he said, “because of your father. You will not pass from here, Moses, unless you repay me [?]. Adam incurred a great debt to me among the trees. Unless you repay me, there is no way for you to pass from here.”

Moses read the document that his father Adam had left, and saw in it [?] dreadful death for all his children. It was written as follows: “I am indebted to Death; I must die. Because I have sinned, I have given all my children to Death. I will repay the debts I incurred, since I have been found guilty. In succession, I have assigned all generations to Death.” Moses saw the document that his father Adam had drawn up. He approached and tasted Death’s cup in great sorrow. All the upright and righteous, the prophets and kings, tasted the cup of Adam, who transgressed the commandment. All the priests who bore the mysteries of God’s house could not step beyond or escape that sentence of condemnation. All the prophets, kings, and priests, the children of Adam, were subject to the sentence passed upon our father Adam. Whenever a priest, prophet, or king arose and was about to pass by, he saw the document and surrendered himself to Death’s cup. As greedy Death passed through all generations, he reached Aaron, the illustrious priest of God’s house. This is the subject of the discourse I am continuing: the priesthood of the sons of Levi and how it came about. Adam bore it from the beginning of all generations, and reached out and handed it to those who came afterward.

That priesthood of our father Adam came down as far as Aaron, who honored it and bore it lovingly. He stood clothed in the mysteries of God’s house, releasing and binding those on earth to those in heaven. He stood over Israel in the Tent of Meeting, and no one among the whole people transgressed his command. Moses had been made like God over the camp, granting release and giving commands like God to the children of Jacob. Miriam was made like a bride of God’s house, and she held a lyre among the tribes. Aaron carried a censer and entered the Tent of Meeting. He burned fragrant incense and made atonement for their sins. He drove dreadful Death from the camp with the censer he offered, and suddenly stopped the destroyer. Moses and Aaron delivered the people from Egypt. Aaron the priest was appointed to grant forgiveness and make atonement. He burned fragrant incense, and the hidden fire received it from him. Fire with fire gave off fragrance before those who watched. Where have you seen fire burning from an ember, except here, where hidden fire revealed its love? With the fire of his heart, Aaron filled the place of atonement with fragrance, and it quickly stopped death from spreading through the camp.

To the tune of Saint Ephrem. Aaron carried fire and fire, and brought them before God. God saw his heart and accepted them both. He carried visible fire in his hand and hidden fire in his mind. The fire of his heart pleased him, and the fire in his hands was accepted. For if the hidden fire of his mind had not been pure, God would not have accepted even the fire he was carrying. Because of the fire of his mind, the fire in his hands was accepted. O atoning fire, which forgives offenses and sins! Offer fire like this, you sinners, and receive forgiveness. The fire in his hands gave off fragrance, and the watchers above rejoiced in it. The fire of his mind gave off fragrance, and the Lord on high rejoiced in it. Where the angel threatened to destroy the camp, he carried a censer full of fire, went out, and held him back from the people. The angel saw the fire and fled from its radiance. He saw hidden fire there and was terrified at the sight of it. The fire drove the watcher away and shattered the spear he was holding. By the command of the Godhead, the priest stopped the plague. Through his incense he restrained the angel from destroying. When he was pressed to the point of death, he did not shrink from death. Aaron always stood between God and the people. By God's command he was appointed to oversee the people.

Eleazar stood inside the Tent of Meeting and watched, to learn how he should attend to the service of God. He constantly watched his father to see how he offered sacrifices, so that he too might offer them as his father did, in purity and holiness. While still a boy, he was learning how to take his place in the priestly office. His mind was pure and clear, and all his thinking was radiant. He also practiced a life of chastity in the Tent of Meeting. His father Aaron stood clothed in the priestly garments. The splendid garment of service was fire that had descended from on high. A crown was set on his head, and a turban above his body. He wore an ephod [?] in truth, and hung onyx stones upon himself. There were golden bells on his garment, and he was appointed a priest of God. He entered the Tent of Meeting to make atonement for offenses, as it is written. God said to Moses, “I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your interpreter to the great people.” “When you have come out of Egypt, he will then serve as priest. It is fitting for such a man to serve in the house of Adonai.” He was to administer faithfully the priesthood entrusted to him. As he stood in the Tent of Meeting, his son was with him in the sanctuary. He was learning the mysteries of the priesthood and becoming perfected in his conduct. His father taught him how to carry the censer of atonement and how to enter and call upon God with a pure heart.

While the young Eleazar was serving in the Tent of Meeting, the debt shared by all arose to demand its due from Aaron. For the time had come for Aaron to hand over the treasures. And it was Eleazar’s time to enter and take his place. While Aaron was clothed in the priesthood and standing in the sanctuary, Adam’s bond of debt arose to demand its due from Aaron. This man, who had served as priest for forty years in the Tent of Meeting, could not free himself from the written bond of the debt shared by all. This man, who had made atonement for the people and over whom the angel of wrath had no power, could not escape the bond that Adam had written. This man, who had driven away death and the angel by means of his incense, could not save himself when the cup of death came upon him. When the time had come for Aaron to taste death, the Lord called to the son of Amram and [?] with him, saying to him, “Moses, listen to what I tell you, and do not grieve over this. “Do not lose heart at the news that reaches your ears. Do not let your mind be troubled or distress take hold of your heart. “Do not let your eyes stream with tears at the sorrow I speak of to you. “Let me see no sadness in you over this secret between you and me. “Do not fall into despair and become weak like everyone else.” Then Moses answered God and said, “Whatever your Majesty desires, I will do according to your will.”

The merciful Lord said, “Now I tell you, Moses: your brother’s time has come to depart from this world. “Your brother’s time has come for another to take his place. “Your brother’s time has come to take off the garments of his ministry. Now, Moses son of Amram, listen to what I tell you. “Get up, lead Aaron your brother away, and take Eleazar with you.” Go up one of the mountains, the one I tell you. The three of you are to complete the mystery among yourselves with gladness. Do not weep, son of Amram, and do not grieve your brother Aaron. There is no way for him not to be distressed, since he is drinking the cup of death. And tell Eleazar not to let his mind be troubled when he sees his father Aaron being buried on the mountaintop. By Mar Jacob. The Lord called Moses his servant and spoke with him: “Rise and take your brother Aaron, as you have been commanded. Take Eleazar along with him, and let him go with you, for he is to go up and put on the sacred garments. He is also to enter and take his father's place. I am making him a shepherd to preside over the flock. I am appointing him as priest to make atonement for Israel. Give him these instructions that I am telling you:

He is to purify himself from every evil in holiness. Let me see no injustice or wickedness in him in any form, and let no hateful deceit approach him and defile him.” These words were spoken by God, and Moses listened with great love to everything he told him. Moses called his brother Aaron and Eleazar and spoke words of pain and sorrow to them: “A journey has fallen to me, to you, Aaron, and to Eleazar, for the Lord has told me that we are to go up Mount Hor together.” Moses took Aaron and Eleazar, and they set out to travel to that Mount Hor, as he had been commanded (sic). They arrived and reached the mountaintop, as they had been instructed, and Moses began to encourage his brother Aaron. Such were the things one brother was saying to the other, amid the great pain and sorrow that had seized them. Moses said, “Alas, I will reveal to you a secret I hold, for there is truly no way for me not to reveal it. Like one limb joined to another, you are joined to me. We entered Egypt together, as the Lord commanded us. Together we also performed wonders among the Egyptians. When I stood before Pharaoh, you helped me. When the staff turned into a snake, it was you who had thrown it down.

When the sorcerers stood against me, we were united. When their staffs became serpents, we stood close together. We did not distance ourselves from one another among the Egyptians. But death has come, and now it separates us from one another. Let the Lord's command be fulfilled in us according to his will. You have repaid my labors well, Aaron, as was fitting, and you have shown me a brother's love without flaw. And now, Aaron, the debt common to us all has pressed upon you, and there is no way for you not to drink the cup of death. Look, the debt document Adam left behind has now arrived, and a brother cannot redeem his brother, as it is written. And now, Aaron, do not grieve because the end has come, and do not let a single sorrowful thought arise within you. See that you do not become estranged from the Lord because of distress, for no one born into this world fails to taste the cup of death. Adam tasted it, and now it is passed down through the generations. Do not grieve, for your son will stand as priest in your place. The Lord has chosen the young man to enter and take your place. He himself told me that Eleazar would serve as priest in your place. Then the Lord gave Moses a sign, saying to him: Why are you standing there? Go forward and strip your brother Aaron. Remove from him the sacred garments of the priesthood,

and put them on Eleazar, the priest whom I have chosen. Remove from him all the regalia of the sons of Levi. Strip your brother bare as he goes to meet death. Your father Adam stood naked among the trees. You too must strip him of the priesthood and release him to go. He entered the world in holiness, undefiled; and since he has not sinned against me, I lead him away in holiness. Moses approached his brother as he had been commanded. Aaron saw him coming toward him and bowed his head. Aaron the priest surrendered himself to be stripped of the priestly garments and then to go to the new world. Moses approached and raised his hands above Aaron’s head. He removed the crown of glory from him and gave it to his son. He removed from him the lovely collar that he had worn hanging about him, and gave it to his son so that he might enter and take up his ministry. He removed the ephod he was wearing, and also the turban, and put them (sic) on Eleazar in his father’s presence. Aaron stood watching him as he stripped him, and he was not distressed as he removed the sacred garments from him. He was stripped and left bare of the priesthood, and the young man came forward and received the mysteries of the house of God.

Then Aaron stood looking at his son, who was wearing his garments and stood resplendent like a Levite. He looked at the young priest, the radiant minister, and rejoiced over him. His heart was glad because his son had taken his place. He was wearing a crown, a [?], and a collar together with a turban. He was also wearing a robe, with a sash over them all. There was also an apron with golden bells arranged on it, and twelve pomegranates depicting a great mystery. Like a bridegroom dressed for the wedding feast, this young man was adorned to become a priest in the tent of meeting. While the two brothers stood on the mountaintop, Aaron was stripped like Adam among the trees. Eleazar was clothed in the priesthood of the house of God, and Moses stood restraining his feelings so that he would not weep. Who could have a heart of stone and not weep when he looked and saw Aaron stripped and about to die? Who could see him standing there, stripped of his priesthood, without bringing forth streams of tears from his eyes? Saint Ephrem. The Lord signaled to the son of Amram: Why are you standing there, Moses? Go up and bid your brother farewell. Release him to go to his dwelling, for look, the angel is standing there, watching you to see when you will release him.

Unless you bid him farewell, the angel will not lead him away. Unless you release him, Moses, death has no power over him. Go up, Moses, and close his eyes, for you have delayed too long on the mountain, lest the people make an idol and worship it, as they are accustomed to do. Moses said to God: How can I go up and close his eyes? He is standing and talking with me. How can his eyes be closed? The Lord said to Moses: Just bid him farewell, and immediately the angel will come and take his soul from his body. While the son of Amram stood speaking with God, the young man approached his father, bowed his head, and paid him homage. And Eleazar was saying these things to his father: Grant me blessings, my father, before you go away from me. Then his father opened his mouth and lifted his eyes to heaven. With tears and sobs he offered a prayer to God: May God, before whom I have stood in purity and holiness, bless your youth, my son, and grant you favor before the people. The Son, who is destined to become a child and save the worlds by his grace— may he grant you conduct pleasing to his divinity. The Mighty One, at whose command everything came into being— may he grant you a mind in which God delights. The Judge, who will come at the end of time to judge his creatures—

may he grant you always to serve before him in purity. He who granted me the priesthood, and before whom I stood in purity— may he grant you to atone for the sins and offenses of the camp, and may he accept from your hands pure and holy incense, and the offering of faith that is offered in purity. The Lord, who gave the priesthood to Melchizedek, the great priest— may he grant you perfection in the rank you have received today. The power with which the heavenly beings are clothed in their ministry of fire and spirit— may you shine in that ministry and overcome every evil. The Good One, who is full of blessings and whose mercy is beyond measure— may he open the gate of mercy and answer your requests. The Righteous One, who is full of joys and for whom the righteous waited— may he grant you joys in which you may rejoice all your days. May the Levites obey you and be guided by your signal. May the people stand in fear before you and not defy the word of your mouth. From you the children of Israel receive laws and commandments. Throughout all generations forever, may the fame of your priesthood spread. May the Lord be your companion and protector at all times. May he entrust you with a priesthood pleasing to his divinity. May God himself, the Lord of all, be your good hope. May he set all your thoughts straight, so that they never cease to attend to him.

May God himself be your overseer and guide. Be guided by the word of his mouth, and do not turn aside from his commandments. You are now his servant; do not cease serving him. Take care not to turn aside from his path and become like a stranger. May the prayers of Aaron your father be good companions to you. May they guard your steps before the ark of God. May the Holy One, whose door is open to [?] who calls on him in love, accept your blessings, my son, and your prayers and petitions. May he who is heavenly and earthly, who is in the heights and the depths, grant that you please him through righteous deeds. May the third person of the Godhead be your guardian and protect you continually, by day and by night. Aaron prayed these things over the young Eleazar. God heard his prayer, just as his heart desired. Moses approached his brother, as God had commanded him. He embraced him lovingly and said to him, “Go; may the Lord be with you.” By Mar Jacob. By Mar Balai.
Moses says, “Go in peace, true brother who was at my side.” Aaron says, “Remain in peace, brother who bore no grudge against his brother.” Moses says, “Go in peace, beloved priest of the house of God.”
Aaron says, “Remain in peace, beloved brother whom his Lord loved.” Moses says, “Go in peace, priest who offered perfect sacrifices.”
Aaron says:

“Remain in peace, brother who performed every mighty deed.”
Moses says, “Go in peace, priest who fulfilled his Lord’s will.” Aaron says, “Remain in peace, brother who brought down manna for the people.” Moses says, “Go in peace, priest who atoned for the people’s sins.”
Aaron says, “Remain in peace, Moses, who divided the great sea.” Moses says, “Go in peace, you who accompanied me in all these things.”
By Mar Jacob. As soon as Moses kissed Aaron, as he had been commanded, Aaron’s soul swiftly departed from his body. The Lord commanded the soul, and it departed from its companion. He commanded the bird, and it took wing from its nest. He commanded the dove, and it flew away, departed, and changed its dwelling. The body remained upon the dust, which shared its [?]. Aaron died on Mount Hor, as it is written, and a new priest arose in his place to minister in his stead. Moses and Eleazar stood in great sorrow, and on the mountaintop a wondrous sign appeared. Aaron lay before his brother and his son, and they were careful not to let even sadness arise within them. What brother sees his brother being wrapped for burial and does not weep for him as they are separated from one another?

Moses gave sorrow no room to rule over him, because he knew that God has another world. The young Eleazar stood looking at his father, and whenever he was about to weep, he restrained his feelings, and his mourning subsided. Those blameless men kept the command that the Lord had given: just as they had been commanded, so they carried it out on the mountaintop. Aaron had died, and they stood to perform the funeral service according to the Law. The Lord came to accompany Aaron the priest together with them. As they stood, they began songs of the Spirit, and companies of watchers came swiftly from on high. They opened their mouths to sing praise over the man of dust, with wondrous voices in their spiritual hallelujahs. The praise of the watchers mingled with that of the earthly beings, and wondrous voices rang out there over the Levite. When that service of the heavenly beings was finished, the new priest, who had suddenly become one, prayed and brought it to a close. That Levite was accompanied with great praise, and the Lord, Moses, and the young man buried him together with the spiritual beings. Earthly and heavenly beings covered him and buried him, and a command went out for the angels to ascend. They blazed trails of flame over the mountaintop, for there they had wisely escorted the priest of [?].

All day long companies of fire were on the mountain, and all day long it blazed with flame. At Aaron’s death the angels marveled on the mountaintop at how greatly his Lord had exalted and honored the day of his death. Lord, who came and reconciled the heights and the depths through his blood, grant peace to your Church, for whose sake you died. To you be praise!
Here ends the discourse on Aaron the priest.
On the Star That Appeared to the Magi
By the holy Mar Jacob. Discourse 6. On the Star That Appeared to the Magi, and on the Slaughter of the Infants.

Great Dawn, who filled the world with your rays, make your light dawn upon my thoughts so that I may tell your story. Radiance of the Father, who poured light upon the darkness, illuminate my mind so that I may proclaim the account of your glory. Image of the glory of the great Light, who came down to earth, fashion within me a word full of light, so that it may reveal your beauty.

Splendid Sun of righteousness, who dawned in our land, pour your light into me so that I may tell your story clearly. Through you all the ends of the earth that were dark have been illuminated, and the earth has been flooded with your majestic light, which was sent to it. Your rays went out to the regions of the world and illuminated them, and now the nations delight in your light, which has made them glad. Your rays tore through all the darkness of idolatry; they entered and set up an image of light for you among those in darkness. You sent a letter to the Magian religion by a star of light; you drew it out of darkness and brought it into your light. Your messenger ran to the dwelling of those in gloom to announce good news; there he opened a road for your dawning to travel along. Listen, discerning people, with great love and without distraction, about the rising of that star of light which was sent. Look, I am bringing to light the subject of this discourse and what it is. Let no one grow weary of a story full of wonder. About that divine radiance which [?] from on high and drew the Magi and brought them to see the great King. About the birth of the Lord of the heights, who came down to earth and called those far away to be made new through his birth. About the messenger who laid out his course in the heights above and stirred up Persia with the rays of his power.

About the thoughts of Chaldean astrology, which were exposed through it: he caught it by its own means, and it became his and abandoned its own. About the preparations of the leaders of Persia who went up to Judea, and about the offerings they lovingly presented to the newborn child. About Herod, the accursed devourer, who sought to kill the young stag, who turned and crushed him with his might. About the slaughter of the children of Zion who were killed, and about the Lord’s descent into Egypt like a fugitive. The discourse has set out these points at which to begin and from which to proceed into the story full of wonder. Stirrings carried this discourse out of the mind, and it harnessed thoughts to a chariot so that it might go out into the world. This story has burst forth to be told by a frail man; but let the wondrous discourse not be frail like its speaker. Do not look at the speaker when the discourse is spoken; marvel at the beauty of the colors skillfully woven into it. It is customary for something great to dwell in a small place; yet what is great is not made small by what is small. Our Lord himself dwelt in a carpenter’s house like someone of no account; and now let him recount his deeds through a weak man. He is accustomed to bending his love toward lowliness, so that he may scorn the greatness of the world wherever it is found.

The rich one dwelt with a poor and needy woman; and here he has established the dwelling of his discourses with a frail man. The King of kings lived among the poor; he was devising how to enrich the world through his poverty. He who watches over everyone in his providence had come to birth, and he sent a messenger to those far away to gather them. By a single letter that he sent to Assyria, she was stirred up; she hurried with offerings to see his face. He revealed his authority through a sign full of wonder, showing that he is the Lord whom the heights and depths obey. He traced a single letter of light for the leaders of Persia, and they took up their offerings and brought them to present them. He sent light to kill darkness in its own land and make a road through that chaos of idolatry. He cast a single beam of his rays into that land, and its dawning tore apart the night of error that had grown strong. He had come to enlighten the whole world through his birth, and he sent word beforehand to the far end of the earth to come to him. To the land far removed from teaching and preachers, he sent a messenger of light, intending to bring it to him. He laid a yoke of rays on the shoulders of the barbarians and set them on the road to come and worship him.

The newborn king drew up his battle lines against the powers of darkness, to show that his side was destined for victory. He cast a stone of light into the night of the Magi's religion, and the forces of darkness were scattered before the Mighty One. From a ray he made himself a fiery arrow; he hurled it and pierced that gloom of Chaldean astrology. With a rope of light he drew the Magi to come to him, and by his dawning he conquered the ranks of Persia and brought them out. For he had been sent to enlighten the whole world, and the nations and the people were equal in his eyes, since they belonged to him. He dwelt among the people and sent word for the nations to come to him, so that his dawning might gladden those far away and those nearby. The king sent a decree of light to the realm of darkness, to bring them out of that night which covered them. He wrote a letter and sent it to the land by an envoy, so that there might be peace in the land laid waste by the Magi's religion. He sent the star to summon those far away by its dawning, because no one on earth was capable of going to bring them. His envoy flew swiftly on its urgent journey and stirred the land with good news. What, then, was the reason for the star that was sent? And why did it summon the Magi with its great dawning?

Why did no prophet preach there as in Nineveh, or a herald bring them good news like the son of Amittai? Why did someone like Isaiah not come down and teach them that a virgin would conceive and give birth to a king without sexual union? Why did prophecy not seek out a road there and summon the Magi through its divine revelations? By what means did the star of light come down in search of them, and with what voice did it sow the news of the birth in their ears? A messenger that spoke only through its dawning—how did it proclaim its teaching and gain acceptance? Why was no prophet sent, as I have said, but instead a star carried out the mission of preaching? Here Chaldean astrology found itself an excuse: it had looked to horoscopes through calculation, and not to a prophet. Through divination the king's birth was revealed to it, and it gave credit to horoscopes, saying that they were true. The one wise in heart caught the crafty one by her own means, yet she did not know how he had trapped her in her own craft. With the cunning weapon it had sharpened, he defeated it, and it was subdued. With its own weapon he slew it, as Goliath was slain, like a mighty warrior. Teaching lay in ambush within the snares of Chaldean astrology,

and beguiled divination and drew it after truth. Truth laid an ambush and hid among the signs of the zodiac. From there he caught the religion of the Magi and led it away with him. He cunningly deceived it, as though agreeing with it, while he was catching it. Once it was trapped, he drew it to himself so that it would belong to him. A hunter too sets out bait with which to beguile his prey, and he lures and traps each kind with the food it loves. For he knows that unless he beguiles, he cannot catch anything. That is why he entices each kind with its own kind, with something belonging to it. What bait was there to catch the religion of the Magi, except something from the signs of the zodiac that it loved? He gave it what it desired while catching it, so that it would come to him; for had it known, it would have fled from its hunter. Had he not shown it something of its own, it would not have accepted him. That is why he gave it what it was accustomed to while it was being caught. It would not have accepted instruction from Isaiah, nor would it have listened to Jonah’s words had he preached. For the religion of the Magi has books opposed to Moses, and it does not incline toward the teaching of the house of Adonai. Chaldean astrology is opposed to prophecy; had prophets announced anything to it, it would have stoned them.

It would not incline its ear to Moses to listen to him. Through its craft it was intent on undoing his words. Its labor concerns [?] and the signs of the zodiac. That is why truth caught it through the very thing it studied. Its mind inclined toward the heavenly lights, to observe them; and from them and through them truth skillfully struck it down. It gazed at the stars and at their numerical calculations, and truth beguiled it into seeing him there while he was trapping it. Its power over human conduct comes from the zodiac, and there the good news of the Son dawned for it, so that it might see his face. The firmament was its book, and it read its lights every day. There the one wise in heart showed it his kingdom. Its understanding was fixed on the movement of the heavenly hosts: at what appointed times and where they travel along their paths. It established twelve houses and seven rulers, and from them it draws grounds for speaking about births. Truth sat within its reading and gave himself to it, so that through what it had learned it might be caught, enter, and see the Son. Had a prophet told it that a virgin was conceiving in Judea, it would not have accepted him unless a sign of the zodiac confirmed it. It was rebellious toward the reading of prophecy,

and its heart was steeped in the study of the heavenly hosts. While she was engrossed in watching the fortunes according to her own thinking, a star of light subtly signaled to her about the king in Judah. Her heart was captivated by the calculations of her craft, and through them she learned that a king had arisen, as we have said. And perhaps, my brothers, on the night of the birth of the one who saves all, the whole company of magicians was observing the constellations. Truth contrived some pretext and brought them out, so that the great wonder might be shown to them all together. While they were counting the hours of the night and making their calculations, and observing the times—where, when, and what courses the stars followed— then the divine Dawn lit a torch, fashioned a new star, and showed it to them amid their calculations. In the familiar place where fortunes are determined, according to their teaching, a light stood to show them the king’s birth. Truth entered into what was untrue to bring them in, for there was no other net that could catch them. There stood a star, beautiful in its light and great in its appearance. Its rising was powerful, its radiance blazed, and its beauty shone. Its flame was kindled, its rays burned, and its appearance was wondrous. It was unique, and there was no other like it.

The new sight stirred them to investigate, but in their books they could not find what it meant. They asked many questions about the wondrous revelation they had seen, but the books of Chaldean astrology were unable to explain it. The form of light overwhelmed their attempts to depict it, and all the colors of Chaldean astrology could not contain it. And as these things were being said by the Chaldeans—what it might be, and how, and who the savior was, and where he had arisen— “Someone great has come into the world through his new birth, and he has the authority to take possession of the whole earth. A mighty man has been born, as we have discerned, and all the ends of the earth will obey him when he becomes known. An exalted rank has arisen today among those born, and Nimrod’s crown will be subjected to it when it is revealed. A powerful man who will hold the world by his might has now been born. Let us investigate and see who he is and where he is. Before this man’s crown all crowns will fall. Let us go ahead, take something, and offer it to him. He will subdue all the peoples of the earth when he grows to manhood. Let us go and show him love while he is still a baby. All creation will tremble at his rising when it becomes aware of him. Let us be the first, and so show our love there.

He will subject kings and harness rulers under his yoke. Come, let us bow down to him freely, not under compulsion. The rulers of the earth will become servants under his authority. Let us be the first and come before his face with offerings. He will govern creation and receive the homage of the nations. Let us go ahead and bow down, and so our goodwill will be seen. Let us go and register our land in his name, beginning now, before the nations tremble at the report of his might.” Let us bring gold and lay it before him to honor him, so that when he becomes mighty in his kingdom, he may show favor to our land. Our craft gains distinction through our recognition of him; and now that we have recognized him, it is fitting that we should not slight him. Let us honor him now at his birth, wherever he is, and when his kingdom is revealed, he will reward us. Before the kings of the earth come with their offerings, let this offering of ours be the first and be presented to him. Before the nations make their way to him with their honors, let us be the first to bring a great gift and see his face. Before gold becomes commonplace in his treasuries among the treasures, let this gold of ours come to him as the firstfruits. Before all the distant islands come, let our land go, take something, and present it to him.

Before the nations come in procession from every region, let our country honor him with tribute, beginning now. Before the crowds press against one another at his threshold, let us be among the first to enter his house. Before he subdues the regions of the earth by his might, let our company go and fall before him of its own free will. The star's radiance is far stronger than those that mark births. Let us now seek out where the king is and reach him. The story of the star of light surpasses understanding, and I cannot refrain from sailing upon the sea of its account. It has joined my mind to that company of the Magi, and now it draws it along to go with them on the road they have taken. With a cord of love it bound my mind and drew it toward itself, just as with its light it drew the Magi and led them. Listen to me, then, with love as I speak, for an account of wonder cannot be heard except with love. Someone who loves can gain more than through learning, for it is love that opens the door for the word to be received. To someone who is not thirsty, even water is not pleasant; it is the thirsty whom a drink refreshes when it reaches them. Let everyone who is thirsty come and drink from instruction. It is a sweet spring by which the soul's thirst is quenched.

It is a light that shines upon the understanding and polishes it, and through the message that blazes from it, it spreads beauty. It is a worker who diligently seeks the benefit of all its hearers, without asking anyone to pay it a wage in return. For their sake, instruction arose and opened its fountain. Drink freely from the sweetness of the great spring. For your sake God also sent his Son, and he came to be born so that you might live through his birth. For your sake he caused light to shine in the realm of darkness, so that you might see how the road leads to the kingdom. For your sake the star of light shone from on high, to announce the great birth of the one who saves all. For your sake the King sent a new light, to summon all the nations by its shining and gather you together. The one who has mercy on everyone seeks to benefit you by every means, so that you too may show mercy on every occasion for his sake. The Magi saw where the star of light rose and marveled, for it urgently spurred them on with its rays. They learned from it that the king had come, as you have heard, and they set their faces toward him to go to him, as has been told. They diligently investigated which country was his and among which people he was, but the answer to this inquiry was not found in their books.

They persistently questioned one another, and in turn one clearly fell short of the other. It stirred up all Chaldean wisdom and its teaching, so that they might discover the country of the king whose rising they had seen. Perhaps, as they searched their writings, they found what Balaam had said to Balak when he prophesied. “A star will rise from Jacob,” he proclaimed there, “and a leader will arise mightily from Israel.” The nations regarded Balaam as a great man. He was a diviner, and his words were precious to them. When a faint breath of prophecy stirred in him, they regarded his message, which was true, as divination. From him they learned about the star and from whom it would rise, and the nations of the earth readily accepted his message. It had been heard that a leader would arise from Israel, and the rulers of Persia set their faces toward him to go to him. They prepared gifts for the king, so that he might be honored and they might enter his presence with offerings when they saw him. While they were taking care to prepare the offerings, Truth stood up to teach them what was fitting for them. Open your treasuries and bring gold, for he is a great king.

And take myrrh for him, for he must also be slain. Frankincense too is fitting to honor him, because he is also God. Bring incense, myrrh, and gold to be offered to him. They took their ancestors’ treasure, intending to present their offerings to the great king. They carried gifts of honor and took the road up to Judea, to see the newborn child in his own country with their offerings. The messenger stood up and urged them on with its rays, so that they would not falter in the journey for which they had prepared. Persia was exalted through the offerings of the Magi, which had been prepared with the provisions of the rulers of the land. The whole country contributed tribute to send to the newborn king whose rising they had seen in their constellations. They equipped themselves in many caravans to go up and see the king worthy of worship who had risen in Judea. They became heralds as they traveled along the roads, announcing the king’s rising to the whole world. Their glory-loving craft urged them not to conceal the reason for which they were going up. To become renowned as learned men in every land, they spoke at length about that dawning light that had drawn them.

Truth raised them on high through their own means, so that through this occasion the good news of the Son would be proclaimed. Both while traveling and while resting, they spread his story: “Our journey is toward the mighty one born in Judah [?].” His teaching shone forth along their roads, and their words were heard at their gatherings. In every lodging where they stopped, they sowed the good news; and while traveling, they spread the story of his birth. Their proclamation spread along the miles of the road, and those stories were recounted at the stopping places. The lands and their inhabitants were stirred by them, and the peoples of the earth learned the stories through their questions. They struck fear into the inhabitants of the cities as they recounted the birth of the great King. They shattered the hearts of the kings whose territories they crossed with the news of the King whose birth they were recounting. They disheartened the rulers when they announced to them that someone from Judah was destined to take possession of all lands. The crowns of rulers trembled at their words, for they spoke of his birth with awe. New good news was being proclaimed through the art of the Magi, and the King's birth was being spoken of throughout the lands.

Truth had seized them to be its heralds, so that, without realizing it, they would recount its stories abundantly. Truth had tricked Chaldean astrology into praising itself, and on that account it sang of the Son throughout the lands. “We know,” they said, “that a king has arisen in the land of Judah, for through our skill we have seen his rising in the signs of the zodiac.” To praise their craft for how much it knew, they spoke at length about the Son throughout the journey. The mighty one arose who, by his birth, undid their horoscopes, and they proclaimed him throughout the lands with their words. The wise one came to erase the tablets of Chaldean astrology, and the Magi became his witnesses to recount his story. The architect rose against the structure of the Magi's art. He came down to demolish it, and they became his workers in tearing it down. They praised him, so that even outsiders would be his witnesses, although he had come to abolish their calculations through his birth. Through him the Magi strayed from the error they had held to. He brought them onto the path of truth, and only then did they recognize him. These wild men took a yoke upon their necks and began to toil in his service on the journey they undertook. They sang [?] to the Son along the roads among the nations.

They reached Judah, the land that had withheld all its harvests. They saw that it was quiet, with silence resting upon its wise men, and that they were unaware of the King who had come to save them. The king’s mother was asleep, and her heart was sunk in slumber. The Magi came and called into her ear, and then awakened her. Persia was stirred by the news of the king who had appeared in the land, while the people of that land were sunk in a stupor and were unaware of him. The mother of the pagans sent a gift to the royal bridegroom, while the bride sitting inside her chamber was unaware of him. The daughter of the Chaldeans sent gifts to the Savior, while the daughter of Abraham, who was in his house, did not honor him. The uncircumcised were carrying their offerings to present them, while the circumcised despised the news of the king, and it went unspoken. Foreigners were hurrying along the road toward the Mighty One, while silence lay upon the members of his household, and they did not respond to him. They came to Jerusalem and knocked on its gates with their questions: “Get up and show us where the king is who has appeared on earth!” The lover of sleep was stirred by their voices, and Truth rebuked her before those from far away because she had been unaware. She sprang up from sleep and answered them, but she would not have noticed if they had not awakened her. Those from far away came to bring good news to all those nearby

about the birth that had taken place among their streets. The land of prophecy lay asleep, without praise, while among the Magi the good news of the Son was being sung. The scribes who were leaders of the people, and the elders of Zion, were complacent, while the Persians stirred up the land with the news that the king was in Judah. The good news came in from outsiders to those within, so that the nations might bear witness to his birth through their offerings. The streets of Zion were filled with news from those far away, and the whole city, which denied the truth, trembled at their words. New messengers from among the nations had entered among the people, and through them the proclamation of the Son’s birth shone forth. “Where is the king who has appeared in Judah, so that we may go to him? We have seen his star and have made ready to worship him. His great light shone powerfully upon us in our land, and it gave us certain news of his birth.” Herod heard the news of the king, and the weak man shook. One crown saw another crown and trembled in fear of it. The one who removes crowns breathed fear into the king of the land, and in terror he arose to inquire about his kingdom. The king was shaken by the news from the Magi, and he began asking how, how long ago, and when he had been born.

He was startled by the reports and turned his attention to questioning. Trembling took hold of him, and he began to learn about the Mighty One. He summoned the scribes and the elders of the whole land to learn from them where the Savior would appear. He summoned prophecy to inform him about the king, for he was afraid because of the news from the Magi. The wretched man’s hands lost their grip on his kingdom, and he began asking where he was and which land was his. Without questions the nations learned about his birth, while through questions the scribes barely grasped his story. The nations came with vowed gifts and offerings to honor him, while the people kept questioning to learn who he was and where he would appear. The former carried the treasures and blessings of their ancestors; the latter wore out the books every day, yet did not recognize him. The king asked about the birth of the great King, and the interpreters of things to come revealed the mystery to him. They held up the lamp of prophecy through their explanations, to show the way of truth through their interpretations. The feeble king questioned them about the mighty one, and they informed him that the King would appear in Bethlehem. “This,” they said, “is what is written in the prophet about Bethlehem: ‘From you will come a king who will shepherd my people Israel.’”

They spoke to him from the revelations of prophecy, and broke his heart with the interpretations disclosed to him. From the scriptural reading they explained to him the removal of his crown, and that a king was arising who would shepherd the whole world. They informed him that he would certainly be replaced, and that another was coming whose kingdom would have no end. The substance of the account spoke of the king’s overthrow, and its interpretation made an announcement about the Son of David. The interpretation came in and took away the crown of the house of Herod, so that they would no longer rule over the kingdom of the house of Judah. Destruction arose from the revelations of prophecy and overthrew the king who had asked to learn about the Savior. He asked to learn, and in what he learned he found his own overthrow. He sought an explanation, and it was explained to him that he would be replaced. The Magi and the scribes surrounded the man who had no kingship, and between the questions and the interpretations he was being battered. The Magi said, “Where is the king? For you are no king.” The scribes said, “He will appear from Bethlehem in Judah.” The wretched man saw with his own eyes how he was despised on every side, for the wisdom of the Magi and prophecy had dissolved his kingship. He saw the offerings in their various forms passing before him, but because he was not the king, they would not let him receive them.

They dishonored the exalted man who had fallen from his kingship, and because he had been deposed, they were not afraid to despise him. “Here are the offerings, but you do not receive them, for you are not the one. Keeper of the place, show us the king, so that we may present them to him. There is another king in the land, and he is its lord. We have brought gifts to present to him; show us where he is. His rising in our land urged us to come to him. He is the one we seek to see and worship, though he is a newborn child. He is the one whose radiant star we saw blazing, and by its appearance it drew us and brought us from our lands. His messenger rode upon a constellation and called us; it poured out its light, and our land was flooded with its rays. The heavens have become witnesses to his kingship, and the heavenly hosts and their rulers obey him.” The great King’s authority extends over the heavenly lights, and through his rays he revealed the dawning of his might. Herod was astonished at their momentous news, which they spoke fearlessly about the newborn child. The Magi of Persia sowed new tidings in that land, and the mystery of prophecy set its seal on their words. Truth brought witnesses to his story from every side, for both insiders and outsiders were speaking of him.

Through the heavenly light, heaven testified to his birth, and prophecy openly sang of him in a mystery. The Magi, who had seen his rising light, testified to him with their offerings, and the scribes of the people explained his story through their interpretations. The star by its rising and the prophet by his voice testified about him. The heights and the depths became witnesses that he is the Son of God. The scribes were asked where the King would arise, and interpretation stood up to reveal his beauty in the reading of Scripture. The beauty of the mysteries that had been hidden was revealed, for the day had come for hidden things to be sung. The veil of silence was lifted from the reading of Scripture, and truth uncovered its face to speak clearly. Teaching stood upon the platform of prophecy and began to explain the Savior to the people of Persia. The circumcised people were reconciled to the blind nations and began to explain about that child who had made peace between them. Those far away came and mingled with those nearby, so that they might receive one teaching of truth from the True One. For he who had made the two one had arisen, and through him that great hostility was dissolved. Truth raised its voice to speak from the reading of Scripture, and the nations became listeners, paying attention to it.

The offerings of the Magi came from among the nations, and the interpretations of prophecy came from within the people. The offerings came in, the interpretations came out, and they met one another. From both sides the King’s birth was being confirmed. The Magi said, “We have seen his star in our own land.” The scribes explained, “Look, his birthplace is Bethlehem.” He was spoken of in the lore of the Magi and in prophecy, and each recounted his birth to the other. Light and voice became heralds of his birth; the prophet and the rising light became heralds proclaiming that he is the Son of God. But Herod was scorched by their words, and their words pierced him like arrows. The Magi and the scribes struck him with their interpretations, for their statements announced another king. The despised crown was insulted by the heralds, for they asked him, as though he were of no account, “Where is the King?” The crafty serpent was embittered by their words and stored up gall to pour out his fury on the newborn children. The despised king was stricken with envy because of the King, and in his bitterness he forged a plot to commit murder. He had planned to kill the king and seize his place,

to overthrow the crown and himself take control of his dominion. A second Pharaoh had laid an ambush for the newborn, to put him to death and carry off the treasure sent to him. He coveted both the authority and the offerings, and he had set his mind on killing the child and taking them. He trembled like women before the mighty man he imagined, and began looking for an opportunity to kill him and escape him. The great crown had shaken the little crown, and the weak one began to fight [?] the mighty one. He saw that he could not fight him openly, so the deceitful man secretly devised a scheme to put him to death. He saw that all the people had become aware that a king had been born, and he schemed to raise a faction and fight him. The crafty man summoned the Magi and questioned them about when they had seen the shining star, as they had reported. He learned from them about that rising light which had drawn them, so that he could establish exactly when the king had been born. “Go,” he said, “and inquire diligently about the child. When you have searched and found him, come and tell me, so that I too may go and worship, just as you do, and appear before him with my offerings once I know him.” Though unwilling, he humbles himself as one who worships him.

Truth compels him to count himself among the worshipers. Whether deceitfully or as a pretext, he spoke the truth: his crown bows down and kisses the dust before the Son of David. “I too will go and worship,” he said deceitfully. Truth made its demand on him, and he gave the Son what belonged to him. It took worship in words from him as the firstfruits owed to the Son by royal power. The king’s statement was mingled with the offerings of the Magi, so that it too might enter the King’s treasury. Yes, Herod, your crown is subject to his crown! Your deceit is your own, but the worshiped King receives what belongs to him. Why, then, are you afraid of him if he is not a king? Be patient until you see where he reigns. If you are already afraid of his kingdom now, by what power will you abolish it when it is revealed? A child has terrified you and cast your kingdom into turmoil, and now you are stirring up [?] to fight a newborn! It has become clear that he is a great king: how greatly he has shaken you! His authority is wonderful: without battles, the news of him has thrown you into confusion. The royal throne was shaking beneath Herod, ready to fall, because the one to whom sovereignty belongs had come. He summoned the Magi and questioned them, as we have said:

He had made a pretense of going to worship, as you have heard. The innocent men heard him, but they did not know what his trick was. They went out to inquire about the king. As they went, the star welcomed them with its shining, and with its rays it made the king’s road easy before them. The messenger who had called them and brought them out came, so that he himself might also open the door and bring them in. It had sent them on their journey and taken the road behind them; now it came here to welcome them like a dear friend. It was also necessary for them to see its rising in the land of Judah. They followed it, coming after the one who had called them. It appeared to them so that they would not be distressed that it had left them, and so that they would be assured that its rising was not deceptive. At first they saw it without an interpretation of prophecy; afterward they became doubtful about its revelation. They turned again and heard the scribes’ words and their interpretations, and again they believed that the king would arise from Bethlehem. After that they saw the shining star a second time, so that at both the beginning and the end it might make its truth known. By appearing to them a second time, it taught them that it agreed with that interpretation of prophecy. With its great shining it began on the path of proclamation,

and it came to complete it, showing that it came from the True One. They saw it and longed for it affectionately. Its great [?] brought them past their anxieties. They rejoiced at seeing it and set out to follow its light. It led them to the place of the king who dwelt in Judah. It brought them to Bethlehem, the mighty town, so that they would not wander bewildered among the roads, asking for directions. It became for them a road full of light along which they traveled, so that they might reach the king’s dwelling without fear. It brightly traced a radiant path before them until it reached the place where the king dwelt. It flooded the road along which they traveled with delightful light, so that through its service as a messenger it might honor the offerings for the king. It went before them until it reached the place where the child was. Here is a wonder whose story is beyond explanation! All the stars travel on high according to their appointed times, and not one of them has ever descended into the depths. They travel in orderly ranks, in the places assigned to their numbers, and the swift onward rush of their movements is not disrupted. Which of them ever left its place and came down to show people the way, contrary to its usual course? Where have you ever seen a star leave the ranks

and lead a company like torches giving great light? When did this new thing ever enter anyone’s mind: that a star should come down and show people their way on earth? At what time did one of the heavenly ranks leave the firmament, come down, and walk with merchants along their paths? They ride upon the firmament and travel along the course of the heights, but they do not lower themselves to walk down below. All the heavenly hosts are harnessed under the yoke of time, and from the beginning they have traveled side by side in an even line. Which of them slipped its neck free from among its companions, came down, and set its course down below, all alone? Everything that happened through our Lord’s hands was new, for he never acted according to nature or custom. Where have you seen a virgin mother except his, or a newborn who shakes kings except him? Who had shining messengers except him? And for whose birth were there heralds except his? For whom did a star appear down below except for him? He made use of everything exalted and boundless. Let the scribes stop explaining his birth, and the interpreters stop questioning his glorious majesty. The inquiry pursued in discourses finds its answer only in praise.

For its words cannot reach far enough to explain his great story. Even his messenger exhausts the scribes and cannot be explained. How, then, can he himself be described as he truly is? At his appearing, the star leaves those who investigate it sitting in wonder: it left the heights and led a company down below. It blazed like a torch, and the Magi saw its light and rejoiced. Along the path of its radiance it led them into Bethlehem. It went out after them like an officer sent by the king, and brought them to see its Lord with their offerings. It drew them onward along the path of its light, and when it reached the king’s door, it opened it with its radiance. It [?] before them as far as the place where the child was, and, as though with a finger, pointed him out to the Magi: “Here is the Savior!” It became their path from Jerusalem to Bethlehem, brought them in, and they saw the king. Then it went away. They entered and saw the child lying there: a needy place, a poor person’s dwelling, a little house. And a young mother without possessions or relatives; poverty, and a king lying there without legions. The Magi looked at him and did not doubt his kingship. They fell before him, offering their honors in supplication.

The mighty leaders of Persia knelt and worshiped him, the leader who had arisen from Israel, as had been proclaimed. The king began to bring back the captives of the nations that had gone astray, and to leave the captor who had carried them away sitting in amazement. He began to gather the worship of the nations, which had been scattered, and he began with that land of Nimrod, which had been so strong. The firstborn of crowns fell down and worshiped him through the Magi, so that other kings would bow before his majesty. That kingdom of the chief of mighty men fell before him, to become a mirror for the world, so that it might follow its example. The hunter’s great land gave hostages, and through its offerings recorded the King as its lord. That kingdom, which is the head of the whole world, bowed before him, so that through it all creation might submit. Truth drew the land of Babylon, where dominion began, to worship that Head of all heads. They saw the stone that had been cut out without hands: the great statue was struck by it and fell before it. It struck the head of gold and bent it down to submit to it; like chaff in the wind, it scattered the whole statue. The dominion of Media fell from its glory before that stone which filled the whole earth.

The head of the world, in the daughter of the Chaldeans, submitted to the heir who came to take back his own from plunderers. The offerings of the Magi came in and were presented to him, the worshiped King who came to his own in poverty. Because the King was despised among his people by those within, he sent to outsiders, and they brought him their offerings. He came to his own, and because they did not receive him, he rebuked them by being lovingly honored by foreigners [?]. He sent and brought from among the nations what he needed, because among his people he had been despised by those close to him. The nations who were last became first through their offerings, while the people who were first remained at the door and did not enter. The Magi fell down and worshiped him in wonder, without doubt. Although they had not seen miracles as the people had, they did not despise him. When he healed the sick among the people, they considered him a madman; and when he drove demons out of them, they considered him the chief of demons. But when the Gentiles brought him their offerings, it was not because they had seen him performing signs that they worshiped him. Not when he changed ordinary water into good wine, nor when he multiplied a little bread and fed thousands. Not when he bound Legion and cast him among the waves, nor when he cleansed lepers by his word, as the one who commands all.

Not when he put mud on the blind man and he saw the light, nor when he spat into the deaf man’s ears and gave him hearing. Not when he trod upon the sea’s savage waves, nor when he rebuked the winds and storms and they obeyed him. Not when he called and brought out the dead man after he had decayed, nor when, with his voice, he returned the young man to his mother’s embrace. Not when he healed the woman with the flow of blood from her impurity, nor when he made well the man who was mute and blind and had a demon. Not when he healed and strengthened those who were sick, nor when he gave life to the dead who lay asleep. Not when he drove demons out of the possessed with his voice, nor when he gave light and hearing to those who needed them. Not when he moistened the leper’s hand, which had been withered, nor when he dried up the moist fig tree from its roots. While he was crying upon the midwife’s knees, they saw his lowliness and did not doubt his greatness. In a poor house, without possessions or grandeur, they saw him lying and fell before him with their gifts of honor. In poverty, which brings dishonor upon all who possess it, they honored him, unashamed of his need. In deprivation, which causes its possessors to be despised,

the King was dwelling, and in it he was honored by foreigners. The Rich One scorned the world’s wealth through his poverty, by which he made kings bow before him through their envoys. Through his poverty he trampled the pride of rulers, and at his threshold he brought them low with their gifts of honor. His humility bent crowned heads to obey him, and harnessed the mighty to his yoke, to work through them. From his lowliness, terror fell upon the powerful, and with offerings they knelt and worshiped him without doubt. Through poverty the Son of the rich trampled wealth, to show that his wealth had been his from eternity. The King’s Son dwelt as a poor man in a needy house, and he sent for the treasures of kings, brought them, and piled them at his door. The Magi fell down and worshiped him, the great King, in wonder; though they saw no worldly wealth belonging to him, they did not doubt. From that time onward they became a mirror for the world, so that whoever worships the true Son should imitate them. They did not scrutinize him when they presented their offerings to him. They honored him with love, unashamed of his smallness. They did not investigate his birth with their questions. They gave offerings and did not press him with insolent questions.

They did not debate his birth before giving him their gifts of honor. They knew him to be King, but did not investigate him in their discussions. They worshiped him with love; they did not seek to comprehend his birth through debates, so that they might be an example to the household of faith. A new church came from Babylon to see the Son. She did not investigate him, for she was certain that he was the King. The proud daughter of the Chaldeans saw him and did not investigate him, so that she might be an example that no one should scrutinize him when worshiping him. The Magi, who investigated [?] with their questions, wisely kept silence concerning his birth. Why is his story not held in such honor by the debaters? Instead, look: the scribes are tearing it apart with their questions. Why do you not possess that simplicity of the Magi, which honored him without investigating him through subtle arguments? Why does not everyone worship the Son of God as the wise Magi worshiped him, without investigation? Why is silence not spread over his story like a veil, with him dwelling within it, hidden from those who cause turmoil? Why do the scribes not kneel before him in simplicity, and refrain from investigating him, just as the Magi did not scrutinize him? Why are there divisions concerning him [?] among the debaters, and distortions of his teaching among the investigators?

Why has the mouth made faith a subject of debate, and why does everyone speak with [?] to establish his own position? Why has contention formed factions for itself in the congregations, and stirred up strife to debate the Son through disputes? Let the Magi be a mirror for whoever worships him, so that what is spoken among discerning people may not be subjected to scrutiny. Let the envoys who came from among the pagans with their gifts of honor teach the matter of faith to whoever investigates him. In the land of Judah they asked only, “Where is the king?” And once they had seen him, they did not return to questioning. Those faithful men saw a child lying among the poor, and they did not doubt and ask again about his kingship. They knelt and worshiped him and brought their offerings before him. They opened their stores and gave him the treasures of their fathers. They had brought gold and offered it to him as to a king, and they gave fine spices in his honor as to a lord. They brought him gifts of distinct forms, to the great Crown from whom authority flows. They knelt before him and begged him to accept them. Though he was a child, they were not embarrassed by his smallness. They fell down and worshiped him with great trembling and fear, asking him not to reject their offerings.

They did not see his crown, yet he was believed to be the Lord of crowns. With great love they sought to please him through their offerings. The hidden Crown filled them with awe, and they fell before him, pleading with him to receive their gifts of honor. Mighty men, leaders of the earth, fell before the newborn child, and with offerings they begged him to accept them. It was as though these things were being said by the envoys to the worshiped King as they gave him their offerings: “Receive, my Lord, the gifts that our land has sent to offer you. You are our king; receive tribute from your domain. The crown of Nimrod, chief of the mighty men, has sent a diadem to pay what is due to your glorious kingdom. From now on our land lives under your name, for you are its king. Receive these things from us and release us to go, for we have been sent. The kingdom of Media and Assyria has sent word through us that you are the King and that rulers obey you. The great region to which all dominions are subject pleads through these gifts that you count it among your domains. The land of kings, from which authority goes forth, has now recorded you as its king from this time onward.” The Magi worshiped the Son and presented their offerings, trembling before his kingship without any doubt.

The mighty men bowed down on their faces and pleaded with him, while the virgin mother wisely pondered these things in her heart. The blessed woman spoke words like these to the Magi who had worshiped her son with their gifts of honor: “Where, men, do you see a king, and who sent you? Reveal the mystery to me: who informed you of his kingship? “What order of attendants have you seen here serving him? Where is his crown, if he is a king as you have said? “Look, you see the poverty that surrounds him, and I, his mother, am needy and destitute. “What ranks of people have you seen surrounding him? How many soldiers are at his gates, paying him honor? “How many armed men are with him, according to your account? How many horsemen are now with him, as you have said? “How many legions has he sent ahead of him into the lands? What troops of his soldiers does he have beside him? “Have you seen gold or treasures, as in a royal household? Does he have wealth or authority for which he is honored? “Are servants standing by, or attendants obeying him? Are ranks drawn up, or does royal majesty accompany him? “Is his crown magnificent, or does he have a chariot in which he is carried in state? Does his clothing gleam, or are engraved gems set in his diadem?

“What is there about him that resembles a king, as you have said? Who compelled you to come before him with offerings? “You have encountered him in need and poverty. Who gave you reliable news of his kingship?” They said these words: “Mother of the king, your son is mighty, and the whole world is his to [?] by his valor. “It is not because the land is quiet and does not know him, and the people refrain from worship and bring him no offerings. “The heavens, together with the heavenly lights, bear witness to his birth, and the people of your land bear witness in their writings to his authority. “The hosts in the firmament proclaimed his crown: he is a great king before whom lords fall down. “The ranks on high recorded your child as king, and an image of might rose for him in the zodiac. “Along the passage of the heavenly hosts we saw his crown, and from it we learned of his mighty authority. “His great image stood above the shoulder of the firmament and showed us his [?], so that we would come to him. “The image of his glory rose among the heavenly lights, and we saw it. The sun in its radiance cannot compare with his splendor. “Look, the heights carry his authority upon their heads, and his crown shines above the heavenly lights in their courses.

“The firmament, together with its heavenly lights, bears witness to his might, for through a wonder it announced his kingship to us. “Among those ranks above he is a great king, and there he has a glorious name for his deeds.” The young woman said, “The account of your revelations is true, and I, though wronged, have been convinced of it for a long time. “Yes, truly, he is king of those above, but those below do not realize that he has visited them.” A messenger was sent to me too from the Most High, and he told me about his birth—that he is the Son of God. The messenger descended from among the ranks of the heavenly hosts, and through a wonder he clearly revealed his story to me. I received light from the Most High through hearing alone, but I do not understand what sexual union is like. In wonder I conceived him, without any thought of intercourse. I received the good news of him from the Most High, and a baby stirred within me. I had no sexual union, yet I became a mother, as you have seen. My virginity is preserved, yet I have a child, and here you see him. I do not know what intercourse is like, yet here I have become a mother, like married women. I do not understand what women's labor pains are like; yet I gave birth in holiness, without having known them.

I have not known a man, yet I conceived outside the ordinary course of things. I am not a married woman, yet I am a mother without sexual union. A spiritual being sowed in me good news full of wonder, and without a man's stirrings I conceived while remaining pure. I had asked him, 'How will what you say come about?' And he explained to me, 'The Holy Spirit will come to you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you in holiness, and you will bear a child whose kingdom will have no end.' At that voice I conceived in a way full of wonder, and I gave birth to a king, but no one noticed except you. I am wronged on his account. Be my witnesses among those who wrong me, so that I may uncover my face and put them to shame for how greatly they have mistreated me. Come, you winged ones, tell his story to those nearby, and rebuke them, for [?] they know him to be the Son of God. Call into the ears of the deaf people, so that perhaps they may hear and become a little aware through your good tidings. They say these things: 'Mother of the King, do not be anxious, for a time will come when the whole world will be stirred over your child. Be patient until his kingship becomes known and all the ends of the earth take up his stories to proclaim them. A day will come when his crown shines throughout the lands, and the peoples of the earth and their judges fall down before him.

A time will come for you to see crowds surrounding him, and you will forget the loneliness of the little house in which he is being raised. You will see ranks of nations falling down before him and honoring him with their offerings and their vows. Before long the earth will be stirred by reports of him, and news of him will fly throughout the regions and among their inhabitants. Time will pass, and the world will awaken to speak of him, and his good news will race to all the ends of the earth to take hold of them. He will occupy a place that none of the kings has known, and he will shake all crowns and bow them down before his majesty. He will hold a rank in which none of the mighty has stood, and there he will trample the crowns and caps of rulers. He will inherit a throne whose height the air cannot reach, and the lofty seats of rulers will tremble before him.' In time, reports of him will shine out among the nations, and creation will tremble before the authority of that great King. Dread falls upon judges because of his authority, and he makes the mighty kneel before him in all their splendor. The emblem of his might is set above crowns, and kings with their dominions become a footstool for him. He shakes the authority of rulers throughout the lands, and thrones and those who sit on them tremble before him.

In his power he shines upon the earth far brighter than the sun. He holds its farthest reaches, and no one can escape his authority. Mary says, “Everything you have said is certain to me, and there is no room for me to doubt your words. I truly know who he is and whose Son he is. I learned everything from the angel when I received him. I have not seen his Father, but I am certain that he is Lord of kings. The one who begot him is hidden, and by his authority the world stands. At his command all created things and their inhabitants hang suspended, and through him the farthest reaches of the earth and those who dwell there stand firm. The prophets testify concerning his birth that he is the Son of God, and I am the virgin who conceived without sexual union. His story was openly sung in prophecy, and now you yourselves have proclaimed his kingship. It is fitting for you to begin this proclamation, because of the people who have closed their eyes to understanding. It is fitting for you to speak about my Son and his kingship, since you are strangers to the disputes of the elders of the people. They are jealous and will not accept that I have given birth to a king. They are drunk with zeal and do not understand the things to come. The heart of the people has grown dull, as it is written. They have shut their eyes and made their ears too heavy to understand.

You speak, for it is fitting for you to understand: the King has lovingly made you his confidants. May the earth be filled with your good news, and may the world awaken at the sweet sounds of your joyful cries. May the report of your offerings go out among the nations, and may creation be filled with fresh news of your triumphs.
