May the King marvel at your offerings, as you have longed, and may he receive you with delight, as you have wished. May you please his Father with the honors you have offered him, and may the gifts you have brought him accord with his will. May the effort you have put into your gifts please his divinity, and may he rejoice in the beauty of your offerings that have come before him.” The King was staying in the little house of a destitute woman, and before him lay heaps of the treasures of kings and their offerings. His poverty subdued the wealth of rulers, to show that he was the hidden King of all dominions. He excelled in both littleness and greatness; he rose above both lowliness and grandeur. He moved in both need and power; he went his way in both humility and kingship. Glory and dishonor assailed him from either side.

He was regarded as the Son of God and as Mary's son. He was being raised in the needy home of a poor woman, yet he was bringing the might of the kings of Assyria low. He was despised among the people and was not honored by those within, but he called those outside, and they answered him with their honors. The priests denied him his due and did not bring him their tithes; the Magi worshiped him and brought their offerings before him. Zion withheld the praise that was required, while the daughter of the Chaldeans faithfully rendered the worship that was owed. The king's servants despised the king who had come to their country, while people from far away honored him with choice gifts. The people's scribes, who had explained his story, did not recognize him, while his new good news was being proclaimed through the heavenly lights. Justice came and would not allow the king to be despised. From among the heavenly ranks she called a messenger to prepare his way. The Magi brought their offerings and presented them to him. Through their worship they paid him his due, so that he would not be dishonored. By its rising, the star fulfilled the proclamation to the nations, so that the Son's glory would not be diminished in any way. It is written that it came as far as the place where the child was. It seems that there it stood, shining at the doorway. It left the heights and stationed its light down in the depths.

It resembled its Lord, who stooped and came down to those below. The servants hurried after the Lord to obey him. Both the angels and the heavenly lights came down to honor him. All the armies follow the king, and wherever he takes up residence, there his legions also stand. The Lord of the heights had descended from his Father's side into the depths, and the ranks on high began to follow in his footsteps. The angels came down, and the heavenly lights also began to descend, for through his birth the earth had become heaven. When he descended, he brought down with him some of those above; and when he ascended, he brought up with him some of those below. He brought down spirit and raised up flesh, accomplishing both: he became a human being and made many divine. He was born of a woman so that we might be born of the Holy Spirit. The Son has two births, and we also have two. He was begotten of the Father in a birth beyond explanation, and again of Mary in a new birth full of wonder. Though he is God, she bore him bodily, in a human body, so that he might become human without change. With a pure body, a rational soul, and a complete mind, he came forth from the womb to renew everything through his birth.

He clothed his hidden nature with bodily limbs and became one of us, so that he might clothe us too with spirit and power, and we might become of him. Through his second birth we learned what to do [?]: another birth is needed for us too, so that we may be renewed in it. Baptism became a second womb and gave birth to us, and this birth is truer than that bodily birth. An old man, advanced in years, enters the womb of water and becomes an infant through the new birth of baptism. Although human birth through Adam was real, through the Spirit and water we became children of God. Eve, who gave birth to us, is not our mother—see this from our Lord. The Spirit conceived us and gave birth to us; let us be her children. Eve’s womb gave birth to flesh through sexual union, but baptism gives birth to spirit and unchanging life. Our Lord showed an example in himself to teach us: he came to birth, although he was ancient in his begetting. Baptism became Mary for him, and he bathed there; he came forth in humanity, to become human a second time. He received a body from Mary in holiness, for he had directed his course toward sufferings, to endure them. The Ancient of Days became an infant through his new birth, so that old people might learn the way to come to birth.

“How,” he said, “can an old man return to his mother’s womb and be born again when his time has passed?” “This happens through water and also through the Spirit,” our Lord explained to the man who was asking to learn from him. Just as the Virgin Mary gave birth to him bodily, the fountain of life gives birth to old people spiritually. For baptism is a second Mary for us, and through a perfect and genuine birth, she is our mother. The Virgin gave our Lord a body so that he might become human, and baptism immersed us in the Spirit so that we might become gods. There are two new mothers for us and our Lord: Mary for our Lord, and baptism for us. He who is spiritual made a bodily woman his mother, and for us, who are bodily, he appointed a spiritual mother to give birth to us. He received a body, and we received spirit, from our mothers, for every mother clothes her child in her own likeness. The King had laid out this road to earth for himself. He came and brought, and he went and carried away, as you have heard. As he descended, the watchers and the shining ones escorted him in honor; as he ascended, the apostles and disciples accompanied him. He came without a body and was raised up bodily. He laid aside and took up, and through both he [?] his journey.

The King descended and established his dwelling among the poor, and the heavenly hosts came in procession from his realm to honor him. Angels came from the Father’s house to announce peace and hope to the world at the birth of the Son of God. The shining ones hurried and gave a signal to the regions, so that the ends of the earth might see his rising with their tributes of honor. His rays went out to the land of Persia, which was gloomy, and there they bound the darkness with mighty strength. His path ran toward victories in an extraordinary way, and he yoked the elements to his service contrary to nature. A star, a watcher, and angels also descended to honor him; wherever he stayed, they stood there to serve him. He dwelt in Mary, and the archangel greeted her. He entered the cave, and it filled with watchers offering their praises. He went out into the wilderness, and angels ran to serve him. He entered the tomb, and watchers descended with him to honor him. Wherever the king’s standard was set up, he gathered his legions; wherever he stayed, the ranks of his armies stood. He entered a little house to stay with a poor woman, and the star hastened there and stood over its doorway as though in the firmament. The chief of the heavenly lights left its ranks in an extraordinary way; it descended and honored its Lord’s doorway with its great light.

“It came with them,” it says, “as far as the place where the child was.” It is therefore clear that it descended into the depths like its Lord. The king and his radiance descended into the depths, to those below, so that soul and body might ascend to the heights, to those above. His radiance stood over the king’s doorway, as we have said, and became a lamp for the Magi so that they might enter his presence. By its great light the offerings of the Magi entered, to be presented to the King of kings who had come to his own. They opened their treasures and presented their offerings to him: gold, myrrh, and frankincense too, with discernment. The newborn king was honored by the envoys. They worshiped him with offerings and returned rejoicing. Just as they were about to go to Herod and tell him, night bound their journey with sleep so that it could not proceed. The stillness of night held the Magi back from traveling and carried them to the land of dreams to teach them. Instruction entered subtly to give them commands, so that even in sleep they would not be deprived of guidance. A dream entered and clearly revealed the secret to them: Herod had secretly devised a plot against the king. It taught them about his wickedness, what he had planned, and what accusation he would raise against the child if he saw him.

It recounted to them his deceit and his bitter thoughts: he had prepared himself not to worship but to kill. It made them understand how he was threatening the newborn child, and that if he learned from them where the child was, he would commit murder. The king’s deceit was exposed before the envoys, and they mocked him for threatening the King of kings. Whatever the king had planned as he lay at ease on his bed, a dream went out and revealed it clearly to the Magi. The deceitful man had secretly laid an ambush, and no one noticed; but a vision of the night exposed his secret before many. In the furnace of sleep the king’s fraud was exposed, and the deceit he had devised was spoken of among the visions. Night revealed his hidden plans through its dream. His secret came out, and the undertaking stalled and did not proceed. The king did not reveal to his confidants what he had planned, yet his plot was exposed in a dream, and he became a laughingstock. Though no one had entered his palace and learned his secrets, all his hidden plans were being proclaimed on the rooftops. While guards carefully held watch at his gates, word went out from the king’s house without their noticing it. A dream went forth and brought out what was in Herod’s house.

And the deceitful king was mocked before people from far away. He was accused by a revelation in the stillness of night, and exposed before the company of the Magi. The Magi changed their route and turned away from the king’s house. They mocked Herod, the very one who had deceived them. Through this too, the good news of the Son was dawning and being proclaimed along the roads of the whole world. They went up by one road and proclaimed the king, and when they went back down by another road, they sang of his victories. With their words they filled the earth with fresh good news, both as they went up and as they came down from the king’s presence. They told his story along the roads of the whole world, for they went up by one road and came down by another, speaking about him. On two roads they spoke at length about his kingdom, so that through their offerings the earth would become fully aware. A dream guided them by another road, and they went down. They treated Herod, who had deceived them, with great contempt. The deceitful king was left suffering in his deceit, while the Son’s road was being opened through proclamation. A section suitable for reading at the slaughter of the children, or at the commemoration of the martyrs.
Then, after these things, the watcher said to Joseph:

“Get up, take the child and his mother, and move to Egypt. The king is about to stir up strife against the child, and the time has not come for him to endure the sufferings for which he is prepared. His face is set toward slaughter and sacrifice, but not now—only at his appointed time, when it pleases him. He is destined to receive the sword and the spear, for this is why he came. But he will not die until he has completed the work of his journey. He is prepared for death, but he will not drink his cup today. Get up and give way to the sword that is sharpened and waiting for him. He will not endure the sufferings of sacrifice in secret. He will be sacrificed openly, before the eyes of many, to save them. He will not meet death in an ambush like a weak man. He will be hung on high so that the worlds may see his might. He will not die secretly through the king’s deceit. The whole people will rise in uproar against him and clamor at him. He will not become a sacrifice in the lap of his young mother. On the hilltop he will endure suffering heroically. He will not come secretly to slaughter at Herod’s hands. He will die before the eyes of all created things and shake them.” Let him flee today, not because he is afraid of Herod, but to give the plot room, so that it will not strike him. Let him go and visit the land of Egypt gently.

And when the king’s fury has subsided, let him return to Judah. He is going to his own land, not crossing into another domain. He walks within his own handspan, and all places are one to him. Joseph did as the angel had commanded him, and took the one who carries everything to Egypt like a fugitive. The Lord rode upon a cloud—the Virgin, full of strength—to go down and visit the land of Egypt, which was sick. He was borne in procession upon a dark cloud—the young woman—and descended to the sick land, which was dark with idolatry. The idols of Egypt saw the Savior and trembled before him. They shook in his presence, as had been proclaimed in prophecy. The lion’s cub looked at the foxes and terrified them, and they made ready to fall before him like weaklings. The powers of darkness saw the great light and hid from it, and with its rays it drove them out of every region. The ember of light clothed itself in a body and went out into the land to burn away from its fields the weeds that were in it. The pillars bearing images throughout Egypt trembled before the one who had come to shatter them through his crucifixion. All the standing monuments of the high places shook before the high priest who had come to offer sacrifice and abolish them. Truth entered, whispered to the idols, and shook them.

And though they could not hear, he summoned them to their downfall. It was as though these things were being said by Justice to the images of Egypt, which were mighty in their shrines: “Fall, you wretched things! You have flourished long enough with borrowed things. The one worthy of worship has arrived. Make room for him to stand in his own place. “You hollow shells, clear a place for the Son of God! Images of error, come down from the heights of your palaces! “You desolate idols, which became snares for your worshipers, come down to destruction! Do not hunt any longer to bring ruin. “Flee, you weaklings, from the mighty one who is coming against you! Stand no longer in the king’s place, for he has now arrived. “You manufactured things that took the name of God and threw the earth into confusion, look! The Maker has set out from his place to expose you. “A wind has gone out to gather the thorns from the fields. Flee, you weeds, from the whirlwind that rules the ends of the earth!” The blackness of idolatry trembled before the mighty one, and the ranks of images were given the news of their downfall. The king had gone out over his lands, which lay in ruins, and the one worthy of worship began to bring them peace through his travels. The light had gone out to kill the darkness of the world, and skillfully hunted it down in every region. He sent a shining star to Babylon so that she would come to him.

And he went down to the land of Egypt so that she would receive light from him. Here and there he cast nets throughout the whole world, so that all creation might be gathered into the fold of life. He began to visit the two regions, embittered by their arts, to sweeten them with his teaching. He drew the daughter of the Chaldeans with a thread of light, and she came; and he himself went down and visited the mistress of sorcery. He began to subdue the arts of the Magi and sorcery, to undo all the knots of wickedness in both of them. He devised the pretext that he was fleeing from Herod, and visited Egypt so that her bitterness might be sweetened. If he had not intended to visit the land of Egypt, why, then, did he not flee to Babylon with his messengers? He opened the way to one region with a shining star, and fled to the other to sow hope in both. He sent word to one, and she came with offerings to honor him; the other he humbly visited on his own feet. To one he showed his might through his great manifestation; to the other, his humility by fleeing. He sent a star to one region concerning his coming; in another land he laid an ambush, supposedly fleeing himself. The powers on high trembled at his journeys.

And along the roads a young woman carried him as he fled. He who makes the cherubim tremble was himself afraid, as it were, and fled from a human being. He who carries creation was being jolted along the roads. To give his bodily existence its due, he allowed himself to grow up in the human way and then to suffer. He fled from the sword, not to escape it altogether, but because he was waiting to give his humanity its due. When he set his face toward suffering, he offered it his full-grown stature; that is why he fled from sufferings while he was an infant. He preserved the ordered course of his bodily life so that it would not be disrupted, and he allotted time for his growth so that he would come into his own. His activity, however, did not cease from doing good, for even while fleeing he was making use of what was his own. In mercy he visited the sick land so that she would be healed, and he summoned the gods of the country to their overthrow. In his infancy he went down to comfort the downtrodden land, which was grieving over the infants who had been slaughtered. He went to the land of Egypt, where his servant Moses had been hidden, to fulfill the symbolic pattern that had been drawn for him. Satan, meanwhile, was joining forces with Herod to cut short the King's course of good deeds with the sword. The wicked man saw that the Magi of Persia had made a fool of him.

He was enraged and wanted to commit massacres on account of the child. He saw that he did not know who the king fighting against him was, and he threatened to destroy the entire army. He thought, “The commander is hiding among the ranks. I will destroy them all, and then he will certainly die there.” “The leader has hidden himself in the throng and does not show himself. Let it all be swallowed up, and look—he is confounded along with his legions!” “He has entered the company, and no one can distinguish him from the crowds. Let the sword come out, and he will die with them, among the multitude.” The wretch did not know that he was fighting a mighty warrior who had gone to visit another country and make a mockery of him. The king had moved to Egypt to carry out his work, while Herod remained, raging over the affair. The lion cub was growing majestic in the thickets of Egypt, while the contemptible fox was frantically struggling to destroy him. The eagle had gone and made his nest in the land of Egypt, while the hawk of Judah was raging against him, seeking to kill him. The deceitful king had laid an ambush, but it had not succeeded. So he began openly to form a battle line for combat. He saw that he had been mocked by the messengers, who had scorned him and gone away, and he threatened to destroy the king to whom they had come as well. The tyrant king drew up his forces for battle against the newborn child.

He began to destroy the children of Zion, though they had done no wrong. He sent the sword against Bethlehem, the king’s town, to kill all the children within its borders. Those two years old and under were being killed, according to the time he had investigated and learned from the messengers. After two years the Magi had entered the land of Judah, and when Herod questioned them, this was what they reported. After witnessing the king’s rising among the heavenly lights, they reached Jerusalem in the second year with their gifts of honor. When Herod began to destroy the children of the country, he began killing those two years old and under. The coward waged a new kind of war and became a laughingstock: he summoned one-year-olds to combat so that he could destroy them. The lot of the children was cast in the land of Judah, and they were being killed in place of the king who had come into the world. As they were killed, they became new martyrs for the Son, and through their sufferings they opened the way for the Son’s death. They were beloved wedding attendants who arrived at the bridegroom’s feast and offered him the first blood from their necks. They were children of the knife, whom the womb of suffering had borne, to become soldiers of Christ the King through the blows they suffered. The sharpened sword became their foster father and took them up.

The blade of the sword carried them like a wing and sheltered them. The mothers cried out as they saw the slaughter of their children, who were being killed at the command of the tyrant king. The vines wailed over their first tender shoots, for a wild boar had come in and crushed them on their branches. The fields of Abraham’s household wept thunderously, for hail had fallen and stripped them of their ears of grain. Isaac’s flock cried out in distress, for a wolf had come in to ravage its beloved lambs. A loud cry of sorrow was heard from the daughter of Jacob, who saw her children being slaughtered by Herod. Rachel wept when she saw that her children were no more, and Jeremiah listened and heard her voice amid his revelations. The prophet heard a voice in Ramah, a sound of great weeping: “Rachel is weeping, and she refuses to be comforted.” He called the congregation by the name of Rachel, that daughter of Laban, the mother of Joseph, whose father wailed over his violent death. The aged Jacob refused to be comforted as long as he believed that Joseph had been killed by bandits. Nor would the congregation turn toward consolation as long as she thought that the King had been killed with the children. Egypt is accustomed to sheltering the saviors of the people,

and while they were thought to have been killed, they were living there. Joseph was alive in Egypt while his father mourned, refusing to be comforted over his beloved son. Our Lord went away there to escape from Herod, while Rachel wept, thinking that he had been killed with the children. The prophet told her, “Be still, for there is a reward for your tears,” as though to say, “The King is alive; do not grieve.” Look, in Egypt is the treasury of abundance who comforts you: the Lord of Joseph, who also gladdened his father there. His descent into Egypt fulfilled hidden mysteries, for in prophecy the Father called him “my Son” out of Egypt. While the King was making his journey among the Egyptians, the little children of Judah were being killed because of him. Herod left alone all the kings within his borders and drew up his battle lines to fight against children. Zion’s little children stood before him to hold him back, and he drew his sword against the beautiful children and slaughtered them. The wicked man slaughtered the King’s troop but did not harm him. His company took the blows so that he himself might escape the knife. The children drew up their ranks against Herod and fought with him. They were victorious, for they did not surrender their commander. They took their stand, and all of them died in the fighting,

but they did not reveal where the King was, lest he be struck down. O Herod, how have the people’s little children wronged you? It is a disgrace to your rank that you wage war against children. You boast of victory over nursing infants, but your side lost the battle, for the King did not die. Children triumphed in the battle and defeated you. Become a laughingstock, for the leader of their company was not mangled by the knife. The troops died [?], but the Bridegroom did not die, because it was not his time. The wedding company was struck, but the master of the wedding feast was not dishonored. The Bridegroom had gone to invite Egypt to come with him, and the sword fell upon all his young men while he was coming. He had come to hold a wedding feast of blood in the land of Judah, and the children of the land were invited to be slaughtered. The blood of beloved children entered the wedding feast instead of wine, so that the whole feast might glow with blood from its beginning. Slaughter was symbolically depicted at the banquet, and [?] whoever came to be a wedding guest shed his blood. The mystery went out and gathered early grapes, and pressed new wine from them for the royal Bridegroom. The Virgin's Son had invited virgin wedding guests for himself, so that with virgin blood they might depict his killing and his sacrifice. The innocent were cut down for the Innocent One, though they had done no wrong,

to clear a path for the holy blood that was to be poured out. The king had commanded that the sword should go out and destroy the one-year-olds and two-year-olds within his territory. The sword was drawn to slaughter the infants, and they were being destroyed wherever they were, without reprieve. The command went out, accompanied by the sword of Herod's household, to seek out the children of the land and kill them. The killers made many inquiries about the boys, and they were being killed without mercy in their mothers' arms. The executioners of Herod's household went out through the land and drenched the earth with the innocent blood they poured out upon it. He brandished the sword over the laps of married women and emptied them of the fruit they carried. They poured out blood and filled the mothers' laps, and [?] died of terror at seeing the sword against their beloved children. One infant was draining a breast when the sword caught him, and they splashed blood and milk over the mother carrying him. Another had his head cut off while asleep in his mother's lap, and passed from sleep to death in profound stillness. Another they took from the knees of his mother, who was holding him; they poured out his blood, and his lovely little cries ceased. Silent martyrs, who did not speak as they were being slaughtered,

so that they might depict the profound silence of the one who saves all. Innocent children, against whom the sword came to destroy them, who did not know how to ask why the sword was upon them. Wronged children, who saw the light only briefly and had not had their fill of it, whom the terrible sword of the pagan king swept away. Condemned ones who did not speak as they were being killed, but silently stretched themselves out before the knife. Confessors who displayed deeds instead of words, and set forth the message of faith without debate. Pure priests who had never known wickedness, and brought their blood before God instead of censers. Choice lambs who were handed over to the knife, and were killed in silence for the Shepherd. Children against whom the wicked raised the sword, and who were slaughtered in place of the King who came to his own. Workers who went out to clear the stones from the road of crucifixion, and through their sufferings sprinkled it with blood that befitted him. Perfect sacrifices, free from every blemish, who in their purity were cut apart for the High Priest. Enviable ones who had wronged no one in the land of Judah, yet the wicked had drawn the sword against them. Children who had begun to crawl along the road of this world:

The sword overtook them and hacked their limbs apart. Infants who died without knowing why; but he for whose sake they were being killed knew. Children at the right hand of the newborn King, who stood with him and suffered at Herod’s hands for his sake. Fire and a sharpened sword came out and destroyed them in place of him who came to cast fire upon the whole world. It was good for them to suffer for his sake, for they had been found worthy to be born close to the time of his birth. A road of suffering had been laid out for him to walk on, and everyone who came to birth alongside him was struck down by the sword. The sword ruled over those born in the year of his birth, so that the road of blood would not cease to be traveled. The beloved children had gone out and opened up that road with their wounds, while the King of sufferings was coming to walk on it. The slain infants of the land became hostages for the Son, and he sent them to guard the place of crucifixion. When they were killed, he sent them to the realm of Death to announce to him that the King was coming to the abode of the departed. It was as though these things were being said by the Savior to the infants who [?] on the road of crucifixion ahead of him: “Go and tell the tyrant king: ‘Look, I am coming!

You are already in a hurry to summon me to the realm of your dominion. For I am coming along the road of suffering laid out for me, and I will strip you of the authority of your dominion. I have a little time [?] to carry out what I was sent to do; afterward I will come to you like a mighty warrior. You have dealt very crookedly with humanity in your rebellion, and now, through the humanity you defeated, I will defeat you.’” Make room for the living to enter your prisons, for look, I am coming, and the ranks you hold captive will come out. Go, children, and remain there in the realm of Sheol until I come and empty it of the dead. Look, in a little while I will reach you in the house of darkness, and I will make a great light dawn for you, so that you may rejoice in it. Go and wait for me inside the opulent city filled with the dead. I will not delay; I will overthrow it so that it will never rise again. Fall asleep away from the world, and rest from the struggle of all generations. When I have brought it to an end, I will awaken you along with many others. Go a little ahead of me on the road of suffering until I come. Through crucifixion I will bring it to completion, so that I may raise you from the dead. Go in and wait for me in great [?], the city of the ranks. When I suffer, I will cry out within it, and the whole of it will fall. Go into captivity with the many whom Death has led away.

Look, I am coming to break his bow and bring you back. The little children mocked him as they were being killed by the sword, for the King's road was being prepared through their sufferings. They laughed at Death, for they did not know what its taste was. They were not distressed as they were dragged toward the knife. The children stood playing with the destroyer—the little ones with Death—and they did not realize that it was bitter. The sword was weaving a crown of little children from Bethlehem for the King who is worshiped, who came to die and raise everyone from the dead. They took their blood as a firstfruits offering and brought it before him, so that innocent blood might be honored by holy blood. My Lord, let the slaughter of the little children be pure incense to you, and through it be reconciled to the world, which needs forgiveness. Let peace take hold among the children of the Church, which holds fast to you. Keep stumbling blocks, schisms, and division away from her. Seal her lofty gates with your cross against disputes, and let no disorderly controversy from those who pry enter her. Let your peace stand over her splendid corners, and let your love mix its wine within her, so that she may delight in it. Let your peace guard her gates watchfully, and let everyone who comes to tread her threshold find peace. Let the might of rulers be humbled within her.

And let her alone possess the earth as its mistress. Let her tread down kings with the exalted heel of your crucifixion, and harness rulers under the yoke of peace. Let choirs be drawn up within her for praise, not for contention, and let the sound of rejoicing rise from her, not the sound of questioning. Let the mighty who have taken possession of lands bow down within her, and let her sweep the dust from her threshold with their robes. Let your cross be a great standard over her buildings, and let all the ends of the earth gather to her with their splendor. May she subdue the strength of all kings by her gentleness, and employ the mighty of the world in her work. May her little ones take possession of lands through their conduct, and may all authorities obey her authority. May the lords of the world become servants who obey her, and may all masters kiss the dust of her feet. May her horn be raised above judges and their powers, and may rulers and their dominions become a footstool for her feet. May she possess the ends of the earth, and may the kings of the world be gathered within her; may all the crowns of every ruler kiss her heels. May she lay her yoke on the shoulders of barbarians, and lovingly place the cross as a collar around their necks. May she extend her ranks over the regions and encompass them.

And may she take possession of all dominions in your name, exercising authority. May she bring the strength of all the mighty low beneath her threshold, and may they enter her presence with their vows, with discernment. May she be mistress over kings and judges in the world, and command them like servants concerning her affairs. May the potentates of the earth become a footstool for her glory, and may she lovingly appoint them to her service. May her peace increase, may her assembly resound, may her children rejoice; may her horn be raised, may her glory grow strong, may her crown grow great. May her bosom be filled, may her enemies fall, may she trample those who hate her; may her mouth be opened, may her voice be raised, may she gladden the heavenly watchers. May she grant forgiveness to people, bind up sicknesses, and heal pains; may she be filled with virgins, rejoice in the perfect, and delight in priests. Seal with your cross both her and her children, for she takes pride in you; and may the sprinkling of mercy reach me too, so that through it I may be forgiven.
Here ends the homily on the star that appeared to the Magi and the slaughter of the children.
On the baptism of the Law, on the baptism of John, and on the baptism that our Lord gave to the apostles.
Again, Homily 7: On the baptism of the Law and on the baptism of John. And on the baptism that our Lord gave to the apostles. By the same author, Mar Jacob the Teacher.

At the dawning of the Son, the creatures that had been dark became radiant, and the blind world, which had not seen, saw the light. The radiance of the divine Being shone forth in the world and gave light, and like the day it drove the shadows from every region. Our Lord, the Light, revealed himself amid the darkness, and the night in which the whole world had been enveloped fled. He came from the Father into the Virgin, Abraham’s daughter, and began to travel the road that he had laid in the world. The Light dwelt in holiness in a virgin womb, and from there he began his journey in the flesh. He came out of the womb without destroying her virginity by his birth—a new deed, the like of which had never happened in the world. He went out into the wilderness to uproot thorns from the lands and sow peace in the earth that the great serpent had devastated.

He went out to renew the old things that had been corrupted and establish on earth a new creation that would not pass away. He became a child who would play with the venomous snake, and he crushed the serpent that had bitten Adam among the trees. He traveled from one lodging place to another like a merchant carrying life to distribute among mortals. He stayed at the first lodging place, which is Mary, and came to birth so that he might visit the world as a human being. He came and stayed at the second lodging place, which is baptism, to clothe the warriors in armor. John became a voice in the wilderness, preparing [?] the way, and opened a gate that brings people into the house of God. Where there was water, he stood like a fisherman, to catch people through repentance for the new world. John came to betroth a bride to the Son of God. He was preparing to wash away her filth, and then she would be betrothed. He brought her down into the water and washed her through repentance, so that she would be clean and then see the royal bridegroom. He cleansed her in the river and took away the shame from her face, so that the bridegroom who loves beauty would not see her filthy. Through baptism he made her clean [?] and pure, and then brought her, holy, into the bridegroom’s bridal chamber.

For this reason the son of the Levites hurried to the river, so that from within the waters a bride full of beauty [?]. He was cleansing her, purifying her, sanctifying her, and making her radiant, so that the bridegroom would see her beautiful. He told her the good news of the greatness of the king, his Lord, and continually proclaimed to her that he was from heaven. He would tell her, “I am not worthy even of his sandals,” so that through his humility he might magnify his Lord as he truly was. He cherished the bridegroom’s sandals above his own head, so that the bride would hear and take pride in the one to whom she was betrothed. As he preached to her, he taught her that he himself was from the earth, but concerning his Lord he taught her that he was from heaven. Every day he set her ablaze with love for him, so that she would await him. But the bridegroom was hidden, and the bride did not know who he was. She had learned from John that he was great and glorious. But Christ was hidden, and creation burned with love for him, longing to see him. The crowds asked one another with great excitement, “Where is he? Where is the one whose coming John announced?” While John was like thunder in his preaching, the bride lay there, lay in her love for the Son of God.

The crowds were asking about him because he was hidden, and baptism longed to receive a double measure of holiness from him. Then the bridegroom rose like the sun and a great light, and John stirred to show the bride his beauty. The Levite bowed in worship and lowered his head in great wonder, for he saw the Light, the Son of Majesty, who had come to him. That radiance of the divine Being shone upon John, and with its rays overwhelmed her, so that she marveled at him. But the son of Levi had not seen our Lord in the flesh since the Virgin Mary gave birth to him. While the Virgin was pregnant with him, he had seen her from his mother's womb, and had received the Holy Spirit from him in that hidden place. When the infants came to birth, Herod was stirred to slaughter the children in Judea in his madness. The Son of God fled from Herod to Egypt, while the son of Levi was hidden in the wilderness of Judea. For when the infants were being killed, Elizabeth took the son born from her barrenness and fled to a deserted place. When the executioners demanded that Zechariah bring his son, they shed his blood at the holy altar. Elizabeth remained in that deserted place in this way, while her son John was brought up by grace.

He sustained himself on roots, leaves, and flowers in the wilderness of Judea, like the wild animals. He saw neither inhabited country nor human food during the thirty years in which he grew up in that wilderness. He was brought up in communion with the Holy Spirit, together with grace, which watched over him like a nursing mother. Understand, you who are a disciple, and see now that John had never seen Christ. The providence of God's household also acted in this way toward the people who were full of stumbling. This was so that people who show favoritism would not say about John, when he became a witness to the Son, “He is his friend, and out of their friendship and their earlier association, they made an agreement that he would testify about him when it would be useful.” For this reason he remained without seeing him throughout his long years, and as soon as he saw him, he showed the bride that he was the bridegroom. The pure man was filled with the Holy Spirit, the revealer of mysteries, and through him he was stirred to reveal the Son of God. He said to the bride, “This is the bridegroom to whom you are betrothed. This is the Lamb who takes away Adam's sin. He abolishes all the sacrifices of the sons of Levi, for he himself becomes a sacrifice on behalf of sinners.”

John trembled when he saw his Lord coming to him and asking to be baptized together with the repentant in baptism. The servant said, “My Lord, I ought to be baptized by you, for you are the one who sanctifies and forgives the whole world. You give holiness to the priests, for you are holy. And look, baptism awaits you, to be sanctified by you.” Then our Lord silenced the servant so that he would not speak, but would fulfill [?] baptism. “Allow it now,” he said. “It is not the time for me to reveal the mystery, lest the ruler of the air perceive whose Son I am. I do not want the demons to know whose Son I am until I have reached the great crisis of the crucifixion.” Be silent now, and let me be baptized with those who repent, so that the devil may be mistaken and think that I am weak. The path of birth has brought me to baptism. Since I have been born, here I am being baptized. Be still and baptize me. John fell silent and kept the mystery secret, as he had been commanded. The bridegroom descended so that baptism might be sanctified through him. The rich man's son hid his wealth in poverty, so that he might walk humbly on his path like a poor man. John fell silent, for he had been commanded to conceal the mystery.

And the Father spoke to reveal his beloved to the crowds. The Holy Spirit hovered and descended upon the Only Begotten, so that the Father and the Spirit might be witnesses to the baptism. The Spirit did not descend to sanctify the water so that the holy Son, from whom holiness flows, could then be baptized. After Christ had bathed and come up out of the water, the Spirit descended to show who he was, not to sanctify him. For Christ did not come to baptism to be sanctified. His path is clear to anyone who wishes to walk on it. John's baptism is a baptism of repentance. It called sinners to be baptized so that it might forgive them. But what sin or failing did Christ have that baptism should forgive him when he descended into it? The Son of God did not become like us in sin, so that he should receive forgiveness in baptism like a sinner. It is clear that, although he had no need, he came to baptism so that the righteousness prescribed in the Law might be fulfilled. He traveled along the path of birth in accordance with the Law, and baptism met him midway along the path. If he had turned aside and not descended into it as he passed, he would have disrupted the order of the path he had begun.

It would not have been righteous for him not to finish as he had begun. Our Lord was baptized to pay righteousness its due. He was baptized in water, not to gain anything or to be sanctified, but to fulfill the righteousness prescribed in the Law. John, however, did not baptize with the Spirit and fire, nor did his baptism give the Holy Spirit. He baptized with water for repentance, as it is written, and his baptism was ordinary for anyone who descended into it. The Son of God gave his apostles his baptism, in which there are fire and the Holy Spirit for anyone who descends into it. There is power in it, and it gives birth to spiritual children. Those born from it call the heavenly one 'Our Father.' This baptism, which the Son of God opened, gives birth to new and immortal children for the Father. It is ablaze with fire and the Spirit and gives birth in a divine way, so that through it human beings may become children of God. The Law also gave baptisms to the circumcised, but they did not give the Holy Spirit to all who were baptized. The Law commanded that anyone who goes in to see a dead person must wash in water and remain unclean all day. Anyone who touches a dead person's bone must wash in water.

Anyone defiled by a nocturnal emission must also wash. The Law provided washings of every kind to portray a pattern of the baptism that gives birth to the firstborn. The washings prescribed in the Law were shadows, and they did not bring the person being washed to perfection. The baptism of the Son of God is greater than these, just as a body is greater than its shadow. Now, then, understand the three degrees of baptism for those who were baptized, as we have said. One belongs to the Law, another to John, and the third is this one that the Son of God opened. The baptism prescribed in the Law is a shadow, and John's baptism is one of repentance. The baptism of the Son of God gives birth to the firstborn and makes them sons, so that they may be brothers of the Only Begotten. Moses portrayed an image of baptism in the wilderness, while John opened it as a baptism of repentance. Christ came and kindled it with the Holy Spirit and fire, so that it began to give birth to new children who would not die. Through his baptism, the great Moses sketched a figure of the baptism through which the whole world is cleansed.

John, however, washed away the filth of his people's children through it, to sanctify them so that they would then see the Son of God. Christ came and opened baptism through his cross, so that, in Eve's place, it would become the mother of the living for the world. Water and blood flowed into it to form spiritual infants, and baptism became the mother of the living. No baptism ever bestowed the Holy Spirit except this one that the Son of God opened through his cross. (Through water and blood it gives birth to children spiritually, and in place of a soul the Holy Spirit is breathed into them. Neither Moses nor John, a descendant of Levi, was able to give the Spirit to baptism. The Son of God, from whom the Holy Spirit receives, himself gave the Spirit so that baptism might be sanctified through him. Although he had no need, he came to John for baptism—a baptism that did not perfect those who went down into it. John said, “I need to be baptized by you,” and openly acknowledged how deficient his baptism was. The one in need was pleading with the one who had no need to be baptized by him. And when our Savior went down, it became clear that he was not baptized out of need. John openly acknowledged that he was in need.

But the Son of God was only telling him to be silent. So that he would not reveal to the crowds that he stood above him in greatness, he told him to be silent, so that the baptism would not be canceled. Now let us see why this baptism of repentance was begun by John. This man was appointed to go before the Son of God and prepare the road ahead of his coming. And so he began to call people to repentance, to cleanse them and wash them free of evil deeds, so that the Son of God would find them holy, blameless, and far removed from evil deeds. And so he began preaching in the land of Judah, saying, “The heavenly kingdom has drawn near.” It was as though he were saying, “The Son of God is about to come. Flee from wrongdoing, for he utterly hates those who do wrong.” John became a voice crying out, “Make the road level! Flee from wrongdoing, and come take refuge in repentance! The king is coming! Let the road he travels be prepared, and let straight milestones of righteousness be set up along it. Clear, clear the road for the Lord, for he has arrived, so that he may find his people radiant and pure, so that the Son of God may come and see humankind

on a road filled with righteousness and uprightness.” For this reason that Levite urged his own people to show the fruits of faith. When necessary, he became stern and angry, even calling people a brood of snakes. With threats, warnings, and every possible means, he struggled to bring people to repentance, so that the king’s road would be cleared of evil deeds, and then the royal Son would come in procession to travel along it. He washed in water everyone who came for baptism, and announced to them the good news of the Savior, who had arrived. The daughter of the Hebrews was asleep when the bridegroom came. The sleep of wrongdoing weighed heavily upon her, and she did not notice him. But John, like a trusted friend and mediator, awakened her and announced to her that the bridegroom had come. Because she was filthy, he bathed her in baptism, so that the bridegroom would not see her in her uncleanness when she received him. He brought her down to the river and washed her clean of the smoke of burnt offerings that had accumulated on her face and stained her. He adorned her in fine clothes, as befitted a free woman, so that she might stand beautiful in the bridal chamber of the Only Begotten.

The herald became a voice between the bridegroom and the bride, so that the bride would become aware of the approaching bridegroom’s procession. It was as though the voice, between the mouth and the ear, were escorting the word so that it might come in procession to the hearing. The voice resounds in an empty place to make itself known, for it has no place either in the bosom or in the inner chamber. John too, who is the voice in an empty place—that is, the wilderness—was singing, and the crowds of Jews heard him. The Levite sang, and the bride rejoiced in his melodies; the wilderness resounded with his announcements of the royal bridegroom. The bridal chambers are ready and await the King's Son. The bride bathes and sits in awe, watching for him to come. Our Lord dawned like daylight upon the darkness, and at the dawning of the Word, the voice was stirred to speak. He showed the bride, the daughter of light, to whom she was betrothed, and the Father became a witness to his Son with a loud voice. The Father bore witness by his voice to his Only Begotten, and the Holy Spirit revealed himself beside the Savior. In the likeness of a dove he hovered and descended in innocence, after he had bathed and come up from baptism. He waited to show clearly that our Lord did not need baptism to be sanctified for him before he bathed.

Once he had come up from the water, the Holy Spirit descended, led him, and went out from among the crowds to a deserted place. The bride saw the bridegroom who had come and knew who he was, and immediately he went out to fight against the wicked one. He left the bride knowing him and taking pride in him, and went to do battle with the ruler who guards the air. He set his face toward doing battle with the ruler, so that, once he had bound him, he could come and show the bride his wealth. He directed his path against the one who had taken human beings captive from the Father's house, and afterward he would shine forth among the assemblies. Once he had been tempted, fought the battle, and overthrown him so that he fell, he would reveal himself through the mighty deeds he performed with heroic strength. Once the adversary's fall had come like lightning, then the Son of God would begin to perform signs. The bride knew who the bridegroom was, but he did not stay for her to rejoice with him; instead, he went out to fight. He would overthrow from his dominion that rebel who had taken the bride captive, and then take her, the daughter of daylight, for himself. The Spirit led him to be tempted and to fight the battle, so that in victory he might reveal himself among the assemblies. He fought the contest, and the adversary fell like lightning. Then he began to walk the path of mighty deeds.
The entire path of the Only Begotten is full of wonder. Blessed is the Dawn who, at his coming, gave light to all creation.
Here ends the homily on the baptism of the Law, on the baptism of John, and on the baptism that our Lord gave to the apostles, composed by the blessed Mar Jacob.
On the Baptism of Our Savior in the Jordan
By the same author, likewise by the same holy Mar Jacob. Homily 8. On the Baptism of Our Savior in the Jordan.

Christ the bridegroom held a wedding feast for the Church of the nations, and the world became aware of the banquet he had prepared for her. The King's Son wished to betroth the battered woman to himself, and he sent her to the spring to wash away her filth. He saw the persecuted woman, who was weak, sorrowful, and weary. He mixed water and sent her to bathe and then be betrothed. He looked at her beauty, which had been altered by the smoke of idols.

He poured streams of light over her face to make her complexion beautiful. First, when he was betrothing her, he brought her down into choice waters, to wash her prostitution away from her through holiness. The foul smell of sacrifices clung to her, and he poured pure water over her to make her body fragrant. She had become foul from the filth of burnt offerings, and he sprinkled holiness upon her so that she might be cleansed by it from impurity. He had placed a robe of glory in the bosom of baptism, and he sent the bride to take it and put it on from within the water. He called his trusted friend, the son of a barren woman, and sent him ahead of him to go and bring adornments to the bride until he himself arrived. John went out carrying the riches of the great treasury, to adorn the daughter of the poor as he had been commanded. He took the Spirit’s bag and opened it above the water, and brought out garments for the Church to wear in holiness. He showed her marvelous garments that she had never seen, which had been prepared on that loom in the house of God. He captivated her with his startling appearance, bearing promises as he proclaimed the kingdom on high to the daughter of beggars. “Look,” he said, “the kingdom of heaven has drawn near! The bridegroom has set out in procession to come to you, so that you may rejoice in him.”

He called the young woman, and she gave herself over to being adorned, for she had learned that the bridegroom coming to her was a king. She called Isaiah to learn from him about John: “Who is this who announces to me the good news of the kingdom on high? “Come, prophet, come explain this herald to me, for I need to learn the truth from you. “I accept your own voice, which speaks on my behalf, for I have long heard the words of your account. “Through your prophecy you gave me confidence in restoration. Come and see whether the time has arrived for me to enter it. “See what the news is about this man who proclaims glorious things, while poverty is plainly visible in his own person. “His appearance is destitute, but the voice of his proclamation is rich. His outward bearing is lowly, but his word is great in everyone’s ears. “From what I have seen of him, the man does not speak in proportion to his standing, and the promise he sows in my ears is not lowly like him. “He makes his words grand, while he himself owns absolutely nothing. He wanders in the wilderness and announces to me the good news of the kingdom on high. “Tell me, [?], whether he is trustworthy, so that I may listen to his words. If he is not trustworthy, let me not be led astray by him as by the others. “Your Lord is coming, and I am ready to go in before him.

“Reveal the truth to me; do not let yourself become involved in blame.” Isaiah came forward to teach the Church about John: “He is the confidant of the bridegroom, your Lord; receive his words.” “This is the voice crying in the wilderness before the King's Son: ‘Clear, clear a road for the Lord in faith!’” “Go, descend and bathe; do not wait for the herald to ask you. He levels the mound to prepare a road for the King who is coming.” The Church, the King's bride, approached John, and he began to bathe her, wash her, cleanse her, and sanctify her. He became her trusted attendant and worked as hard as he could to adorn her. He taught her and gave her wisdom so that she might be put in order, for she was in confusion. She heard his voice and was drawn after his words. She thought that he was the bridegroom to whom she was betrothed. She embraced the servant lovingly as though he were the master, because Christ was hidden from her among the tribes. The faithful man saw that the bride he had betrothed was clinging to him. He began shaking out the folds of his robe and crying, “I am not the bridegroom!” He pushed her away from him so that she would not be mistaken about him, since he was a servant. He kept her waiting in hope of the bridegroom while he remained far away. He humbled himself, saying, “I am not worthy even of his sandals,” so that, as a faithful servant, he might preserve his master's supremacy.

He saw that the young woman's gaze had settled on him, the consecrated man, and he hurried to cut off the cause of stumbling from her mind. He bound her by an agreement to await the bridegroom and not look to him, proclaiming to her, “He comes after me, but he is before me.” She began watching for when she would see him coming to her, examining those being baptized one by one. She cast her gaze far over the many people, hoping to see among them the one and only one to whom she was betrothed. Whenever someone went down for baptism, the crowds surrounded him to examine him and see whether perhaps he was the Christ who was to come. The Church gathered and stood in the wilderness beside John, searching with her eyes to see which one was the bridegroom. She went around the river and cast her eyes among its streams, so that she might receive the true bridegroom from within the waters. The beautiful woman stood watching for the bridegroom, waiting for him to come, so that she might enter with him into the embrace of the waters to be sanctified. She spread out the hem of her robe and waited for him beside the waters, so that when he bathed he might be received in holiness. John too was waiting for him to come, so that through him his baptism, which was incomplete, might be brought to completion.

He kept the secret that was between him and the Father, and watched for the Spirit to bear witness to the true one. As he laid his hand on those who came to baptize them, he looked upward because of the agreement that had been made there. He sent his eyes sweeping over the many people beside him, to see which one the Spirit would point out when she was sent. He watched for that winged one, the mistress of the heights, to see how she would descend and on whom she would rest, to bear witness to him. He waited for the swift wings that uphold the ends of the earth, to see whom they would receive from within the waters. He longed to see the wing that flies without flapping, so that when it appeared he might bear witness to the Savior. He listened closely to that mighty voice of the Father, to hear from it about whom it cried, “This is my beloved Son.” The bride stood beside the faithful man, the son of a barren woman, waiting for him to signal, “This is the bridegroom.” She looked to him to tell her about the Savior, while he waited for the Father to bear witness to his beloved Son. Whenever someone came to go down and be baptized, she pressed close to him,

so that, if he was the bridegroom, she might receive him lovingly from him. He would tell the crowds, “Look, the bridegroom stands among you,” and these words added fire within the bride. He also proclaimed, “I am not worthy even of his sandals,” and again he set her ablaze with love for Jesus and his majesty. The bride of light hurried and stood beside John, so that when he showed her who the bridegroom was, she might fall before him. The bride kept her eyes fixed on everyone brought to be baptized, until he came up again. Thousands were baptized, but no Spirit descended upon them. Tens of thousands bathed, but the river remained cold, without the hovering of the Spirit. Crowds went down, but the waters remained ordinary, just as they were. Many came up, but the Father’s voice remained hidden as before. And when the bride had been made perfect with the ornaments of repentance, and had bathed and come up from the baptismal waters, and when the entire wedding feast was ready with all its arrangements, and only the bridegroom delayed coming to attend to what was his, when the wedding guests had received a bath that cleansed them, but had not been clothed from within the waters with the garments of the Spirit, and when all the nations stood naked, waiting for the bridegroom to come and clothe them,

and when the bride’s filth had been washed away in the water and she had come up, and everyone was looking for the white garments the bridegroom would bring, and when baptism lacked forgiveness, and no one had received the Holy Spirit from the waters, and when the whole wedding party was looking for the bridegroom, wondering where he was, the King’s Son came out from among the crowds to approach the river. While he was still far away, baptism boiled up to meet him, and the river overflowed and proclaimed him without speaking. The Holy Spirit had gone out from him and stood over the waters, and the heat of his might set them ablaze. His fire blazed among the currents before he went down, and the river leaped with the great boiling heat of the flame. Baptism yearned for him as he approached her, like the horn of anointing coming to meet David. She did not boil up to meet him in order to sanctify him, for he was holy. His beloved was eager for her own bosom to be sanctified by him. She rejoiced in him because he was the one who perfected and sealed her, and she spread her wing so that the holiness of the Son might be received within her. John saw the river seething and its currents turning back, and he knew that the Holy One had come to be baptized.

He drew back his hand so that he would not baptize those who were coming, so that Christ, the Bridegroom, might be revealed and stand alone. He shouted at the crowds and drove them away from the river, so that everyone might know on whose account the baptismal water had seethed. He rebuked the flock so that it would withdraw from the spring, so that the sacrificial Lamb might separate himself and come out from the flock. He signaled to the attendants, and they made room for him among the crowds, so that the Bridegroom might be revealed in glory to all peoples. The crowds surrounding the place of baptism fled, and the royal Son stood alone, all by himself. The faithful servant ran to bring the noblewoman good news about the Savior. He called the modest woman to show her that this was her Lord. “Church, I betrothed you to this Bridegroom from the beginning. Ever since I came, I have kept you waiting in hope for him. This is the Lamb who brought himself to be a sacrifice. This is the one who takes away the sin of the world through his sacrifice. Look, this is the one I have long been teaching you to trust. In his name I had you sit and wait for him. I carefully guarded you for him as a faithful servant. Give him thanks on my behalf, for I did not let you be stolen away by me.”

While the King's bride was being instructed by John, David, the singer of the Spirit, approached and sang to her: “Listen, my daughter, and look; incline your ear to glorious things. Forget your people and your father's household, for they are divided. Yes, he truly is your Lord. Come near and worship him. Do not doubt the Savior who has come to you.” The Church learned from John and also from David, and she became certain that he was the Bridegroom to whom she had been betrothed. She approached and stood watching how he was baptized, so that when he came up out of the water she might fall down before him. Christ approached John to be baptized by him. John saw him and held his hand back from the Fiery One. He bowed his head before the Son and said to him, “It is I who ought to be baptized by you, for you are holy. I was looking for you so that I could entrust baptism to you. Here is your treasure; now release me, so that I may rest a little. I was only keeping your place, for the authority is not mine. Take your position; I have no authority over your domain. A king does not receive authority from a beggar. The ranks of all rulers proceed from the crown itself. What does baptism have that is not yours?

And what pardon is there for you to go down and receive from the water? If pardon flows from you to humanity, and if forgiveness is yours, as is the forgiveness of sins; if the whole priesthood is in you, since you are the High Priest; and if it is kingship, you are the one who binds crowns on kings.” Holiness flows from you to humanity; and as for priesthood, behold, the world stands at your right hand. And since the fullness of divinity is with you, what does this little river have that could make you complete? Our Lord said, “I lack nothing except one thing: I must find Adam, who is lost to me. Let me go down and seek Adam, the beautiful image; and when I have found him, my whole desire will have been fulfilled. I had a great quest concerning him, and that is why I came. If I do not find the lost one, something is lacking. This alone is lacking to me: finding him beside me, so that I may regain Adam, who chose to perish at the hands of the Evil One. Through this finding, my desire reaches fulfillment, for I still lack Adam’s entry into his inheritance. Let me, then, take hold of and polish the image that he corrupted, so that he too may not remain lacking when you hold me back.

The grace that called me to come to birth—that very same grace has called me again to come also to baptism. Great compassion drew me to descend and become an infant; this same compassion drew me to descend and be baptized. The embrace of baptism is no more confined than the womb, and the river’s waters are no darker than the womb. If you think you are showing me honor, you should also have kept me from conception and birth. If this is a disgrace to me, which place is more lowly: a womb of flesh or the greatness of baptism? If you had stopped me from coming to conception while you were in your mother, you could readily have objected to my being baptized as I was sent to do. If you turned me back from that stage of being born, come, turn me back from the rite of baptism. If you had kept me from swaddling bands, so that I was not wrapped in them, drive the river’s waves away from me so that they do not cover me. If you had stopped me from tasting lowly milk, you would have kept me from taking hold of the spring. If you had prevented me from resting in Mary’s lap, I would also have passed by the embrace of baptism. But now that I have traveled and come along the path of those who are born, how can I turn back from it unless I complete it?

For it is fitting for me, who was sent, to do this too, so that the entire path for which I descended may be fulfilled in me.” John recoiled, trembled, and was terrified before the King’s Son. He bowed down to him and acknowledged him, crouching low with a thunderous cry. “I beg you, my Lord, I am not able to approach you. Straw is too weak to lay its hand upon a blazing fire. How can grass take hold of a flame, or a speck of chaff lay its hand upon a burning coal? The heat of your might has reached the river, and behold, it sets it ablaze. How, then, will you not scorch my hands of flesh? Nor is it necessary for you to be baptized by me as though you lacked something, lest a rumor spread through the world that you are deficient.” Go, Son of the King, rescue the captive people, who are looking to you. You do not lack weapons that you must take them from the water. Your crown has been yours from eternity and does not change. You are not enriched from the treasury of baptism. Hurry on your way! The exiled people thirst to see you. You are not waiting for someone to accompany you. You were born amid the Father's purple robes, from his own being. You do not need to clothe yourself here before you can save. There is battle on earth; do not delay its deliverance.

Go out and take the captive nations away from their persecutors. The Father's kingdom and yours are one, Lord of kings. You do not gain your strength to rule from here. The exiled people have passed beyond peace. Why are you standing still? Go and bring them back from the stumbling blocks through which they departed. Look, captors have raided the land! Quicken your pace. Go out and bring back the captive people who have gone out from your dominion. Baptism adds nothing to what is already yours. Why, then, are you so eager to go down and bathe? Be still, John. You are not adding anything to me. The waters need the hovering presence, so that they may be filled from me. I have not come down to the spring to take a shield for myself, but to forge mighty weapons for the warriors. I am eager to polish people for the arena of battle, so that everyone who comes to the struggle may fight as I do. I am making baptism into an armory: unless someone enters and clothes himself from it, he cannot fight. If I pass by without being baptized, as you have tried to prevent me, no one can take weapons from the water. Like an army commander, I have taken the lead in the struggle,

so that I may be an example to the armies coming after me. If I turn aside from the road I have taken and traveled, they too will turn aside after me, following what they have seen me do. If my troops are not equipped from within the waters, they will not meet the great battle like valiant warriors. Although I have no need of the furnace of water, I am entering it, so that people who have worn out may be recast in my own mold. I am encouraging them to come to the spring as I do, so that they may be spiritually stamped with my coinage. I am bringing human beings down into the grave of water, so that at the resurrection I may make them immortal. I am bringing them into the eager womb, so that it may conceive them and, without labor pains, give them a new birth. It is right that I should be baptized by you; do not delay. Come, open the road, for the world is waiting to be renewed through me. The timid man approached the mighty one and asked him, “How, my Lord, can this be possible?” I said this to the bride of light who was betrothed to you: “Your Lord, the bridegroom, baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire.” Look, she is watching for you to baptize her, as I taught her. How can she now approach and see you being baptized by me?

I acknowledged before her that I am not worthy even of your sandals. How could I dare to lay my hands upon your head? I was baptizing her in your own name so that she might be adorned with you. But in whose name I should baptize you, the Holy One, I do not know. Look, my word stands pledged to her, and she is mindful of it, for I told her, “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.” How can I now reverse my words and change what I said, and baptize you, who baptize everyone, in water like the rest? I become implicated in falsehood, and you are diminished, and the bride thinks there is some deficiency in her betrothed. How shall I speak when I baptize the one who forgives sins? With what words shall I observe the order of baptism? Shall I baptize the Son in the Father's name? Look, you are in his embrace, and there is not the slightest trace of separation between you and him. Shall I invoke the Son? You alone are the one who sanctifies the water. Since you are holy, why should you bathe your holiness in baptism? If you are baptized in the name [?] of the Spirit, how is it possible to descend separately into the water [?], when you are with the Spirit? The Father is wholly in his offspring, and the Son in his Father; and the Spirit who proceeds from him is one dominion with them, without confusion. How can I, wretched and weak, do this and introduce a division into that indivisible unity?

John, leave these questions behind and be silent. Do not inquire here about these things. I have not come to baptism so that it may sanctify me. Nor is it necessary for you to say anything when I am baptized. Come silently and simply place your hand upon my head. It is for the Father to decide what to say about his Son. Stretch out your right hand, lending it to me. Without any word from you, the Spirit bears witness to the true one. When the son of barren parents was trembling over these things, he then allowed the Son to be baptized as he wished. He approached trembling, bowed down in acknowledgment, and touched him with shaking hands. He trembled and was terrified, but power supported him so that he would not fall. The Holy One came and reached the water to go down and be baptized. His fire swept through the waves and set them ablaze. The river leaped in the pure womb of baptism, like John in Elizabeth at the approach of his Lord. The waters blazed with flashes of flame, for the living fire had come to baptism to bathe in them. The fire that burns the worlds cast its flame upon the spring, and its heat set the river ablaze with holiness. The ordinary waters were mingled with rays of holiness,

for mercy had gone forth from the Holy One and set them ablaze. The fiery coal descended to bathe among the streams, and there it poured out the burning heat of its holiness. The flame came and took off the garments it was wearing, and descended to cast fire into the waters of baptism. The heavenly beings marveled at that bathing of the flame, as its radiant body was laid bare to sanctify the waters. The streams of water mingled with rays of light, and the river shimmered with the radiance that dwelt in it. The flowing waters fashioned a canopy of waves, and flashes of lightning from the flame surrounded it on every side. Astonishment and great wonder fell upon creation as the flame descended to be baptized by John. All the air grew hot and blazed with holiness, because the Son of the Holy One descended to baptism, though he lacked nothing. The wind was fiercely kindled with fire, so that in radiance it might receive the Bridegroom from the midst of the waters. Splendid glory blazed from every direction and formed an escort of honor for the royal Son. Clouds of light flew from the farthest reaches and stood there,

to form a bridal chamber for the glorious Bridegroom who descended to be baptized. The mists came forth like towels from the royal household, so that when the King's Son bathed, he might be received in them. The Father spread out choice garments above the air: radiance, glory, wondrous flashes of lightning, and mists as well. He wrapped the river in marvelous, intangible colors to magnify the wedding feast of his only Son. He tore open the heavens and raised his voice mightily: "Look, this is my Son! This is truly my Beloved!" The Spirit flew from the Father's side in a great wonder. She flew, descended, settled, and remained upon his Beloved. She came innocently in the bodily likeness of a dove, to build there and place her nest in baptism. She put on the form of a dove, pure among the birds, and came in her innocence to bear witness to the True One. It was not to sanctify the Son that she descended when she was sent, for the worshiped Word had no need to sanctify himself. She did not sprinkle holiness upon the Holy One by her descent. When she appeared, she bore witness to the Savior. The Spirit became a finger for the Father, and through her he pointed out: "This is my Son; do not doubt his coming."

If the Spirit had not descended upon the True One, who would have known to whom the Father's voice referred? Along with that word proclaimed from the Most High, the Spirit pointed out, as with a finger, that this was the King. For if she had not visibly settled [?] upon him, the voice would have wandered among the crowds, over many people. They would have heard the voice saying, "This is the Beloved," and would have asked in doubt, "About whom did he say it?" The Spirit descended to dwell upon him in holiness; for he did not lack holiness and become complete through it. The Law too calls two witnesses to his side, for one alone is not accepted, even when he is truthful. The Father and the Spirit together testified about the Only Begotten, so that, according to the Law, they might establish the righteousness of the one who is true. The Father's voice and the Holy Spirit descended together, so that no one would reject their testimony when it was revealed. The Father's voice split heaven open and came out of it, and an endless sea of light stood over the river. The Spirit took up great glory on her wings and came, and the wilderness was flooded with the radiance that poured down from the Most High. The Church, the bride of light, marveled at the royal bridegroom,

at whose bathing the heights and the depths were reconciled. She saw the river, its currents trembling and its whole expanse ablaze, and she heard the Father's voice proclaiming his Beloved. She sent for David, that lyre of the Spirit, to come and sing songs suitable for the wedding feast. Come, son of Jesse, and bring your songs with you, so that today we may vie with one another at the banquet of your Lord and your son. Polish your melodies and stretch the strings of your lyre, and raise songs that gladden me with their clear meaning. Do not speak to me in symbols when you sing. Let your words shine out, and let the truth thunder in your melodies. Reveal and explain to me why the river trembles, and what power compelled the deep, so that it shook and was terrified. What is this voice descending from the heights to the depths, and why have these many lightning flashes set the air ablaze? Raise songs of praise to the bridegroom, David, so that we may explain this event to the Church just as it happened. The waters saw you, O God; they saw you and were afraid. The depths also shook, and the clouds of the sky poured down water.

All of nature sensed that you had visited them: the seas, the depths, the rivers, the springs, and the pools. They crowded against one another to be blessed by your footsteps, for your great manifestation over them filled them with awe. You stepped upon the Jordan as upon the head of all the seas, and the foundations of the depths and the floods shook at your power. The whole nature of water was stirred by your hovering, for through your baptism you made all waters fit for the forgiveness of sins. Though the waters of the seas are far away, they are not far away, for the power of your holiness moved unseen and visited them. For this reason the waters saw you; they saw you and were afraid. The depths also shook, because by your descent you filled them with awe. The clouds sprinkled water in the river—water in the river—as you were being baptized, so that they too would not be deprived of your hovering. Look, the heavens again gave voice through your Father on high, so that through his testimony the earth might recognize that you are the Only Begotten. Your lightning bolts lit up the world, and it saw a splendid light, for the earth was troubled in darkness before you came. The waters saw you and feared you as their Lord, for the surge of your might made them seethe as you descended. David explained the reason for this event as he sang:

And Zechariah came and roused the Church to point him out to her. “This is the man I told you about, whose name is the Dawn. Look, he has shone forth, and the ends of the earth are lit by his rays.” John approached and lowered his hand onto the blazing fire, while the ranks of the Watchers hid in their chambers in terror. The heavenly powers marveled at the wonder they saw: a speck of dust touched the burning coal without being scorched. The heavenly beings marveled at the awesome sign that took place there: a hand of flesh was not harmed by the flame. The seraphim cover their faces before his blaze, yet a hand of molded clay rests above his head. A brick molded from earth held the sea; it laid its hand on the flood and did not dissolve. It is a wonder to tell: while the fiery beings are powerless before him, he descended to baptism under the right hand of the son of a barren woman.
