He is carried by the cherubim, majestic on the chariot, concealed from the Watchers, hidden from the ranks, glorious among the assemblies, and awesome to the heavenly orders. The ranks cover themselves, the assemblies shrink back, the orders are terrified, the powers quake, the companies tremble, and the thousands shudder. The flame stands aside, trembling, while he descends to be baptized by the dust his hands have molded.

Heaven is torn open, and the Father cries out concerning his beloved. The Spirit shines and stands ready to testify concerning the Only Son. A voice came out from the inner chamber of the royal palace to declare that the King's Son was no stranger. A hidden word, not from a mouth, was stirred to come forth and testify concerning that offspring of the Godhead. That voice, hidden from everyone, was revealed as it cried out concerning the hidden One who had come into the open. A mighty voice thundered in heaven without a tongue, from [?] the bodiless One, concerning his beloved who had taken on a body. He did not speak through an angel at that moment, nor did he make his proclamation through the blazing mouth of one of the Watchers. He did not borrow a word or a voice from the heavenly beings, for he spoke from his own being concerning his Only Son. The Father himself truly spoke in his own person to declare that his offspring was truly his. A new word was heard among the assemblies, a mighty voice whose like had never otherwise been uttered. A melody that had never been planted in human ears, an awesome thunder that made its voice heard in a unique way. He had never spoken a word like this at any time:

For he had no other child on either side. The Mighty One thundered to show his love for his Son among the crowds, to let them know that this was his true Son. Fatherly affection overflowed toward the Only Son and cried out about him to show that he was its beloved. The Godhead, exalted above all, was not ashamed to see its Son clothed in a body and bathing in water. That greatness was not diminished when its beloved went down to baptism, which was intended for salvation. It was not that any deficiency in him was being made up by the water, so that the Father should disown him and refuse to acknowledge him because he was deficient. He was perfect before he went down and after he went down, and the Father could openly acknowledge his Son. This was the reason that called him to come to baptism: that the hand of the priests should reach its culmination in him and go forth from him. The Father had entrusted a deposit to Moses on the mountain and sent his Son to receive it from John in the water. It had been handed down through the tribe of Levi, and the lion cub of the house of Judah arose and took it from that tribe. Holiness had poured down upon Mount Sinai from the Most High,

and through John it was poured out upon our Savior. Our Lord received it from its beginning so that he might complete his course, rather than follow another path like a stranger. That priesthood which had been handed down from the house of Aaron went forth from our Savior into the world through the apostles. It was not because the High Priest lacked priesthood that he received it at baptism and then gave it. So as not to disrupt the path of truth that his Father had laid out, he renewed the old things from what was his own. It is not because the ocean lacks fullness that all the streams and rivers pour into it. Water naturally runs toward the sea, though the sea lacks nothing, and the whole sea does not grow beyond what it is. It was not because Christ was in need that he received the hand of Aaron, nor because he was deficient that he received kingship from the house of David. Kingship flowed along with priesthood and rested upon him, although he himself is the High Priest and King of kings. Holiness streamed forth, came, and fell upon him like a rivulet into a full sea that lacks nothing. Kingship came from the house of David and was poured into him,

although his kingship was far richer than the sea. He came up as he had gone down, holy as he is, and was welcomed in the embrace of the voice of the one who begot him. The Spirit wrapped the baptized Bridegroom in wings of glory, and the Church was assured that it was he and fell down before him. Perfect One, who came to make the imperfect perfect in water, let your great compassion overflow from you upon my imperfection. Blessed is he who came and was baptized by his messenger, as he was pleased to do. He is the one who sanctified baptism; to him be glory.
Here ends the discourse on our Savior’s baptism by John.
On Holy Baptism
Also by the same author, Saint Jacob. Homily 9. On Holy Baptism. Son, who made us children of his Father through the water, through you I will speak about your spiritual birth.

Only Begotten, who gave us his Spirit in baptism, give me words with which to sing to you lovingly. Lord, who wished to become a brother to wicked servants, fill me with your teaching, so that I may proclaim your goodness every day. Great Sun, who caused his light to dwell within the water, dawn within me, that I may shine and tell of your beauty in wonder. Son of the Virgin, who gave us too a virgin mother, let my words give birth to you with discernment as I stand in wonder. With the mind stirred, let my tongue proclaim a discourse of praise without confusion, its voice free from contention. Let baptism be the occasion for the account I have begun, and let the discourse proceed toward the appointed celebration of the Only Begotten’s glory. Let this mother, who gives birth each day to immortals, stir my words, that they may go out and carry your stories through the world. The daughter of the shining ones, who gives birth to bodily suns, has invited me today. Come, let us delight in her delicacies. The mother of life, whose children are raised above darkness, has asked a discourse of me; if I remain silent, it is an injustice. The King’s bride has prepared a wedding feast for the whole world. Nations and all the world, come to Christ’s banquet.

She has opened a channel of living water from the Father’s house to the world. All you who thirst, drink hope from her spring. Who is this to whom the nations of the earth have gathered, who distributes garments of light to clothe them? Who is this bride who has come up from the water, resembling the fragrance of a censer, chosen from all aromatic spices? Who is this whose beauty awed the river Jordan, so that it prepared before her a bridal chamber of waves in which she might be married? Who is this majestic woman who sits within the spring and gives birth to children who will become brothers of the Son of God? Who is this before whom the priests and high priests of the earth stand trembling, consecrating her with the movements of their hands? Who: without limit. Who: Who is this who leans upon the Only Begotten, is steeped in his blood, and embraces him, rejoicing with him? Who is this who draws people to the spring and mixes fire and Spirit into the water to give them drink?

Who is this whose appearance is like a cloud of light, who has captivated everyone who comes by her beauty, in holiness? Who is this who, as soon as she opened her lofty gates, shut Sheol, which had stood open to the generations? Who is this new mother who takes old people and conceives them, so that at birth they may become children? Who is this living nurse who, within the water, weaves a garment of light for everyone who comes to her? Who is this mistress of glory, full of splendor? Look, all creation is stirred by her to rejoice with her. It is baptism, the daughter of day, who opened her gates, and night fled. She who had been hated [?] the king, whom she labors to bear; and the Only Begotten supports her with his Father's Spirit. The sun's betrothed, through whom all creation is illuminated, and the world grazes lovingly in the meadows of her light. Baptism is the gate that leads into the kingdom, and through her a person enters God's presence to be with him. Baptism is a new ship that carries the dead. In her they are raised to life and cross over to the land where no one dies.

Baptism is placed between one world and the other, and through her a person enters the land of life from the realm of death. Baptism—on this side of her is the gate of Sheol, and beyond her is the gate that leads into paradise. Baptism—in her the cross is set like a ladder, and it carries people from within the water to the heights above. Baptism is a bridge built between the two sides, and no one crosses over to God except through her. Baptism is a womb that gives birth to living people every day and sanctifies them to become brothers of the Only Begotten. Baptism gives Adam the robe of glory that the serpent had stolen from him among the trees. Baptism is a great furnace filled with light, and in her people are recast to become immortal. Baptism is the great road of the kingdom, and she brings whoever walks on her into the land of light. In baptism the treasures of God's house are stored, and whoever enters finds limitless wealth. Baptism gives birth every day in her virginity. She is a mother and she is a virgin, and she is beyond scrutiny.

Baptism became our mother, and in her we became children of the Father, so that we might lovingly call him our Father. This womb formed us spiritually, so that through her we might become God's children in holiness. For if she had not given us a second birth, how could we call the heavenly one our Father? From Eve we are earthly people and children of death, but from this new mother we are children of God. From her onward we have a Father above in heaven, and we call upon him, confident that he is our Father. How do we have a Father in heaven, or since when? For look, our father Adam is in Sheol upon his ashes. If birth from Eve remains in force, let us then say, “Our Father in Sheol,” not “in heaven,” where he is not. The serpent bit our first father and cast him down into Sheol. Look, there he lies in destruction, thrown down and abased. He lies sprawled in the dust, surrounded by ranks of maggots. Worms are his clothing, and he has [?] as a covering. Maggots are beneath him, and vermin settle above him. The dust has humbled him; his dwelling is empty, and he wastes away in Sheol. This is our first father, and this is his place.

And if he is not replaced through baptism, great is his abasement. As long as our race remains in this birth from Eve, this is our father, and we must seek him below, not in heaven. Flee, listener, from this great abasement. Seek another father for yourself, the one in heaven. Run to baptism, take refuge in her, and seek her as your mother. She will give you a Father who is rich and full of blessings. She gives birth to you even if you are an old man, so that you may become a beloved child whose Father is a king. She teaches you to say, “Our Father in heaven.” From then on, our Father is above, not in destruction. It is a disgrace to acknowledge the one in Sheol, who is so poor and so abased. Take for yourself a Father who is entirely wealth. Baptism writes your name above in heaven, in the assembly of the firstborn, where the Father sits on high. Be baptized, listener, and call upon our Father who is in heaven, for from now on your descent from him is heavenly. Through baptism, take another in place of the one in Sheol. From now on, look upward when you call, toward where he is. The one who became your Father through the water is truly your Father.

Look, he is in heaven, in his exalted place, majestic and glorified. Above the mountains, above the expanses, above the heights; above the principalities, above the glory of the powers. Above the assemblies, above the ranks, above the orders; above the companies, above the countless thousands. In a place higher than the angels and their assemblies, in a height hidden even from the Watchers and their shouts of praise. Where there is no place for the Watchers to minister, nor does any spirit step inside to hover. In the place higher than the chariot and its movements, where neither the creatures yoked to it nor the flying creatures travel. In the sanctuary where the Trinity dwells, which even the seraphim cannot approach when they have covered themselves. Where fire [?], if it approached, would immediately burn up, and a flame would be scorched if it entered. In the place where the light of the sun and the moon [?] lies insignificant and discarded outside its door, so that it may not be sullied by their shining. In the tabernacle that is neither made nor composed of created things, where he alone dwells—the one who established baptism for you. Send your mind soaring to this meeting place when you call out:

“Our Father,” to your Father through our spiritual birth. Ever since the chosen waters of baptism gave you birth, your family has been above, where the Father sits on high. There you have a brother, Christ, whose Father is your Father, and kinship with the Holy Spirit, who sanctified you. You were wretched and needy on the dungheap; mercy lifted you up and made you great, so that you might even be called a son of God. The waters gave you birth in place of that bodily birth, and now your voice rises to call out, “Our Father who is in heaven.” The Only Begotten came down and raised you from the dungheap. He gave you his Spirit in baptism and made you his brother. From within the waters, those baptized gained a new mouth and a loud voice, and became new children of the Father. And because through the waters they became brothers of the Only Begotten, his Father is truly their Father, and they call him “Our Father.” For this reason, from our birth through water onward, we have a Father above in heaven, not in Sheol. We have forgotten Eve, and baptism is our mother. Had she not cast us up to the heights, the depths would have swallowed us. We have left Adam behind, because God has counted us among his children.

How angry Sheol would have been with our race if we had abandoned him! That poor, needy, ruined man, our father Adam—we no longer call him our father, since he has been replaced. We have found ourselves another Father, full of riches, and that rich one has taken the place of that poor man. His compassion compelled him, and in his love he brought the children of the poor, so that he who possesses riches might fill a father's place for them. The rich one saw that poor man, full of woes, deprived and needy, with children in deep misery. The Exalted One saw that if his children inherited from him, they would be choked by the curses among the thorns that he bequeathed to them. He saw that he had possessed a great garden full of blessings, but the serpent threw him into confusion and drove him out of it, leaving him poor. He saw that he had nothing to bequeath to his children except thorns, cruel prickles, and Sheol, the abyss that swallows the dead. In his love he wished to become a Father and bequeath to Adam's children all the hidden treasures he possessed. That rich one sent his Son to the poor. He chose a virgin and made her the mother of his Only Begotten. From within the womb he became a brother to Adam's children.

They enrolled him among human beings, together with those below. He is called the Son of Man throughout his whole course, so that human beings may be sons of God with him. In exchange for the mother he took for himself from those below, he gave a mother who descended with him from his Father's house. Baptism is a pure womb filled with light, giving birth every day divinely and virginally. She transforms human beings and makes them sons of God; she receives bodily beings and makes them spiritual as well. In her, race mingles with race in holiness, and she makes those below become members of those above. She makes Adam's household kin to God, so that when they call upon him, they may call him “Our Father” by nature. He caused the Holy Spirit to dwell in the waters and brought them down, so that through birth they might become brothers of the Only Begotten. He became for them a Father beyond suffering in baptism, in place of that father who had been bitten by the venomous serpent. The Father sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, and through the Spirit we truly cry, “Abba, our Father.” The Son of God is the Son of Man bodily;

and human beings are sons of God spiritually. Mary gave the Word a body so that he might become incarnate, and baptism gives human beings the Spirit so that they might be renewed. Because he became our brother in the womb, he made us sons in baptism, so that we might call the heavenly One “Our Father.” Because he brought our race near to that great lineage, nature moves us to call him “Our Father,” though he is in heaven. We have been made kin in his divinity, members of his race, and from within the waters we have truly become sons. From this we have attained the right to call the hidden Father “Our Father,” for he gave us his Spirit in baptism. Come, outsiders, enter among the sons! The door is open, the house has room, and the Father is glad to welcome you. Come, you who are far away, become near through baptism! There is room in God's house for all who come to him. Come, strangers, become members of the household through the waters! Gain a new Father on high and call him “Our Father.” Come, debtors, enter and receive your debt certificates back without payment! In the waters, wipe away the debts you yourselves owe. Come, you poor, grow rich through spiritual baptism! In the great treasury, forget the lowliness of poverty.

Come to baptism, wandering sheep belonging to the Lord of the flock, so that through you the full number of one hundred may be complete. Come, weary, worn-out sinner, full of trembling, and cut away from yourself the burden of wrongdoing through baptism. Come, you darkened ones who became blind by choice! Be baptized, have your eyes opened, and receive light from her, the daughter of daylight. Come, you lost ones, for the good Shepherd has gone out in search of you! He has appointed a meeting at the spring to gather you together. Come, you who have been scattered through the worship of dead images; be baptized and be made holy, freed from the impurity of [?]. Come, you who went astray and were enslaved to emptiness; from within the water learn the way to the house of God. Come, you old ones who have grown filthy and worn out with paganism; gain renewal in the new womb of baptism. Come, you unclean people of the earth, and be made holy in pure water; receive cleansing from the fountain of holiness. Come, come, you precious coin of the Godhead! Look, the master of the house is lovingly searching for you. Come, repentant one, whom mercy has drawn to baptism,

so that the heavenly hosts may rejoice at your coming. Come, daughter of the nations, the Church who prostituted herself with little gods; put on your bridegroom and live with him in a pure union. Come, prostitute, and give your hand to the Only Begotten; he will make you a virgin through the water, in holiness. Come, dark woman, whose complexion the sun has marred with its rays; clothe yourself in splendor through the purifying water prepared for you. Come, darkened woman, who has become foul-smelling in the smoke of sacrifices; shine with radiance, and let your fragrance become sweet through anointing. Come to baptism, old woman who has aged in idolatry; through the water become a splendid and glorious young woman. Come down and put on the garment woven by God; then come up and show us your sweet beauty, so that we may rejoice with you. Come, adorn yourself from the fountain that pours out light; let the world see you wearing the jewels of the Holy Spirit. Braids of gold for the bride who has come up from the water! Let silver studs add beauty to the radiant lady. Let pearls come from Cush for her lofty head, and strings of precious stones from India. Let the sea bring the beautiful blood of purple shellfish,

and its companion, the dry land, stones of [?] and [?]. Let the mountains offer all their emeralds and fine signet stones, and let the depths send jacinth from their treasures. Glorious stones from between the eyes of serpents, and gold from Ophir for beautiful necklaces! Multicolored necklaces and neckbands for the neck of the crowned bride! Her bridegroom is rich; let them increase her adornments with their designs. The bride says: “I have the cross instead of jewels, and through it all my beautiful ornaments are arranged upon my limbs. He dyes my clothes with his blood and adorns me; I do not want the sea-blood of purple shellfish. He places his mark between my eyes and makes me radiant; I have no use for braids of gold or pearls. With his anointing he makes my face shine with joy and makes me holy; I will have no silver studs, for I have no use for them.” Instead of jewels and fine signet rings, he gave me his nails, so that I might forge from them all the adornment of brides. How beautiful you are, daughter of the Gentiles, how beautiful you are! Your whole veil resembles the morning with its splendid dawn.

Upon your forehead rests a great light; even the sun, if it looks at it, is immediately dazzled. Your pure mouth resembles a scarlet thread, and it seems to me that your lips too are dyed with blood. Your beauty shines in the assemblies in two colors: in the blood and water that flow to you from the Beautiful One. Your bridal chamber is in the water, and your dwelling is in the thick cloud of the Most High. The Crucified One is your beloved, and your hope is at the Father's right hand. You are dressed in richly colored fabric, like the high priest in the place of atonement. A garment woven of fire and Spirit is yours, and it is entirely light. O daughter of the nations, you were betrothed to the Light in the water. Guard what has been entrusted to you from the darkness that would snatch it from you. You have an enemy filled with envy; beware of him, lest through his enticements he blemish your chastity. O bodily person who became spiritual in the water, sanctify yourself so that you may become a temple for the Godhead. Child of the poor who became a brother to the Son of the Rich One, take care not to squander your great wealth on lusts. You who were baptized in water have become brothers of the Only-Begotten. Do not let him be dishonored by your fleshly deeds.

You are his member; do not unite it with a prostitute. He has united you with his Father; cleanse yourself of transgressions. Do not let baptism, which is entirely light, be defiled by deeds that are not pleasing to God. Someone wearing new clothes guards himself against both dust and filth, so that neither comes near him. Man, you are clothed in baptism; flee from wrongdoing, lest it tear from you your priceless garment. The Son of God freely gave you a splendid robe. Do not treat it with contempt, lest it be stained by your sins. The serpent is accustomed to stealing garments through his hateful counsel and bringing those who wear them to utter nakedness. You put on in the water that robe of glory which was stolen among the trees, and the evil enemy envies you. If you lend him an ear through your lusts, he will strip you naked, as he has been accustomed to doing from the beginning. Daughters of Eve, guard the purity of baptism, for Eve's bond of debt has been torn up in the living water. Do not let the serpent come again and enter as he usually does, finding his opportunity through the whisperings of love for the world. Have nothing to do with that fruit of lust, which is entirely death

and is deeply hateful both to God and to your husbands. In baptism you were joined in marriage to God, and if the thief finds an opening, he will cause a rift. Baptized one, you have found that glory which Adam cast off. Do not lose it again through sin after finding it. Soul, you have been betrothed to the Son of God in baptism. Do not give yourself to Satan to torment you. You who were carried off by demons, the Father consecrated you and gave you to his Son. Remain faithful to him, so that they do not corrupt you after your consecration. O soul, you have paid your debts in baptism. Do not begin writing another bond of debt. You were baptized and forgiven; sin has departed—let it go. Do not let the sore return to its place through hateful wrongdoing. The high priest cleansed the leprosy with which you were clothed. Do not let uncleanness return again upon your purity. Look, wrongdoing has been drowned in the choice waters of baptism. Do not bring it back to life through shameful desires. Soul, you have risen from the fall into which the serpent cast you. Do not fall again into the hands of your enemy, who clings to you relentlessly. Baptized one, you are clothed in a robe of glory filled with light.

Flee from filth, so that you may shine among the angels. Do not throw your splendid garment into foul mud, lest the enemies who envy your protection laugh at you. You wear this garment, O man, from within the waters. Its warp is fire, its weft is the Spirit, and it is a flame. The Father prepared it, his Firstborn wove it, and the Spirit spun it. You went down into the waters and put it on in a divine way. The Trinity kindled a fire in baptism, so that wrongdoing might burn and the soul might live with God. In baptism our race found what it had lost. Blessed is he who gave us a womb of water in which to be renewed.
On the prayer that our Lord taught his disciples: Our Father in heaven, may your name be hallowed.
By Saint Jacob. Homily 50. On the prayer that our Lord taught his disciples: Our Father in heaven, may your name be hallowed.

Son of God, from whom all speaking beings receive their riches, give me a word with which to speak about you. Lord, who came to become a brother to the servants you redeemed, make me your own, so that I may sing you pure praise with a loud voice. Discourses, words, and songs are yours. From what is yours, my Lord, accept praise from one who is weak. The mouth, speech, and tongue are yours, my Lord. Grant the mouth, though unworthy, to sound your praise. The intellect, understanding, and mind are yours. Grant the intellect, as it gazes on you, to tell your story. The movements of the soul and its thoughts are yours. Grant the soul to see your beauty and speak to you. Give me your word, O Word who came to become flesh, so that with it I may speak about your coming, which is full of wonder. You came to us and remained in your Father; you are above and below. Heaven and earth are filled with you, Son of God.

Fill my mouth with praise, as you have said, “Open it, and I will fill it.” Open it and fill it, even if it is not open, for it is lazy. You are the one who opens closed mouths to speak, for who can open his mouth without you? Once even a donkey spoke, so that everyone might know that it is easy for you to give speech even to an animal. Open my mouth for me yourself, for I have closed it through the wrongdoing of my hands. It befits you to do good things. Open it and fill it, for you are the one who opens everything that is shut. Through you, closed mouths are opened to offer praise. Who, my Lord, opened a doorway in the rock in the wilderness, so that rivers flowed out of it for a great people? Who opened the dry bone that Samson held and brought fresh drinking water out of it for the thirsty man? Who opened the jar and the horn in the widow’s house, so that, through a great wonder, they supplied enough food during a famine? Through you all the gates that had been shut were opened: the eyes of the blind, the ears of the deaf, and the mouth of the mute. The blind were to see, the deaf to hear, and the mute to speak. So open my lips too, that I may speak. Open the ear too, so that it may hear your story with understanding.

For you are the key, and through you all creatures are opened. Let the soul see you, for if it sees you, it shines with light from you and speaks to you clearly through you, O radiant one. The world darkens everyone whom it has bound with desires, but a person shines with light from you if he gazes at you lovingly. The human eye has no light of its own by which to shine, but if it is clear, it can receive light. It receives light either from the sun or from fire, and once it has received it, the light becomes its own, and the eye in turn belongs to the light. So it is, my Lord, with the soul when it sees you: it receives speech from you and goes out telling your story. It is not radiant, but when it gazes at you, it shines with light from you. Through you it sees you and speaks abundantly about you. Even the eye cannot see the sun except through the sun itself. It gives the eye fire so that it may see it lovingly. It looks upon the eye and clothes it in its own radiance, and in that radiance the eye shines so that it may see all created things. Look upon the soul, just as the sun looks upon the eye, so that it may clothe itself in light from you and speak about your revelation. Come, go, O mind, and see Christ as he stood among the crowds, resembling the Gihon, full of mercy.

He flows onward, pouring out every kind of healing upon the afflicted, and the land of Judea is drenched in him and in the help he gives. Great compassion gushes from him like a flood, sweeping away diseases and pains to destroy them. Through him the blind saw, through him the deaf heard, and through him the dead came to life. From him light shone upon the whole land, which had been dark. Everyone who met him received healing and then went on his way. He gave help to everyone who came, and then went on his way. Through him the fallen rose, through him the outcasts [?], and through him the hungry were satisfied. For this was why he came: to raise up those whom the world had thrown down. He walked the earth to uproot thorns from its regions and sow peace in the place laid waste by the destroyer. He chose apostles for himself to send to the lands, so that through them he might bring the whole creation to the one who begot him. Christ the sun took twelve hours for himself, to gather them and make one day of great light. Twelve steps by which the sun rises and descends, spreading its radiance over the darkened lands. Twelve rays went out from the sphere of righteousness like lightning after the night that had covered the earth. He took from the world twelve men of renown:

Clear-hearted, straightforward, innocent, and without evil. He chose fishermen who were neither rich nor learned, for the Son’s way does not require learning. To bring down the world’s wealth and its learning, he chose uneducated men to carry his proclamation out to the earth. They loved him, held fast to him, and followed him. They were enlightened by him, united with him, and enriched by him. They left the world and followed him because of their love for him. They rejected possessions so that they might lovingly gain him. They left relatives, children, brothers, and fathers, their homes and families, and went with him according to his will. They obeyed his word—everything he said, just as he said it—and took care not to walk except in him. He taught them not to acquire gold or silver, and they seized his command as a great possession. He taught them not to worry about what they would say, and they did not wish to speak except through him. They said to him, “My Lord, teach us to pray,” so that they would never utter even a prayer without him. They held back even from the speech natural to them, and lived for him, for him alone.

He commanded them not to worry about speaking before judges, and they went beyond his command. They resolved not to speak in prayer, either before his Father or before him, without him. “My Lord, teach us to pray,” they said to him, “so that we may not send even a prayer to your Father unless it comes from you.” The disciples asked him to teach them to pray, and this loving request to the Son of God shone with beauty. The great teacher began to teach his confidants how they ought to pray when they prayed. So that unnecessary words would not be spoken in prayers, he placed what was needed in the prayer he taught them. For first he commanded them that, when they prayed, they should not speak excessive words of their own. He carefully taught them not to prolong their prayer, so that prayer would not become insipid through lengthy words. In this discourse that I have come forward to deliver, the beautiful prayer that our Lord taught shines forth. The discourse requires a hearing free from evil, and love of the Lord, which is the highest of good things,

and love, which is the great strengthening of faith. With these things, the discourse is pleasing to its hearers. Even if a discourse contains every sublime beauty, if the hearer does not love it, it will not please him. The prayer that the Son of God taught his confidants will be explained to you, if you listen with love. The disciples asked him to teach them to pray, and, knowing that their request was good, he did not refuse them. He said, “Pray like this when you pray: Our Father in heaven, may your name be held holy, as [?] is holy. May your kingdom also come to us from where it is, and may your will be done on earth as in heaven. Give us from your treasury the constant bread of each day, and forgive our debts and pardon our sins, as we have forgiven. Do not bring us into temptation, for we are weak, but deliver us from the evil one, for your power is great. For yours are the kingdom and the might, and also authority, together with glory, forever. Amen.” The Son of God placed a mighty weapon in prayer and gave it to his apostles, so that they might confront the devil’s battle line. The countless thousands of prayers that a person prays—the Son of God encompassed them in ten phrases.

The full force of every petition of all who are in need he enclosed in this little prayer and gave it to his apostles. At that first word, “Our Father,” which he taught us to call out, all the enemy’s strength is bewildered. For the commander of our army knows our enemy: how brazen he is and how much he hates human beings, how envious he is, how fiercely he wages war, and how wickedly he acts. Wherever he finds an opportunity to prevail, he wreaks destruction. He is eager for destruction, devoted to wrongdoing, and a lover of evil. Killing comes easily to him; he delights in blood and stirs up strife. He teaches warfare and stays alert for combat in the contest. As soon as someone stands in prayer, he stands beside him. If he could, he would violently shut the mouth of everyone who prays, whenever they pray, so that they could not pray. He hates prayer, obstructs it, throws it into confusion, and strikes it down. If he could, he would stop it altogether. Lances and arrows do not terrify an unarmed person as much as prayer terrifies the evil one, and he hates to see it. For this reason he stirs up evil thoughts and disturbs the soul with anxiety about all kinds of affairs. He spreads his smoke over the mind so that it will not become clear,

so that by every possible means prayer may be deprived of purity. He stands there when the person praying prays, watching to see which way the movements of his soul incline. If he sees that the person is full of fervor and discernment, alert and standing ready to ask boldly for mercy, he devises schemes, acts cunningly, and contrives how and by what means he can distract his soul from supplication. He casts one utterly hateful thing after another into his heart and hinders the person praying so that he will pray no more. Once he has cast evil thoughts into the mind, he turns around and makes the person feel remorse for having thought all these evil things. Through distressing thoughts he seems to despise him and rebuke him, saying, “Why are you thinking these things?” He beats him down and silences his supplication, so that, although he has not sinned, he feels like someone who has. Through that distress, the prayer he loved is brought to an end, for it torments the devil unless it stops. Even if he were dying, he would not fear seeing death as much as he fears seeing prayer before God. He does not even move away from the place where the person praying meets with God until he sees how he comes away from supplication. He also disturbs him through the affairs of the evil world,

and once he has drawn his mind toward himself, he takes him, leads him away, and leaves. If he encounters a soul occupied with affairs, he lies in wait for it and even reminds it to do a good deed. He also makes it think about that good deed, claiming that it is prayer. Whether it is done or not, look—prayer has stopped! Anyone who approaches to pray stands in battle, and Satan also stands beside him to injure him. The prophet saw Joshua the priest, son of Jehozadak, praying before God in the Holy of Holies. He saw Satan standing at his right hand, seeking to cast down the priest’s spirit in the house of God. He sought to disrupt the high priest’s supplication, and if that angel had not restrained him, he would have disturbed him. This is the evil one’s habit toward those who pray: if he can, he betrays them in the house of God. For this reason, at the beginning of the prayer our Lord taught, he instructed his apostles to say, “Our Father.” As soon as you approach to pray, say, “Our Father,” so that the evil one who fights against you may hear who your Father is, so that he does not come with his tyranny at the beginning of the battle,

unaware that you have a Father above in heaven. And when he despises you as belonging to a weak race, he will wage war against you and scorn you in his tyranny. For this reason you were taught to call the Father “Our Father,” so that from the outset he may know who your Father is. As soon as he hears that you have a Father above in heaven, he becomes confused, and his foot trembles as he fights. You are like a child who is weak but has a mighty father: when he is attacked, he calls his father into the fight. As soon as his enemy hears him calling his father, he lets go and flees, because he is weaker than the mighty man. So you too are commanded to call out “Our Father,” so that the evil one may flee as soon as he hears who your Father is. You say to him, “Our Father in heaven, may your name be made holy.” May we be made holy, for your name is upon us. Make us holy, my Lord. Your name has been invoked over us; may it be made holy in us for your sake. You are holy; may your name be made holy in us who are weak. The prayer that the Son of God taught is full of riches, and from it you can learn who you are and how great you are. It teaches that you have a Father who is a great king, and your soul is exalted at the stature to which your dust has risen.

The Son of God came down from on high and became human, and from the depths he raised you up to become a son of God. He became your brother from within the womb full of holiness, and he made you his brother from within the womb of baptism. He became human for your sake, though he is God, so that you might become a son of God with him, though you are human. He became poor for your sake, though he is rich, so that you, who are poor, might gain riches through him. From within the water he made you a son of God with him, so that, though he is the Only Son, he might gain brothers through the second birth. For he too became human through a second birth, and through that second birth he made you a son of God. And so that you would not forget who your Father is when you pray, he taught you to call out “Our Father in heaven” at the beginning of your petition. This is so that your soul may be exalted by remembering your noble lineage, and your enemy may fear because you have a mighty Father. For if he despises you because Eve is your mother, let him turn back in fear because baptism has given you birth. And if he is emboldened to bind a lowly son of Adam, let him tremble when he hears that you have a Father above in heaven. And when he fights against you to defeat you through his tyranny,

let his foot falter in battle at the news of your Father. Let him tremble before you because of your Father, who is stronger than he is, and be diligent yourself to do good deeds every day. Flee from deeds that are not good, because God, who is full of beauty, is your Father. Be pure and without blemish because you are a son, turning aside and passing by evil deeds for your Father’s sake. So that, when you sin, he may not be dishonored because of you—the one who was pleased to become your Father, though he knew you. Consider whom you call “Our Father” in the place of forgiveness, and purify yourself for his sake, so that he may not be dishonored. See, you have risen to great honor because of him; do not let him come to great dishonor because of you. Through him you become great; do not let him be diminished through you, if you have understanding. Preserve the honor of the Father, for he is great, and through him you become great. This is why our Lord taught you to call the Father “Our Father”: a noble name demands a very noble lineage. Since you call God himself “Our Father,” take care to please him, as befits one who has become a son of God. To make your enemy tremble before you, he taught you how

to say “Our Father,” whose name makes created beings tremble. You gain courage when you learn who your Father is; your enemy is afraid when he hears that you have a mighty Father. He wished to direct you to the birth of baptism, reminding you that you have been born spiritually. So that you may have great hope in God, who became your Father, while you became his son through the second birth. When you pray, you call upon the Father to come and rescue his children, who have been enslaved to the devil from ancient times. You say to him, “I have indeed been taken captive and sold. I have become a slave, and now I am held in bondage among strangers. Sin bought me, and I fell from freedom. They led me away from you, and I became a slave to emptiness. The evil master I acquired yoked me with a harsh yoke, and now he mistreats me in a house of slavery filled with suffering. I have been sold, my Lord. How can I return to freedom? For I went willingly with the evil master. The crafty serpent obtained a written signature from me. Together with Eve he drew up a deed, and they made me a slave. I gave my consent and became a slave, though I had been freeborn. The devil who bought me imprisoned me in his emptiness.

But you, Father, have not put your signature on my deed. You did not sell me; do not leave me with the wicked one. Let the deed of sale that the serpent wrote without you be brought forward. Look there: you will not find your signature. Dispute with him over how that rebel dared to buy a son without his father, and felt no fear. If a child goes and sells himself without his father, who will buy him, confident that he has a valid claim to him? Let the deed of sale be brought forward, to see whether the Father has signed it. If not, let both buyer and seller be set aside. I was sold, my Lord, without your knowledge, though you are my Father. Do not let an agreement made without you be upheld. Do not let the evil one rejoice over me, thinking that he has a valid claim to me. You did not sell me; do not neglect me, for I am yours.” Your hand is not set to my deed; let it not be confirmed. Annul the sale that the serpent made with great deceit. I bore your name, which is your image, and it became defiled. Our Father in heaven, may your name be hallowed for your own sake. Father, do not leave the children who ran away in slavery. Come, lead them away from the rebel who enslaved them. Let nothing done without you remain in force.

Because you are the Father, let your word stand, and take possession of what is yours. Without her husband, Eve sold her children to destruction. In the judge’s court, a woman’s deed is not accepted. The serpent is the scribe, and the seller is a woman. And I ended up in slavery, far worse off than either of them. They are not trustworthy; let their deeds not be accepted. Tear down, destroy, and undo all the deceit. You are the master, and there are servants who bear your image. A tyrant lay in wait for them and bought them. He brought them out from your dominion, which is full of beauty, and dragged them into slavery, which is full of woes. Do not compensate the one who bought your servants without your consent. Take them for yourself; do not allow him to own them. He wanted to become master over your property by seizing it. Take possession of what is yours, and cast the plunderer into destruction. You are master and Father. Come, rescue your own from the rebel, who unjustly seeks to possess what is not his. When you say, “Our Father in heaven, may your name be hallowed,” you have included all these stirrings of the heart in your prayer. For these reasons our Lord taught you to call out, “Our Father,” so that you might obtain every benefit through prayer.

So that you may take pride in having an exalted Father, and the evil one may fear the greatness of your exalted Father. And let all the earlier and intervening dealings made concerning you without the Father be brought forward, and let him annul them. And because you were a child and were sold without your Father’s consent, let the agreement for that sale be canceled, and let you be set free. Sin, which made the sale through the serpent, knew that the agreement made by the robber was being annulled. For the Father sought his children, that they might return to him. And now they call upon him—who can prevent them? That is why the Son of God taught you to call out, “Our Father,” so that through the Father’s name you might obtain every good thing. When you say, “May your name be hallowed,” he is teaching you yourself to be holy for the sake of your Father, who is full of holiness. And let sin give way within the unholy soul before the awe-inspiring renown and the great name of fatherhood. May your name be hallowed, and may your kingdom also come to us. For if the kingdom advances to come, the rebels tremble. That is why the Lord taught you to call for that kingdom: because of the insolent ranks of demons surrounding you. They set traps and hide snares and nets.

They shoot arrows of wickedness at the soul to wound it. So that you will not be defeated by the bloodthirsty army, call for the kingdom, and immediately the unclean demons will flee. The forces of the evil one seek to wound your soul. They have surrounded it like a walled city, seeking to breach it. As soon as they hear that the kingdom of God's house is coming in procession, the legions of darkness flee. For this reason our Lord taught you: When you pray, call for the kingdom, and see, the rebellion is defeated. The evil one hears that you are calling for the Father's kingdom, and he understands that he cannot withstand the kingdom. In prayer you do not call upon a righteous person to help you, nor upon a prophet to come and assist you when you pray, nor upon an apostle to drive your enemy away from you, nor upon one of the commanders of the heavenly armies to deliver you, nor upon Gabriel to come to you and help you in that petition, as he came to Daniel, nor upon Michael to draw his sword against those surrounding you, as he accompanied Joshua son of Nun. You leave aside the heavenly forces, their commanders, and the rulers, and call upon the kingdom itself—you call upon it to come against the rebels.

Our Lord did not teach you to call upon angels, the upright, or the righteous to help you when you pray, but to call upon that kingdom of God's house, before which all the enemy's forces tremble. Call for the kingdom, full of light, to come to you, and immediately all the demons, the children of darkness, will flee. As soon as the demons hear you calling for the King to come, they do not wait for him to come and find them. They flee at the news of him. For who can fight against the great King when he comes to help? If an angel or a righteous person came, the devil might or might not fight. But if that kingdom advances in procession to come, how does he have the strength to withstand the procession of that majesty? For this reason the Son of God taught you to [?] when you pray, so that the kingdom itself might come to you. And when you have invited it to come to you, prepare, for your part, a place suitable for that army, where it will be honored. Look, you are calling for the kingdom to come. Prepare a place: a house that is clean and entirely filled with holiness. At the entrance of the house, which is the mouth, hang upon its doorway

door curtains [?], painted and fully adorned. Sprinkle the interior of the house, which is the heart, with purity: all thoughts that love beautiful things every day. In the soul, which is the courtyard of the coming King's house, spread the fragrant perfumes of good deeds on every side. On the floor of the house spread the carpet of pure love, for wherever he stays, he wants to see love there. In prayer you have called for that kingdom to come to you. What you have called for is coming; prepare a place where it will be honored. Look, the one who was drawn up for battle against you is fleeing! The King is coming to you to dwell where that one dwells. See whether you are angry; see whether you are troubled; see whether you are in turmoil. See whether there is love of money or greed in your soul. See whether there is deceit in you, a foul smell, or sexual immorality, the filth from which the King flees. See whether there is treachery and speech that turns in two directions, or whispering and an ear inclined toward slander. If these things are present, drive them out, for the King is coming. If he comes and finds these things, he will not dwell in you. And if he turns away after you have brought him, there also returns

that rebel, who abuses you with his tyranny. Let your soul be a place worthy of the King's lodging. Let him come and dwell, just as you invited him to come to you. This is why you learned to call for that kingdom to come to you: so that you would prepare a clean place for it. Then, as soon as it comes in procession, the accuser will flee, and you will purify yourself and receive it in holiness. For you call out, "May your kingdom come to us, my Lord; may your will also be done on earth as in heaven." You say to him, "My Lord, may your will be carried out among us human beings, as among the spiritual watchers." It is fitting for one who prays before God to entrust all his requests to God's will. Our Lord himself also prayed this way and said to the Father, "Not my will, but yours." This is how he taught you to plead in your prayers: "My Lord, may your will be done on earth as in heaven." Just as the angels never transgress your will, so may human beings also obey you. May the earth resound with assemblies praising you, just as heaven teems with hosts serving you. Bend your will over ours, so that ours may become yours,

so that our will may be in harmony with your will. Will that we find our desire in you, so that whatever you desire, we too may desire, and that we may no longer desire anything except that all your desires be fulfilled. My Lord, may your will be done on earth as in heaven. May human beings give praise just as the angels also give praise. Just as those ranks of Gabriel's company serve, may the churches on earth also serve without contention. As these companies of Michael’s host shout for joy, let us raise joyful praise to you in our assemblies with pure love. As that radiant assembly of seraphim proclaims your holiness, may the company of humankind proclaim your holiness throughout the earth. As that chariot, awesome to behold, gives blessing, may the Church cry out with trembling, “Blessed is he from his place!” May all the orders of those who offer praise in heaven obey you and serve you spiritually. May the whole earth carry out all your wishes, just as heaven never departs from your commandments. May the priests on earth, like the angels in heaven, obey you and serve you in holiness. In every form, in every manner, and by every means, may all your wishes be fulfilled on earth as in heaven.

This is the prayer that can grant every request to the one who prays, through its divine provisions. Whoever wishes to be among the perfect in God’s household should persevere in this prayer with discernment. This is the prayer that the receiver of prayers himself taught us, showing how anyone who prays should pray. The Son, who brings every petition before his Father, taught you how to speak to his Father when you pray. He composed a petition according to the mind of the hidden Father and placed it in your mouth, so that you might pray to him according to his mind. He wanted to show you how he wishes you to speak to him, so that you might speak according to his will when you pray. You ought to pray just as you have learned, for in this prayer you find everything you need. Ask God, “Give us our regular daily bread.” For what does daily life require except bread? Gold and silver, pearls and beryls, topaz stones, finely spun linen, and fine clothing— These splendid riches are not among life’s necessities, for the body needs only its regular daily bread. Even if you give it pearls from Cush and India,

but withhold bread from it, it grows faint, dies, wastes away, and is worn down. The body needs bread to live, and nothing else; yet because the world is vain, it asks for superfluous things. For the body does not eat gold if you give it some, nor hyacinth gems, nor precious stones. A pearl has neither taste nor smell; it cannot be eaten or drunk, and yet it is precious. Why is it precious, except that the world is vain and empty of understanding, and is eager to acquire superfluous things? The king receives his daily bread from his kingdom, and the laborer receives his daily bread from his labor. The king and the laborer receive equal shares of what the body requires, what it needs, and what sustains it; in these they are equal. Although the king has the revenue of the whole earth, they give him nothing from it but his daily bread. And although the laborer has only his daily wage, they do not withhold his regular daily bread from him. What benefit does gold or revenue bring the king, when all he receives from his kingdom is a laborer's bread? Human nature has roasted grain and bread to live on;

and the poor man has roasted grain and has bread. The gold the rich man possesses brings him no benefit, for his regular daily bread alone is enough for him. Thus God has given an equal measure, a ration per person, to live on each day. If you force your nature to eat extravagantly, to take more than the prescribed measure, it is put to shame, is convulsed, and becomes weighed down. It stops eating because it has taken too much. He ate two days' ration at one sitting, and because of this he goes a day short of food, so that today's ration, which he ate yesterday, may be deducted from his allowance. Then he takes food in an orderly way, as he is able. Nature stands over the glutton like a debt collector, and if he grows greedy for food and eats too much, it demands back from him the excess he ate. It also makes him sick and expels that excess. Then it gives him only his regular daily bread, for this is enough to sustain life comfortably. For this reason our Lord taught us to pray: “Give us our regular daily bread, so that we may live on it.”

No one should ask for gold or silver when he prays, nor for possessions, pleasures, or profits. So that no one would covet and seek these unnecessary things, he limited the prayer that asks to receive to daily bread. He established the prayer for rich and poor alike, so that it would rebuke us if we became greedy for more. For if a poor man asks for anything other than bread, he will be accused by the Giver. And the rich man, too, when he prays, “Give us bread,” will be put to shame, because he has ten thousand loaves. He will recognize that the surplus stored up with him is not his, but belongs to those hungry people outside. The daily bread that is lacking in the poor man's house is stored in his own house, for he has been made a steward for his fellow servants. And unless he brings it out and gives some of it to the hungry, he is bound to receive blows from the Judge in the presence of justice, who will accuse him: why did he hide his brothers' ration while they went hungry, and take pride in what was not his? For this reason he taught him to pray, “Give us our regular daily bread,” so that he would give away the surplus he has.

Let him put himself on an equal footing with the poor by sharing his possessions, and eat with them from what God has given him and increased for him. Let him pray, “Give us our daily, enduring bread,” with confidence, together with the poor, who are his brothers. How beautiful is the prayer that the Son of God taught! Blessed is anyone who places it within his soul and adorns himself with it. All the beauties of righteousness and perfection are found in it by anyone who learns it and prays it. Through it, all beautiful and precious requests are answered for the soul that asks of God. Through it, all gifts full of riches for everyone in need are given from the treasury of the Godhead. The Son of God taught you to say, “Forgive us our debts.” He wants to forgive, and that is why he taught you what to say to him. For if he were not intent on forgiveness, he would not have taught you to say, “Forgive me my debts.” But because he is eager to forgive the guilty, he also taught them to plead for forgiveness. My Lord taught his confidants to say to his Father when they pray, “Forgive us our debts and our sins.” He gave them encouragement that he wants to forgive the guilty,

and that is why he taught them to plead with him for forgiveness. Who would not rejoice in a creditor who himself teaches him what to say when he comes in to see him? He wants to hear “Forgive us our debts” from the guilty, so that he may give his justice a reason for forgiveness. This is so that, when he forgives, he will not be reproached by his justice: “Why are you forgiving them when they have not pleaded for forgiveness?” He also questioned the paralyzed man in this way when healing him, so that he might learn from him whether he wanted to be well. And he taught the guilty to pray to him, “Forgive us our debts,” so that he would not forgive them without their asking. He wants to forgive, and he wants them to ask him for mercy, so that the petition they make may also enhance the beauty of the gift. He requires discernment from them when they pray, so that there may be no laxity when he shows mercy. Look, the record of your debt is deposited with God, in the keeping of his justice, and without pleading no one takes it out of her hand. Because he does not want to distress his justice when he forgives you, he taught you to plead for forgiveness when you pray. For as soon as his justice hears you pleading with him, she too overflows with love and pours out mercy upon the guilty.

You also say to him, “Forgive us, my Lord, as we have forgiven.” Here he taught you that unless you forgive, he will not forgive you. He gave you a measure and settled with you that, just as you measure out, you too are to measure and receive for yourself when you receive. “You know how much forgiveness I give you: as much as you forgive the one who needs your forgiveness.” It is a great cause for fear for anyone who needs forgiveness if he does not forgive when he prays. His judgment and his acquittal come from himself; his judgment comes from his deeds. He himself has pronounced the sentence, and it happens just as he himself has said. “Forgive us our debts as we have forgiven,” you say to him. And this is how he answers and deals with you: according to what you have prayed. He knows what you have forgiven; do not try to deceive him. The measure rests with him, and with it he measures out what he gives you. Be bold, then, and ask forgiveness from God, just as you have forgiven your fellow servant if he has wronged you. But if you have not forgiven, how can you have the face to ask him to forgive you, when a condition has been laid down for how he will forgive? Forgive your fellow servant, and forgive him generously, however much he owes. Then come and ask the same from God, and you will receive it. Let the poor man also hear here what he is to forgive:

For this is a matter common to everyone, both the rich and the poor. Let everyone forgive, for the Son of God taught this prayer to everyone, desiring every day that everyone should live. Let anyone who has gold forgive the gold owed by his debtors; and anyone who holds contracts or accounts should cancel them. If he holds other people's debt certificates, let him tear them up, and let him come in confidently to ask aloud for forgiveness. Let him not doubt that the great debt certificate standing against him will be torn up, if he tears up the small, insignificant one. But let the poor man also forgive, though he has no business dealings or accounts, no debts owed to him or claims to pursue. If someone has despised him, if someone has persecuted him, if someone has struck him—whatever the matter that has distressed him, let him forgive it. If someone has cheated him of the wages for the work he did for him, and he wants to curse him, let him relinquish the fruits of his labor without cursing. If he has ever been insulted or taken away for forced labor, let him put these things out of his mind and forgive as well. If a fellow poor man owes him a single small coin, let him forgive it, and he is counted like someone who has forgiven a talent. And if no one owes him even one coin, let him forgive a word; if he has heard it spoken maliciously by someone, he too is among those who forgive.

The Son of God taught this prayer to all humanity, so that all might become rich through his teaching. Let everyone forgive: one, debts and accounts; another, anger; another, rage; another, insults. Let his companion forgive a word, and another an affront if he encounters one, for everyone is required to be forgiving when he prays. Glorious and great, and full of the beauties of righteousness, is the prayer that the Son of God taught people to pray. Everything that human nature needs to receive from God he placed in the prayer and gave it to the apostles so that the world might learn. “My Lord, do not lead us into temptation” is in the prayer, because all human nature is weak when it is put to the test. Here the discourse calls for more than ordinary listening, for among the knowledgeable it stands far above its companions. Those trained in discipline understand with great discernment the trial that a person prays not to enter. And if it does not weary the listener, I will also explain the kind of trial that the Son of God included in the prayer. When the devil fights against a human being, that person has help from God. Like a watchman who neither slumbers nor sleeps,

so the hidden power guards human beings. When Satan stirs up a struggle against a person, there is an angel helping that person without their knowledge. This is like what happened to Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, who was helped by an angel. For while he was unaware, the angel rebuked the devil. The prophet saw what happened, but the priest did not. In the same way, every day there are angels beside every person, holding back the ranks of demons from harming them. When someone wishes to please the Lord through their conduct, the devil sets himself against that person to fight them. Without the person's awareness, an angel also comes secretly and helps them overcome the evil one, if they are upright. Whenever someone stands in prayer before God, Satan also stands there to mock them. Then an angel also comes like a watchman, rebukes the evil one, and keeps him away from that person. And when Satan has been defeated many times and the godly person has triumphed in victory, the insolent one pleads, as he pleaded concerning Job,

that God remove from that person the help that guards them. In his wickedness, he asks God this: that the Lord leave that person without assistance and bring them down alone into battle against the evil one, with no one helping or supporting them in the struggle. This is the trial concerning which our Lord taught a person to pray not to enter it. This is the great struggle to the point of bloodshed, of which Paul says, “You have not yet reached it.” In this battle the soul either conquers or is conquered, for it is a battle in which it either kills or is killed. Without assistance it goes down into battle against Satan, and the encounter is terrifying for a soul deprived of help. This is the trial that a person prays not to enter, as they learned from the one who knows everything. Job went down into this battle when he fought against Satan without divine help. That righteous man both felt and said, “Look, his help is not within me now that I am being tested.” Wherever this battle takes place, it is very terrifying.

Only a few emerge from it victorious. For this reason our Lord taught a person to pray, “Do not bring me into temptation to be tested by it.” Satan asked God concerning Job that he withdraw from him the hidden power that helped him. The Lord told his adversary, “He is handed over into your hands,” for he knew that the contestant would not falter. One human being fought a battle with Satan, while the Lord stood apart from them both like a spectator. The Lord brought that righteous man into testing, and from the great, bloody contest he won victory. Because the struggle is so hard, our Lord taught a person to pray not to be subjected to testing. A person should not seek to conquer without divine power, lest he boast about the victory. Whoever flees from temptation humbles himself and entrusts the battle to the one who is victorious, so that he may triumph. For he says to him, “Do not bring me into temptation, but rescue me yourself from the evil one, whose power is great. Do not hand me over to the adversary to fight against me without your help. Instead, conquer him yourself through me, weak as I am.

Let your hidden help not withdraw from me: it is the power that goes down with the athletes into their contests. Do not test me, for I have come to know that I am weak. Let the whole battle be yours, and may you triumph. Yours are all the victories of all who conquer. Conquer, for that befits you, and do not bring me into temptation. Rescue me from the adversary who fights against me, for I cannot conquer him without your help. Do not look to me to conquer in the great, bloody struggle. Take the battle upon yourself, and take the victory that befits you. Rescue me from him, and let the crown and the renown be yours. Credit me with neither victory nor triumph. Rescue me from him, and let all the glory of the athletic contest remain with you, for you are the one who conquered the adversary. Rescue me from him, and let the blame follow me, as I confess that I was defeated and you gave me victory. Without you I cannot conquer in battle. Let me not be tested; rescue me from him without a trial. In mercy rescue me from Satan, who fights against me, for it befits you to claim all victories. Rescue me from him, because yours is the power,

and also the kingdom, the authority, and the glory.” Whenever anyone conquers, it is through you that he conquers, for all strength and might belong to you. The prayer that the Son of God taught his confidants is appointed against the ranks of demons, to drive them away. Likewise, it is directed against all the forces of the Evil One, so that through it a person may fight against the ruler who guards the air. Through it he calls upon the Father to come down to him in the depths and drive away from him the demons that hunger for the soul’s blood. Through it the children of the Spirit are strengthened to cry, “Our Father,” and they shake the devil with that great name. Through it a person calls for that kingdom to come to him and drive away from him the forces of the Evil One that surround him. Through it a person declares that he submits to the Father’s will: let it be done on earth as it is also in heaven. Through it a person asks for the day’s bread without greed and leaves aside all unnecessary excess. Through it a person also asks God for forgiveness, having promised that he too will forgive those who are indebted to him. Through it a person escapes the trial of the great battle, pleading with God amid groaning that he may not enter it.

Through it a person calls upon the Helper to come to him and rescue him from that enemy of humanity who fights against him. It teaches you that all power, glory, and authority belong to the Lord Jesus. To him be glory!
Here ends the discourse on “Our Father in Heaven,” composed by Mar Jacob.
By the same holy Mar Jacob. Discourse 51. On that young man who said to our Lord: “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” (Matthew 19:16; Mark 10:17; Luke 18:18. E. N.)

Your word, our Lord, is full of light for whoever loves it. Give me your word, so that I may walk by it without stumbling. The world is dark, but you are radiant, Son of God. Let me journey by you, my Lord, for you are greatly beloved by whoever follows you. The world’s path is tangled and full of every stumbling block. Woe to anyone who walks on it—how wretched he is!

The evil world is dark and deceitful, full of snares, slippery places, and every kind of evil for whoever travels through it. You, our Lord, are a good companion, a great light, and a path full of life and blessings for whoever walks on it. Blessed is the one who has hated wealth and possessions, bent his shoulder, and taken up the yoke of your poverty. Someone who possesses nothing in the world, if he possesses you, is far richer than the rich of the whole world. But if someone possesses the whole world and does not possess you, he is poor and needy, ashamed and despised, and full of woes. You are a great treasure, our Lord, Son of God, and a pearl that cannot be stolen from its [?]. The world deceives, and whoever trusts in his possessions leads his own soul astray, for the wealth he has found is not lasting. Yesterday he sprang up and today he grew rich, but tomorrow he is gone. And where is the wealth whose owner is no longer there to enjoy it? Only a fool rejoices in the wealth of a dream and loves possessions that last a day. A person is rich while asleep, but when he wakes, the wealth is gone. Why does he rejoice, unless he is being misled by an illusion? Even if possessions are not passing things, O owner,

you, their owner, pass away from your possessions. Either they leave you and pass away from you while you watch, or you leave them to others against your will. There is no way for all your wealth to be yours unless you hate it and distribute it among the needy. If it is yours, then give it to someone in need, so that it will be available to you when you need help. Why does it mislead you, entice you, and trouble you, so that every day you run after gain that is never exhausted? Look, you run to add to your possessions every day; and all that you have gathered, in a single hour [?]. Look, you are wise; look, you are shrewd; look, you are busy. Look, you are diligent; look, you manage; look, you accumulate. Diligence, wisdom, and shrewdness have filled your house with all kinds of abundant good things. But if a slight attack of fever reaches you, all your diligence and shrewdness come to nothing. All your wealth-loving wisdom comes to nothing, and everything you love becomes hateful to you. You become an obedient slave to illness, and you loosen your grip on your possessions, because they cannot save you.

Where is your bustling activity? Where is all your wisdom? Where is the anxious care you devoted to gains? Look, you are weak; look, you are dazed; look, you are idle. Look, you are burning with fever—and who will bring you relief? Call for your possessions, bring your gold, gather your wealth! If they save you from distress, they are yours. If wealth cannot put out a fever, how does it help? And if it does not help, what benefit does it bring? Do not toil for it, for it does not love you as you have loved it. It is not yours. Why do you wear yourself out over what is not yours? Look, it is stored up and guarded, and you watch over it so that it will not go away. Yet it remains, while you are led away. What will you do? If you wished, it would be easy for your wealth to become yours: send it along the King's road through the hands of the poor. It would go ahead of you to the lofty place filled with blessings, and it would all be yours to enjoy. Why do you hurry to furnish a house that is not yours? Your dwelling is a tent, yet you are very anxious about its affairs. The tent of this passing time is pulled up and folded away. For that great building of yours will be folded away, [?] forever. Do not labor so diligently for strangers.

For whatever remains here after you is not yours. Why have you gone astray when you are wise, you diligent man? Why are you diligent about empty things, you wise man? Why do you love a house that is falling down, you knowledgeable man? Look, your soul has fallen through wrongdoing, and you do not raise it up. Build up, build up your soul, which you have overthrown through the wrongdoing of your hands. Then concern yourself with building a house that is not yours. This is wrongdoing: the house is built and filled with good things, while the soul, which is the King's palace, lies in ruins. You have despised what is yours, yet you are diligent about what is not yours. Your soul is uprooted, while your house is prosperous and filled with good things. I did not wish to become your teacher, good friend, for no one lacks the knowledge of how to live. Everyone is wise and knows what benefits him, and every human being has knowledge of what he should do. Everyone knows, but not everyone is willing to act. For it is a good will that is lacking, not knowledge. The road that leads to life is well trodden and full of light, and all the commandments are arranged along it like lamps. For anyone who wants to enter life, the gate is open. Nothing is asked of him except that he be willing, and he enters immediately.

It is not teachers that are lacking in this evil world; rather, the world itself hates the teaching that comes from God. God himself became a teacher to human beings, and through the commandments he set down in the Scriptures, he made them wise. He gave the Law, full of light, from Mount Sinai, and with watchposts he marked out the road to the kingdom. He sent his Son like a day of great light, and through him the whole world became bright and beautiful and gained life. And after this teaching, so full of wonder, through which the whole world learned and became bright as day, a certain foolish man was asking the Son of God, “What should I do to inherit life with God?” An arrogant, empty-headed young man, full of foolishness, asked with evil intent, though there was no need for the question. With a haughty spirit and a mind full of pride, he put his question to present himself as knowledgeable. Yet from his very words one can tell that he is not knowledgeable, for if he knew, he would not be asking, “What should I do?” Tell me, wretched man: are you wise or ignorant? Do you want to learn, or do you wish to be a teacher? The road of life, for the whole human race—

God has revealed it so that they may walk along it without anything concealing it. But if the road of life is still not visible to you, why, if you are wise, is it hidden from you when it is plainly revealed? If you know and still ask, you are insolent; and if you still do not know, you are ignorant. In any case, your question shows your lack of understanding: wealth has puffed you up, and here you are speaking presumptuously. “What must I do to inherit life?” he was asking the one who knows everything, who looks into the thoughts of the heart. He considered himself righteous, climbed up to stand on the heights, and began speaking with our Savior as though he were discerning. He wanted to present himself to the crowd as a wise man who had gone out in pursuit of new life to obtain it. He was rich and spoke with confidence in his wealth, for the spirit of wealth raises its voice in gatherings. Poverty’s mouth is shut wherever it is, and in this world no one gives it room to speak. The poor man is silent, and no one listens to him at all; even if he is wise, they do not let him speak. But the rich man, even if he is ignorant, is haughty; he speaks openly and has room to speak.

As a rich man, the foolish young man wanted to speak with our Savior, imagining that he was winning praise. “What must I do to inherit life?” he was asking him—an obvious matter about which there was no need to ask. Our Lord heard him, though he had known him before he spoke, and in his humility patiently endured that arrogance. Our Lord said, “If you want to live, keep the commandments.” He left on his sore the first dressing that Moses had applied. He did not change his dressing, since he saw that he had not benefited from the first dressing that the great prophet had applied. Moses brought down a great dressing from Mount Sinai and with it bandaged the sore of the wounded people. Like a medicinal root full of compassion for the wounded, he applied the Law to the people, bandaged them, and they became well. But when the sore of wickedness burst from its swelling, the Son of God came and replaced its dressing with another. Moses commanded that no one should commit adultery, and he forbade adultery; but his Lord said, “Do not even look at a woman with lust.” In his teaching full of wonder, the Son of God forbade a person even the thought that gives birth to adultery.

This dressing, which does not leave even a scar from the sore, the Lord of Moses applied to the soul as he bandaged it. Moses commanded that no one should covet what was not his own, and he taught the soul not to be greedy for more. But our Lord came and taught people to give even what was their own to anyone in need. The Son of God changed the dressing for the world’s sores, but the physician’s purpose remained the same and did not change. Little by little he disturbed the sore as he dressed it, so that the sick person would not flee from him if he treated him by force. If he had told someone committing adultery not even to lust, that person would not have listened, because his teaching would have been far too hard for him. And if he had told someone who plundered his companions to go out and give from his own possessions, he would not have answered. First he restrained the onrush of evil among those who practiced it, so that they would first stop the evil deeds they were committing. With the Law, as with fetters and chains, he bound the evil world so that it would cease from evil deeds. And once people had been trained to learn good things, he brought them up another step toward goodness. And like a teacher full of love for his pupils,

little by little he drew them toward his teaching. A skilled teacher does not write anything further for a child until the child has repeated the first lesson he received. And a good physician does not change the dressing on a wound until the wound itself shows that it has improved. For this reason our physician and teacher, the Son of God, did not give that rich man any further teaching.
