Instead, he required him to train himself in that earlier Law, and then he could rise to spiritual things. “Young man, remain with the commandments of the great Moses. Read the Law and do everything written in it. Unless you have carried them out, I will not teach you anything further about what you should do. That Law itself brings you into new life. Read it, read it, and it will teach you what you should do.” “If you want to enter life, keep the commandments.” The fool said, “Which ones are they, so that I may keep them?” That deficient man did not even know them, and that was why he asked to learn which ones they were. He presented himself as righteous and wise,

but showed that he was both a sinner and an ignorant man. He was not even aware that righteousness existed, and wisdom had never come his way—the fool who dared to speak. He did not even know what the divine commandments were, those through which the world lives. Without having read or kept them, he approached our Lord to question him in the assembly, in full view of many people. He stumbled and stood there, exposed as someone without understanding, a fool who had begun discussing a subject he did not know. The wretched man asked, “What must I do to inherit life?” He was told, “Keep the commandments,” but he did not know them. He began to inquire which ones they were, so that he might keep them, and the skilled teacher repeated them without growing weary. “You shall not steal,” he said, “nor ever give false testimony in the world. Honor your father and honor your mother, and you will have life, for whoever keeps the commandments lives by them.” The arrogant man began to act stubbornly, saying, “I have kept all these.” He lied greatly, acted with great presumption, and went far astray; in his pride he fell into the pit of falsehood.

Because he presumed to ask without knowledge, he became confused and began to insist stubbornly. He professed to have kept all the commandments, and further insisted that he had kept them since his childhood. Yet as a young man he did not know what they were! How, then, had he kept them all as a child, as he said? In his youth he was ignorant, contemptible, and full of faults. What could he have known in his childhood except how to sin? Our Lord did not wish to impart his spiritual teaching to him, because he saw that he was fleshly. For this reason he left him in the hands of Moses the scribe to train him; afterward he would let him read the book of perfection. But he began insisting that he had kept the commandments, practiced them, and fulfilled them since his childhood. The fool began goring with that lofty horn, raising his voice and multiplying lying words: “I have kept the commandments ever since my childhood! Add something new for me from your teaching.” “Tell me, young man, do you despise Moses and his observances? And do you demand that I tell you something still greater? All the commandments of Moses have been kept, as you say,

and now you are asking for other, new commandments! Then you are above the law and the commandments; you are higher than Moses himself, who laid down the law! You are perfect, you are spiritual, as you say, and you want to hear perfect teaching in a spiritual way. I have great and spiritual teaching, but I held back out of pity, because I saw that you were fleshly. The wound of your soul is not healed enough for it to reach perfection. For this reason I left you to Moses, the physician, to examine you. You have not understood the lesson Moses left, and for this reason I have not given you the great book. You are deficient in the old one, which you have not finished, yet you boast that you will read the new one with understanding! It is not that I lack lofty teaching to offer you; it is you who have no ear that hears spiritually. But if you wish to be perfect, as you say, go, sell all your possessions and give to the needy. Keep nothing for yourself in the world from all that you have acquired. If you leave yourself two garments to wear, you are not spiritual. Distribute everything you have on earth among the poor,

and leave yourself nothing at all from your possessions.” Sell all the possessions you have, along with the products of your labor and your belongings, and give to the needy without holding anything back. Give everything you have to the poor with joy. Treasure will be stored up for you on high; then come, follow me. When you have emptied yourself of the things of this evil world, I will teach you how to live with my disciples. The young man heard words that rose above the Law, and he trembled at the matter because he saw that he was not equal to it. The demand cut into his thick abscess, and the weak man fainted. He could not endure the incision, for he was sick [?]. His heart was broken by the spiritual teaching, because he was clinging to those material possessions. He saw how high the rank of perfection was; he faltered and fell, and he could not ascend to it. He was troubled by distressing thoughts, and he could not give our Lord an answer. Distress rose like smoke from his mind, and the light of his face faded and went out from sorrow. The suffering within folded up and carried away his outward beauty. The whole crowd saw that he had become ugly and that contempt for him had increased.

The once-flourishing color of his face changed, and the rich man's lofty talk was brought into contempt. He who had walked with his neck held high bowed his head, and his spirit fell—he who had thought himself righteous. He saw the path on which the perfect person walks, but he turned back and could not walk on it. The whole crowd saw and recognized that he was false: he was a talker and a boaster, not a truthful man. The humility of the Son of God shone forth, along with his wisdom and the brilliance of his teaching. The crowd understood that he had indeed been showing compassion to the rich man, and had not given him that teaching from the beginning. His compassion and kindness were revealed: how greatly he desires everyone to have life, wherever they are. And how he heals people without exposing them! Instead, he is patient and gently binds their wounds. The young man asked him, “What must I do to inherit life?” Yet he knew that the young man would not accept instruction. Although he knew this about him, he did not rebuke him before the many people, for it is not his custom to expose anyone who approaches him.

He did not say to him, “You cannot do it. You are not equal to it. You are not truthful; you are a liar. Move away! Go!” Instead, he welcomed him, listened to him, and spoke to him kindly. He applied a bandage that would have healed him if he had listened to him. If he had listened when he told him, “Keep the commandments,” and had gone and kept them, he would not have come to that public exposure. Instead, he wanted to seize a rank that was not his, and he fell and became a laughingstock among the crowd. How presumptuous he had been! Love of the world had seized him like a fever. It silenced him, and he could not speak. He was bound to his gold and his possessions, and because the Son of God sought to free him from them, the weak man lost heart. The road of life rises far above those who walk it, and few are the people on it who journey to the heights. It has milestones and resting places of righteousness, and there is room on it for people of every rank to walk. If someone gives a cup of water to a thirsty person, he is walking on it and has a reward from justice. If he merely says a good word about his neighbor, he is close to the road of life and walks on it.

However much he increases his good deeds, there is room for him to travel on the road, and it leads him radiantly into life. If that rich man had kept to the commandments of the great Moses, it would have been easy for him to inherit new life. And if he had sold everything he owned, as he was commanded, and given to the needy, he would also have lived by running along his road. He would not have been able to reach the lofty summit of the road, not even after scattering all his wealth among the poor. Our Lord had something else to tell him, and for this reason he said to him, “Come, follow me.” For when someone distributes everything he owns among the poor, this alone does not make him perfect and spiritual. A person has indeed emptied himself of possessions when everything he owns has been distributed so that he may gain his life. He throws off the world's weight so that it may be easy for him to run along the road of righteousness without being encumbered. “Go,” he said, “sell and give to the needy, and come, follow me, and I will show you the whole road of perfection.” If he had sold his possessions and followed him as he told him, he would then have heard a teaching higher than the first.

If he had been willing to follow him, he would have told him, “If you are struck, offer your cheek to the one who strikes you. And if evil people take your tunic from you, leave it in their hands and let them take your cloak as well. If they hate you and persecute you, bless them; pray for them when they strike you, and love them. If they put you on trial, do not worry about what to say; and if they persecute you, move away in love, without an uproar. Do not take a staff for the journey, or a bag, or a purse, or food for the whole day. Do not worry at all about what you will eat, if you are my disciple. And if you go beyond these things, you are of the evil one.” That rich man grew weak even before he had heard these things. He became afraid and turned back, and did not remain to hear them. He heard talk of his property being sold and became troubled, because he did not want to sell any of his possessions. He loved those possessions, which lasted for a time, more than the whole great road of perfection. Because he heard that it was to be distributed among the poor, he did not stay to listen, for he was entirely filled with the love of wealth.

When someone sells everything he owns and gives it to the needy, he needs to begin walking the path of perfection. It is like a tree: when it is uprooted from one place, planting it in another requires work. When someone distributes everything he owns among the poor, so far he has only uprooted himself from the world like a tree. He needs to labor to plant himself in the new world, and he needs watering and every practice of righteousness. And if he does not love those who hate him, as he was commanded, and if he is unwilling to offer his cheek to the one who strikes him, and if he grows negligent, let him be concerned that tomorrow he will not thrive in the land of the living, where he has been planted like a tree. He is uprooted from here once the poor have received his possessions, and he is planted there, but much is required for his growth. If godly practices do not water him, they will not let him bear fruit in the new world. Even when he is uprooted from this world and has scattered his wealth, he will not thrive there unless he lives spiritually. Even when he is planted in the land of the living, he does not bear fruit if his mind wanders among worldly concerns. Nor can he, merely because he owns nothing in the world, inherit

new life if he longs to acquire something. For this reason our Lord had pity on the rich man and did not show him the path of perfection. For he knew that the man could not walk it, because he was tightly bound to possessions and would not let them go. But when the young man pressed our Lord, he taught him what to do; and once he had learned, he was unwilling to do as he had been commanded. The love of wealth, which was darkness, strangled his soul. May we possess you, my Lord, for you are great wealth to those who possess you.
Here ends the homily on the young man who said to our Lord, “What shall I do to inherit eternal life?” Composed by the blessed Mar Jacob, the teacher.
By the holy Mar Jacob. Homily 52. On the son who squandered his possessions.
Your word, our Lord, is entirely light to whoever loves it. May I be enlightened by it to tell your story in the world. You are a great day, our Lord, to whoever journeys in you.

In your light I will set out to walk without stumbling. The world is dark, but you are radiant, Son of God. In your light, with you and in you, I will walk toward the one who begot you. The world's road is full of stumbling blocks and snares. Be a smooth road for me, our Lord, and I will walk in you. Your companionship is light [?], and you are the Sun of Righteousness. With you I will journey in a place clear of stumbling blocks. The world is full of pits, snares, and slippery places, but whoever holds fast to you is high and exalted above falling. You are peace and light and a smooth road, our Lord. Give me your hand so that I may walk in your peace and see your beauties. See, created things stir up your praise through their forms. Open my mouth too, so that I may praise your might. See, days and nights, within their appointed limits, open and close, spreading the account of you throughout the earth. Evenings and mornings, at their watches and appointed times, awaken people to praise you with understanding. Summers and winters, through their changes and their [?], teach the earth that you are the one who changes their seasons. Cold and heat, which come and go in their appointed courses,

tell of you, of how skillful you are in your works. The hours of the day and the four watches of the night all offer distinct praises to your creative power. The sea, with its ships, its storms, and its [?], tells in wonder how awesome your workmanship is. The turbulent waves, together with the mighty winds, sing of you, of how wonderful your might is. The great deep, and Leviathan with the sea monsters, depend on you within their bounds in the depths of the seas. All the dry land—the earth and its mountains and heights—[?] praises you, because you support it so that it does not fall. See, the heavens tell your glory through their natures, and the firmament displays the work of your hands, showing how mighty you are. The great tent that your creative power wove and spread out stands stretched over every boundary, filled with your glory. The sun and moon, with their rays and their risings, awaken the world to your praises through their great course. Stir up your praise in me too, our Lord, like a rich man who freely gives everything needed to those who ask him. May my speech about you be for your praise, in simple words, without presumptuous probing.

Speechless creatures praise your name abundantly. Stir me all the more, [?], to praise you. It is fitting for your image to sing your praise with understanding, more than these things that have no freedom and are compelled by you. I alone among created things have freedom, while they praise you through the compelled courses of their natures. For the sun shines and the moon is beautiful not by their own will, and the swift, compelled course of the heavenly hosts is held in check. Your great power compels them all to praise; it is not their freedom that chooses to praise your awesomeness. For me, a free person, it is good if I choose praise, because my will has authority either to remain silent or to stir myself to praise. If I remain silent, I receive blows from justice, which requires free people to praise [?] with understanding. For this reason I will praise you, my Lord, trembling, because I am unworthy; yet here I am, daring to do so, though I am inadequate. Every mouth owes you praise; let whoever is worthy sing praise. You, my Lord, are worthy of praise from all creatures, with words and voices, and silently through their forms. Stir yourselves, you who have understanding, to offer praise on behalf of the creatures

that are silent, for it is fitting for you to offer praise. Who can repay the Son of God, who came into our world for our sake, even by never ceasing to praise him? For—for sinners the Son of God went up on the cross, to turn them toward repentance, yet look, they remain idle. His mighty voice, which split the rocks and tore open the tombs, did not frighten us into seeking his face in repentance. Love of the world has seized us like a fire. The physician touched us and gave healing, but it did not release us. Love of gold, an ulcer that defies those who dress wounds, has sprouted in our soul and will not yield to healing. Sins have lain in ambush for us like robbers on the road of this world, yet we do not call upon the Deliverer to help us escape them. Our soul has grown dark from the possessions it has loved. The light has dawned, but it will not open the door for him to enter. The one who disciplines us has struck us with blow after blow like a judge, but our hard heart has not been corrected and turned away from evil. Like thieving slaves, we have been beaten for our wrongdoing, yet after the blows we have rebelled still more. To make us hate the world, he buffets and strikes us within it. Yet because love for it is woven into our soul, we have not let it go.

To make us flee the world, he shakes us with terrors. Because we have loved the world so much, look how we are crushed. Evil has grown strong, and love of money has spread among people like a blazing fire; look, they are burning in it. It has corrupted the world and ruined its beauties and its works. Now it is overturned and disturbed, full of falsehood and deceit. Love of gold has corrupted the road to the kingdom. Now it has laid its hand even on the holy ones to corrupt them. Into the pure place where the Trinity is worshiped, it has entered like the serpent into Paradise, and now it is disturbing it. It has led the priests astray into acquiring gold. Who can be healthy where the salt of the earth has lost its taste? Satan has muddied the fountainhead with his hateful counsel. Who can become clear when the whole creation has been muddied? We were commanded not to possess two of anything in this world. Yet now we have many things in duplicate—what can I say? He does not permit us to take shoes and a staff on the road, yet now we carry even beds and their coverings. He commanded us to travel through the lands without a bag, yet now we have bags of gold stored away. Who would not weep? That teaching of John and his followers is not found among us:

And the one from Simon’s company, whose whole beauty gold corrupted. That discipleship of Paul has now been corrupted, for look, the disciples have acquired even towns and their hamlets. Flocks of sheep and shepherds for the Christians who had been commanded to tend the sheep of the Son of God! Look, instead of souls, the disciples have acquired animals. And when the owner of the sheep comes, what will they say to him? Your master taught you to give what is yours, disciple. How, then, are you now rich from what is not yours? For disciples, acquiring possessions is theft. Judas taught it; Simon is not the master of this. Ananias stole from his possessions and his proceeds, and when Simon Peter discovered it, he struck him down dead. What, then, will happen to someone who steals what is not his? For look, Simon’s Lord watches him and remains silent toward him. The Just One has certainly not neglected punishment. The Light blazes; he will cast the greedy into Gehenna. He is patient, to bring them to repentance. But if they do not come, look, the flame will investigate their case. Tremble, disciple, before the Light who tests human beings. Teach and make anyone who does not tremble at Gehenna tremble.

Do not acquire possessions yourself, and teach those who listen to you likewise: the world’s wealth is a noose for whoever acquires it. The Tishbite, who acquired nothing, is now in heaven; but Gehazi, who acquired possessions, is clothed in leprosy and a foul reputation. Simon Peter, who left what was his, became the steward; but Judas, who took a bribe, bought himself a noose. Now judge between the one who acquires possessions and the one who does not: who has disgrace, and who has a good name? The great serpent who drove Adam out of Paradise is the one teaching you to acquire gold, disciple. From that gall which dripped from him among the trees, he spews up a drink for you when he teaches you to acquire gold. The teaching he once put into Eve’s ear he puts into your heart when he draws you toward Mammon. The love of wealth is that fruit full of death which Eve plucked from the tree of knowledge. The tree of life wishes to give human beings life alone, when they do not acquire superfluous possessions. Christ teaches, “Hate gold, and come, acquire life.” But the serpent whispers, “Acquire gold and take pride in it.”

And look, the teaching of the Son of God is despised and rejected, while the whole world runs after the serpent’s teaching. Wealth is loved, and even the disciples are corrupted by it, though they ought to have acquired nothing but our Lord. And look, they have gone after wealth without discernment, and the love of money burns within them like a flame. The serpent’s counsel is greatly loved, though he is a murderer, while the teaching of the Son of God is despised and trampled underfoot. No one makes room for the word or for instruction, for wickedness has increased, and teachers have been swallowed up in ruin. Students do not want to profit from instruction, nor does the teacher put silver on the table. Through love of gold, learning has fallen asleep, as in slumber, so that everyone may grow rich, as in a dream that never comes true. Everyone knows that wealth does not benefit its owners, and everyone says that the world and its wealth pass away. The one who acquired nothing in the world is praised, yet no one wants to hate wealth as he hated it. Everyone loves and praises righteousness, yet everyone runs away from it and does not practice it.

Sin is hated, yet no one wants to flee from it. They revile it while serving it by their deeds. Whenever the lofty story of one of the righteous is told, everyone says, “Who would grant me to be like that?” He is buried in sin, yet longs for righteousness, and despises himself because, if he had not wanted to, he would not have sinned. Righteousness is easy for the whole world to acquire, and if the whole world wanted it, it would acquire it. Wealth is not easy for everyone to acquire, though they love it, and not everyone who wanted it became rich as he wished. But before God, everyone who wished became righteous, for no one is prevented from acquiring righteousness. For God gave human beings freedom, and by his freedom a person acquires righteousness. Likewise, freedom also commits wrongdoing and is not restrained, for if it were restrained, it would not be freedom. You understand from the teaching of the Son of God that human beings possess freedom equally. If this were a time when teaching was loved, I would also speak about freedom, which is equal for all. It is not that one person is unfree and another free, for everyone is equal both in nature and in freedom.

For God gave human beings bodily members, bodily constitution, and freedom equally. Whoever wishes to do wrong has the power to do so, and God does not restrain anyone who practices righteousness. You learn from that parable of the younger son that human beings possess freedom equally. The teaching of the Son of God is full of light. O you who are darkened, be illuminated in the daylight of righteousness! In the story of the younger son who squandered everything he possessed, you can learn about freedom, which is equal for all. “A certain man had two sons,” he said: an older son and a younger son, both born of one father. In the parable he called God the Father himself the man, and the whole human race the two sons. Because he has both righteous people and sinners, he called them the older son and the younger son. He called the righteous the elder son, because they had been with God and had grown in their love for him from the beginning. And the son [?]—in the end they did not draw near to God. The younger son, who said to his father, “Give me my share,” was like someone saying, “Let me do whatever I want.”

The father divided the property and gave it to the two brothers. It was freedom that he called the property that was divided. “He divided his property between them,” it says, meaning that he distributed that freedom equally among human beings. The righteous person and the sinner have the same freedom: the Lord gave it equally to both. That property which the father divided between the two brothers is the freedom he gave equally to human beings. That sinner who was called the younger son took freedom as his share from his father's house. He went out and traveled to a country far from his father's house, and there he lived recklessly with prostitutes. The property his father had given him when he divided it, he squandered shamefully, and he became destitute through his wicked way of life. The distant country to which that sinner went is the evil will that is far from God. A person distances his heart from God and then sins, as though he had gone to another country to sin there. As though the Lord were not there and were not watching him, he goes on sinning, with no thought of the Lord in his mind. That is why it is written that he went to a distant country,

and squandered his possessions while living recklessly. He distanced himself from God as he sinned, and enslaved his freedom to serve worthless things. Virginity, that great treasure belonging to human nature, he defiled through adultery and sexual immorality, and it was lost to him. He also despised holiness, the second rank, and did not discipline himself to live a holy life. He became enslaved to gluttony and lust, and in his foolishness destroyed all his freedom. When someone is far from God, he does these things, as though the Lord were not there to see his wrongdoing. As this man lived recklessly, deprivation and poverty overtook him there. Anyone who is far from God is very poor: he is hungry and weary, and can never find life for himself. Anyone who hears our Lord's word with understanding is afraid to sin, lest he distance himself from God. The evil will that the younger son had acquired placed him far from God as he sinned. When he had been brought low and sin had defiled his freedom, he became subject to one of the masters of that country, to serve as his slave.

The Son of God calls the demons the masters of the country, for through error they had become masters and even gods. In that very country, people had gone far from God, and gods and masters had entered to be worshiped there. There the lofty horn of idolatry was raised, and people were enslaved to serve emptiness. Demons arose at the lofty summit of idolatry, and they became like masters over the world, to be worshiped in it. In that country where great sin is practiced, demons and evil spirits are its masters, as has been said. When the younger son had gone far away from his father, he went out to one of the masters of the country and became his slave. The sinner went astray when he went far away from God, and he enslaved himself to the demon who loves worthless things. The demon of love for the world, to whom he had enslaved himself, seized him and handed him over to the evil passions of desire. He sent him, it says, to tend pigs, and he longed to fill himself with carob pods, but no one gave him any. In the parable our Lord called the passions pigs, and likened the desires of the evil world to carob pods. Let everyone tremble at the explanation of this great parable,

and let no one sin if he hears it clearly. The parable teaches beyond dispute, to anyone who understands, that when someone sins, he is far away from God. It also makes known to us that when someone falls into sin, he attaches himself to the demon who inflames him with desires. That very demon, who loves worthless things and has time for them, uses them to entice the person who enslaves himself to him. As long as he is made a herdsman for the pigs, he keeps running about, serving emptiness for nothing, without any benefit. Alas, sinner, where have you been cast down when you sin! Into a country far away from God, where he is not present. Woe to you, miserable one! What a master you enslave yourself to: the demon who has taken you captive through worthless things, so that he may drink your blood. Hate sin because of the demon who is its master: he is the one who makes desires look attractive to sinners. Do not enslave yourself to one of the masters of the country of wickedness, for you have the Master of all countries. You have one Master; do not go to other masters. The Lord is your Master; renounce the demon, who is not your master. Hate sin because Satan loves it.

You are freeborn; do not enslave yourself to worthless things. Do not corrupt the freedom that was given to you by God and enslave it to desires. Do not leave the Father's house through the wickedness of your hands for a country far removed from freedom—from freedom and stability. In the fearful parable that the Son of God set down in his book, tremble at the wickedness that has corrupted human freedom. The weak son attached himself to one of the rulers of that country—to the demon who leads human beings astray from God. This ruler sent him to tend pigs, and he longed to fill his belly with carob pods, but he could not. For desires produce hunger, not satisfaction, like carob pods, which are not nourishing food. He longed for them, but they would not let him fill his belly. For no one can make his deeds keep pace with his desire. The person held captive by the love of money craves gold, for he cannot acquire as much gold as he desires. The adulterer, too, wants to defile his neighbor’s wife, but the honorable woman flees, and the fool is ashamed because he has not carried out his purpose. With his hateful desire, he wants to commit sexual sin with many women.

But some of them do not yield to his wantonness. He wants to wear fine clothes, but they are not available to him. Perhaps he also clamors for foods, but he does not have them. For he cannot fill his belly with carob pods, and they do not let him fulfill his will as he wishes. He desires much, but his desire is never fully satisfied, and every day he needs to satisfy those desires. There is no way to be satisfied with carob pods, nor can anyone be satisfied when he desires empty things. The sinner toils, but his soul gains no benefit from his toil. He tends pigs: the work is hard, and the wages are shameful. He wanders over mountains and heights and stumbling places, and the flock is unruly and torments the one tending it. Brutish passions are evil and full of death, and the fool runs after desires without ever being satisfied. Sins are snares, and the love of gold is a noose. Debauchery is a desire full of foul dung. The desire of the eyes is slippery ground in a smooth place. Anger is a snake that spits out gall that kills the soul.

The sinner wears himself out with great toil on his way, and unless he turns back from the stumbling places, the end is fire. Sin wore down the younger son, who had labored so much in its service, and he lingered among the desires he loved. The wretched man wasted away, unable to satisfy those desires, and they would not let him obtain them as he wished. The wretched man became distressed over his stumbling, his suffering, and his enslavement, for he remembered that he was freeborn. The sinner reflected that if he had not wanted to, he would not have sinned, and that if he had not wished to serve wickedness, no one had forced him. As though waking from the sleep of desires, he stirred and wailed, for he saw what a contemptible life his soul was living. He came to himself. Come, listen and marvel, discerning one: whoever sins becomes distant even from himself. When, it says, he came to himself, he spoke this way: “How many hired workers have their fill of bread in my fathers’ house!” He came to himself, for he had been far even from himself when he was far from God and practicing wickedness. Someone who knows what the soul is finds it hard to sin, lest its lofty, natural beauty be spoiled. As soon as a person forgets God, he forgets himself;

and he remembers neither his soul nor God. He came to himself because he wanted to come to God, and immediately he recognized who he was, whose son he was, and what condition he was in. He looked at himself and examined his own person. He trembled because he had sinned and turned back to go to his father’s house. He saw how that beautiful nature he possessed had been corrupted by ugly desires. He saw that God had created him beautiful and without blemish, but that by his own choice he had fallen into sin and become ugly. He came to his soul, for while he was sinning he had not been near it. He recognized what it was and felt pity for its beauty, which had been spoiled. As soon as he came and saw himself, he saw God, and he despised himself for having gone far from such a one while he was sinning. He remembered his father’s great house, its servants, its visitors, and its beautiful possessions. He remembered his father’s great table, full of abundant food, while he himself was wasting away in poverty. The miserable man thought about his father’s slaves and hired workers, and about the table from which even outsiders ate their fill. For as soon as repentance draws near to a sinner, he remembers God, his greatness, and his servants;

and the holy ones, how close they are to God; and the righteous, how splendid their rewards are; and how much beauty the chosen have in God’s house, and at what rank the perfect stand in triumph; and how many upright people God has who are close to him, while he himself lies cast away and far from God because of the wickedness he has done. As soon as a person turns to come to repentance, he [?] over all these things as he sighs, embittered over these beautiful things he has lost, grieving over how his freedom has been degraded, while shame stands over him like an accuser, making him bow his head like someone ashamed of the wickedness he has done. The sinner is despised because he has lost these beautiful qualities that belong to his nature. He has become ugly and suffers tremors. He sees others living in virtue, perfection, and righteousness, while he himself is brought low. Everyone who has drawn near to God has triumphed and been glorified, while he, the sinner, is ashamed and ugly, and everyone rebukes him. He bows his head and finds it hard to look up to heaven. His mouth is closed, and he has no strength to pray. He sees that he has spent most of his days in emptiness,

and has sinned greatly and ruined his soul, which was beautiful. The wretched man is far from God because of his wrongdoing, while other people, in their different conditions, are close to him. Although he and the righteous have the same freedom, he fell into sin and became a sinner because he chose to. The Son of God called him the younger son in the Gospel because he delayed and came to God last. He came to himself and began, with sighs, to speak words that would bring back a father's love and compassion. “How many hired workers there are in my father's house,” he said, “who have plenty of bread, while here I am dying of hunger among strangers!” As long as a person has not fallen into sin, he is a son of God, beautiful and beloved, and has a nature full of beauty. God saw that his creation was very beautiful; and the child is beautiful like his father as long as he does not sin. His whole nature is beautiful and full of righteousness, and because of his beauty he is worthy to be a son of God. But when he falls in love with the world and begins to sin, he loses his lofty, natural beauty. He is brought down from the exalted position of sons, for the beauty belonging to his nature has been ruined.

Then a person begins, through the labors of righteousness, to heal the sores that sprang from his freedom. Like a hired worker who works to fill his stomach with bread, he needs to apply himself diligently to the work of righteousness. A little from there and a little from here, and again from there, with remorse of soul, with tears of sorrow and supplication. He clothes the naked, feeds the hungry, and cares for orphans, hoping to find mercy so that he may return to God's house. The younger son sought to stand at this rank; he was not longing for the honor belonging to sons. A son does not sin, because his seed is in him, and he is not enslaved to doing wrong, because he is pure like his father. But when he sins, he comes down to the rank of hired workers, so that he may pursue righteousness and save his soul. Through work, supplications, and almsgiving, he may enter through the door of the house so that he does not perish. Because he was a son and ruined the beauty belonging to sons, he became a hired worker and labors to gain his livelihood from the house. Until he approaches repentance, the person who sins and is not [?] in the course of his journey belongs among strangers.

Through his desires he is enslaved to one of the rulers of the country, and there among strangers he labors for emptiness. As soon as he wishes to return and come to God's house, the rulers of the country cannot hold him there. If God did not prevent him from leaving when he wished to leave, how can the evil one prevent him when he wishes to return? The sinner wanted to sin, and he sinned as much as he pleased. Then he wanted to return, and nothing could stop him. He fell as he wished and rose as he wished, and he had control over himself. For free will cannot be forced to do anything. The younger son wanted to return and see his father, and the whole throng of desires did not stand in his way. Nor did Satan, who had worked with him, stop him on his way. Nor could the demons thwart his good intentions. Nor did love of the world bind him as it usually does. As soon as he wanted to come, he came, and no one restrained him. O sinner, as soon as you want to come, you can come. There is no power that can keep you from what benefits you. Make your choice and leave that pasture whose wages are shameful: pigs, [?], evil passions, all of it error [?].

Come to your senses, as that foolish heir did. As soon as he came to his senses, he became wise and [?] his father. See that you do not forget the great household of God. Look, you are far away, cast out from it like a stranger. There the upright delight in the course of their lives, and the perfect are praised for the beauty of their conduct. Its banquet is filled with all the righteous in their honor, while you are far away, brought low and cast down among strangers. Come, sinner, come and see your father, who is waiting for you. You have delayed a long time. Come in before they close the door. Through repentance the soul is restored when it has gone astray, and through repentance it regains all the beauty that had been ruined. Repentant one, acquire the younger son's attitude, for the Son of God told his story for your own instruction. Come to your senses and ask for mercy as he did, for the Father is willing to embrace whoever seeks him. Sinner, adopt the younger son's attitude, and it will bring you in to be an heir in your Father's house. Come to your senses, as he did after his stumbling, and seek forgiveness with a remorseful mind. Hunger tormented him—a hunger for pleasures that you do not have.

And they do not let you satisfy yourself with them. Why are you standing there? Come to the table in God's house, where there is food in abundance, and fill your belly with its spiritual delights. Consider, sinner, how everyone who has drawn near to God has been satisfied with his good things and is being richly fed on his luxuries. Hunger and want left the younger son empty, and only then did he turn back to return to his father's house. He remembered the luxury in which he had been raised. His soul was distressed, and he began to speak through his tears: “How many hired workers have their fill of bread in my father's house, while here I am dying of hunger! What shall I do? I will return to my father and weep and wail and plead with him. I will say to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you.’” I am not worthy to be your son from now on, because my sin is far too great for forgiveness. I am not a son, for my offense is not that of a son. I will be a hired worker, and it will be a kindness to me to live with you. If from now on I have my fill of bread with your hired workers, that will be a luxury for me—the bread of your house, which provides food in abundance. The repentant son had turned back to come and see his father. While he was still far away, a father's compassion went out to meet him. He wanted to return, and because he wanted this, his father's heart burned for him.

He went out and welcomed him while he was still far from his father's house. His father was deeply moved because he saw the dead man alive, and he rejoiced over the living man who had turned back to return from destruction. He welcomed that lost son as though from the embrace of Sheol, and rejoiced at the resurrection of the dead man who had risen from the grave. In his joy he threw his arms around his son's neck and embraced him. He kissed him as though he had brought wealth into his house. He did not reproach him for leaving or demand to know why he had delayed. Nor did he question him about what had happened to his property. He did not require him to bring back the share he had taken with him before the heir who had returned to his father's house could be welcomed. He was not grieved over the property that had been squandered, nor did he distress him by demanding an account of the wealth he had lost. He welcomed him just as though he had gone away and brought back riches, treasures, and every kind of precious possession to his father's house. He rejoiced over the heir and was not grieved over the possessions that he had recklessly wasted on worthless things. The sight of his son and the burning love one has for one's children filled the place of wealth for the father, and it was his son he wanted. The young man said, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I have done wrong, and I am not worthy to be your son.

I will be a lowly hired worker in your house, working, enduring insults and blows, and bearing it all. No one can measure how high the heavens are, nor is there any measure for how great my wrongdoing is.” That confession of the returning heir was precious, and his father received him as though he were a very great treasure. He welcomed him in this way, without blame or complaint, and cherished him as though justice had found no fault with him. He embraced him, kissed him, and honored him. His father loved him as though he owed him a debt. At once he ordered his household members and servants to bring the finest robe the father possessed. They were to put a ring on the hand of the returning heir, and the young man was to put on shoes from his father's house. The father gave the order, and the fattened ox was slaughtered for him. The servants did as the master of the house commanded. The house resounded with the sound of praise and songs, and with the celebrations held for the returning heir. The father's household rejoiced over the dead man who had come to life, with great jubilation, songs, and voices mingled in great praise. While they were celebrating, the elder son, who had been in the countryside, arrived.

He heard the sound and began asking about the jubilation. “What is this?” The servants said, “Your brother has come, and your father is rejoicing because he is safe and well. Come, rejoice too!” As soon as he heard, the elder son became angry and turned back. He did not want to go in and rejoice over the heir who had returned. But the father, whose compassion is never divided, went out after him too, to bring him in as well and rejoice with him. The elder son began to challenge his father's compassion and reproach the blameless man, saying to him: “Look how many years I have worked for you as a servant, my lord! You have never lent me a young goat so that I could enjoy myself with it.” His father said, “My son, you are with me all your days. No one moves you away or takes you far from your father. Everything of mine is yours, for you are the elder. You are the heir, and your brother comes in through kindness. Here you are with me, but your brother who has come was not with us. He was dead and has come to life. Because he has come to life, come, let us rejoice over him! Because he was lost and now we have found him, let us rejoice today. Who would not rejoice over an object he had lost if he found it? Your brother was lost; do not be upset because we have found him. Your brother was dead and has come to life today. Who would not rejoice?”

Who would not marvel at the father, who is entirely full of mercy and is wholly a boundless sea of compassion? He welcomed the younger son who had come, so that he would not go away, and lovingly pleaded with the elder so that he would not be angry. His love was wide enough to embrace both the younger and the elder in his compassion, without abandoning either of them. The people were jealous of the nations who had been lost. Because God welcomed them, the people became angry and went out. But God wants to gain all the nations, and all the nations that seek him are his heirs. He wants to give life both to those who come last and to those who come first, for they are all one to him, and he wants to bring them all back. Likewise, he opens his door to both the righteous and sinners and calls them all to give them life. He wants sinners to come to repentance, and he watches over and cherishes the righteous, to give them their inheritance. Because of his love, he bears the burden of both groups, for his compassion is sufficient to give life to them both. The righteous person is with God all his days, and for this reason he was the elder son and the first. It is to him that the words are spoken: “Everything of mine is yours.” For the righteous inherit the earth, and it is theirs.

The sinner too, if he comes to repentance, finds compassion and inherits life in the Father's house. Look how many years I have served you as a slave, my Lord! I am righteous, yet I plead like a sinner. I have not sinned, yet every day I plead as though I had sinned. You have not let me think that I could find rest on your path. I have feared you, your threats, and your commandments, your warnings and the laws of your severity. In your teaching you did not allow me to possess two. And if I looked at a woman and desired her, you said that I had committed adultery. If I call someone an empty-head, I will fall into Gehenna; and if I call my brother a fool, the judgment becomes severe. If my tunic is taken from me, I must surrender my cloak; and if I do not do these things, I will suffer [?]. Look how many years I have been a slave to the fear of you! You have not allowed me to violate or despise a single one of these things. I have never transgressed the commandments of your severity, nor have I stooped to the slightest failing by breaking your words. I have kept them all, though they are hard and severe; and since I came to know you, I have found no rest on your path.

This is what ‘You did not give me a little goat’ means: ‘I have not stooped to commit even the slightest failing.’ These are the words the perfect man has before God, speaking boldly, raising his voice, and demanding his wages. He has no need to ask for mercy at the judgment before justice, for he has not experienced sin so as to ask for mercy. And therefore, when a sinner enters into judgment, the perfect man does not think there is any possibility that he will live. And therefore the elder son wanted to be angry, because he saw that the penitent had entered to receive an inheritance through mercy. The elder son said to the father in a loud voice, ‘I have never broken your words or your commandments. But this son of yours acted foolishly in worthless pursuits and gave his entire inheritance to prostitutes. He squandered and wasted everything he owned on unclean women, yet look: you have honored him with a fattened calf for him to feast on!’ God, however, rejoices in this man who is unashamed, and wishes to offer a hand so that whoever has fallen may rise. And if a sinner wishes to come to repentance, he makes room for him in his mercy, so that he may live there.

As soon as a sinner becomes one of the repentant, he seats him with the righteous and gives him a place at his table. When the younger son returned from his stumbling, they clothed him in the finest robe the father had. There was one robe for both the last and the first, not torn apart so that each of them might take half. That finest robe was given to the younger son, and there was no other: the elder son was to wear that very same one. For God there is one faith and one baptism, and one garment that he gives to the baptized from within the water. There is one sacrifice through which all sinners have been forgiven, and the treasuries of God's house are sealed with one signet ring. The bride who came up from the water has one sandal: a shoe of fire with which she tramples serpents. The Son of God is the lover of repentance. Come, sinners, recline at his table, so that he may give you joy. The compassionate Father's mercies are spread over sinners. Who would not come, except someone who hates his own life? He made the younger son an heir alongside the elder, for repentance raises the dead at the Father's command.
He had been dead and came to life, becoming a hope for all sinners that they can easily come to life through repentance. Blessed is he who shows mercy to everyone!
Here ends the discourse on the son who squandered his possessions.
By Saint Jacob. Discourse 53. On the Pharisee and the tax collector, of whom our Lord said that they went up to the temple to pray.

The teaching of the Son of God is full of life. Lovers of life, come and delight in his teaching! All his words are light to those who have discernment. You discerning people, shine through the good news that is full of light! From his lips rivers of living water flowed out into creation, to water the earth that had become desolate. On his tongue are blessings and riches beyond comprehension, and he distributes them to his listeners in their assemblies. When he opens his mouth to speak, death flees, and his power gives resurrection to the dead, awakening them.

From his words life dawns upon souls, and those that had been bitten by the venomous serpent are healed. When he speaks, his voice falls upon the ears of the dead, and they stir as though from sleep and rise to give praise. He carried remedies and brought them to our land from his Father's house. He distributed them freely to the afflicted and healed them. He shone upon diseases like the sun upon shadows, and drove them away from every afflicted body. Through his teaching he healed the soul that was sick, and his word bandaged the dead body that had been wounded. He drove sin from the soul—the blemish that was killing it—and from the body he drove the pain and the ulcer that were tormenting it. The sins of the soul and the pains of the body, numerous as they were, vanished like smoke in a strong wind. Wherever he saw sin in a soul, he granted forgiveness; and whenever bodily pain confronted him, he granted healing. As he taught, he pronounced woe upon the scribes and Pharisees: a cautery for the disease that resisted healing. He saw pride and had compassion on the soul slain by it. He made an incision in it and applied a cautery to heal its ulcer. He saw the poor distressed by their poverty, and he bestowed a blessing upon the poor to encourage them. 301 He saw the rich who had no compassion for the poor, and he revealed [?] the rich man and Lazarus. Through the man who begged for a drop of water and was given none, he taught them to have compassion on the poor. Against the soul’s wickedness, which is a hidden ulcer, he revealed and showed it the fire of judgment, so that it might become beautiful. He recounted one of the events of the new world to help both the rich and the poor. Through the drop of water that the man begged for but was not given, he struck fear into the rich so that they would not become proud. And through Lazarus, who was reclining beside Abraham, encouragement was given to anyone bound by poverty. As he taught, he portrayed the world through ten virgins, revealing and explaining the foolish and the wise. So that the soul would prepare for itself the oil of good deeds, he showed it how the wise virgins enter with him. He warned the soul that unless it shines with good deeds, the door will not be opened for it to enter into his presence when it pleads. Again, he portrayed himself as a shepherd who took care to separate the goats and the sheep, on the right and on the left.

He placed the sheep in the light and the goats in darkness, for even the goat’s color is dark to anyone looking at it. As he taught, he revealed what he would say to those whom he places on his right and on his left. Those on the left hear him say, “Go away, you accursed!” And those on the right hear him say, “Come, enter and inherit!” He spoke these words of the end beforehand to help anyone who hears his teaching. Thus, before going to the place of judgment, a person would know what the judgment is and prepare good deeds for himself. The Son of God takes care to benefit human beings by every means through his teaching, which is full of wonder. In one place he spoke in parables and riddles; in another place he showed the soul threats and punishments. At other times, through gifts and praise, he stirred the soul to love good deeds. There he spoke about the tax collector and the Pharisee, telling a story that greatly benefits anyone who hears it. He wished to show, concerning pride and humility, which is condemned and which is vindicated before the Judge. He sought to crush both boasting and arrogance,

through which the soul is brought low and stands condemned before justice. Because of his love, he wished to deliver the soul that does good deeds from pride and from all reproach. Thus, after its toil, it would not be stripped of its good things and lose its labor through a proud spirit, should it acquire one. He struck fear into the righteous person: even though he is righteous, he is never permitted to recount his good deeds. And he encouraged and supported the sinner: if he humbles himself and asks for mercy, he can readily receive it from God. For this reason, he set out a story full of [?] about that tax collector and the Pharisee as he prayed. He said that two men went up to the temple to pray: one a Pharisee, and the other a greedy tax collector. Among the Hebrews, the name “Pharisee” is like “righteous man.” Now listen to the Pharisee, who was righteous. It is clear that the tax collector was a sinner. These men went up to pray in the house of God. They went up to pray, one righteous and one sinful: the Pharisee and the tax collector, before the Judge of the whole earth. The Pharisee began to speak with an arrogant spirit, because he trusted in the good deeds he had done. He looked at himself and saw that he was pure and had no blemish.

He trusted in his purity as he stood to pray. He began to say, “God, I thank you that I am like neither sinners nor robbers. I thank you that I am free from blame. There is no injustice in me, and I am not like evil people. There are adulterers, there are sexually immoral people, and there are oppressors. I have never been like them, nor am I like them now. I am not like evildoers and the wicked. Rather, I am pure and clear of evil deeds. I thank you that I have not been deceitful, unjust, or contemptible, and that my conduct is not like that of evildoers.” O righteous man, what are you saying in your prayers? These words you are speaking are not words of prayer. O Pharisee, this is not how someone who prays behaves, nor does he dare recount his good deeds before the One who knows everything. You have praised yourself; you have not brought praise to your Lord. You are occupied with yourself, recounting your good deeds now. This is not how prayer goes [?] before God; rather, in sorrow it asks the Judge for mercy. This is not how a soul stands before God.

Rather, it is bowed down, trembling, shaking, and filled with awe. How have you come, and why have you come to pray? Look, you have not prayed, but have praised your good deeds. If you have no need to receive anything from God, there are others in need. Why do you not plead for sinners? If your soul does not seek to have beauty added to it, there are others in need. Pray for them as a good man should. This man looked at the beauty of his own soul and became bewildered. He did not know to look at God and see how beautiful he is. Whoever looks closely and sees the beauty of that Majesty finds his own soul ugly in his eyes, however beautiful he may be. If a little lamp encounters the great sun, it disowns its own light, which has been obscured by daylight. So too, when a righteous man becomes attentive and looks at God, his righteousness grows dim and small in comparison with God. For Abraham, who gazed on God's greatness, called himself dust and ashes, although he was righteous. Simon Peter said to his Lord, “I am a sinner.” And who is righteous when speaking with God? If Abraham called himself dust and ashes, and Simon Peter was a sinner, as he himself said,

who dares to look at his own good deeds and recount them when speaking with God? This Pharisee was righteous in his own person, but he had not perceived how beautiful God is. He did not have that hidden vision which peers into hidden things, with which to gaze on the beauty of that greatness. He did not have a great mind and an exalted understanding that boldly ascends and enters among the angels, and trembling, uncovers the entrance to the fortress of light, while waves of the radiance of that greatness wash over him, and his sight is dazzled by these incomprehensible beauties, and he despises himself if he has imagined that he possesses beauty. If the eye of his soul had been clear as he gazed on the beauty above, he would not have seen his own beauty. Anyone who sees his own beauty is not beautiful, for if he were beautiful, he would consider himself full of blemishes. A clear soul does not look at itself when it is beautiful; it gazes on the beauties above and is dazzled by their radiance. Someone who is righteous thinks deeply that he is not righteous, like the disciple who cried out to his Lord, “I am a sinner.” This Pharisee had become righteous through the law,

through observances and bodily commandments. For he did not know that there was another degree of righteousness above his own, one that draws near to God. Love for the Lord is commanded by the law, and it does not even look to him for a reward in return. The more beautiful the soul becomes, the more it thinks it is not beautiful, for the exalted beauties of the Godhead stir it. But the Pharisee, who was righteous according to the law, was pleased with himself and stood up to recount his good deeds. He looked at the tax collector, who had also gone up to pray, despised and scorned him, and spoke about him contemptuously. He thanked the Lord in a spirit full of conceit, compared himself with the tax collector, and saw himself as greater than him. “I thank you that I am not like this tax collector,” he said to God, mistakenly thinking that this was prayer. He did not look at Moses, or Elijah, or Jeremiah, but at this man, and in comparison with this man he was righteous. He dishonored himself while thinking that he was praising himself, for he compared himself with the tax collector and appeared beautiful in his own eyes. He did not compare his light with the light of that Beautiful One, to see which beauty was beautiful and which was dull.

He compared his dim light with the tax collector’s darkness, and by looking at darkness rather than light, he thought himself bright. He did not look at Joseph, the young man who conquered lust on its own ground, nor at Daniel, who rejected the king’s delicacies. He did not look at Job, that sea of virtues and trials, nor at Jacob, who wrestled with angels. He looked at the tax collector, and his own righteousness grew great in his eyes. Because he saw someone ugly, he thought himself beautiful. Therefore, anyone who wants to enrich himself in righteousness must look at those who are virtuous and exalted. And if he has reached the stature of the perfect, let him look at God, so that, comparing himself with him, he may be ashamed before his greatness. When a rich man sees wealth greater than his own, he sees himself as poor and does not exalt himself. But if he looks at someone who lacks his daily bread, he mistakenly supposes that no one in the world is greater than he is. If the soul looks at those who are perfect and spiritual, it descends deeply into humility, which is full of virtues. But if it looks at wicked people, it becomes proud, and pride produces faults in whoever possesses it. Rather, though it is ugly, it thinks it has become very beautiful,

by comparison with the wicked, and falls into the pit of pride. This is what happened to the Pharisee as he prayed: he saw the tax collector and thought himself greater than him. He began to disparage him and point him out to the Lord, saying, “I thank you that I am not like this tax collector.” Two evils were committed through a haughty spirit, and those who discern recognize harm in both. For someone to look at his companion’s sins is evil, and to be pleased with himself is also evil. No one benefits from looking at a wound that is not his own. Instead, let him wisely attend to his own wound. No one benefits from dwelling on his own good deeds. Instead, let him forget them altogether, if he has done any. As it is written: “I forget what lies behind me, and I stretch forward again toward the good things ahead of me.” “If I did a good deed yesterday, it has been done, and now I am running to do another, if I can. I forget yesterday’s good deed along with yesterday itself, for if I dwell on it, it keeps me from doing good. I have put behind me the good deed I did, if indeed I did it, so that I may run forward again after another good deed.

Let yesterday’s good deed be preserved in yesterday’s life. I am alive today; let today have what belongs to it.” The sun likewise forgets and leaves behind the times that have passed, and runs on toward those that are coming, to pass through them. If the sun stopped to reckon up yesterday’s course, its course today would cease to advance. Day after day, it throws its past courses behind it, and again seeks to run onward like one who is diligent. Paul resembles the sun on the road of apostleship: he would forget yesterday’s course and take no account of it. Why recount the good deeds that have been done, so that they become a reason for other good deeds not to be done? The Pharisee’s good deeds became a cause of harm to him, for when he sought to count them up, he was not justified. Yesterday he had been eager and had done good deeds; today he stood counting them up and became idle. All good deeds are laid in the Lord’s hands, and he does not forget them. Why are you anxious to count them up? Why have you stopped doing the work of righteousness and begun calculating what you have done for God?

He does not forget; do not stop doing good. Do not remind him of what you have done, for it is written down before him. Deeds and words, actions and thoughts, gestures and movements of the soul—he knows them and keeps watch over them. Since he does not forget, why have you reckoned him deficient? Look, you recount your good deeds to remind him! It is necessary, my brothers, that no one dwell on your good deeds, for that righteous man is reproached precisely because he dwelt on them. Let anyone who sins set his sin before his face; and if he acts righteously, let him throw his righteousness behind him. Look at your sin, for if you look at it, it disappears. But do not look at your righteousness, lest you wipe it out. If you practice righteousness, forget it completely; for if you forget it, the Lord watches over it so that it will not be lost. For if you dwell on your sin, God forgets it; he disregards it and forgives it if he sees that you are crushed by it. But if you forget the sin you have committed, the Lord does not forget it and let it pass; instead, he calls it to account. Look at your sin, whenever you have one, as you would at a wound. For who can forget his wound when it hurts him? As long as someone with a bad wound keeps groaning,

the sound of his groans rouses his physician to care for him. But if he does not groan, he gives the impression that he has no wound. The physician neglects him and does not dress his wound, since he feels no pain. Likewise, as long as the sinner keeps looking at his sin, God himself cares for his wound and heals him. But if he becomes careless and does not look at it, the healer ceases his work, and the wound remains without healing, receiving no help. If someone remembers his sin while despising it, a broken spirit obtains mercy from the Judge. He is like that tax collector whose sin lay before his eyes, and who could not look toward heaven because of it. He was unwilling to lift his gaze from his wrongdoing, for he kept looking at it and did not dare to look upward. He kept the sins he had committed before his eyes, and it was not easy for him to see heaven, which was veiled. He looked at nothing but the wrongdoing his hands had committed, and he could see nothing else alongside it. He stood bowed down like a thief before a judge, and because he felt despised, he could not lift his eyes. He feared and trembled before Justice, who sits on high,

afraid to raise his eyes toward her, lest she become angry and raise her rod and strike him to destruction because he had dared to look confidently in the place of judgment, though he was guilty. For this reason he did not dare look toward heaven, toward the fearsome Judge who is a terror to sinners. He looked at his sins and was moved to seek great mercy, for nothing but mercy can bandage the sore of wrongdoing. He stood praying in shame, despising himself; but God did not despise him, because he had humbled himself. His soul was enlightened, and he saw his sins and struck his hands against his chest in trembling as he cried out before the Judge. He called upon God, saying to him, “Have mercy on a sinner! Your mercy is life; bring to life the dead man whom wrongdoing has killed.” The account of this tax collector and the Pharisee has overwhelmed me, for it is a matter of great trembling to tell their story in wonder. And if I do not venture to speak boldly, I cannot tell these things as they are to those who hear me. The Pharisee’s good deeds became a cause of evil for him: through them he darkened his soul with boasting and pride. That tax collector’s soul, however, was enlightened because he had sinned; it trembled and longed to seek mercy from the Judge.

The righteous man grew dark because he counted up his good deeds; the sinner grew bright because the wrongdoing he had committed made him tremble. The righteous Pharisee went astray, even to the point of reproaching God; but the greedy tax collector recognized that the Lord is full of mercy. Yet it cannot be said that evil springs from good deeds, nor can it be understood that goodness dawns from evil deeds. What, then, shall I say? Because of his good deeds, boasting puffed up the Pharisee, and he praised himself—and now he is reproached. But the tax collector’s sins opened his soul before the Judge, and he sought mercy; he is praised as a wise man. Let us therefore accuse, not the good deeds that were done, but the error [?] and pride of the Pharisee. And again, let us praise, not the sins the tax collector committed, but his soul, which looked and saw how ugly it was. Through his story he became like a mirror for those who practice wrongdoing, so that they might stand in God’s house with great humility. He urged the soul to seek mercy from God, and it came to know that if it asks him, he gives it mercy. Our Lord told this parable to help both groups through it, if they listen to it with discernment.

Both the righteous and sinners benefit from him, for the Son of God desires to benefit them both. O righteous person, never despise a sinner. He is God's image, even though he sins, and he is your fellow. Do not boast if you do good deeds, lest you fall from that height of righteousness. You have given to God from what is his, not from what is yours, yet you reproach him over the tithes you give him. When you fast, do not boast and recount your fasting, for Daniel fasted in humility when he fasted. Humble yourself in God's house when you pray, for your prayer is not accepted when offered in pride. Even if ten thousand beautiful qualities are placed and arrayed in you, they are not beautiful unless you clothe yourself in humility. Even if your deeds make you more righteous than Job, your good deeds are not accepted when offered with a proud spirit. And you, sinner, benefit from the account that was told about the tax collector, and stand in prayer with shame on your face. Justice does not permit you to look toward heaven, for the place of judgment is a great terror to those condemned there. Tremble in prayer and seek mercy in humility, and you will receive it from the giver of good things.

Be silent and humble yourself if you are rebuked by a righteous person, for that tax collector too remained silent when he was belittled. Say to God, “I beg you, my Lord, have mercy on a sinner,” and he will have mercy on you because of the compassion woven into him. Our Lord's parable is entirely life to whoever hears it, and it can help both the righteous and sinners. This parable is not merely a parable; it actually happened just as it was told. On one occasion, a Pharisee and a tax collector met and stood in prayer, and they spoke these things in God's house. The Son of God listened to them together with his Father, for he is the one who receives all petitions and prayers. For no prayer enters his Father's presence without him, and no gift comes forth from his Father except through his hands. He receives and brings in; he takes and brings out from the Father's house, for he is a mediator between us and his Father, so that he may forgive us. The sacrifices of Levi and the tithes of righteous Jacob—he received them and brought them into his Father's presence. He received Hannah's prayer in the holy temple, and he brought out for her from his Father's house the mercy she had requested. He listened to Jonah's prayer from inside the fish, and brought it into his Father's presence like an offering of firstfruits.

Sacrifices set apart, the incense offerings of priests, and whole burnt offerings; prayers, petitions, all tithes, together with all vows; the words of the mouth and the thoughts of hearts—he is the one who receives, listens, hears, sees, and remembers. He listened to the Pharisee and that tax collector as they stood praying in the holy temple. And as he listened to the petition of the whole world, he did not forget to recount them as they had been heard. And since this was an event that had once happened, as it was related, he made it a parable to benefit whoever heard it. And because the tax collector who prayed humbly pleased him, while the Pharisee who prayed proudly did not please him, he preserved the account and made it a parable full of benefits. He placed it in the Gospel so that all who heard it would benefit from it. He taught the world that whoever exalts himself is humbled, so that everyone would flee from pride, which is abhorrent to him. “Whoever is proud in heart,” it says, “is abhorrent before God.” And who, if he has understanding, would not tremble at pride? Vices are hateful and displeasing to God, but this expression, “abhorrent,” was used of pride alone.

He hates them all and wants none of them to exist, but of this one alone it is written that it is abhorrent before God. He does not merely hate it as he does its companions; rather, he abhors it and recoils greatly from it. All sins feel shame before God, but pride wants, as it were, to wage war against him. The Lord is exalted, yet he wishes to dwell among the humble; but whoever exalts himself has stepped toward God to claim greatness. And because it is written, “The Lord reigns and is clothed in majesty,” it is hateful for a human being to exalt himself or act proudly. For this reason it is written of pride that it is abhorrent before God, for anyone who listens with understanding. And for this reason the parable of the Pharisee was written, so that whoever does good deeds might learn wisdom from it: that he should flee from speaking about his good deeds, and from pride, the passion that is abhorrent in God's house. It is good for you to flee from every passion; it is good for you to hate every vice. It is good for you to hate sins in every form, but flee especially far from pride, because it is abhorrent. And humility is full of the beauties of righteousness,

so that even a fault is covered up wherever humility is present. The tax collector was hateful, and his faults were many; yet because he humbled himself, see how favorably he is spoken of. And the Pharisee was righteous and possessed virtue; but because he wanted to recount his virtues, see how hateful his story is. With one medicine our Lord healed two sores, and he can easily treat both the righteous and sinners. From one parable he made a remedy for both sides, so that both the sinner and the righteous person might benefit from it. He cast fear upon the righteous person, so that he would not boast and his good deeds would not be stripped away by his boasting. And he taught the sinner to feel sorrow and humble himself, to know himself and find mercy before God. The Son of God seeks to benefit everyone through his words. Blessed is he who desires everyone to live through his care.
The homily on the tax collector and the Pharisee is complete.
By Saint Mar Jacob. Homily 54. On the parable our Lord told about the workers whom the owner of the vineyard hired.

Open my lips to speak lovingly about you. Son of God, grant me to speak abundantly of you. With you I am bold: I will steal every treasure from you. Lord of treasures, give me your riches, so that I may be filled with them. Reveal your mysteries to me, so that I may reveal them to the whole earth, and all the earth may sing praise to your divinity. All the riches your Father possesses are yours. Give me some of them, so that I may become rich and enrich whoever hears me. Give me your word, which is wealth to whoever possesses it. Let me acquire it and impart it to anyone who eagerly seeks what is beneficial. Let me multiply the roses of your words on my tongue from your readings, and bring forth and scatter your stories sweetly among the assemblies. The invited guests look expectantly to drink life from your bowl. Let your living cup quench the thirst of the assembly that longs for you. Your good wine came forth to creation at the end of the ages, for your Father had kept you so that you might be the world's consolation.

Your sweet taste now stirs my tongue to cry out praise to the Father who sent you, so that all who are bitter might become sweet through you. Jesus, the honey that came out of the carcass of the lion—death—to sweeten the world's bitter palates. The star ran and, by its rising, called the lands to bring gifts: great praise to the Father who sent him. Let the whole earth be stirred to praise you, my Lord, for all of it has been illuminated by your divine rays. You are living water. Everyone who sought and drank from you found delight in you and is filled from the spring that is full of mercy. Your teaching sprang from Golgotha, God's Eden, and went forth to water all creation, which had been laid waste. The thirsty, exhausted earth drank its fill from you. It rejoiced and became like a paradise full of blessings. Your stories entered the world like river channels, and now all creation meditates on your teaching. Pishon, Gihon, the Tigris, and the Euphrates fell short of the flow that poured from your disciples for the world to drink. The cross opened a single spring from Golgotha. It divided itself toward the four quarters, and now it gives us drink.

It stood on the height and opened a well down into the depths, so that through its lofty flow it might cover the whole earth. He laid channels toward the nations and the lands, and they all drank and were spiritually filled with your words. All creation, which had been asleep, heard your voice. It stirred, rose, and clapped its hands in praise. Come, let us delight in the teaching that is full of life, beloved children whom the womb of baptism has borne. Bring with you all your gathered thoughts, for this is what the account of the Son demands of those who hear it. Let your whole self come, if you come for instruction, for Christ wants your whole self, to give you life so that you may be with him. The gospel is light for darkened souls. At its dawning it gave light, life, and delight. The Son’s words carry life to distribute throughout the whole world to whoever listens with love. He carried blessings and riches and brought them to us from his Father’s house, and he made the poor treasurers over his treasures. The Lord of kings became poor because he chose to, and now all creation is rich through his poverty. He spoke with us because he was pleased to become one of us.

And with his teaching he salted souls that had become tasteless. He became our physician and bore the pains of our sickness. He became our shepherd and gathered the sheep that were lost. He became bread for us and drove hunger from our souls. He became water for us and relieved the thirst that was choking us. He became our road and led us along it so that we might reach his country. He became our door and through it brought us in to the one who begot him. He became our brother so that we might become his kin and be with him. He made us his own family, joined us to himself, and became one of us. He dawned in our world like a day full of light, and the darkness in which all creation had been wandering came to an end. The radiant Son spoke in parables and riddles, so that through study he might make the soul wise enough to seek out his teachings. As he taught, he portrayed his kingdom through one image after another, so that through its images the whole world might long for it. In one place he portrayed it through ten virgins, a wedding feast, and the lamps of the wise virgins. Elsewhere he compared it to a talent and the profits of great wealth that comes back multiplied to the master of the house. There is also a place where he portrayed it through a small seed that became like a tree, in which a bird made its nest.

Again, he compared it to a little yeast that a woman hid in dough; all of it rose and was made pleasant by it. Along with these, he also portrayed his kingdom through a householder who went out and hired laborers for the vineyard to work with him. Let us now speak about this parable that the Son of God told when he portrayed his kingdom through laborers. He said that the kingdom of God’s household is like a man who went out to hire laborers for his vineyard.
