He called laborers at daybreak and agreed on a denarius for each of them, and brought them in to work diligently. At the third hour he saw other laborers and called them. He brought them in to his work alongside the first. At the sixth hour, in his eagerness, he hired still others, without specifying how much pay they would receive from him. At the ninth hour he again saw workers and brought them in, for his vineyard calls all creation [?] to work with him. After this, the owner of the vineyard went out at the eleventh hour and saw other workers standing idle. The owner of the vineyard began speaking, reproaching the workers who had spent the whole day without working: “Why, men, are you idle and doing nothing,

and why do you spend the whole day foolishly, without work? Why are you not working alongside your companions in the vineyard that can give life to those who work in it? Why has idleness led you along all day? Evening has arrived, and you stand there looking ashamed.” The workers said, “No one has hired us to work with him, nor has the owner of the vineyard called us to his work.” He said to them, “You go too! The vineyard needs workers even for an hour, for there is work for everyone who comes to it.” The workers came, and evening arrived, when they were to receive their wages. The master of the house called his steward and said to him: “Get up and give good wages to the workers who have worked with us. When you pay them, give those who came last a denarius each. Begin with them, and give each of them a denarius. In this way, treat them equally and give to the last and the first alike.” The steward got up to pay the wages as he had been instructed, and he gave those who came last one denarius each. But when those who came first saw the wages he gave those who came last, they thought they would receive more than their companions. They were thinking, “If he gave those who came last a denarius, how much, then, will he give us who came first when he reaches us?”

But the steward gave a denarius to those who came last, to those after them, and to those in the middle, without adding anything. They all passed by, and those who came first went in to receive their wages. Again he gave them likewise one denarius, with nothing extra. But when that first worker saw the denarius, he drew back his hand, distressed, and would not take it. His wage had been agreed upon, but because he had expected more, he forgot the agreement and wanted to become angry over the pay. He began speaking, accusing the master of the house because he had treated them equally and given those who came last as much as those who came first. He said, “I have worked the whole day, from early morning, in toil, weariness, and hardship. I endured the heat and bore the burden of the whole day. What have I gained if my wage is the same as that of those who came last? Look, these men received one denarius for a single hour. Then twelve are owed to me, if you are just! A denarius for one hour, and one denarius for twelve hours—it is not justice for me to receive this way, as you say. No, employer, do not depart from your duty and let the one who works and the one who does not work be equal in your eyes.”

It is not because you gave more to the last workers that I complain; rather, I am bitter because you have wronged me. You gave these men more, and they received a denarius without labor. Look at me, who have labored, and give me more too, if you are good. Then the vineyard's owner, in his uprightness, began to rebuke that first worker, saying to him: Your wage is fixed. Why do you expect more? See, I have not wronged you. Do not blame me as though I were stingy. I agreed with you on one denarius when I hired you. Here is a good denarius; take it. Why are you complaining? If I gave your fellow worker more, what do you lose? For I have not wronged you under the agreement we made. If I am generous with what is mine, what have I deprived you of from what is yours? Look, I have given you one denarius, just as I promised. I did not agree on two, for I have only one; I give it to the last as well as to the first. I have not deprived you, lied to you, or shortchanged you. The agreement is clear, and my word stands. What is the complaint about? Perhaps you are envious and complain because I have given your fellow worker the same good wage as you.

Or do you think I have no right to do as I wish with what is mine? I will give equally to the last and to the first. Take what is yours, as agreed for you. And if I wish to make your fellow worker equal to you too, that is not your affair. In his compassion and with a good heart, the vineyard's owner gave wages to the last workers just as to the first. Now we must turn to the spiritual meaning and to the interpretation that clothes the saying in beauty. The Son's writings are like the sea, and within the sea a pearl lies cast down, hidden from the merchants. The interpreter descends after it like a diver, searches the depths, and brings the pearl up with him. Once it has been brought up, it is carried to the merchants, and they all profit from it when they acquire it. Like a diver, the mind descends into the reading to bring up with it the word of life, the pearl. O listeners, receive the word like merchants, and all of you profit from it and become spiritually rich. Someone who buys a pearl pays its price. Come, receive freely the word of life, which is full of riches. The mind descended and dived into the Scriptures, though it was unworthy,

and felt for and grasped the pearl of God's house. Now the tongue carries it to cast it before the listeners. Hang the daughter of light on your ears, and adorn yourselves with her. Our Lord opened his mouth in parables, as it is written, and on his lyre he sang riddles to the whole world. He veiled his words so that whoever cares about gaining benefit might uncover and see the hidden beauties in his parables. Let us now hear who the master of the house is, what the vineyard is, and who the workers hired by him are. And why did the owner of the vineyard hire workers in the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and even at the eleventh hour? And why, then, was that steward instructed to pay the last workers before the first? And what is that denarius which the steward gave alike to the last and to the first, without any addition? God himself, who established the worlds, is the master of the house, and the vineyard is the work of righteousness. The workers he hired are the human race, whom he called to live well and become heirs in the kingdom. The first workers were Adam's household, whom, at the beginning

of the world's morning, he brought to work in Eden. And that denarius which he had agreed to give the first is his beloved Son, whom he gave to the last at the end of the ages. And these workers of the third hour, if you look closely, are Noah's household, whom he set to his work. Those of the sixth hour are Abraham's household in the land of Aram, who clothed themselves all around in righteousness like the first. And these workers of the ninth hour are Moses the great, Joshua son of Nun, and the whole company of prophets. All the workers [?] God entered and were gathered into the Lord's vineyard, which is the course of righteousness. The path of the righteous proceeded from Adam himself, reached Noah, and continued onward until it came near Abraham. The path passed onward and reached Moses the great, of the ninth hour, who ran its course earnestly through the observances of righteousness. The workers labored diligently in the vineyard of the Beloved—those whom he hired at four different times and brought in. They all ran as they worked in righteousness: the households of Seth and Enosh, from the beginning of the great world. Noah's household was added to them and lived righteously; Abraham and Isaac arose and worked diligently.

Moses came, and with him the prophets of God. They became good workers in the vineyard and labored diligently in it. They stood like smiths and clothed themselves in love for the new life, and they labored well in the vineyard of spiritual fruits. They bore the burden of the evil world in their revelations and endured the disgrace of the love of worthless idols. They uprooted the thorns and thickets of error from the lands, and cleansed souls, like vines, of evil deeds. In chastity, purity, and holiness, they raised up their lives and produced the fruits of faith. After these, when the world was already nearing its end—as though to say, when the day was approaching sunset— the owner of the vineyard went out from the palace at the eleventh hour and saw the nations idle, unoccupied, and without work. Degraded and ruined, idle and lazy, dissolute people who slept the whole day without working. People who lived throughout the world without knowledge, without pursuing righteousness and uprightness. They did not enter and work faithfully in God's house, nor did they produce good fruit to glorify the owner of the vineyard. Instead, they passed their time in the world living evil lives. And in error [?] the time of the world in evil lives, and in the error of loving worthless idols.

The owner of the vineyard saw these people standing idle, and he began to [?], reproach them, and scorn them. “Why, people, are you idle all day, doing none of the work of righteousness? Why are you so asleep when it comes to good deeds, with no one calling out in righteousness and faith? Why have the times thus run out and lives come to an end while you sleep, without work or understanding? The day is setting; the world has reached its end. Get up, you idle people! Be diligent in this precious hour of repentance. Why have you remained idle while all the ages of the world have passed, without working in the blessed vineyard of God's house?” The nations say, “No one hired us to labor with him, and that is why we are idle and unoccupied. No law, no commandments, no observances, no prophets, and no revelations of the truth. No one hired us; no one taught us or gave us wisdom. No one asked us to enter and work in God's house. They called Abraham from Aram to the land of Canaan, and they called Isaac to be a sacrifice on the mountains of Jebus.

They called Jacob to the ladder of the heavenly beings; they led Joseph away to provide food in abundance for all Egypt. Moses is entrusted with prophetic revelations, and Aaron the priest enters confidently into God's presence. The Most High descends on Mount Sinai to the Hebrews, and the people eat bread freely given from the thick cloud. The congregation drinks blessed water from the rock, and the Jordan is split open so that she may enter and take possession of the Amorites' land. Joshua son of Nun uprooted high walls before her, and the sun was held back so that he could open the gates for her entrance. David is sent after her to bring her to God, and Samuel is pure and ministers to her in the place of atonement. Elijah threatens and devastates the land as he instructs her, and the prophets of the Most High are made servants for her. The prophets taught her, made promises to her, and agreed on her wages; through their persuasion they brought her in to work in God's house. But as for us, the nations, none of the seers hired us, nor were revelations sent to us from the Most High. No prophet from among us arose in our midst to prophesy to us, nor was there a herald to show us the vineyard where we could work.” And look, we have been left behind as though we were surplus and outsiders.

We are idle, empty, and unoccupied. There is no one to hire us, no one to seek us out, no one to advise us, and no paymaster to encourage us to labor with him. No one! Yet if there were someone to hire us, here we stand, ready to work diligently. The owner of the vineyard opened his gate to the nations of the earth, and all creation entered and worked in the house of God. At the end of the world, at the close of times and seasons, all the nations entered the great house at the eleventh hour. They diligently began the race of good deeds, and they wove righteousness and clothed themselves in it bodily. They broke and cast away their idols and images, and undertook an earnest race on the path of faith. They came to know the Father, believed in the Son, and honored the Spirit, and they all became chosen temples for the Godhead. They entered at the eleventh hour and justly received the denarius, which is our Lord, the reward of all righteousness. The first, who sowed and fell asleep with their generations, were left behind; and now the last carry the sheaf full of nourishment. The nations who were last became first through the body of the Son, for they put him on from within the waters of baptism.

Enosh, Noah, Abraham, and the household of Moses are far away, while the last workers have received the denarius and are now rich. The tax collector is justified, and look, the robber triumphs in the garden. The prostitute, too, kisses and embraces the Son of God. Moses is far away, while the sinful woman holds his feet and lovingly bathes him with oil and tears. Abraham, who longed to see his day, was left behind; and now all the nations gaze upon his crucifixion. After all the world's lifetimes had been spent and come to an end, the nations realized that God exists and immediately followed him. They entered at the eleventh hour and applied themselves diligently to repentance, and now they are clothed bodily in the Son of God. They came at the end, after all the ages had been completed, and now they have become first through the good news that is full of life. The last workers are the nations who entered at the eleventh hour, in the fivefold pattern by which the owner of the vineyard hired workers. The human body is sustained by five senses; the Law, which is full of mysteries, has five books. The Lord established five covenants with humanity; five times the owner of the vineyard hired workers. He established the first covenant with Adam among the trees,

and the second with Noah, the righteous man, son of [?]. The third was with Abraham, the good friend; the fourth was that of Moses, and the fifth that of the Son of God. In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and also at the eleventh; and there is no further covenant in the world [?]. A human being has no senses other than the five, and the right hand has only five slender fingers. There is no further teaching after the transaction of the crucifixion, for in the fifth stage the world reaches completion and attains its full measure. A human being, too, must ascend through five stages, as though by steps, and then reaches maturity and becomes a grown man. He is an infant, and afterward a little child; after being a boy, he becomes a youth, and then a grown man. There are infancy, early childhood, boyhood, and youth; then he reaches the stature of a grown man. Beyond this fifth stage there is no room for any further addition to the stages of human life. The world has reached the fifth stage, that of the cross. It has reached maturity and become a grown man, and it grows no further. The time of the infant, Adam the first, has passed, as has that of the little child, righteous Noah, who settled the earth;

And that of Abraham the boy, who ran with God, and the time of Moses, the watchful and godly youth. The last age has arrived and begun—the fifth, that of Christ. The ages have reached completion, and from now on it is the end, for anyone who understands. The morning when the workers entered the great vineyard has passed, and the time of the bright third hour has passed. The sixth hour and the hot ninth hour have passed and gone, and now the world is running through the cool eleventh hour. Noon has passed, and human love has grown cold. Evening has drawn near, and now the world totters, ready to come to its end. You of the eleventh hour, quicken your pace in repentance! You nations who came last, become first in righteousness! The Lord's word is very much like a pearl: to anyone who looks at it, it is filled throughout with radiant facets. To anyone who has spent most of his days in emptiness, the parable of the Son of God offers a helping hand. And to anyone who sinned in his boyhood and youth, and reached the end of the loom of his life while acting foolishly: You, old man, aching and bent with age, who wish to repent: enter at the eleventh hour, and you will be accepted.

An hour of life remains for you, and if you make an effort, in it you can find the whole of life without end. The evil one enticed you with desires while you were sinning. See that he does not shut the door before you when you repent. Do not let him say to you, “How can there still be any opportunity for you to be accepted in repentance, when you are incapable of work? You have no strength to bend yourself down in supplication, nor is it easy for you to undertake fasting like a diligent person. Your body does not lend itself to toil and weariness either. You have sinned greatly, and how will you find favor if you repent? Your strength has failed, your eyesight has diminished, and your body is weak. From now on, give up the work of righteousness.” The Evil One gives this advice to the sinner: to cut off his hope and not approach repentance. But you, worker who entered at the eleventh hour, do not doubt: your wages are ready alongside those of the first workers, if you repent. The last workers are dear to the Son of God, for he himself came to visit the earth at the end of the ages. The impetuousness of youth carried you away while you were sinning, and your days passed in the idleness of an evil life. Give God that little remainder of your life,

for he is willing to give a worker’s wage for a single hour. It has been demonstrated how our Lord gives wages, and he has testified how dear the last workers are. He encouraged anyone to repent: if he works for a single hour, he becomes one of the first. O sinner, who has spent the span of his years so badly, look! The giver of wages has his door open and is scattering his treasures. And if you repent at the end of your life, when wages are paid he takes account of you, though you were among the idle. If you have no strength for the labor of righteousness, give God your willingness itself, and it is accepted. Hate the sin you have practiced for so long, and give yourself to righteousness, which has never seen you. Turn away from wickedness, even now when your days are spent, and become a last worker who receives good wages. Sit down, judge yourself, and become your own accuser. When your conscience rebukes you, be ashamed of your evil deeds. Say to your soul, “O wanderer, sheep that has been lost, leave the shepherd even a trace, and he will find you.” Sins, those wolves, have savagely torn you apart among the mountains.

Enter the fold of the one who binds up the wounded sheep. The day has declined, and look! The shadows of death surround me. Be a sun for me at evening, our Lord, so that I may see your light. Do not let the day of death set on me outside your vineyard. Your eye is generous; accept an hour of repentance. My days have run their course while I worked at worthless things. Accept the final stretch of my life; let it be yours. There is no time that is not a time for repentance, and unless someone has reached the gate of Sheol, he has not lost it. As long as the soul remains and dwells in the body that has sinned, there is hope of repentance for all sinners. As long as blood flows through the arteries and the limbs, there is room for both sin and righteousness. As long as there are tears for the eyes to shed over the face, there is mercy to deliver the one who has sinned. As long as you can weep, you can ask for mercy; and if there is weeping, there is compassion for all sinners. Even the sick person, when he groans on a bed of pain, can easily receive forgiveness if he pleads for it. If someone draws near to God in a single hour, that hour is far better than a whole lifetime. Unless a person has entered Sheol and its bolts have been shut in his face,

he is not beyond the power of repentance. Unless the ship of life has reached the quiet grave, the cargo of riches is not taken away from those who repent. As long as you are alive, you can repent if you wish. But if death meets you, it snatches away your repentance. Only in the grave is the door of repentance shut, for the dead are not allowed to repent in the place of destruction. Even in the hour of death there is room for you to repent, and even then good deeds can be done, if you wish. Even when the soul stirs to rise out of the body's limbs, if it acquires a good resolve, it will find life. When death enters, stands at the door, and shoots its arrow, hurry and set your affairs in order righteously. If anyone has been robbed, return what you took, and then depart, lest the person you robbed bring a complaint and cause you distress through it. If there is a worker who has not received his wages, pay him what is his, so that you will not stand accused at the crossing if he meets you. If a widow has been wronged by you, call her and release her, before her voice shakes the door of the Judge's house. If you have taken anything from an orphan, give him what is his, for at that door the complaint of orphans is readily accepted.

If a time of laxity has caught you in bodily sins, send gifts to the monks and the holy ones. Plead, weep, lay yourself bare, and uncover your wound. Ask them to beg for mercy on your behalf. It is still an hour of life, and there is room for righteousness. You have entered at the eleventh hour: hasten your race of good deeds. Look at the house that has been amassed for you through anxious care, and use it to buy yourself water for the fire that threatens you. Bring out and distribute a ragged cloth to one person, a garment to another; clothing to this one, a covering to that one, and bread to another. Call the poor and the beggars, and through their hands send a bribe to the fire, so that it will be still when you pass through. Ask your heirs, plead with them, and disregard them, so that they will not be distressed if you take care to save your soul. Whoever is distressed should be regarded [?] by you as a great enemy, for he wants you to burn while he inherits your possessions. Rouse yourself to seek what benefits you at the hour of death, so that by every means you may bandage the many wounds within you. Tear up the debt documents and throw them into the fire: it will accept them from you. If you give it debt documents, it will be satisfied and will not approach you.

You have run through the world and toiled greatly for emptiness. Make provision for yourself before the door is shut in your face. You have no excuse to say, “No one has hired me,” for the master who hires is stretched out on the cross and is waiting for you. Look, his hands are outstretched, and he stands on Golgotha, calling everyone to come into the vineyard of righteousness. He cried out loudly on the cross, and the earth trembled. He awakened all the idle to repentance. Look, the denarius is placed in your hand: his body, which he broke. He appointed you to work for a good wage. Why are you idle? He has made you the envy of both the first and those in between. Be wise in the hour of life that remains to you. Make friends for yourself with the unrighteous wealth you have acquired, so that they may welcome you into their radiant dwellings. Pay your debts while you are in your own country, among those who know you, for in that other country every debt is exacted with fire. Look at the cross as at that bronze serpent, and ask it for medicine that heals your wounds. You have only an hour. Seek forgiveness in faith, for faith never returns without receiving everything it asks for.

Even the robber was fastened with nails and was [?], and the arrows of death were striking him at Golgotha. In that very hour of death he asked for mercy and found it, just as he had asked, because he asked in faith. Through the good wage he gave to those who came last, he gave encouragement to anyone who comes to repentance at the end of his days. So the world may learn that he welcomes everyone who comes. Blessed is the First, who gave a good wage to those who came last!
Here ends the homily on the workers whom the master of the vineyard hired.
By Mar Jacob. Homily 55. On Zacchaeus the tax collector.

For the sake of the wicked, our Lord set his course through the world, to gather those who had wandered from his Father’s house. He directed his journey toward sinners to bring them back, and sought out those who had gone astray so that they might be found, for they were lost. He left those who had been found and zealously sought the lost.

He left the perfect and went about among the repentant. He accepted kisses from a prostitute. They invited him to be with sinners, and he would feast. He was called a friend of tax collectors and prostitutes. He carried bandages and loved none but the broken. The good physician did not come down to bandage the healthy, for only the sick needed his help. Someone who has not died has no need of resurrection, and forgiveness is unnecessary for someone who has not sinned. Someone who is broken seeks a bandage to be applied to him, and someone who is wounded calls for the physician to come to him. Medicine for sores is never applied except to sores; only the sick seek a dressing for diseases. The brokenhearted need only encouragement, and those distressed in spirit urgently need consolation. Anyone who has sores needs medicines, so that, as he is healed, his wounds may find relief. Whoever greatly loves his creditor has his soul hanging on forgiveness, because he is in need. Anyone whose soul has been wounded by wrongdoing and who feels the pain of his wound—

it is fitting that the medicine of mercy should be brought to him. Anyone whom sins have bitten and who cries out with understanding needs a healer to devise a remedy for him. Anyone whose limbs have been struck by the arrow of wickedness seeks compassion to draw out the shaft of his suffering. Anyone upon whom sin has fallen like a lioness seeks mercy to rescue him from destruction. Rightly, then, did our Savior come to sinners, to visit them as a healer visits the wounded. Through Zacchaeus the tax collector, he made a marketplace for repentance, so that everyone might come and trade in it without hindrance. Through that plunderer he gave encouragement to evildoers: if they repent, they will not be held captive by justice. He placed him before their eyes like a mirror, for them to look into: if they turn back, their offenses will not be remembered. Who would cut off his soul's hope while looking at him—the companion of tax collectors who became a companion in the apostles' ministry? Who could think that his debts would not be forgiven when he sees the extortioner mingling with the disciples? Who would not run to take refuge in repentance,

which has the power to turn even hawks into doves? Who would not follow this good shepherd, who catches wolves so that they may become lambs within his flock? Who hates his own life so much that he would flee from this physician, whose power triumphs over wounds? He mingled the tax collector with the disciples as a means of awakening in extortioners a desire to imitate him. Who would not marvel at whom the Son of God caught—the greedy tax collector, to become an apostle to the repentant? This man had filled his house with plunder drawn from people's groans, and had amassed abundant loot that was not his. This man had seized everything he could find from merchants, and did not know how to conduct himself without extortion. This man had sinned openly all his days, empowered by the law and by authority. He sinned confidently and made use of authority; he practiced wrongdoing with his face uncovered as he did it. His sin was public, yet the judges did not censure it; his wickedness was known, yet they did not rebuke him for doing it. The conduct of the tax collector and the prostitute is open wickedness.

The sinner does not steal in disguise to avoid being exposed. He seizes things while people are watching him and does not hide it; he plunders while they look at him and feels no shame. Sin rebels against concealment and [?] the law; it does not hide from onlookers when it is practiced. The tax collector’s wrongdoing loudly proclaims the one who practices it: daily plunder, renewed in every form. This man had heard that Jesus was passing through the land of Judah, and he went out after him in love, to look at him discerningly. He was sick with wrongdoing and heard the news of the physician who had come. He carried his pain and went out to see him, so that [?] he might bandage him. There was a great, stubborn sore in his soul, and he hurried to bring it out to our Lord, the medicine of life. Greed saw that righteous Son and shut its mouth; with good thoughts it stood to gaze at him. The plunderer heard, “Look, the Judge is passing by,” and abandoned the habits by which he had lived. Through grace, light had dawned in Zacchaeus’s soul, and he recognized the Son as the one who forgives sins, in whom he could take refuge. He had entered repentance as though entering a walled city,

to take shelter there from that marauding band of greed. The wandering sheep had heard the news of the shepherd who had come, and ran after him to gather itself into his flock. He saw the great crowds surrounding him and the ranks of people running eagerly ahead of him. His soul yearned to see the Son, but the crowds would not let him: they pressed in from every side to cling to him. He was short, and the people were crowding together—what could he do? His pain was severe, and the physician was hidden from his sight. Oppressed by sins, he longed to see the one who had come to visit. The little man was held back by the great crowd and could not manage to see the Son whom he loved. Zacchaeus was not as small [?] as he was in appearance, for he was broader and wider even than the world. He was shorter than many of those near him, but in his love his mind passed even beyond the clouds. If you look discerningly at this man, he was a renowned giant in his lofty understanding. A great soul was visible in a small body; its stature rose above created things and their structures.

His limbs were short, but his thoughts reached far. He was small in appearance, but on examination greater than many. He saw that he could not manage to see the Son as he wished, and the wise man ran to a fig tree to carry out his plan. And Zacchaeus was saying these things to the fig tree: “Make a way for me, as you have been accustomed to do from the beginning. “You clothed Adam with leaves when he was exposed; through you let my need now be met, so that I may see the Son. “Give me your height. Let me climb up and stand on your branches, and gaze upon the Lord of Eden, who has come to visit us. “Make room for me at your lofty top, so that I may stand and see the one who made all trees grow, together with the Father who begot him. “Bear with me a little while I look and gaze upon the fruit of life sent to us from the Most High. “I am short, and unless I stand upon your height, I cannot manage to see your Lord among the crowds. “I have no height, and you have no fruit, for you are bare. Be height for me, and I will be fruit upon you. “Make up for my lack of height when I climb you, and I, in return, will fill the place of fruit upon you.”

The wise man climbed up and stood in the fig tree, and there he gazed upon our Lord as he approached, with the crowds surrounding him. His short stature was not enough for his faith, so he added borrowed height to himself, that he might see the Son. Love drew him, and he climbed up and stood upon the tree, so that his whole vision might be filled with the Son of God. He saw that he was low down and could not manage to see the Son, so he seized a height that was not his own and stood gazing upon him. His faith had made him a new stature, so that in a single moment he might grow taller than the entire crowd. The lowly man climbed up and stood high upon the tree, to see how far the Exalted One had descended into lowliness. He had raised himself to gaze upon the one who had lowered himself; he had climbed to the heights to look upon the one who had come into the depths. The chief tax collector gazed upon our Lord and was made righteous. He saw him from afar and loved him as though he were near. Zacchaeus, the chief of extortioners, had been bitten by the hidden serpent. He gazed upon the Son, and the venom subsided in his limbs. The biter’s wound had caused him pain when he became aware of it, and he ran to see the one through whose symbol the Hebrews had received life. Our Lord took the place of that bronze serpent

for the chief tax collector, whom wickedness had bitten like a viper. Sin had spread through his soul like venom, and when he gazed upon the Son, it subsided within him, and he was made righteous. The sight of our Lord made the tax collector a new creation, for as soon as he gazed upon him, he was changed from his wicked ways. He merely gazed upon him and found complete righteousness, for wherever one desires to look, love does its work. Whoever looks at something with desire and affection has willingly entered into fellowship with it, even though he is not near it. The impulses of desire bring a creation into being in a godlike way—either building up or overthrowing the one who possesses desire. Hateful desire commits wrongdoing even by its gaze, but true desire is wholly united with God. From the tree Zacchaeus saw God with longing, and the fervor of his love united him with him in fellowship. Whatever a person's soul longs to contemplate, however far away it is, it is near because of his love. There is no mountain that can keep desire from union, for as it gazes, it is wholly united with what it beholds. Zacchaeus stood far away from the entire crowd;

and because he gazed at Christ with longing, Christ united him with himself. The fire of love had blazed fiercely within him. He gazed at the Son and, with longing, carried him in his thoughts. If love had not performed its work there, who would have been farther from our Savior than Zacchaeus? Outside the crowd he stood upon a fig tree to contemplate him, but love brought him closer than everyone who was there. He gazed with love and beheld the Son with longing. Who else was as close as he was? And while his blessed gaze thirsted for our Savior and drank from him as from a spring full of life, and while he seized the Son with his eyes from among the crowds, so that he alone might delight in him, the sweet fruit, and while he rejoiced that he had found a place to his liking, high enough for him to see the one he loved, then our Lord looked at the tree as he passed and saw Zacchaeus standing on its branches. He looked at him with love and began to speak to him: “Come, Zacchaeus! I too have seen you, just as you have seen me. Come, tax collector! Be my apostle to those who repent,

and teach them that I have mercy and forgiveness. Come, sinner! Go out and proclaim me with my disciples, for I welcome whoever turns away from his evil deeds. Come down, plunderer, and run along the road of proclamation! Proclaim hope to the wicked [?] in a loud voice. Come, I will send you to the wicked to teach them that I have compassion and welcome whoever seeks me. Come, let me paint a beautiful picture of repentance, so that the whole world may long for you and imitate you. Come, be an advocate for my mercy toward sinners, for I greatly desire to forgive the sins of whoever seeks me. Through you let peoples, worlds, and lands learn of me: that I am a shepherd, and the wandering sheep is dear to me. Come down, Zacchaeus! I must be in your house today. Come down and prepare for me, for I will delight in your hospitality.” This is the guest who came of his own accord, by his own will; though they had not invited him, he made himself ready for the evening meal. He did not ask him, but said, “I am staying at your house.” He saw love in him and was very glad to go with him. Oh, the farmer who cultivated the rebellious soil until he could turn even weeds into wheat!

He poured the water of his teaching over the evil thorns until they bore sweet fruit throughout the whole world. He accepted tears from the prostitute as firstfruits, and made the chief tax collector an apostle merely by looking at him. He brought fruit even out of rocks through his persistence; even flints gave him drops of water when he demanded them. In the wilderness, bread; in inhabited country, good wine; for the hungry, satisfaction; and for the sick, every kind of help. He passed through no place without collecting tribute from it, for he demanded that even the barren fig tree give him fruit. From the sea he took a coin in an extraordinary way, and from that tree devoid of fruit, a sweet fruit. Lovely is the fruit of this tasteless fig tree, which Christ plucked from its branches as he passed by. He saw Zacchaeus like an early fig in the tree, and hurried to pluck him so that he could enjoy his sweet taste. Not even in Eden had he ever found fruit like the fruit he plucked from that fig tree as he passed near Jericho. He was not like Adam, who fled among the trees and took leaves from that fig tree, but nothing more. He eagerly longed to see the Son from the tree,

unlike Adam, who hid from the Creator. He had ripened in love and was full of the flavor of repentance, until he became so sweet that he could be offered even to God. From Jericho and from that tasteless fig tree, Christ produced this fruit through his skill. The ruined city and the tree devoid of produce gave the gospel a sweet specimen, so that it might be honored through him. Great is the power of repentance when it shines forth, for it has the strength to rebuild even ruins. It produces fruit where there is no yield at all; in Jericho it hung a lovely cluster on a barren tree. The Son of God did new things on the road he took, and by every means he draws the world to repentance. He took Zacchaeus from among sinners as firstfruits, to be a model for those who come to repentance. “Come down, Zacchaeus!” And the discerning man hurried down, to welcome the Lord of kings with a good heart. He was eager to bring inside the great wealth he had encountered, for he had not expected to find such a treasure. The greedy tax collector had set his eye on the merchant, and led him inside to plunder great wealth from him.

He saw a load of mercy passing along the road there, and eagerly brought it inside, so that all of it might lodge in his house. A caravan came down, carrying compassion from the Most High. Zacchaeus seized it to take his share before letting it go. The chief tax collector seized the company laden with blessings, which had come down from that hidden place to those on earth. With love he seized that merchant of mercy who had come, and brought him into his house to grow rich from his treasures. Oh, Zacchaeus, you seize both earthly and heavenly things! You plunder people, and you also lodge God in your house. All the merchants are plundered by you along their routes. Oppressed orphans cry out against you over their accounts. All travelers complain about you at their stopping places. Those lodging there also grumble against you in their lodgings. Mercies came down and walked upon the earth, and you seized them. Compassion was coming from the Most High, and you welcomed it. Grace came to pass through your region, and you seized it too. Forgiveness dawned upon the world, and you boldly plundered it. The gift of peace came to earth, and now it is in your house. You boldly and diligently strove to gain heaven and earth. You have defeated me, Zacchaeus, and I do not know what to call you.

I stand amazed at you, O victorious one, full of victory! Should I call you a tax collector? You are an apostle to the repentant. You are a disciple, O plunderer among robbers! You are skilled in all these things, and I am too weak to speak of you: a chief among tax collectors, a kinsman and companion of the apostles. Your wealth is in the world, and your name shines in apostleship. You are not destitute, and your praise is mingled with that of the disciples. You are secure in possessions and diligent about revenues. You have it in you to seize, and giving things away is not difficult for you either. You are nimble and adept at gathering and scattering. You have the power to act unjustly, to plunder, and to give alms. In one place your hand is full of robbery and plunder; on the other side it distributes all kinds of alms to everyone. There is wrongdoing in your way of life, yet the Son of God is inside your house. That is why you have defeated me, so that I must cease praising you. The Son of God invited himself to Zacchaeus’s house to give life to those who needed forgiveness. The physician entered to drive out the diseases of wrongdoing, and the blind crowds reproached him while he was healing. “Why has this man entered the house of a tax collector full of evil deeds? Why does he mingle with sinners and love them?

Why does he not turn away from the wicked and leave them? And because of this he mingles and lives at peace with evildoers. Why does he not reject those who practice wrongdoing, if he is true? Why does he eat with the wicked, and why are they dear to him?” The shepherd was reproached while searching for the sheep that had strayed, but he was intent on his search like a diligent worker. The caregiver was diligent, cutting open the abscesses of hateful wrongdoing, and they grumbled against him because he was healing the wounded. Hope for the wicked and for sinners at that banquet, where the forgiver of sins reclined among the repentant. Zacchaeus saw the great wealth that had entered his hall, and he despised his possessions so that he could acquire the treasure he had found. His soul was enlightened, and he saw that the world's wealth was unjust. He began seeking to cast it away from himself by distributing it among many. He saw the Lord of the world reclining at his banquet, and he despised the world and began to flee from its evils. He approached with discernment and bowed down to the Son, saying to him, “I worship you, the physician who visited me when I was wounded. “Let the soul stained with wounds give thanks to you, my Lord, so that, polished by your mercy, it may see your beauty clearly. “The wounded man, full of many sores, begs you:

“Do not shrink from tending my wounds with your care. “Let my feeble mouth give thanks to your mouth, which called sweet words into my ears so that I would turn to you away from stumbling blocks. “Let my lips kiss your footsteps, physician full of remedies, for since you visited me, my limbs that were sick have found relief. “I will lick the dust from your holy footprints, for by your footsteps you drove away the injustice that dwelt with me. “Let half my possessions be the payment for your feet, physician, for I was not worthy of your visit, that you should come to me. “Everything I have taken away I will repay, my Lord, rejoicing, and I will turn the injustice I have practiced into righteousness. “What I plundered I will return with interest, and everything I seized I will repay many times over to the person who was robbed. “Far be it from me, from now on, to let injustice enter through my gates or let hateful wickedness be practiced within my halls. “The gate through which the great King entered to stay with me—I will never again open it for sin to enter.” Christ performed a great deed at that banquet, for it was not merely to eat bread that he hungered without a purpose. There in the tax collector's house he held a great wedding feast for repentance, and he invited all sinners to it.

It was a feast at which righteousness was being gained, and our Lord went to rejoice there with the repentant. The Son of the Righteous One entered and drove out the injustice that was there, for darkness could not dwell with the light. Zacchaeus began to scatter his possessions among the needy, and he distributed all his property among those in distress. He carried alms on his right and on his left, and he diligently distributed them with both hands. He was as eager to scatter as he had been eager to gather, for in every respect he was diligent in whatever he undertook. His gates stood open, and he carried things out to those outside. He raised his voice, calling for everyone who had been plundered to come and receive. “You who have been robbed, come and take what is yours from the robber! It is the day of repayment; let no one delay in coming to me.” Come, poor people, receive alms from an oppressor! Needy people of the land, help me a little to distribute my possessions. O needy people, become my workers for good wages! Carry away and remove this injustice that my sins have piled up. It was fitting for him to hurry to give alms and scatter his possessions among everyone who came from every direction. The plunder that had come in little by little while he rejoiced,

he brought out and gave away in a single hour, rejoicing. He had seen the Son, and his eye was filled with his beauty; he could no longer look lovingly upon the world. Christ had yoked him to the light yoke of apostleship; would it have been right for him to bend his shoulder toward Mammon? He pledged half his possessions to the gospel when it met him, and he did not delay in going out to give what he had promised. His hands were full of alms to distribute; his eyes were open toward the poor, ready to welcome them. His feet ran along the roads toward passersby, so that he could lovingly distribute his possessions to anyone in need. This was the work he was doing at that banquet, while fools complained, “Why is he eating with sinners?” Bringing a dead man back to life after he had decayed was not as great as this: that a tax collector should become an apostle. Yes, truly, it was a miracle full of wonder that a greedy man should distribute and scatter everything he owned. For a soul to come to life out of wickedness is greater than for a body to rise from decay. This is the great sign that the Son of God performed: in a single moment he made a sinner into a righteous man. Where are the crowds who complained when he was entering

the tax collector’s house to eat bread with sinners? They did not know enough to look at him and see what he was doing. He was wise at heart and was acting for their benefit. That discerning fisherman cast a hook and, in his mercy, caught the ruler of the whole town. He had enclosed the chief tax collector in the [?] that he cast there, for no one had ever caught anyone this way except our Lord. The Son of God cast his net into the sea of the world. It enclosed the tax collector and drew in his possessions along with him. If our Lord had not gone in to eat bread there, this catch would not have entered this net. If he had passed by and had not agreed to come to him, the man would not have found this opportunity for repentance. For he knew what he was doing wherever he was, and for this reason he was not afraid of criticism. Our Lord saw Zacchaeus and rejoiced in the boy he had gained, and he began to call him a son of Abraham because of his love. “Today,” he said, “life has come to this house,” for life dawned in it, and death, which had reigned there, fled. Here is encouragement for all the wicked and for sinners: through repentance they can become good.
Here are the new things the Son of God did along his way. Blessed is he who proclaimed good news to humanity!
Here ends the discourse on Zacchaeus the tax collector and the meal.
Again, Discourse 56: On the Rich Man and Lazarus.

To you, the Giver, I entrust my requests as I worship, and from you I will receive everything I need whenever I ask. Trusting in you, my Lord, I will set out my petition with discernment; by your will, abundantly supply what I lack. Stir in me the will to entrust my life to your will, so that I may live well for you, my Lord, even now. Make a spring flow within me, gushing with living water, so that the flock purchased with your blood may drink from your fountain. Your symbol pierced the rock that brought forth rivers; let your cross stir my soul with wonder, so that it may bring forth accounts of you.

The barren soul, too, resembles the barren rock. Make it bring forth discourses about you, for even the rock brought forth rivers. Your praise can easily be spoken even by stones; how much more by souls that are aware of you! My Lord, may I not fall silent from praising your divinity, lest stones take my place before you if I am silent. It is written, “If you fall silent, the stones will cry out.” So I will cry out, lest the stones be called upon to praise in my place. Give silence to the stone and fitting speech to me, my Lord, so that a speaking mouth may voice your praise with discernment. Our praise does not benefit God, O discerning people, for he is exalted and glorious as he is, and full of blessings. Whoever strives to praise him is himself helped. Let us therefore fill our mouths with praise, so that through it we may benefit. He gives abundant rewards to those who praise him; although praise does not benefit him, he buys it for a price. Although the one who praises him gains greatly throughout his life, he has also pledged to give him the kingdom as the reward for his praise. But to whoever withholds praise he has promised hell, so that by threatening him he may win him over to spiritual life. As for the lazy man who kept his talent without making a profit:

He banished him to chains and stocks and to dreadful darkness. He greatly frightens the idle and casts terror upon them, so that by threatening them he may benefit them when they draw near to him. By every means he seeks for everyone to gain life, so that by every possible way he may gather the worlds to his Father. He opened the kingdom to entice the weak through it, and established hell to frighten the slack through it. And look, he uses encouragements and terrors as means to bind human beings to himself in love. For someone who loves, neither the kingdom nor Gehenna is the reason for binding his love to God. Love seeks neither encouragement nor terror, for it is bound bodily to God without any other motive. For someone who stands at that level of great love, both the kingdom and Gehenna are superfluous. He is not stirred by payment to serve God. He fulfills God's desire, for he does not look to the reward that comes from him. Nor does the fire frighten him into fleeing evil, for he utterly hates evil deeds without being frightened. And as for someone whose love is thus close to God,

he neither entices him nor frightens him, because he belongs to him. But when someone slips from that level of love and falls, God draws near, encouraging, supporting, and heartening him. He opens the kingdom, sets out promises, and multiplies blessings, so that he might win him over to himself, even through the reward he promises him. And for someone who is weary and unwilling even to be a hired worker, he lights the fire, kindles Gehenna, and threatens him, so that through threats, terrors, and warnings, he may fear him and not approach evil. Thus there are three orders of righteousness, and through all three runs the road to the house of God. One is motivated by love, the second by reward, and the third by a person's dread of Gehenna. The one who loves is an heir, for he does not work for a fixed wage, as it is written: “Everything that is mine is yours.” Then again, someone who longs for the kingdom of God is an honest hired worker who receives his wages with confidence. And someone who fears Gehenna, while being righteous, is a good servant who keeps himself from harm. There are three groups in the Father's house who are dear to him: hired workers, servants, and also children, who are his heirs.

The servant fears blows, and this is very good, for as long as he is afraid, he does nothing wrong in his work. The worker rejoices in good wages and is encouraged by them, and for their sake he works all the more diligently. But the son, whose love is bound to his father in his very soul, truly loves him and cherishes him affectionately. Nature moves him to love his father, though he does not know why he loves his father, except that he is his father. And even if he has neither a kingdom nor Gehenna, the son loves and honors him because he is his father. Among the discerning, God is loved because he is God, and they serve him without any other motive, out of love for him. Another person labors for the blessings reserved for him; this too is the second form of excellence in the house of God. Another is virtuous because of the terrifying report of the fire; to avoid being burned, he does not go near evil deeds. But now let us show ourselves in which rank we are recognized, and in which order we possess goodness. Let us reflect and pursue what is good.

Children love, hired workers work, and slaves fear; but we neither love nor work nor fear. For we are not close to the love that belongs to children, nor have we entered into the work that belongs to hired workers. We do not fear blows as slaves do. Whom in the household do we resemble? Not a single order. We have not remained in the high rank that belongs to children, nor have we persevered in the work that belongs to hired workers. The fear that belongs to slaves has been taken from us and has departed, so that we do not even have a place in the house where we can remain. Evil deeds have placed us far from God; they have made us strangers to him. Where shall we go? He called us children, numbered us among hired workers, and placed us among slaves; but we have abandoned all three orders and wandered away. He formed us in his image: this is the portion that belongs to children, that we should be with him, [?] what is his, and become like him. Because we abandoned him and forgot the love of his fatherhood, he came down and stirred us to work with him and receive our wages. When he saw that even this was tiresome to us, he threatened us with fire, so that we might turn back to him in fear.

He revealed and showed us the abyss of fire and the great pit of flame, so that we might run to him in terror. The Father's only Son mercifully made us his brothers, and revealed and made known to us all the mysteries in his Father's house. He told us about Gehenna and the rich man, and about Lazarus [?] the kingdom of God's household. He wanted to tell us about the chasm between them, and how the two sides see one another in great suffering. He revealed to us the mysteries of what is there before we go, so that the report of judgment might correct us in place of punishment. When he came, he brought frightening reports to our land, to warn us through his accounts of the great judgment. He wanted to teach us the customs of the land from which he came, so that we might be prepared to face the fire that threatens us. He saw the rich man burning in Gehenna, and came and revealed this to us to rescue us from his torment. He disclosed one event among the events of that land, so that when we heard it, our hearts might recoil from evil deeds. He loved us greatly, and to let us know how much he loved us, he disclosed the mystery of the new world for our sake.

He would not have revealed the mystery of his world in our evil world if he were not showing us his love so clearly. He revealed the hidden things in his Father's house to assure us that he had made us his confidants, friends, and brothers. He showed in our own place what took place there in its own realm, so that before going there one might learn what happens there. Who would have known the dreadful story of that rich man if our Lord had not revealed his story to warn us? Or who would have known the story of that Lazarus if he himself had not told it to encourage those in need? Because the new world was hidden and invisible to us, he came and showed us its whole story through a single event. Through that Lazarus, wretched with sores, whose story he told, he taught this: those in need should not complain. And through the proud rich man whom he showed us, he also taught us how fitting the fire of [?] is for the rich. In his teaching he taught that no one should amass gold, and then he showed the rich man burning. This was so that everyone might know, from what happened to [?], that wealth prepares fire for its owners if they acquire it.

On another occasion he pronounced woe upon the rich, but the reason for that woe was not made clear there. Through that rich man who was tormented, whose story he told, he showed everyone why there is woe for the rich. He also pronounced a blessing upon all the poor, but it was not clear why he said, “Blessed are the poor.” Once it was heard how greatly Lazarus had been exalted, the blessing he pronounced upon the poor was explained through him. Our Lord’s word is entirely light for those who hear it, and it is wholly filled with hope, life, and every benefit. He spoke so that we might benefit. Let us therefore benefit from his teaching, so that his word may be fruitful among those with discernment. When he told the story of Lazarus and the rich man, what need was there to bring their deeds to light, except to benefit humanity through their stories, and to help all who hear through what was revealed about them? Let us therefore direct our discourse toward what is beneficial, and speak about this only in order to help. In the dreadful story of that rich man in Gehenna, the speaker has abundant material for every kind of benefit.

Let us all listen with discernment now, and let his story benefit us as it is told. It is written in the Gospel that there was a rich man who wore fine linen and purple, and was proud and boastful. He indulged himself, fattened himself, and exalted himself, living every day in complete arrogance and conceit. A wretched poor man lay opposite his gate, needy and distressed, despised and deprived, and full of pain. He longed to fill his stomach with the crumbs of that rich man who was opposite him, but they gave him nothing. That poor man was full of sores and wounds, and the dogs kept licking his ulcers. Listen, you who have discernment, to the account of the rich man and Lazarus, their lives, and the differences in their conduct. That poor man was not merely reduced to poverty; he was also tormented by pain, as you have heard. He was battered by poverty and illness. There are two evils in the world, and both were with him. Want and sickness surrounded him, and he was battered by both without grumbling. For someone poor and healthy was better off than a sick rich person.

Yet someone rich and sick finds comfort in his wealth. Set healthy strength against gold, listener, and compare poverty with sickness, weighing them equally. Where either one presses upon a person, he bears it with great suffering and becomes bitter. But when both are present, anyone who can face them without grumbling is far more victorious than other victors. Look: Lazarus was poor and sick, lacking bread and covered with sores and pains every day. When there is suffering, friends, if there are any, are a comfort: they strengthen the heart, and through their conversation suffering subsides. But Lazarus did not even have friends in our land, and so dogs became his companions. Our whole world's face is stained with favoritism, and it knows how to love the rich insincerely. For its love follows fortune, and anyone to whom fortune lends a hand, it loves greatly and honors unjustly. But the poor man has neither friends nor relatives, because the world's love is not for God but for outward appearances. But if someone is poor and lies helpless, who acknowledges him,

except dogs like those that gathered beside Lazarus? He was covered with sores, but doctors would not touch him, because he had no fee to give them, since he was destitute. He was deprived of friends, food, and health; he had sores and poverty, and dogs were his companions. He had no possessions in which to find comfort and forget his sufferings, nor health from which to take courage in his destitution. He did not even have friends to strengthen his heart in his troubles: dogs, pains, and want—and nothing else. There was no one to bandage his many sores, and no one to support his heart, broken by need. He was in pain, hungry, and full of misery. What could he do? Yet even in such a condition he did not complain, because he was discerning. Now hear also about the rich man at whose gate he lay, thrown down and abandoned: how proudly he lived, surrounded by good things. His body was healthy, and he was rich in possessions. His clothing was splendid, and his food was excellent. His table was full, his house resounded, and his estate was imposing. He was rich and healthy, and everyone loved and honored him. Fine clothing, a healthy body, and a full purse;

a splendid life and every good thing, without any losses. He rejoiced in his wealth, was proud of his clothes, and looked splendid in every way. He lived comfortably and in good health, and paid no attention to the poor man. But Lazarus lay at this proud man's gate, full of misery, seeing the good things and yet not complaining. He longed only to satisfy his hunger with crumbs; he did not ask for the luxuries that were there. He was not eager for clothing or wealth, nor for the many dishes on the table. He needed only the crumbs that dogs eat. Even this his nature demanded, and only then did he long for it. If his nature had not stirred up great hunger, he would not, of his own choice [?], have longed even for crumbs. Desire is hateful when someone asks for luxuries, but when nature demands what belongs to it, that is proper. For someone to long for daily bread is natural; but when he seeks a variety of dishes, his desire is death. That discerning man did not even desire a whole loaf, but only to satisfy himself with crumbs and relieve his hunger. When his nature rose against him and pressed him like a creditor,

he longed for little things to offer it. He longed to fill his belly with crumbs, but not even this was given to him, so that his virtue might increase. He longed, but he did not blaspheme, nor did he grumble against the one who had given him poverty. The lot of poverty had come to him from God, and because he knew it was from God, he accepted it and remained silent. He was patient in hunger, illness, and need, and bore his pain like a discerning man, without complaint. Thus he bore poverty without grumbling, as a gift that had been given to him by God. He looked to God, who apportions wealth and poverty, and did not grumble because God had given him poverty. He regarded the one who apportions as upright and discerning. He did not consider himself wronged, but considered the one who apportions to be just. A sick body and an empty house fell to the afflicted man's lot, and he did not seek to change what had fallen to him, because it was just. He saw that his portion contained neither wealth nor possessions, and he did not long to acquire what was not his. He saw the crumbs that were going to waste at the rich man's house, and only then did he long for these to be given to him.

If they had been useful or of benefit in the rich man's house, he would not have coveted them, lest he be condemned by justice. He desired them after they had fallen from the table, when they were being trampled underfoot, so that the master of the house would suffer no loss. He longed for the things that had been lost, but they did not come to him; and he continued to endure his poverty without complaining. He did not envy the rich man, his table, his clothing, his health, or his comforts. His desire stooped to the crumbs, seeking them; and when they did not come to him, he remained quiet and gave up even on these. But the rich man lived in pleasure and pride, without looking at the wretched man who lay at his gate, full of pain. His eyes were haughty, his heart carefree, and his whole being joyful. He despised the afflicted man, though that man never went far from his gate. He went out puffed up and came in arrogant; he sat down proudly and stood up grandly; he went away cheerful and returned rejoicing. He lay down enjoying himself, reclined and fattened himself, splendid in his clothes; he reclined over delicacies, dwelt amid comforts, and occupied himself with displays of pride. His house was secure, his belly full, and his body healthy; all the good things in the world were his in abundance. But Lazarus was sick and poor, brought low and destitute,

ill and hungry, distressed and abandoned, despised and deprived. His belly was empty, his dwelling desolate, and he was covered with sores. He had pains and a miserable life, and he endured tremors. His misery grew severe, his distress increased, and his torment lasted long. His appointed end arrived, when he would leave the world and its miseries behind. His weary ship was being driven about in a world of pain, and it drew alongside death as though it were a harbor offering rest. Poverty rose against him like a surging wave, and pains pursued him like storms on the great sea. Because he was wise, he steered his ship without loss, and from amid his sufferings he gathered merchandise of great value. One day at a time, his miserable life slipped away, and like a merchant he entered a dwelling full of rest. The years of suffering and distress pushed one another along, and he passed through them all like a shadow, until they were no longer noticed. He gathered up his years and endured his days with sighs. His weary journey came to an end, and he entered rest. He leaped and strode onward. The months of his pain, one after another, toppled over one another, passed away, and moved toward their end. Evening [?] and morning carried him along, bearing him from one to the next,

and he left behind all those harsh times and their pains. The wheel of his life turned toward its end; it carried him out of suffering and set him in a lofty place. Lazarus died—yes, truly, his death was rest. But perhaps I should say that he came to life, for he had been dead while alive. The poor man fell from the dunghill into the royal palace; he slipped from his place into the glorious place of a good life. He fell from the depths, and the heights of Abraham’s dwelling received him. The suffering man died—or, one might say, he came to life, for he had been dying. Lazarus died, and the children of light gathered to honor him. The heavenly ranks received him with a great procession to pay him honor. The angels spread out their holy robes, and they laid crowns of light along his road to the kingdom. The heavenly armies extended their ranks so that the man worn out by pain might come to the home of the angels. Clouds of light, like white sponges, passed over his sores, and he forgot his wounds. Diseases fled, and pain and poverty ended. The man entered and stood in the land of blessings and splendor. The angels came out and bound a crown on him as on a bridegroom.

They escorted him in procession and brought him in to see the bridal chamber in Abraham’s dwelling. The courageous man passed joyfully through terrifying regions, and through the dreadful passage of fire, without trembling. Companies of light accompanied him as he traveled through the dreadful sea filled with darkness, and he was not afraid. The ready company of Gabriel’s household crossed with him through the realm of death, and he did not tremble like a weak man. He crossed the great abyss with the help of Michael’s household. They carried him and placed him beside Abraham in the kingdom. He had descended to the station of poverty like a diligent worker. Without grumbling, he triumphed in it and ascended like a victor. He stood in the contest of hunger and pain and proved himself in it. The Watchers marveled at how steadfast he was without complaint. Because he had triumphed, the angels came out with their crowns to welcome him, while their companions honored him. He entered [?] the furnace of poverty as choice gold. When his beauty shone out, they took him and placed him in the kingdom. He lay on a bed of pain like gold upon an anvil, and sufferings hammered him until he became a great crown. The poor man reclined in Abram’s bosom in the kingdom, and the time came for the rich man too to die in earnest.

The rich man died, and this man’s death was indeed death. He died [?] and was buried; his burial testifies that his death was death. It is written of Lazarus that he died and they carried him to Abraham, and of the rich man that when he died, he was buried and descended to Sheol. Discernment is urgently needed alongside reading. If someone does not discern, he should not even read. Everyone certainly knows how to read, but discernment is something you find among only a few. It is urgently necessary to cut back a little on reading, so that the soul may linger over discernment with clarity. Even animals hear the sound of a word, but people with intelligence and understanding discern its meaning. Let the mind, then, open its ears to instruction, for it is the mind that can see the beauty in the reading. It is not written of the poor man that he was buried. Why is that? Because his precious death was not death. His passing drove him from troubles to blessings. He lived like a living [?], and it is not written that he was buried, because he was alive. But of the rich man it is written that he was buried, because at his death woe awaited him, a cramped place and a great pit. When this man died, they indeed buried him, because he was dead.

He descended to Sheol, which was not where Lazarus was. They buried this man; they did not carry him away, as you have heard. They were sent away, one to heaven and the other to the abyss. It is written of this man that, while he was being tormented there in Sheol, he raised his eyes and saw Abraham and Lazarus. From the statement that he raised his eyes, it became clear that he was in the depths, while that poor man was in the heights above. This wretched man died and was buried, as has been said, and descended to face a fiery abyss in great suffering. Like a fleeting evening shadow, his good things passed away, and every kind of endless misery gathered around him. As though in a dream, he grew rich, became proud, and forgot himself. Then he awoke and saw that he was crushed, distressed, and full of suffering. Like a flower beautiful in color, he shone in his clothing. But as soon as the heat of the fire reached him, he withered and was ruined. He grew fat on delicacies, wines, and luxuries. But when the fire of judgment struck him, he shrank and was brought low. Time dislodged him from his lofty bed, and he fell into a hollow depth that has no bottom and is full of fire. His splendid, adorned couch was overturned. He descended from it, and blazing coals received him.

Death overturned his table, laden with good things, and made a place for him in Gehenna, where there is no water. The weak man left behind the clear drink in his splendid dwelling and descended to a place where they would not give him a drop of water. The world mocked him and [?]. Because he loved it so much, fire loved him, and he became food for the flame. He descended into the abysses and inherited darkness in the dwelling of Sheol. Terrors, sufferings, pains, and every kind of distress surrounded him. While he was being tormented there in Sheol, he raised his eyes and saw Abraham and Lazarus in the kingdom. He saw that needy man, who had been trampled at his gate every day, now enjoying abundant splendor in a lofty place. He saw the lowly man wearing a crown among the victorious, glorious on high and filled with heavenly blessings. He looked at him reclining at the table in Abraham’s house, eating light and drinking radiance to nourish himself. He saw him reclining over a bowl full of life and drawing every delight from it spiritually. He appeared to him in a place where sufferings do not enter and pains never approach its inhabitants. He saw him in the bridal chamber that the Father had prepared for his friend Abraham:

that he too had been granted [?] there among the saints. He realized that this was the needy man who used to beg opposite his door, whom he would look at without showing him mercy. He recognized him as that suffering man whose sores the dogs used to gather around and lick with their tongues. The Gospel is a fountain of light in all its words, and on every side it has radiant faces. It has taught us about the revelation of the new world, its forms, its activities, and its ways of life. Through it we have been able to know clearly, here, what lies beyond and what the great judgment is like. If the Gospel had not shown us, who would have known that the two sides see one another in the new world? From what happened to the rich man and Lazarus, we understand the whole scene of the two sides there. They see, recognize, and hear one another's voices; otherwise there would have been no conversation or requests from one to the other. The Judge is just, and because his great judgment is upright, this is openly arranged: the two sides will see one another there. Thus the wronged orphan will look out from the kingdom and see the one who wronged him being tormented in the fire.

The widow will stand on high, on the right, and look at the man who robbed her, cast into Gehenna. Thus treacherous Cain will see from the left Abel, whom he killed, reclining in splendor on the right. Thus the oppressed will see their oppressors receiving their punishment, and will acknowledge the Judge's righteousness, because his judgment is just. For this reason the two sides face one another, so that the Lord's judgment may not be hidden from his creatures. Whoever saw someone wronged here and was deeply grieved will rejoice there when he sees the oppressors in the fire. Whoever thinks that things here are in confusion will rejoice there, because even a little word spoken by the mouth is subject to scrutiny. The nations will know that the Lord is righteous in all his judgments, and that he judges everyone justly according to their deeds. For this reason he set the lofty place of the kingdom opposite Gehenna, turning it toward it and aligning it to face within. So that he would not judge human beings in secret, he revealed his great judgment before his creatures, making it as clear as light. He gave his uprightness a face, so that the nations and the world could look upon it and see that it does not bend toward favoritism. All hidden things come out into the open at his great judgment, and for this reason the two sides are arranged opposite one another.

Thus, when the judgment is made public and its sentence is issued uprightly, both sides will cry out, “Righteous is the one who judges all!” How just it was that this arrogant man should see that poor man in the greatness in which he was dwelling! And just as the poor man had longed to fill his belly with his crumbs, so he would yearn for a tiny drop from the hollow of the poor man's hand. For justice weighed their deeds equally and repaid their sufferings according to the fair measure of their actions. She set a drop of water against the crumbs, to repay the sufferings there equally, as though in the pans of a balance. That one longed for crumbs, and this one for a drop. Since that one received nothing, this one received nothing, so that there would be no injustice—no injustice. He saw him from afar in the kingdom, just as he had seen him before; once again, from afar, justice strikes him through him. That hidden watcher saw the poor man longing for crumbs, while no one gave him any. He himself made the rich man suffer, longing for a drop of water, while those with Lazarus gave him none. He himself spread a bed of fire for him inside Gehenna, in exchange for the bed of pain on which he had seen the poor man. In exchange for his purple and the fine linen in which he took pride, he gave the needy man radiance and splendor to wrap himself in.

And in exchange for the luxurious life this man had lived, Lazarus received that kingdom which never passes away. In exchange for that rich man's meals, he gave the needy man a table of blessings whose provisions never run out. Now compare the flame with the sores, and the fire of judgment with that poor man's fever. And compare the great thirst that surrounded the rich man in the fire with that poor man's great and cruel hunger. Just as the needy man had begged for crumbs here, the rich man begged for a drop of water in great anguish. He lay cast into the fire, with the flame wrapped around him. The wretched man wailed, but those with Lazarus showed him no mercy. Fire clung to him, and he cried out in torment. Mercy stood far away from him and did not answer him. There, amid the blaze, thirst for water tormented him, and he began crying out, “My father Abraham, have mercy on me!” He saw the support of the righteous dwelling in the heights above, and from Gehenna he offered a plea in great anguish. He saw Lazarus, known and loved among the holy ones, and asked that he come to him in the fire to relieve his thirst. He saw that, if that poor man were sent from that company, he could give him relief from his torment.

He saw that, if he came, he would rebuke the fire and it would obey him, and the flame wrapped around him would subside a little. For this reason he cried out in supplication to Abraham, asking him to send Lazarus, so that [?] he might give him a little relief. “My father Abraham, have mercy on me,” he pleaded. “Send Lazarus to me,” he pleaded. “Let him bring a drop of water with him from where you are, and let him moisten the tip [?], which is burning with thirst.” Alas for the rich man, proud of his drink and his wines! To what depths he had fallen, to beg for just a single drop! Alas, alas for the man proud of his delicacies and his luxuries! What a great thirst surrounded him inside Gehenna! Alas, from what heights to what depths he had fallen, from his purple robes to needing a drop of water and not receiving it! Alas for the wretched man! How proud he was in this life here, and he went away and found a miserable life full of every torment! Alas for the exalted man! How far above the many he had stood, and time cast him down into a torrent filled with flame! Alas, he had been proud, pampered, and fattened! But distress overtook him, and now he rolls about on burning coals! Alas, he had been attractive, handsome, and lovely as a flower! But the fire of judgment blazed up, and all his beauty faded away!

Alas for the rich man who used to alternate between every kind of wine! He asked for one little drop, but they denied him, and his suffering grew. Alas, he had boasted of his cupbearers and his bakers! But he thirsted for water in the fire and cried out, and no one listened to him. Alas, he had been accustomed to a crowd of slaves and attendants! But he begged the poor man to give him water to drink. “My father Abraham, send my brother Lazarus to me.” He certainly knew him: he was the very man who had been opposite his gate. It was as though someone were saying, “He knows me, and I know him. He knows who I am and what I used to be.” The rich man saw that his associates, his advisers, and those of his own rank were not at the banquet in Abraham’s house.
