He did not see his table companions there, nor his loved ones [?], nor his friends, nor the handsome men who had been his companions. Of those he had known here, he saw no one there except that poor man who had lain before his gate. If he had seen a friend or relative in the kingdom, he would have asked that man to come to him instead of Lazarus. But when distress overtook him and none of his own people were there, he asked for the man who had always been at his gate, every day, to come. It seems to me that this man’s friends were with him.

That is why he saw no one from his company beside Abraham. Of that whole crowd that had been at his great gate, he saw the most downtrodden of them all there in the kingdom. He asked for him by name, as an acquaintance, to come to him. This very thing strongly condemned him as an unjust man. He began calling for him to his own condemnation, so that on this very ground he would be accused by justice. For when the man lay cast down at his gate, why did he not acknowledge him? And after he had gone far away from him, why was he calling for him? He asked him to come to him in the fire as though he were a dear friend, yet the man’s lowliness and abject condition testified that he had not been his friend. He had lain opposite his gate in pain and need. Since he had not acknowledged him then, why was he calling for him now? He trampled him when he went out, knocked him down when he came in, and forgot him when he enjoyed himself. And now that the man had finally come to rest, look, he was troubling him too! He had barely escaped his sores, his pains, and his poverty, when the rich man began calling for him to come, to plunge him into Gehenna! When his table was full of every good thing, he did not know him; but once a sea of fire surrounded him, he made him his friend. While he reveled in his delicacies, he kept his distance; but once he was brought low among the burning coals, he became close.

“My father Abraham, have mercy on me,” he pleaded, “and send Lazarus to me to relieve my suffering.” The rich man cried out in anguish from Gehenna, and Abraham answered him from the kingdom, saying: “Remember, my son, that you received your good things, while Lazarus endured his many hardships. Now, here he is at rest, while you are tormented. Yours were there, and his are here. What are you asking for?” The Gospel needs no explanation among those with discernment, for it is entirely light and is itself the explanation of the mysteries. The sun grows dark, but its light does not change; the moon sets, but its dawning shines upon creation. Let us only open the eyes of our hearts, which are closed, and behold, it appears clearly in its beauty. It has shown us, if we look with discernment, that this world is the opposite of that world in every respect. For its good things are truly bad things, and its bad things, in turn, are certainly good things. All the good things of this world are full of death, while whoever endures its hardships gathers life from them. For whoever enjoys rest in it, afflictions are prepared and kept in store; but whoever is afflicted in it will have rest in the new world.

This is what our Lord’s Gospel teaches humanity, and if anyone chooses not to understand, that is his own doing. He said plainly, “Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life in the world will find it again.” The one who loses his life is the one who toils, is persecuted and afflicted, and is crucified every day in opposition to his passions and desires. He dies every day because of his hope for the world to come, and lives only as someone superfluous in the world that does not love him. The one who loses his life here goes on to find a desirable place and a life of light without end. He finds his life full of blessings in the great world, and the saying is fulfilled in him: he finds his life if he loses it. For the one who lives luxuriously and at ease, who sins and boasts, and has at his disposal the life of this world and all its splendors, who loves wealth, whose soul is bound to possessions, who hates afflictions and takes great pains to flee from troubles, and who finds his life in luxurious living without distress—this man loses and condemns the life he has found. He goes on to inherit a sea of fire like the rich man, who received all his good things here, as was said. Oh, how bitter are the comforts of this world!

For from them spring every torment for those who possess them. Alas for the clothes, the purple robes, and the possessions that give birth to suffering, pain, death, and every torment! Alas for the foods, the delicacies, and the wines—what thirst they earned for that rich man! Alas for the great table, filled with every luxury, from which every distress soon springs! Alas for wealth, which honored its owner for a little while, then carried him away and hurled him into an endless sea of fire! Alas for possessions! What have they done to that feeble man? He acquired them as though in a dream, and now he is tormented forever. Alas for gold! How much it leads people astray, without ever being exhausted! It puffs them up, makes them arrogant, and finally throws them into the fire. Alas for the honors that passed like a shadow and vanished, from which disgrace, shame, and every evil sprang! Alas for the proud man's breakfasts and dinners—what sufferings they earned for him in Gehenna! Alas for the good things that a great flood swept away! In their place, time brought every evil. Alas for the world! How much it leads human beings astray! With its desirable things it entices, chokes, and destroys them.

I renounce you, world! How ugly your beautiful things are, and how evil and full of woes are all your good things! You are to be feared! Blessed is anyone who hates you intensely and considers you his great enemy, as indeed you are. Woe to those who love you, and woe also here to those who hate you! Whoever loves you burns, while whoever hates you is worn down and weary. It is time, then, to flee from your good things, evil world, for in them a person finds scourging, fire, and great judgment. Let everyone fear your gift, if he has discernment, for when you give, you put bitter things inside the honey. You are sweet, yet you choke, for even your sweetness is bitterness. Your good things are evil things, as it is written. From now on, let no one fear your evils; rather, if he has understanding, let him fear your good things. For those evils of yours that the poor man endured were the means by which he found that kingdom in Abraham's dwelling. Who can set his heart on your evils and love them, except someone steadfast like Lazarus? But if someone loves the evils of this world, it is well known that through them he inherits every good thing. For a person is not allowed to receive here and also there. He enjoys rest in only one world, whichever he loves.

Anyone whose soul has gone out in longing for this world here, and who has loved it greatly, has no place in that other world. For whoever wisely sets his face toward that world considers the comfort here a thorn that strikes and wounds. You can understand these very things clearly from the words Abram spoke to the rich man. He said, "You received all your good things, and he his evil things. In exchange for these, he now enjoys rest, while you are tormented." This saying is very hard to hear, and who can bear it, except someone who hates pleasant comforts? That rich man is now being tormented because he lived in comfort, and fire has swallowed him because he was proud during this life. It is not written that he sinned, but that he lived in comfort and was proud, that he enjoyed himself and gave nothing to the poor man. Justice did not accuse him of plundering or stealing, nor of acting unjustly or wronging his fellow servants. No orphan complained against him that he had seized and carried off his possessions, nor any widow that her property had passed inside his gate. He was accused before the Judge of this alone: that he was proud and paid no attention to the poor man. When the rebuke came from Abraham,

the righteous man recounted to him all his passions and deeds—recounted them to him. If there had been anything else he was involved in, the righteous man would not have concealed it and covered it up for him. Truth rebuked him for these things that were his, without wronging him, for he told him only that he had received all his good things. He did not reproach him for theft or plunder, for if these had been found in him, he would have exposed him. For he was indeed reminding him of what had happened, and he told him nothing except that he had received all his good things. What, then, happens to someone who acted unjustly and wronged others—not merely someone who was proud, but someone who made his fellow servants cry out? This man burns because he neglected the poor man. What, then, will happen to someone who even plundered the poor man himself? That man was tormented because he enjoyed his own possessions. How fierce, then, is the burning of someone who took a hungry person's bread? Because his clothing was very splendid, he was clothed in flame. What, then, is the judgment of someone who even stripped a widow? Why was this man's story told at length, while the plunderer and thief have no story told? They cast this proud man down into fire because he was proud. What place, then, has fallen to the plunderer there?

This man became known within Gehenna because he had lived in comfort. Where should we look for someone who crushed his fellow servants? It seems to me that the plunderer descended to the bottom of the pit. The flame closed over him below in the abyss and did not let him see Abraham and Lazarus. This man, who had not plundered, saw Abraham and Lazarus, but the thief lies cast down and brought low at the bottom of the pit. The fire swept him away, brought him down, and placed him below in the depths. His story is absent because he was covered by the flame. He was buried in burning coals, and his story fell silent and is not told. The pit swallowed him, and speech and conversation about him ceased. The great judgment of this proud man is known and revealed, and his story, his words, and his exchanges are written in the Gospel. Let the account of this man strike terror into the rich, and let trembling fall upon anyone who is proud at the telling of his story. Let great sorrow stir my words to tell his story, and let the mouth speak of him with sighs, for his pain is great. He cries out in the fire and raises his voice from Gehenna. He keeps knocking, but the door is shut, and no one answers him. Where there was no door open to mercy, he was asking for mercy. After the door had been shut in anger, he knocked, seeking to enter.

Alas for the world! What has it done to that weak man? It bound him with love for itself, and because he delighted in it, he suffered anguish. Because he lived at ease and filled his belly with bread in it, now he is crushed and dejected, thirsty and howling from the burning. He pleaded with the royal household for a drop of water, but they considered it too precious, because he had not asked for it at the proper time. The great door of the kingdom had been shut against him, and it was not the time for them to incline their ears to petitions. The bridegroom’s bridal chamber was held in honor, and he had entered his wedding feast. He was not receiving another guest at that time. The bride had entered her chamber to be married. Whoever knocked was unwelcome, and no one answered him. Noah’s household had entered, and the door of that [?] had been shut. Those outside had remained there, and entering was no longer easy. The sea and the floodwaters swept away anyone who had not entered, and he could not enter the ark of life. The door was shut against the great flood of fire, and those inside who had been saved would not open it. God is not devoid of mercy in his great judgment. It was the time appointed for that rich man that was without mercy. Evil had brought this about and had gone out against the wicked.

And they entered. The friends were honored there in the kingdom. Once the judge has delivered the verdict, he holds no further inquiry. Whoever has been condemned is condemned, and whoever has been acquitted is acquitted; there are no further inquiries. After the great judgment was concluded, that rich man began pleading, and for this reason they would not even listen to him. The lot had fallen into the mouth of the flame, and the judge was no longer willing to hear his words. The inquiries had taken place, and the judgment had been issued justly. There was no room for either a petition or a plea. For this reason that righteous man would not send a drop of water to the man who had delayed and only then asked for it. “You have received your good things,” he said to him, “and you did not acknowledge Lazarus when he was with you. “If he had been accustomed to sitting with you at your table, he would not now keep away from your company. “If you had refreshed him with your evening meal, he would have become familiar with you and would come to you as a friend. “If he had drunk from your bowl, which was [?], perhaps now a river would have broken through the flame.” I did not pamper him there with you with delicious food. He has no way to come to you. Whom are you calling?

Besides all this, a chasm lies between the two sides, and there is no crossing by which anyone can go to the other and return. There is no crossing from here for anyone to come to you, nor is there any opening for you to come from there to us. The bridge is cut off, and the pit is deep and full of fire. The chasm is terrifying, and no one can travel through it. Wrath has cut off the road between the two sides so that it can no longer be traveled. Everyone must remain quietly in his own place, wherever he is. One place no longer admits another to render service in it, nor can assistance pass to one side from the other. My son, why did you delay so long in seeking mercy? You forgot and neglected your petition, and only afterward presented it. Where were you until now, keeping silent instead of pleading? Now no one hears your voice. Why are you wailing? The time for repentance was freely available in the time that has passed. Now it has been rejected and will no longer be accepted. Until this point, grace listened to voices; from this point onward, look, justice carries whips. Why did you neglect all this length of time? The time for repentance passed, and only then did you present it.

The places are cut off from one another, and an unbridged pit lies between them. What are you doing? Burn in the fire, wretched man, and stop your howling, for no one crosses from here to there as you ask. It is a great sorrow for anyone who listens with understanding to the dreadful account of the fire of judgment and how fierce it is. Who will grant me the ability to weep and make those who hear me weep? For the story of the wretched man cannot be told without tears. His story is a lament. I will cry out in sorrow and then speak: How dreadful was the hour when he spoke with Abraham! At the great gate they slammed his petition back in his face, and his plea remained rejected, hated, and unaccepted. That answer full of wrath was returned to him, and the wretched man knew that there was no room for his request. He saw that time offered him no opportunity to repent, and he became certain that there was no mercy to rescue him. He sank entirely into despair within Gehenna, and his cries of petition to Abraham ceased. His life became worthless in his own eyes, and he abandoned his pleading. He thought in his heart that those with Abraham would show him no pity. A cloud of fire enveloped him on every side.

The burning coals of the flame battered him in that place of anguish. He learned and saw that there was no possibility of escape, and he understood that his torment had no end. He cried out repeatedly, but it had been decided that no one would answer him. He asked for a drop, and the answer came back that none would be given to him. He learned that petitions were not customary in that place, and he saw that the two sides were separated from one another. No one from there is allowed to cross over to him; and if he would go, the road is blocked so that he cannot travel along it. The bridge is cut off, and no one crosses as he had hoped. The door is shut, and they do not open it for anyone who knocks. The place is bounded within its own limits and no longer allows anyone to enter or leave in any way. There is no physician to come and examine his great pain, and no caregiver to do anything for his wounds. He learned that the sore would last forever, without healing, and in his heart he gave up petitioning, never to offer a petition again. At that time he hated his wealth and his good things; he despised and scorned his comforts and his pomp as well. He cried woe over all his gold and his possessions, and he greatly reviled his clothes and purple garments.

There he learned what he had been unwilling to learn here: desirable things stir up fire against their owners. The flame became his teacher, and it taught him that he should never have despised the poor man. He was beaten with whips of fire and learned from the Judge that he detests it when someone turns his eyes away from the poor. Gehenna became like a school, and in it he learned how the owner of wealth ought to manage it. Perhaps he uttered these cries within Gehenna: “Blessed is the one who has seen wealth as I have seen it! Blessed is the one who wore rags in the world and went about begging, for the fine linen I wore stirred up the flame against me! Blessed is the one who was needy like Lazarus, reached his dwelling, and inherited the blessedness of Abraham’s household! Blessed is the one who was hungry and thirsty there, for here they would give him water if he asked! Blessed is the one who did not eat his fill of bread in the evil world, for I, who ate my fill, am now burning bitterly! Blessed is the one who did not grow proud during his life there, and who came here and lived well, like Lazarus! Blessed is the one who was sick and hungry like the poor man,

and whom they placed beside him to live with him without suffering! Blessed is the one whom sores pursued in the world over there, and who has not seen here the fiery coals that surround me! Blessed is the one whom pain and poverty disfigured, and who has not been battered like me amid waves of fire! Blessed is the one who had no abundance of daily bread, and who escaped here from the blaze that threatens me! Blessed is the one who was a slave to poverty, and was not called a master of wealth only to burn like me!” He disowned clothes, possessions, and purple garments, and the pomp and good things of the world over there. If only someone had made me a nest for pains every day there, and allowed me here to approach the place where Lazarus is! If only dogs had surrounded me in the world and licked my sores, and he had delivered me here from the bites of the flame! If only there were a way into Gehenna for my lord Death [?], so that I could depart from it just as I departed from my proud pleasures! All my good things passed away like a dream and like a shadow. But here there is no end to my miseries. What shall I do? If only someone would give me a person from among the dead to go and tell the world beyond what sufferings overwhelm me here!

The wretched man was tormented by these terrors in Sheol. With groans he raised his voice, but no one answered him. He pleaded for a tiny drop, but they would not give it to him. And even if he had received the drop, how much help would it have been to him? O great, proud rich man, steeped in arrogance, why is your request so small when you ask? What could a drop of water do for a sea of fire? How far would it go in that wilderness of flame? A tiny drop for that boundless blaze—if the drop you requested had reached you, what could it have done? Your request is small, although your need is very great. Why do you ask for so little from the king's household? The wretched man says, “Even as it is, look, I have received nothing! If I had asked for something great, what would have happened? If my petition was refused when I asked only for a drop from there, what would they have said I should receive if I had asked for more? With something small I tried to learn the customs of this place, and now I have learned that granting requests is not its custom. Loans are repaid, and whoever has made good loans receives from justice according to the measure he himself measured out. My loans are bad, because I never showed mercy to the poor.

That is why they show me no mercy: they are just. The wretched man says, “My deeds have now settled my judgment, and there is no room for mercy to come and rescue me. My father Abraham, send someone from among the dead to go and tell my brothers about the torment in which I lie! Let me send word to my father's household, to my loved ones, and also to my companions, telling them how I am and what sufferings batter me. Let someone from among the dead go and proclaim it in the streets of the whole world, so that everyone may fear luxurious living. Let him take from here a letter full of terrors and [?] distress, and carry it to the rich people of the world. Let me paint a picture of my great torment in words of suffering, and let it be taken and placed among the rich for them to look at. Let me send them word not to imitate me in their deeds, and not to trust in the world's possessions as I did. Let them hate wealth, for it is because I loved it that I am burning now. Let them cling neither to comforts nor to fine clothes. Tell them about hell, how harsh it is, and how fiercely the fire of judgment threatens the rich. Advise them that if they see a poor person in the street, they should bow before him and embrace him in their arms.

Teach them how very great is the freedom to speak granted to the poor here in this great world. Show them that whoever neglects a poor person will beg for a drop of water, and no one will give it to him. Let them learn wisdom from me, so that the world does not ambush them and lead them astray with its enticements, as it led me astray and cast me down here. Let my story be a mirror among the rich, so that they may look at me and not imitate me and burn as I do. Tell them about the blazing fire and the burning, and how bitter are the torments of those who possess gold. Let me become a subject of discussion, a tale, and a parable full of suffering among the rich, and let them speak of it with trembling. Let them remember me and loosen their grip on their possessions, for from those possessions springs the flame that will burn them. Let me become a story full of terrors, and let them tell it to one another with great reproach. Let me be reproached and keep them far from reproach, and through my own case let them escape punishment. Now let someone from the dead go, as I have pleaded, and tell them there what is here, so that he may benefit them. Look, you discerning people, how wise that rich man became

through punishment—he would even have taught, if they had let him. The fire of judgment finally makes all rebels wise, and it teaches them the way of truth that they had not learned. Whoever has not gained wisdom through words and teachings is beaten with rods of fire and learns, like the rich man. Whoever rebels against the commandment and the law [?] learns in the flame of judgment what was right. Ah, the rich man who neglected instruction here! Once the fire reached him, he was eager to teach. While he lived in wealth, he did not examine what was before his eyes; but once he was tormented, he looked toward the course of right conduct. Then he learned, when learning was no longer any help. For if someone sows on fire, what will he reap? Within hell his soul cried out for his loved ones, and he tried to find a way to send them instruction. When he had something in his hands, he gave no relief to anyone in need; but when everything he had was gone, he taught without being asked. He wanted to send a messenger from among the dead to bring instruction to the world from hell. Abraham answered him like a teacher of truths: “There are prophets and Moses in the world to teach them.”

From this, too, there is a benefit for humanity: they need not be uncertain about what that world is like. So that no one may say, “Who, then, will give me someone from the dead to tell me what is there and what they are like? Let him speak to me about Gehenna and the kingdom, and explain that judgment to me at length.” This is what that rich man asked: that a dead man should be sent into the world—if only they had listened to him as he wished. So that no one would ask for what he asked, it was made known that it was unnecessary for a dead man to teach human beings. Look, there is Moses, and with him the prophets and the preachers too. Let the whole world learn from them what it needs. Anyone who wants a dead man to come and tell him about that world [?] has a heart like the rich man’s. Abraham told him that it was unnecessary, and that a person could find every explanation in the prophets. The Scriptures are physicians for the soul in this world: in them you can find every remedy for every sickness. They teach human beings the way of life and, through their revelations, open the door into the kingdom. They are set in the world like lamps of great light, and they drive error from souls like darkness.

In them a person finds height and depth, breadth and length, and all the wealth and all the treasures of God’s house. In them a person also finds the thought of the Godhead and comes to grasp the lofty mind of the divine Being. Look, the whole life of human beings is in the Scriptures, and they teach you how to draw near to God. If there had been any use in sending a dead man, he would have been sent, as that rich man pleaded. For God wishes by every means to help human beings and bring them to repentance. If that rich man’s request had been beneficial, God would have accepted it and sent someone. He who sent his only Son, who came to the dwelling of mortals, would not have prevented a dead man from coming, if that would have helped. What would a dead man have had to tell human beings, if they had sent him and he had come from among them to our land? The Scriptures have left us lacking nothing in instruction, and they have said everything that needs to be said. It was written in Moses that no one should neglect his own flesh and blood, and that he should give alms to the poor and the resident foreigner. And that when a person harvests, he should not reap the edge of his field completely, nor glean his vineyard, for the sake of those in need.

It is also written in the prophets that you should share your bread with the hungry and bring the stranger into your house when he is in distress. He also pronounced blessings on anyone who cares for the poor, and promised to rescue him on the day of trouble. If that rich man had listened to all these things, they would have been enough for him to live rightly by them. Moses taught that a person should love his neighbor as himself. Why did that rich man not listen? That poor man who lay beside him was close at hand, and it would have been easy for him to bring him in and seat him at his table. Because he neglected his own flesh and blood who lay at his door, the Just One neglected him and did not give him the drop he requested. He had heard, “Blessed is the one who cares for the poor.” Had he cared for him, he would have been shown mercy and would not have been burning. The Lord would have rescued him on the day of trouble, as he promised. But because he had not cared, he was not rescued from distress. The day of trouble is that day of the great judgment, and whoever cares for the poor will be rescued. This is why that man was not rescued from the fire: because he had not cared for the poor. All these things are written in Moses and also in the prophets.

There was no lack of teaching in the world by which he could have gained life. It was unnecessary for a dead man to come, as he was requesting, for that would not help when Moses was teaching in the world. Abraham answered him justly, saying to him, “Look, they have the prophets; let them listen to them.” The wretched man said, “That is not what I ask, my father Abraham. Rather, let a dead man go to the world and teach them.” The righteous man said, “If they do not listen to the Scriptures, neither will they listen to a dead man's teaching if he goes. If they despise the prophets there, the children of the divine mind, who can teach them? If Moses' speaking harp is not accepted, who is capable of making them listen through teaching? If that great man, full of revelations, is despised when he teaches, what will they do when an ordinary man goes and speaks? They reject Moses; whom, then, will they listen to when he speaks? My son, it is pointless for a dead man to go, since they will not respond to him.” That righteous man spoke well to the rich man. He justly refused his request, and it was not accepted. At that moment, the afflictions of the tormented man doubled.

He dwindled, shrank, wasted away, and was consumed by great suffering. At that moment, all his words were lost, and there was no opportunity for him to speak with Abraham again. At that moment, his requests and pleas came to an end. His voice fell silent, his discourse died away, and his fire blazed. At that moment, when he stopped speaking with Abraham, perhaps the flame took hold of him even more fiercely. At that moment, when two petitions had been presented and rejected, his anguish doubled in great pain. At that moment, the sea of flame roared against him, and he was tormented in a great storm of fire. At that moment, wave after wave battered him, and burning coals handed him over to burning coals to increase his suffering. At that time, when all his pleas had come to an end, and there was no word from Abraham’s household to comfort him; At that time, when the righteous man fell silent and no longer spoke to him, and he heard only the sound of the fire roaring fiercely; At that time, when wrath turned his words back at the gate, and he had no recourse but to say, “Woe to me!”; At that time, when he was inwardly filled with bitterness,

and cried out in anguish, his voice mingling with the blaze; At that time, when he lowered his eyes from Abraham and neither looked at him nor saw him nor heard him; At that time, when he looked to the right and to the left, crying out, and there were no loved ones to rescue him; At that time, perhaps, he raised a lament full of trembling, speaking in anguished tones: “Where are my friends, companions, and loved ones, who do not rescue me from the burning flame? Where are my advisers and my close companions, who puffed me up with indulgences so that I would squander my life? Where is the wealth that deceived me and did not remain with me? It stoked the fire still higher for me, then departed, and now it is gone. Where is my table that was full of every good thing? Look, I am asking for a drop of water, and they will not give it to me! Where is the gold that I chased after to gather? If it could be exchanged for a single drop, let it all go! Where are the garments of fine linen and silk? Here I am clothed only in a fabric of fiery coals. Where is my power? Where are my possessions? Where is what I trusted in? Where is the world that made me an object of disgrace and gave me a foul name?

Oh, fire that burns forever, what can I do about you? There is nowhere on any side to escape from you! Oh, great Gehenna of judgment, how bitter you are! No breeze of mercy blows within you for someone like me. Oh, blaze that wealth gave me, enough of you! Be still, if possible, even for a little while, so that I may find relief from you. Oh, torments that I acquired through purple garments, I do not know where I can turn aside from you! It was not the judge who twisted the judgment against me; I was the one who sinned, for I shut off my compassion from the poor man and did not help him.” Anyone willing to open his ears to this account will gain much, for it is full of suffering throughout. Through it a person learns about the kingdom and about Gehenna: the one is desirable, and the other terrifying, to those who have discernment. Who can hear about that rich man’s torment without shuddering at his burning and hating his way of life? Or who can learn how greatly Lazarus was exalted without loving poverty, if he has understanding? Wealth is there, while poverty is here; and there things do not change, but remain true.

Here the times ride on wheels, passing on, and wealth and poverty are carried along in them every day. Someone rich today may become poor tomorrow; someone poor now may become rich before long. The sick recover, and the healthy become sick, for this world and its affairs are interwoven with changes. A child grows, an adult grows old, and an old person dies, for there is no completely unchanging condition in this world. Morning passes and noon comes; the afternoon declines, and evening comes and takes the place of them all. Daytime is delightful, its light beloved, and its beauty lovely; but night creeps in to take its place and destroys it. Over there, the times are not harnessed to wheels like this, nor are the seasons subject to changes and passing away. There is no passage for evening to follow morning, nor for night to displace daytime. On the right is a day that has no evening, and on the left rests a night that has no morning. They do not revolve but remain unchanged, for between them is a great chasm with no bridge. The road is cut off before the seasons, so that they cannot revolve.

The wheel's axle is broken, and it is released from changes. Light has no bridge by which to cross over to darkness, nor does darkness have a way to lay a road toward the light. Everyone who has deeds and righteousness there possesses all his wealth as his own, and it lasts for him. But whoever is poor is truly poor, for time does not change there and alter his condition. So let us call that rich man a poor man, and Lazarus a rich man, for the names— [?] of this place everyone leaves behind in this world, and there acquires a true name from his deeds. For light has dawned upon creation through this teaching and driven away from us the darkness of the world that blinds us. It is a new world that was unseen by us because it was hidden; Christ came, revealed it, and showed it to us clearly. He revealed to us the woes and blessings in that place, and told us the conversation between the two sides and everything that took place. That rich man begged Abraham for a dead man to come, and something greater than that has happened for our sake.

God himself became a human being and came to our land, and revealed the whole story of the new world just as it is. Instead of the dead man whose coming he requested, look, the Lord of the dead has come and spoken of everything to help us. He saw that the event would be very helpful if recounted, and the Lord of all did not wish to leave it aside, as he had promised. A dead man was not sent to come, because that would not have helped; look, the one who raises all the dead has come and spoken to us. So that not even this should be missing from what helps us, it was recounted as it happened, to help us. The Lord of all places departed from his own place and came and revealed to us what was said in that place. Although that rich man's petition was not heard, what he had requested was accomplished by our Lord. He was begging that his story should be told in our land, and pleading with Abram that his troubles should be recounted to us. It was not because he had pleaded, but because the Father wished it: he sent his Son, who came and told us the whole story. Since a dead man could not cross over and come to our land, look! The Living One came and disclosed the mystery of the world. He brought to our world the voices that came from Gehenna,

and the speech that went out from the kingdom to the rich man. He brought a picture of suffering from that place to our land and displayed it in the streets of the whole world for everyone to see. With words instead of pigments, he made a great portrait of the world beyond, drawn from what happened to that rich man. He proclaimed his story in the hearing of all the living, so that they would know what was said in that place. This was so that no one else would again ask, as the rich man did, for a dead man to come out of Gehenna and teach us. And so that it would not be said, 'If he had come, he would have helped; and if the world had heard the story, it would have benefited.' The excuse has been taken away, and there is no saying to God, 'There was another means that could help, and he withheld it from us.' What did he have that was as hidden and dear as his Beloved? And once he had given him to us, what could he possibly withhold from us? His Son brought out to us all the mysteries in the Father's house, and now the Father has nothing hidden from us. Our Lord even revealed to us the drop of water that a certain rich man requested, to show us how merciful he is.

Even his plea that a dead man should come, which they had not granted him—the whole petition was fulfilled by our Lord's own coming. The rich man showed his love from Gehenna, and he was begging to send us a message through a dead man. Come, let us all now plead on his behalf, just as he pleaded with Abraham on our behalf. Our Lord, who came and recounted his words to us, go and tell him, 'We have heard about your burning and your torment.' 'We have also learned that you were pleading for a dead man to come and tell us about your distress and help us.' We are not asking you, my Lord, to send someone. Go yourself and tell him, just as you came and taught us. For you alone the road is open to come and go, both to Gehenna and to the kingdom, since this is easy for you. The chasm does not prevent you from crossing over to those places, visiting their inhabitants, and meeting their needs. The chasm set between the two sides does not deter you from making your way from there to here, if you wish. Go to him, my Lord, and come to us as you please.

And if you so command, grant him relief yourself with even that drop. For Lazarus could not carry water, leap across the chasm, and travel a road that was not his. Look, for us you have taken the place of the dead man who was not sent. Take the place of that Lazarus for him too, by bringing water. You did not spare your blood, but let it flow so that we might be forgiven through it. Since you have come and brought it, go, my Lord, and carry good hope. Mercifully offer blood to those here and water to those there. Abraham ruled that the dead man would not be sent, and also that the drop would not be given to the one who asked for it. That happened to him; may this happen to us through you, who show mercy to all, so that in both you may be glorified, here and there. My Lord, have pity on me too, so that through mercy I may live at your right hand and not be tormented there by thirst like the rich man. Let me cross the sea of fire in a boat of water, so that the terrible realm of flame may not cause me anguish. May baptism shelter me there from the burning, and spread its wings over the blaze when I pass through. May this spring of living water accompany me.

And may I not, my Lord, need a drop among the thirsty. May I not, my Lord, ask Abraham for water there, for I have learned that they do not give it to the one who asks. If my path [?] leads to the fire because of the wrongdoing of my hands, may I see you there as Hananiah saw the fourth figure. If my sins cast me there beside the rich man, [?] there like Azariah through that angel. If justice commands me to enter the furnace, may I forget the fire through you and come out like Mishael. You are living water, our Lord, and I have taken you as my provisions for the fire, so that I may drink from you if I thirst. Be a bridge for me over the chasm set between the two sides, so that I may cross over you to your Father and live with you. Here and now, accept the tears that are dear to you, and give me living water there so that I may not be tormented. From this moment I implore you, my Lord: accept my petition, so that I may be kept far from Gehenna, which makes me tremble. May the fire recoil in shame from my limbs when the fragrance of your body and your forgiving blood, mingled within me, strikes it. Good One, who rules over the kingdom and over Gehenna, may I be rescued through you from Gehenna into the kingdom.
May your great compassion rebuke the fire that threatens me. Blessed are you by all, you who show mercy to everyone in the great world.
Here ends the homily on the rich man and Lazarus, composed by Mar Jacob.
Again by the same author, Saint Mar Jacob. Homily 57. On the Canaanite Woman.

A great light dawned here on earth in the days of our Lord, to destroy, in its own place, the darkness that had blinded the world. The radiance of the Father shone its brightness upon those below, so that by its dawning the gloomy road might become bright for those traveling on it. The Sun of Righteousness had come down and walked on earth, and from [?] his beauty the many shadows fled. He spread his rays over the regions and gladdened them, and the world, which had been gloomy before he dawned, became bright. He drove away the error that had abounded among all the nations,

and showed the world the way of life, so that it might walk in it. He sprinkled healing upon humanity, which was sick, and the many pains of the afflicted subsided. He poured out his healing upon those in pain and strengthened them; he blew upon the afflictions of the weak and extinguished them. He poured out his gift to enrich the world through his acts of help. He opened his treasuries, and everyone in need plundered them and became rich. The blind were seeing, and the paralyzed were being healed; demons were driven out, and those bent over were being straightened. He gave hearing to the deaf and light to those without light. He cleansed lepers and gave forgiveness to sinners. He came down like rain upon the land of Judah, which was sick, and the sick sprouted like plants from their beds. He drove away the diseases that had gained power over humanity, and with the breath of his mouth he rebuked the afflictions and drove them away from many. He healed freely, while they wronged him, and he did not become angry. He tended their pains, while they insulted him with their questions. The people hated him, although his healing was mighty; and although his acts of help were many, he was reviled. The uncircumcised nations believed in him and in his acts of help,

while the circumcised people doubted his healing. For the Canaanite woman, a report was enough for her to believe in him; but not even the Scriptures taught the daughter of the people to believe firmly. The report that he was the Son of God sped to Tyre and Sidon, while in Jerusalem he was insulted as the son of Joseph. As he passed through the land of the pagans with his disciples, faith in him was being sung by the Canaanite woman. He passed into the territory of Tyre and Sidon and astonished them, and their worthless gods began to tremble. By his dawning he tore apart that darkness of unbelief, and began to spread his light throughout the lands of the world. The leaven of life had fallen into the dough of the pagans and settled there, and began to draw the whole mass toward its sweetness. The farmer of truth passed into the territory of the Canaanites, sowed his seed, and began to gather a sheaf from it. The nations warmly welcomed the good seed, and it quickly produced abundant fruit. Through the woman whose daughter a demon had seized and was tormenting, faith was being proclaimed in song to all the nations.

The evil demon had seized the young woman to torment her, for he always wishes to corrupt those who are beautiful. The murderer took the girl to abuse her, and in his cruelty he tormented her bitterly. The companion of destruction seized a virgin to corrupt her, for he greatly desires to defile the human race. The strong man entered and carried off the daughter of pagans as plunder, dragging her about cruelly and making her stumble. The whole earth was symbolically portrayed in her: it resembled her both in her sickness and in her healing. Satan took the earth captive too, drove her mad, and made her pagan. He dragged and battered her as he pleased and increased her sufferings. He filled her with madness and introduced the worship of idols into her. He poured falsehood into her so that she would serve emptiness every day. The evil demon battered the earth with all its error, until the great Savior appeared and rebuked him, driving him away from her. Grace became a mother to the earth and pleaded aloud, like the woman whose daughter the demon had battered: “My Lord, the oppressed earth has raved like this long enough! Come down and rescue her from the error that abounds in her.” A plea from Grace came before the Majesty,

and the merciful physician was sent to the wounded. The mighty warrior came and bound the strong man by his power. He restored the mind of the earth, which had gone mad through idolatry. The good physician traveled through the world and tended it, giving healing to all the sick who encountered him. As he traveled through the land of the pagans, as we have said, the reports stirred the Canaanite woman to come to him. She saw that the demon was tormenting her daughter and throwing her about, and she began running after Jesus to make her request of him. She heard the news that the Judge of the world was passing by, and she went to lodge a complaint against Satan because she had been wronged. The one who administers justice and righteousness was passing through her country, and she went out to complain against the plunderer who had seized her daughter. The mighty warrior [?] to the territory of [?], and she cried out before him that a raiding band had come and taken her daughter captive. The hunter and driver of demons was traveling through her country, and she asked him to drive out that demon in her daughter. The good shepherd had gone out to seek the lost, and she told him, “A wolf has snatched away one of your ewes.” He came to the territory of Tyre and Sidon, as you have heard.

And the Canaanite woman went out after him to make her request of him. Reports that Jesus was passing by spurred on the woman, who was full of courage, and she hurried to take refuge in him. She began crying out among the crowds and pleading with him: “My Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me, for I have been robbed! Look, my daughter is being cruelly controlled by Satan! It is for you to set this right, if you are willing. The enemy of mercy has snatched the girl away, and now he is tormenting her. Take her away from him, and in her restored health she will be yours. The foul one has carried off the beautiful young woman, and now he is crushing her. Rebuke him, and he will leave; let her mind, which he has confused, be restored. With plaintive cries she went out after him, filled with wonder. With lamentations she pleaded with him for her daughter: “My Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me and heal my daughter! A demon has hold of her, and unless you crush him, he will not let her go.” The daughter of the pagans acknowledged that he was the Son of David, while among the people they were calling him the chief of demons. The Canaanites were certain that he was the Messiah, but envy had blinded the Hebrews, and they did not believe in him. The pagans recognized that he was a good physician and drove out demons; and the priests of the people—that he was a good physician and drove out demons. And the priests of the people nicknamed him Beelzebul when he performed these deeds.

The daughter of the pagans sang out among the crowds that he was the Son of David, and through her story she reproached the Jews for how greatly they had wronged him. The new good news was being proclaimed by the Canaanite woman, while prophecy was being wronged by the daughter of the people. Those who knew the Scriptures despised the revelations of prophecy, while worshipers of images became the first to proclaim the message. The pagan woman knew that he was the Son of David and drove out demons, while the believing synagogue wronged him even as he was healing her. The pagan woman cried out among the crowds with a loud voice, to make known how great the faith of the nations was. The nation of pagans despised its worthless images and pleaded with no one but Jesus to drive out demons. She complained to the king about the rebel who had greatly increased her suffering, for he could bind the strong one by his power. She did not run to the gods of the Canaanites, for she knew that Jesus was destroying their idols. She became a harp for unwavering faith as she cried out, “Son of David, have mercy on me! That rebel, wicked in his conduct, laid an ambush and took my daughter captive. Come, bring her back from the snares! The demon who obstructs good things has broken into the girl

and drives her to madness. Command him, and he will leave the afflicted girl.” The tyrant who has hated the human race ever since Adam has driven my daughter mad, making her lose her once-peaceful mind. King of the land, drive the foreigner out of your domain! You are the Son of David: be zealous and kill him as David killed Goliath. Do not let the uncircumcised one play with my daughter and mock her. Take her away from him, and she will be yours when you have rescued her. David your father rescued the assembly and became king, and he removed the Philistine’s disgrace from the camp. David himself killed a wolf for the sake of a lamb, carefully guarding his flock from harm. You care for your flock, my Lord, more than David did. Command the demon to release the girl he holds captive. Compassion drew the Canaanite woman after Jesus. She pleaded with him in prayer, but he did not answer her. He knew that the woman had no doubts about the True One. While she cried out, he disregarded her so that she might triumph. Although he loved her, he ignored her and did not answer her, so that through her perseverance her faith might grow greatly. The loving voice of the believing woman was sweet to him.

He let her cry out among the crowds that he was the Son of David. He did not answer her immediately, so that she would not fall silent at the outset. He disregarded her so that she might add to the victories of her faith. He acted indifferently and passed by, seemingly ignoring her, to show that true love does not waver. When she disturbed the apostles with her loud voice, they approached our Lord to plead with him on her behalf. Because her clamor had disturbed the whole crowd, they begged him to dismiss her so that she would stop following them. To add still more beauty to the image of her faith, he again disregarded her and her plea before the disciples. The Father sent me after the sheep of the house of Israel, and it is fitting that I now seek them and find them. I have gone out to seek the scattered flock of the house of Abraham, and I want to gather it by every means. I was sent only after the sheep that went astray—as though to say, all the nations are already found. As soon as the nations realize that I have come, they come to me. I have gone out to seek the sheep of the people, who do not seek me. The nations are free to come to repentance.

I have now gone out after the people, who are stiff-necked. Calling the nations is very easy once they are summoned. It is over the difficult people that I toil, in the hope that they may turn back. The nations need only a slight signal, and they come. The toil lies with the people, who are so heedless of correction. I was sent only after Jacob’s sheep. I seek them because they have strayed from righteousness. Our Lord gave the people no reason to be angry with him. In every way he supported them as one supports a sick person, yet they received no benefit. He rebuffed the faith of the nations even while loving it. Great as it was, it did not diminish through waiting. He rebuked the Canaanite woman so that she would stop raising her voice. But because her faith was sound, she would not be restrained. She pressed her way in among the crowds and pleaded with him: “My Lord, help me, for I need your help.” He said to her, “It is not right to take the bread belonging to the children and throw it to the dogs, who are not worthy. “Let the heirs eat first and live from the table. Then the dogs, who are not beloved, can be fed from it. “Let us leave the dogs aside, and let the children receive food. Let the children eat; let no animals trample the bread.”

She said to him, “Yes, my Lord, but the dogs also eat the crumbs belonging to the children and live alongside them. “For where can a dog find food or nourishment unless the bread of its masters’ children sustains it? “The heirs give to the dogs so that they may live alongside them. For who keeps a creature alive except its owner? “The master feeds both people and animals, and joyfully keeps hired workers and dogs alive along with the heirs. “The children eat from the table as heirs, and the dogs gather up the crumbs as creatures belonging to the household. “Children and dogs alike live on the father’s bread. He feeds them all from his table, because they belong to him. “Even the crumbs the dogs eat are bread. The same dough keeps both the dogs and the children alive. “The son, as heir, rightly eats from the table, and the dog gathers what falls from his bread so that it may live alongside him. “No one prevents the dogs from eating the crumbs. There is enough in the house both for the children and for the animals. “You have enough, my Lord, to keep both the dogs and the children alive. The nations and the people are satisfied by you, for they belong to you. “Your table is full, both for those inside and for those outside.

“You are entirely abundance, both for those far away and for those nearby. “You can feed both the children and the hired workers, and let the dogs eat the crumbs and live alongside them. “There is enough in your treasury for the people to grow rich from your treasures, and for the needy nations also to be sustained by your provision. “You are a great sea, and even if all the nations draw from you, they take only a little from your divine waves. “You are the bread of life. Ranks and thousands, nations and the people, bands and crowds are satisfied by you, and you do not run out. “You are a good physician, and every kind of help flows from you. A little of your power heals thousands, and they are few in comparison with it. “You can drive out the people’s demons and heal their pains, and the wounds of all the nations can be healed through you.” A drop of your power raises the dead, if you wish; for your treasury cannot run short of riches. My Lord, give my daughter some crumbs of your healing, and through them she will live and truly become yours. You need only give a sign, and demons flee in terror; you need only will it, and diseases vanish like smoke. If you command by the breath of your mouth, demons perish. You are a great treasury, and every kind of help is found in you.

Your bread is not so scant that it can nourish only one people. All nations eat from it, and there is still enough. Physician, your medicines are not so lacking in healing power that you can cure diseases among one people but not among another. Your wealth is not something that runs out or diminishes. It is a great spring, and the more you draw from it, the more it increases. Give your people bread to eat their fill, as children, and throw crumbs from it to the Gentiles, as to dogs. I have not come to ask you to withhold help from your people. You have enough to give to me, to them, and to many others. Who can exhaust your wealth, O King, or diminish it? A drop from your treasuries has greater power than all the nations. Who can drain you, great sea full of good things? The waves of your love can cover the whole world. Storehouse against famines, who can empty you? You have enough to feed all the ends of the earth, and they are too small for you. Offer [?] my daughter one crumb of your help, and from it she will eat her fill and gain strength and health. In the Canaanite woman the faith of the Gentiles grew great. From that moment, a sample of them all was taken in her.

She pleaded and was scorned, yet she kept pressing for help. He ordered her to be silent, but she kept crying out about her need. The crowds rebuked her, but she did not cease her pleading. The disciples grew agitated, but she did not stop following them. The shameless woman was even counted among the dogs, yet she kept pressing her plea without denial. It was explained to her that she was not counted among the children, but she did not relent, fall silent, and turn away from the Savior. He answered her insultingly and called her a dog, but she was not so disheartened that she turned away from him, for she was steadfast. The apostles rebuked her but could not silence her. Her voice drowned out the whole crowd, and she stood her ground. Though she was insulted and reprimanded by many, she argued against everyone and boldly prevailed. While the crowds rebuked her to make her speak softly, she disregarded them all, pleading in a loud voice. Even her very humiliation became a resource for the blessed woman, and from it she drew strength to prevail through her replies. From the reproach against her sprang something that gave her victory, and she used it to argue discerningly with our Lord. That very rebuff spurred her on, so that her faith would grow.

And her discernment stood out all the more because of her humiliation. By the very fact that she was counted among the dogs and was not to eat, she argued that she too was entitled to eat her fill. “Even the dogs eat some of the crumbs,” she said. From the very midst of condemnation she proclaimed victory. She showed in truth that she was entitled to receive mercy, for she justly demanded to receive what was due to her. “The master is obliged to feed the dogs as well,” she said. “While he shows abundant mercy to the children, he also keeps the dogs alive.” In the very case that had been brought to record her condemnation, she was found standing firmly on the ground of victory. When Truth had confined her with his words so that she would stand condemned, she won her case from that very argument through her decisive reasoning. “Even the dogs receive life from the crumbs,” she said. Truth vindicated her claim that she too was entitled to receive. Like a creditor, she took hold of the Son to receive from him, and she showed him that he was obliged to give mercy to her too. “I am willing to be a dog,” she said, “provided that you are my master. Feed what belongs to you from the crumbs you have in abundance.” “The dogs eat and are filled from what belongs to the children.

It is your responsibility, my Lord, to keep both the heir and the possession alive.” “Who gives a dog its livelihood except its master? It too eats from what belongs to the children and lives alongside them. If I am a dog, you are the master, for all my life is given to me by you alone.” Someone who loves is not reproached, even for being bold. Whatever love says to its beloved is accepted. It was love that drew the Canaanite woman to our Savior, and for this reason her argument too was accepted. No one ever talked back to him while he was teaching except this woman, who was full of love and faith. He condemned the scribes of the people and the debaters by his words, but when love stood up to speak with him, he gladly accepted defeat. Love thus clothed itself in a woman for the contest and came before our Lord, to show that it could win even through the weak. There love answered back to the Lord of the worlds through the Canaanite woman: when he said “No,” she said “Yes.” He said “No”; she said, “Yes, even the dogs eat.” She did not agree with him that it was not right for the dogs to eat.

But he agreed with her, praising the greatness of her faith. He saw that she was ablaze with the fire of love and was arguing with him, and he consented to let a woman defeat him with her replies. “It is not right,” he said, “for the dogs to eat from what belongs to the children.” She said, “Yes, my Lord, they eat from the crumbs.” He saw that her argument was wise, lovely, and full of love, and he gladly allowed her to win and receive mercy. He marveled at her, for she was stirred by grief and spoke to him; and before the crowd he praised her: “Great is your faith!” The Wise One wove a great crown full of beauty, and before the crowds he stretched out his hand and placed it upon her faith. “O woman, your faith is very great! From now on, let it truly be done for you as you wish.” He saw how close her will was to righteousness, and he appointed her as steward over his entire treasury. “Let it be done for you as you wish,” he told her. He granted her will the right to receive as much mercy as she desired. And because she wanted the demon to leave her daughter, it departed; for there was nothing else troubling her.

Love granted her that whatever she wished should be hers, for he had the power to enrich in every way whoever called upon him. Here is an example full of reassurance for anyone who considers it: no one approaches God except through love. Faith can conquer lofty fortresses; not even demons can stand before it when it shines forth. It rebukes demons, and they flee from it and depart. It breathes upon diseases, and through it all who are afflicted find relief. Although the power to heal belonged to our Lord, he exalted faith, for no one can see him except through it. Approach God in faith, and you will take hold of him; and you can receive whatever you desire, if you love. What image do you see in the Canaanite woman? She is a mirror: if you look into her, you will find beautiful things. You too have a soul that you should love more than a daughter; perhaps it contains a passion far worse than the evil one. That woman's daughter was being tormented by a demon, and she was distressed. Sin is crushing your own soul: do not neglect it. The soul's passion is far worse than the girl's demon. Plead for your soul, and see—it will be healed just as that girl was.

He is the same Jesus who answered that woman when she called upon him. Today too he answers, and he has the power to give to whoever asks him. If a passion torments you, persistently press the Physician, and he will easily drive it out, just as he did that woman's demon. Do not take pleasure in an evil passion when it torments you. Call upon Jesus the Physician: he will apply some of his medicines to it. Complain about wickedness as that woman complained about the demon, and he will breathe upon it, and it will flee from you just as that demon fled. Plead for your soul as that woman pleaded for her daughter. It is dear to you, for it is your only one, unique. You have only one soul, and if sin carries it away from you, come to Jesus: he will breathe upon sin and make it depart. Take for yourself the Canaanite woman's faith and love, and Jesus will put impure passions to flight if they assail you. Even if he ignores you, do not stop pleading. He wants to make you victorious; do not grow weary of prayer. There are times when he ignores and disregards the one who loves him—not to neglect him, but to make his faith greater. Bold persistence opens his treasuries—it is easy for it—and draws as much wealth as it wishes from his stores.

If the Canaanite woman had given up when she was rebuked, the boldness of her faith would not have been praised. Jesus is glad when you pound boldly on his door; and if you do not give up, he will magnify your faith. The woman held him fast among the crowds with her loud voice, and though they rebuked her, she would not stop seeking help. She would not listen even to him and turn away from him without receiving anything. She held him fast with love, and he granted her requests; only then did he move on. She argued with him, and he praised her for overcoming him, for love can act boldly without being condemned. “O woman,” he said, “very great is your faith!” He revealed it to the crowds so that everyone might be bold and follow her example. Take her wondrous boldness for yourself, O man; through it you can drive out suffering if it enters you. When you ask, do not doubt the giver. He is a great treasury from which all who are in need become rich. He is the way along which a person travels to see his Father, and the gate of life through which those who enter overcome death. He is the physician from whom remedies flow, and the spring that pours out life upon those around him. Through him demons and evil spirits are driven out of humanity.

He is the one who heals the pains and infirmities of the afflicted. Through him the soul’s life is made clear, and it shines with light from him. Through him the sins of the world, which were many, are slaughtered. He is the one who makes tax collectors righteous through the power of his preaching, and makes sinners perfect through forgiveness. He drove out the demon of the Canaanite woman who had pleaded with him, and he will quench the suffering of your soul if you look to him. He is the one who bears the world’s weight with his might. All created things rest upon him and have their existence in him. He is the sun of righteousness and the great light. He is the physician and the healer of all who are sick. He is wealth, the son of the rich one, and the one who enriches all. He is the strength of [?] those who are weak, and through him they are strengthened. He is the one who binds up pains and diseases and drives out demons. Blessed is he who came down, visited the world, and healed its pains!
Here ends the homily on the Canaanite woman by Saint Mar Jacob. Amen.
Again, Homily 18: On Palm Sunday, delivered by Mar Jacob.

O fountain of life, from which the dead drank and came to life, open yourself to me; quench my thirst from your spring. O stream that flowed through the thirsty earth, so that it bore fruit, let me drink from you and proclaim openly how sweet you are. O new well that they dug with spears on Golgotha, give me a drink; provide water for my mind, which needs your spring. Son of God, who called yourself living water, let me drink and be satisfied from you, and speak of you. Spring that descended from the highest heaven to earth, let my mind, watered by you, bring forth fruits of praise to your Father. Let me speak of you, not to set limits to you, for you are limitless, but to proclaim to whoever hears me that you cannot be comprehended. For who can comprehend you and speak of you, our Lord, as you are, except love, whose story rises above those who speak? As far as love has room, let it speak about your revelation.

Give me words that tell of the beauty of your humility. From the chariot to a borrowed colt, the foal of a donkey, your love brought you down. Who is capable of recounting your story? From that immeasurable legion of cherubim to a humble mount in our land—how can I do you justice? From among the wheels, the faces, and the wings of flame, compassion carried you away, and now the foal of a donkey bears you in procession. From the majesty of that throne filled with light to lowliness, whose embrace is open to children. From that back, full of eyes as they revolve, to this mount, than which there is nothing more despised in the world. From among the ranks and troops formed from flame to the little crowd carrying branches in the streets of Zion. Where, then, should the speaker recount your story? In what place should a mouth speak of you, if it speaks of you? Look, [?] your radiance dazzles the heavenly beings, yet the colt that carries you among earthly beings is frail and ugly. You are blessed by the movement of the speaking wheels [?], and you are praised with palm branches in the crowds. You are above and below, in greatness and in lowliness. In the heights and the depths, who can do you justice in speech? Emmanuel, for our sake you are like us.

And with the one who begot you, for his sake, you are like him. Look, the cherubim of fire bless you with the fluttering of their wings, and the children too praise you with their hosannas. Look, every realm honors you in its own way: the heights with their light, and the depths with branches from their trees. Above, you are the mighty one whom the flame fears; below, the humble one clothed entirely in poverty. The heavenly watchers prepare his way with flashes of fire, while the inhabitants below throw their rags before him. The mighty one set out from his Father's house to visit our land, and willingly reached the utmost poverty. The one who fashions crowns borrowed a colt to enter Zion, so that by his humility he might scorn the might of rulers. He destroyed the horse and also the chariot of the kings of Ephraim, and carried and brought peace to Zion, which had been in turmoil. He scorned and rejected the adorned mounts of rulers and rode a colt to make his journey in humility. The Hebrew children saw the humility of the great King and took up branches to greet him as he entered. The elders had withheld the glory due to the King who came to the land, but the children of the land were stirred with wonder to praise him. The young people were paying the debt owed by the elders of the people.

And there the praise that was required was set right. The priests and scribes shut their mouths and offered no praise, but the children formed groups to shout joyfully with their hosannas. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” cried the innocent, and the road of the King who had come thundered with new praise. The trees bent down to give branches and prepare the way for the sweet fruit that the blessed vine had given to the world. The children joyfully wove a crown of glory for the Ancient of Days, who had become a child among their gatherings. The one older than the ages came and became a young man in our land, and so the young people were stirred to praise him. The prophet Zechariah took up his spiritual lyre and ran before him, singing and rejoicing in prophecy. He plucked its strings and raised his voice as he sang: “Rejoice, daughter Zion! Shout for joy and cry out, for your King has come! Look, he has arrived, riding a colt, the foal of a donkey. Open your gates to him, for he comes to you humbly. Rejoice greatly and cry out praise in a loud voice, for look, he is coming, just as I assured you through prophecy.” Zechariah sang to the daughter of the Hebrews so that she might rejoice with him, but the contemptible bride did not rejoice as she had been summoned to do.

She was debauched and distressed that the bridegroom had come, and so she did not rejoice when she welcomed him. Her heart had been taken captive by the calf, her lover, and she was infatuated with him. She would not listen when the prophet told her, “Rejoice!” She was entangled with the hideous image with four faces and could not open the gates to the King who had come. She was intent on serving her idols, but had no concern for the service of praising her Lord. She worshiped Ishtar and mourned for Tammuz. She loved Milcom and offered sacrifices to Baal, her companion. She openly worshiped Kaiwan, Chemosh, and Ashima, and held festivals for the gods of all the nations. She was occupied with Egyptian [?] and had no time to sing praise with the disciples. She was busy preparing sacrifices for demons and did not go out to carry branches with the children. The children bless and praise the King who has come, while the old woman polishes her images and refurbishes her idols. The prophets knock at her lofty gates and try to awaken her, but she lies asleep in love with her many companions.

“Rejoice, daughter of Zion!” But she, the companion of calves, did not rejoice, for she was distressed that the Father's heir had come. She knew that he would expose her, and she hated him; she was unwilling for him to be praised by the children. Envy was in her heart, and she became mute and silent, offering no praise; she was intent on silencing those who praised. It was not enough that she was unwilling to offer praise; she was also eager to stop the praise of others. They were praising, and she was angry at their voices. She threatened them so that they would stop praising, but they would not stop. Isaiah cried out, “Awake, awake, and put on strength!” And Zechariah cried out, “Rejoice greatly and be glad, for your king has come!” The children cried out, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” And praise thundered abundantly along the king's way. But the Hebrew woman was unwilling to hear them—neither Isaiah, nor Zechariah, nor the children. She would listen neither to the prophets nor to the children; she was distressed and angry at their voices. In her insolence she was very intent on making them stop, and she sought an opportunity to silence them on any pretext. But those who praised would not stop praising, for the revealed truth had moved them to offer praise.

The Son's journey was a marvel to those with understanding, and the praise of the worlds and their inhabitants was too little for him. Michael's hosts stood in great amazement when they saw the Son riding a colt through the streets of Zion. The heavenly beings looked and saw the Only-Begotten, humble and quiet among the crowds of earthly people. The fiery beings trembled, wondering whether he had come down from the chariot, and they all bent down to look at him, to see whether he was there. They saw him on the majestic throne in his lofty place, and they also saw that it was he who was riding a donkey's colt. The angels marveled as they looked at him in both places, in the height and in the depth: he was not two, but one. They looked at him, seeing that the throne had not been emptied of him, and they saw him among these people with their hosannas. He was riding the cherubim and riding a colt, and it was a marvel that he dwelt in the height and traveled in the depth without being divided. Among the heavenly beings, flashes of fire were subdued before him on his way; among those below, he was being honored with palm branches. The cherubim trembled as they blessed him in his lofty place, while young people below praised him with their hosannas. But the daughter of the people grew envious and acted recklessly as he was praised.
452
She was intent on stopping the praise from every mouth. She agreed neither with the heavenly beings nor with those below, who were praising the Son's journey, so full of wonder. She struggled hard to silence those who praised, but because truth filled their mouths, they were not silenced. The elders of the people envied the children and their hosannas; the priests grumbled, and the scribes complained at their voices. The watchers praised the Son in his lofty dwelling, and down in the depths innocent children praised him with the disciples. The Jews, who hated everything good, hurried over and approached him, pleading with him to silence them. “Do you not hear what they are shouting?” they said to him, as though he were receiving borrowed praise that was not his own. He was being praised from the overflow of his great glory, yet they envied him as though he had stolen someone else’s praise. They shouted only a small part of his praise in their hosannas, yet the scribes were jealous, as though he had never possessed glory. They told him to order them to stop their praise, as though, if the children fell silent, his praise would cease. O Jews, haters of the light, how can they cease praising him, when heaven and earth are filled with his praise?

Even if you silence the children who have taken up branches, he has multitudes in his own dwelling who cannot be silenced. Ten thousand times ten thousand and a thousand times a thousand heavenly beings are praising him. Who can reach them to silence them? Even if it is easy for this little crowd to fall silent, who can command that legion of Gabriel’s company? They told him to order them to be silent, and he answered them, “If they fall silent, the stones will cry out in praise.” And it is indeed as the teacher of truth said: if they had fallen silent, the stones would have spoken, just as he had said. It was a time when praise was owed to the Son, and if they had withheld it from him, the stones would have paid him that praise. If the children with their palm branches had not praised him, the mute rocks would have praised him with their lyres. The Lord of kings was riding a colt, the foal of a donkey, and nature stirred to give praise for his humility. The priests, the scribes, and the leaders of the people were bound to voice the praise that was required. Because the elders withheld the praise whose time had come, the children rose to greatness by giving praise with their hosannas. And if they had fallen silent, praise would not have ceased there,

for the stones would have stirred and sung that song of praise. Nature was eager to pay its Lord the praise it owed him, and if those gifted with speech had not spoken, the mute would have spoken. And even if they had fallen silent, the stones could still have given praise. At that moment praise could not be silenced: either human beings or stones would have voiced it. Creation marveled at the humility of the Son of God and was eager to give praise with a loud voice. If the children had not shouted for joy, the stones would have spoken, for there was no possibility of praise ceasing then. Who, then, can now explain the hidden things to us: if the stones had cried out praise, as was said— For us who know, the Son’s word is trustworthy: as he said, the stones offered him praise. Let us now tell anyone who needs proof that it is easy to learn about hidden things from visible things. At the crucifixion, when those who gave praise were silent, the stones and rocks cried out the praise that was required. In place of the disciples, who did not throw their cloaks before him,

the dead came out and gave him praise with their harps. In place of the trees, which did not send him any of their branches, the sun cut off the strands of its light to honor him. In place of those who crucified the Savior and blasphemed against him, the mute elements praised him in their own ways. His friends had fled, and his enemies remained at Golgotha, and it was time for praise to rise to the crucified Son. When human beings fell silent, the stones stirred to give praise, so that the crucified King would not remain without praise. Through these things that [?] then at the crucifixion, that saying was revealed: “If they were silent, the stones would speak.” If the children had not praised him there with branches, he would have been praised just as he was praised at Golgotha. The [?] stands clearly before the hearers: if they had been silent, the stones would have cried out, as was said. The elements never withhold praise from the Lord, for all creation is stirred by him to give praise. He can easily be praised by stones and by pieces of wood, for his hidden command stirs the elements to give him praise. Created things sing praise in their own ways,
