both those that speak and those that are silent, each in their different ways. The sun, with its light and the rays of its heat, gives praise as it is able while running its course. The moon, in its rising and the changes of its waning, stirs up praise to the Lord of the seasons, who does not change. The sky, in its expanse and with the lights arranged in it, sings praise night and day to its Maker. The earth and the seas, with the high mountains and the floods, give praise in their own ways, according to how they were created. All the forests, the fruit trees, and the cedars give praise every day in great wonder. Heaven and earth are full of his praise, as it is written, and everything that exists utters praise to its Maker. All his creatures sing praise in their own languages, but you can never hear how they do so or how much they sing. Truth bears witness that all the elements praise him, but no one can comprehend how they do so well enough to tell it. No one knows with what mouth or with what voice the earth sings its Lord’s praise when it is called upon. David bears witness that it offers praise, when he called

even upon the elements to offer praise according to their natures. Fire and hail, ice and snow, and also sea monsters; all the depths, the earth and mountains, and also the hills. David laid praise upon these as a tribute, so that praise might rise from the Creator’s creatures to him. He urged the winds and also the storms to offer praise. Had he realized that they did not offer praise, he would not have urged them. David was moved by the Holy Spirit and stirred them up, along with the heavenly beings, to offer praise [?]. The sun and moon, and the lights [?] in the sky; the earth and mountains and hills, and also the trees. “Praise the Lord,” David said to all these. Because he knew that they praised him, he roused them. But how, or in what manner, they offer praise—do not ask me, for it is difficult for me to explain it to you. There is a hidden mystery between God and his creatures, and he hears when they offer praise in their own forms. The stones cry out his praise when they are called upon, and he alone knows how to hear their languages. They stood ready, as he was borne in procession on a colt, to praise his humble journey.

[?] Because the young men had taken up branches to offer praise, there was no need for the stones to offer praise then. Had those who took up branches there remained silent, the stones would have stirred and praised the King who had come. When the Jews sought to silence the praise of the Son, he answered them that the stones would cry out on his behalf. Indeed, they would truly have cried out, just as he had said, for there is no way that his praise can cease among created things. Speaking mouths praise you, my Lord, with their tongues, and speechless creatures sing your praise through their forms. All creation, renewed in you, gives thanks to you, my Lord, for all of it owes thanksgiving in wonder at your humility. The heights bow down to you, who lowered yourself to those on earth, and the depths praise you, who are higher than the heavenly beings. The redeemed assembly of the Church of the nations shouts joyfully to you, my Lord, because you freed it from the snares of lifeless idols. The daughter of the pagans rejoices on your day and is glad in you, whereas the daughter of the Hebrews became gloomy, scornful, and angry. Look, young men praise you with branches from the trees, and the sound of the elders’ praise mingles with that of the children.

Look, shepherds and their flocks bow down to you, in place of that flock which crucified its shepherd on Golgotha. Look, assemblies of the nations bless you in every land, in return for the insults you suffered from that band in the house of Caiaphas. Look, in their gatherings they cry out to you, “Holy, holy,” in place of the people’s assembly, which cried out, “He deserves death!” Look, every voice from every mouth sings your praise, in every tongue that you have stirred to praise you. The fiery seraphim, with awesome voices of holiness, proclaim your praise while covering themselves before your blazing light. The glorious cherubim, harnessed for you from the blazing fire, bless your awesome majesty every day with great trembling. A thousand thousand heavenly beings sing your praise, never ceasing from the praise that accompanies their hovering. Look, the virgin church, whom you brought back from her captors, my Lord, thunders in you, is rich in you, and rejoices in you. Everything gives thanks to you, because at your coming everything was renewed. You are blessed by all; praise be to you in every tongue.
The homily on Palm Sunday is finished.
By Saint Jacob. Homily 59. On our Lord’s question, and on the revelation that Simon received from the Father.

Merciful Father, who redeemed us by the blood of his Only Begotten, from you I will receive strength for a discourse on your Only Begotten. True Son, who came to us to set us free, through you I will speak about your revelation, for your sake. Holy Spirit, teacher of the ignorant and uneducated, through you I will become wise and bring forth a discourse that is entirely wonderful. Father who begets, give me words concerning your offspring, so that I may speak richly and lovingly of his story. Begotten Son, reveal your beauty in me for your Father’s sake, so that my mouth may speak, raising its voice in new praise. Spirit, the Advocate, through whom the whole gospel is sung, through you may my feeble tongue turn to your praise. Father, who sent his beloved Son to become our brother, open my lips to speak about your Only Begotten.

Only Begotten, who gave us all his Father’s riches, may my words go forth to the listeners with the riches of your mysteries. Spirit who went out and leveled the heap before the disciples, clear a path for the wondrous discourse that has stirred to shine forth from me. Father, from whom everything comes and for whose sake all things came into being, from you I will receive a starting point for a discourse that has no bounds. Son, in whose hand everything rests, and apart from whom there is nothing, through you I will sing praise full of discernment to your Father. Spirit, treasury of prophecy and apostleship, give me riches from your treasures so that I may speak. Father, who in his love handed over his Son for sinners, speak in my place to the listeners about your offspring. Son, who humbled himself to become one of us, though he is our Lord, shine wondrously within me, and let your light shine from my words. Spirit, who levels all the rugged heights, prepare a path for my feeble words. Who, then, will give me love that stands like a demanding creditor before the listeners and draws them toward instruction? Who, then, will stir the ear to the voice of teaching, so that the sweet drink, free of dispute, may be pleasing to it? Who, then, made rivers of great love flow

from the speaker and the listeners, united in one purpose? Now [?], everyone runs toward the one will of God, who wishes everyone to benefit from him without his being diminished. Let everyone strive to gather what is beneficial, whether they are speakers or listeners of the faith. You who speak, take care to bring benefit when you speak. If you bring no benefit, practice silence. And you, the listener, gain benefit yourself as you listen. If you gain nothing, why are you wasting your time beside the speaker? Let love bring you here, for love also moves me to speak. Benefit cannot be gathered except through love. Do not listen craftily, trying to catch my words, for love never consents to lay a trap. This discourse is free from cunning and cleverness. So cleanse your hearing too for simple things. Come down from the height of wisdom where you stand, and humble yourself before me, so that I may speak to you plainly. If the Son of God had not come down and humbled himself for us, who could have reached him to speak with him where he is? If he had not lowered himself in love into poverty,

who could have spoken of his spiritual riches? If he had not willingly come and clothed himself in weakness, what mouth could have recounted his might? The exalted one came down and gave himself to us so that we might speak of him. Let us not, then, listen proudly to his revelation. No one can walk on the great road that the Son of God laid through the world unless they clothe themselves in humility. No one can speak about the Only Begotten except through love, which is the source of beautiful things. You who listen to me, hear my words as I speak them, with the love of a soul that knows how to love simple things. If you are discerning, recognize from the speaker himself that the discourse he has begun to deliver is beyond him. Who can speak of the Son of God, whom speakers cannot express, unless [?] speaks of him without dispute? What scribe or sage or scholar can explain the wonder that cannot be explained? Let whoever claims to know the Son explain his name, for no one except the Father knows who the Son is.

Or who dares to speak about the Father? For only the Son knows the Father, who is like him. And you, the listener, if you are fair, how can you demand that we speak in limited terms about that birth which has no limit? Your own ear cannot reach the limit of the Son, nor can a speaker describe him as he is. Do not claim to have ears that can grasp his story, for I have not claimed to have words that can reach him. Anyone who thinks he can set limits to the Son of God is utterly mistaken, whether he is a listener or a speaker. I reject knowledge that thinks it can reach the Son’s limits, and a mind that thinks it has comprehended him or can comprehend him. If you want to comprehend his limits, do not listen to me, for I have no words that can reach the Son’s height. For who can climb inaccessible heights, ascending to speak a discourse that is beyond speakers? The Son is in his Father, and who can measure the Father’s height? His offspring is in him, hidden in his bosom in his very being. Who can speak about the one who is hidden in his Father’s bosom, yet, without departing, dwelt in the Virgin who is full of wonder?

The true Son is in the hidden Father and in the virgin mother. Let anyone who would explain him be silent; he can only marvel. He traveled without moving, and came to us without departing. He was in the heights and in the depths, and who can describe him? When he dwelt in the depths, the heights were not emptied of him, for he was wholly in everything, and was in Mary and in the one who begot him. He came not to be confined within limits or explained, but to visit the sick sheep and return to his own place. The world saw the Great One within the bounds of littleness. Speakers multiplied, but they could not describe him. People saw him come in the flesh, though he was God, and they did not know what to say about his coming. They saw him full of power, strength, and might. His appearance was lowly, but his mighty deeds were beyond what tongues could express. He opened the eyes of the blind, cleansed lepers, made the deaf hear, healed the sick, and raised the dead as God. When they saw him in weakness like a human being, they turned and saw him in might like God. At times he was hungry like a human being subject to suffering, and at times he fed others like God, who has compassion. And amid this new way, full of wonder,

the onlookers marveled, and did not know how to say who he was. They stood caught between greatness and littleness, and could not say who he was without confusion. To say of him that he was God was difficult, for they saw him as a human being in their streets. Yet the mighty deeds he performed would not let them regard him as a human being: they testified that he was God. He mingled with people and performed mighty deeds as God, and no one on earth knew how to say who he was. Not knowing, they invented names, trying to say who he was, though their own wisdom did not give them knowledge. One said that he was Elijah because of his mighty deeds; another said that he was Jeremiah because he [?]. One person was bewildered and did not know what to call him, but called him one of the prophets whose name was unknown. They began calling him one [of the prophets?] whose name was hidden. O seers, do not give him a name that is not his! Do not give the Son of God a foreign name. Do not call the Son Elijah or Jeremiah,

nor a prophet whose name is kept with his Father. They chose borrowed names and gave them to the Son of God. These did not please him, and he was preparing to flee from them. He had compassion on the world, which was bewildered and searching for his name, and he wished to teach it what his true name was. Our Lord, the Light, led his twelve away to teach them clearly what his name was. He led them through the whole country, and they entered the realm of that knowledge which reveals divine mysteries. They reached the realm of great light and revelations, and the Master began to question his disciples. “Who do people say I am?” he asked them, to open a door there for the mysteries to be spoken. The scribe who teaches good things led the children and questioned them to teach them wisely. He became a questioner, not because he needed instruction, but to reject the borrowed names the people had given him. He saw that the disciples were not asking to learn his name, and he himself asked in their place, to teach them. He wished to silence the false names, the uproar, and the talk. That is why he asked what the many were saying.

When a teacher asks a child for an explanation, he trains the child and exercises him so that he may become enlightened. He questioned them, not to learn from the disciples, but so that they themselves might truly learn from him. In asking questions, he too resembled his Father, so that not even in this would he be less than the one who begot him. The Father asked among the trees, “Where are you, Adam?” From Mount Sinai he asked, “What is this that you have in your hand?” The Father questioned Moses and Adam, and likewise his Son also asked, “Who do people say I am?” He looks into the minds and understanding of the whole world, and examines every heart and its thoughts. A heart cannot stir a thought apart from him, nor can a thought move within a mind without his noticing it. Hidden things and visible things are alike to him, and things past and things yet to come are one to him. The Father once asked questions, and his Son also asked, so that the person questioned might come to know the one who examines everything. “Who do people say I am?” he asked, although he knew what their thoughts were saying even when they were silent.

Very loving was that moment and that question, which arose from the All-knowing One to be spoken with love. The sun stood speaking with its rays, and the great realm of faith was filled with light. Twelve lights accompanied the daylight of righteousness: the hours of the day, whose dawning gives light to the world. Twelve rays from the disk of the sun, our Lord, stood beside him so that he might teach them what his name was. A company full of light, life, and delight, of truth, hope, peace, love, and faith. Twelve dawns that drove the night away, making it leave the lands that the light had betrothed, so that it might gladden them. Twelve commanders who went out with the King's Son to establish a peaceful border for faith. Twelve seal-stones that the Son of God set in his crown; before him fell the diadems and crowns of vanity. Twelve men whom the good heir chose and took for himself, so that through them he might rebuild all the ruins that had been demolished. Twelve workers whom the skillful Son took with him, so that they might diligently fence up the breaches in the world.

The bridegroom stood ready to build a house for the bride he had betrothed. He brought twelve stones to mark out its foundations. He looked at them all, considering which he would choose to lay first. He left it to his Father to reveal its beauty through revelation. Within the realm of life he erected a bridal chamber for the glorious bride, and lovingly crowned her with promises. He marked out the house with the twelve, who were full of light, and chose one stone for its splendid foundations. He kept the mystery so that the Father might then be the cause of that stone being built up by the Son's hands. He began to ask, knowing what he was doing, so that through the occasion of that question the Church might be established. “Who do people say that I am?” he asked, as though he did not know. They began to tell him what was being reported outside. “My Lord, some say that you are Elijah, and some Jeremiah; others have taken you for another of the prophets of old. “The people are divided into many factions, and Judea is full of divisions and discussions because of you. “Each person has formed an opinion of you according to what he thinks, and there are many disputes and disagreements because of you.”

The disciples repeated the sayings of all the people and what was being said among the crowds about our Savior. Our Lord said, “Look, the outsiders have all spoken like outsiders. You speak as insiders. “You have told me what those far away are saying. Now tell me what you yourselves say, as those who are near. “I have heard what is being said among my enemies. You are my friends: now reveal your thoughts to me.” The question moved on from the starting point where it had stood, and went inward to the disciples to examine them. [?] Our Lord did not need to learn what the outsiders were saying; rather, he made it an occasion for his discourse. If he questioned them to learn what was being said, why, after hearing it, did he repeat the question to the disciples? He had already heard what the people were saying when he asked; and if he had questioned them to learn, he would not have asked again. He clearly showed that the question about outsiders brought a demand upon the insiders, so that he might examine them. He laid out a course for the heralds of the faith, so that, as trustworthy witnesses, they would declare his name and who he was.

A great demand was placed upon the disciples there: to say who the hidden one was whom the people did not know. He left aside the opinions being expressed by the Jews and demanded that the members of his household say what he was. He set aside and rejected that way of thinking belonging to Judaism, and began to question the thinking of the apostles. He demanded that they say who he was, as trustworthy witnesses, for they held the key to the treasury of God's house. “Who do you say that I am, my disciples?” And the disciples trembled at the wondrous question they heard. Our Lord had made them stand as living people among the dead, so that they might know who he was; and if they did not say, they would be held in contempt. Simon heard the true Son demanding that he call him by his name, and he trembled at speaking without his Father. The chief of the disciples sent his mind soaring to the heights above, and in his thoughts he rose to the dwelling of his Father. He ascended from the earth and from the visible creatures, leaving behind created things, worlds, and everything in them. In his mind he stepped beyond the structure of the temple of the world,

and he left the lower heavens behind and rose still higher. He entered and stood in the hidden Holy of Holies of the One who is, before the Father, and began to plead with him with a pure heart. “My Lord, who dares to give a name to your only-begotten Son? You begot him; you teach me what to call him. It is fitting for a father to give his son his name. This is your right, my Lord; command me to call him according to your will. It is not mine to give your only-begotten Son a name. Reveal to me who he is, and I will go down and reveal him after you have taught me. But how am I to call him? I will not name him. You call him by his name, and command me also to call him that.” The plea of Simon, the chief of the apostles, came before the Father, and he revealed his mystery to that trustworthy man. A revelation went out from the Father's house to that disciple, and he took it and descended, as though carrying a royal decree from the king's house. He displayed a seal bearing the signature of the hidden Father, and on it was written: “You are the Messiah, the Son of God.” And he raised his voice to our Savior, as the revelation had commanded him: “You are the Messiah, the Son of God.”

His true name was hidden in the Father, and Simon learned it. He came and showed the Lord who bore that name that he knew it. Learn and repeat the worshipful name of the Son of God, which admits neither addition nor subtraction. The Father revealed to Simon, the chosen one, the truth about his Beloved; yet who had revealed the great mystery to him remained hidden from him. And the Son, who knows the hidden Father and his revelations, showed Simon who had revealed his name to him as it truly is. When Simon addressed him, he called him this as though it came from himself; but our Lord showed him that this revelation was not his own. “Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you”—as though to say, “You did not produce this name yourself, without revelation. It was not through your own knowledge that you knew to call me this. My Father revealed it to you, for no one but he knows me.” With the beloved name that Simon brought from the Father's presence, he addressed his Lord: “You are the Messiah, the Son of God.” Immediately he received a crown, as though from the King's own hand: a great blessing for faith that does not waver. He gave that disciple a gift in return for his confession, so that everyone might confess as he confessed and receive a blessing.

This, too, was why our Lord asked his question: to give a blessing to everyone who holds firmly to the faith. Through revelation Simon brought the name from the Father's presence, and he received his reward: a blessing, a divine crown. He gave him the blessing as a seal upon the faith, so that this confession might have the force of law throughout the whole world. He showed Simon that he had been in his Father's presence when the hidden mystery was revealed to him, so that he might bring the true name into the world. He showed that he was equal to the one who begot him, in revelations, in hidden things, and in the explanation of all wisdom. “O disciple, you were in the Father's presence when he revealed this to you, just as now the Father is with me and is not far from me. The Father did not give you revelation apart from me, nor do I give you a blessing apart from the Father. The Father did not reveal this to you without my knowing, and I did not give the blessing without the Father's agreement. Your soul is worthy both of revelations and of confession; it is full of truth and does not incline toward doubts. You are Peter, the rock, and I place you among the foundations of the great house, and upon you I place the church that I have chosen.

Your foundation is firm: it will bear the weight and not give way. I will place you first in my building, because you are steadfast. Be the foundation of the holy temple that I am joining together for myself, and upon you I will lay out all the courses of the daughter of the day. I have betrothed a bride, and a great wedding feast is prepared for me. You shall recline first at the table, because you are faithful. I will entrust you with the chamber of the daughter of the day, and upon you I will build her, for your building rises above disputes. Your steadfastness is a rock; therefore you are Peter, the rock. Upon you I will build the church that rises above doubts. You are Peter, the rock, and upon you I will build the glorious church. The barriers of Sheol will not overpower her with their schemes.” And what are the bars of Sheol, O listeners, but Death and Satan, who laid the earth waste? The lofty gates behind which they imprisoned Adam—and there all the captives remain, in the dwelling of darkness. The bars that blocked the path of life so that it could not be traveled, and closed the passage so that no one could cross over to God. The gates and bolts that were shut against Adam, so that he could never again emerge from the darkness in which he was wasting away.

Concerning these, the bridegroom promised the bride that they would neither imprison her in their palaces nor overcome her. Light has betrothed her, and she cannot be imprisoned in darkness. The Living One [?] her, and from now on Death cannot overpower her. He began the house, chose a stone, and laid a foundation. He gave her the exalted position of overcoming Death and Satan. He promised her that the bars of Sheol would not overpower her, so that she might give herself without fear to be with him. The great apostle became the foundation of the great house, so that the bride might enter a structure that cannot be destroyed. He erected a bridal chamber for her and, so that she would not be afraid, promised her that destroyers would have no power over her buildings. He began to build her, and on that great stone he had found he laid her structure, so that her height would rise even beyond the clouds. He had arranged twelve stones in the fortress of light, and had chosen one so that the whole house would rise [?] upon it. He outlined, marked, and carved the great stone he had found, and set it deep within that great building whose foundation he laid. The bridegroom had chosen it, and his Father carved it through that revelation.

The Spirit completed it and placed it among the foundations of the church. He drew revelation from the Father's hidden knowledge, and came down and prepared a house for the Son to use. The bride was betrothed but did not know who the bridegroom was. The Father revealed him to her, and she confirmed the terms of her betrothal. The bridegroom asked her whether she knew him, and because she knew him, he pronounced her blessed for having attained the Father's revelation. He promised her, “You will not be overcome by destruction,” and invited the nations and the regions of the earth to rejoice with her. He took the bride away from snares and stumbling blocks. He broke the snares, prepared a path, and led her to himself. She had two adversaries who hated her, and he granted her that they would not overcome her. The tyrants of Sheol had trampled her within their territories. He bound them and set her foot upon their necks. He placed her in the light and overthrew darkness before her. He drove the shadows of death away from her paths. He built her upon the great stone, chosen and full of beauty, and established her walls upon his company of twelve, full of light. He opened gates for her facing the radiance of the apostleship.

So that she might dwell securely in the radiance of light. He set his cross in place for her like a pillar bearing creation, and lifted and raised stones of light for the great house. With the upright wood of righteousness he completed her dwelling, and with its arms extending this way and that he arranged her shelter. With the nails in his hands he secured her stout beams, and for her adornment he painted colors with his blood, to honor her. He gave her blessedness as a gift full of riches, so that every day she might delight in his divine light. He rebuked death and overthrew Satan through his suffering, and the bride rejoiced in the bridegroom’s goodness and his promises. Because that disciple had called the Son by his name, he pronounced him blessed and built the Church upon that apostle. He made him a rock and placed him among the foundations of his house, because he saw that he held all the courses of masonry firmly and did not give way. “I give you the keys of my kingdom,” he promised him, so that he would be both the foundation and the steward of the house. “If you bind on earth, it is bound in heaven too;

and if you loose on earth, it will be loosed in heaven.” He gave the apostleship authority in the heights and the depths, so that it might command above and below with a master’s authority. The rich man betrothed the daughter of the poor and registered her in his name. He gave her the keys so that she might be mistress over his possessions. He entrusted to her the wealth of the depths and the treasure of the heights, so that above and below she might be mistress, subject to no commands. Her lineage was despised, and so that she would not think he despised her, he placed all his keys in her hands, because he loved her greatly. He allowed her to open all his Father’s gates, so that she might see and rejoice, and her heart might expand at how rich she was. He made her mistress over those above and those below, so that the heights and the depths might obey her in their respective stations. He saw that she loved him, the good heir, and did not turn aside, and immediately he gave her all his treasures and their keys. Though she was poor, her lineage wretched, and her family needy, he gave her his keys because he saw her faithfulness. He took the daughter of the poor from her lowly place and from the dunghill, and she soared to the heights, until she commanded among the heavenly beings.

He authorized her to open the lofty gates of that heavenly Holy of Holies, because he saw that his Father loved her. He had seen the Father give revelation like a necklace, and he himself gave a ring full of keys, to act in harmony with the Father. He saw that his Father loved the glorious woman, and he brought out and gave her the keys and blessings of the whole house. There was a secret between him and his Father, and he saw that the Father had revealed it to the Church. Immediately he made her mistress of his house. The bridegroom had seen his Father give his name to the bride, and he wished to do the will of the Father, who loved her greatly. He saw that she had taken him from the Father's house in that revelation, and he gave her the keys to the great riches and the whole treasury. The Father loved her because she loved his Only Son, and his Firstborn welcomed her when he saw that his Father cherished her. Come, you who watch, marvel at the deed of the royal bridegroom: he saw that the poor woman was faithful and gave her a crown. He built her a house upon the disciple who loved him, and because of his love he gave her the keys to the heights and the depths.
He gave the free woman authority to seal the treasuries and undo the seals. Blessed is the rich one whose coming made the poor rich!
By the holy Mar Jacob the Teacher. Homily 20. On Simon Peter, when our Lord said to him: “Get behind me, Satan.” (Matthew 16:23; Mark 8:33)

In all my homilies I call upon you, true Son. May all my words be offered through you as glory to your Father. May a voice of thanksgiving rise from me to you in songs, as I recite a homily in your praise among your congregations. May my mouth be a censer of sounds for you, Son of God, and instead of incense accept praise from a weak man. May my mind grow fervent in the fire of your love so that it may speak, while the beauty of your story blazes forth before the listeners. May the homilies about faith in you be a perfect sacrifice.

Accept them at the place of atonement as an offering. May my tongue honor you with songs instead of sacrifices, and with every sound may every thanksgiving be sacrificed to you. You are the one for whom sacrifice and blood are not fitting. May my sounds of praise be gifts that please you. Son, who gladly became a sacrifice for sinners, may my mouth sing pure praise to you in a loud voice. Your word is exalted above all speakers. May praise well up within me and stir my voice to sing your praise. I cannot reach high enough to ascend and measure the height of discourse about you. Let it descend to me, since it can easily become like you. Let it humble itself and, in its humility, be spoken through me, for I cannot ascend to where it is. If your story does not lower itself into the great depth, who can reach it and speak of it as it is in its own place? Let discourse about you look to you, who lowered yourself to those on earth. Let it follow you, and behold, it will be spoken by the weak. Your Father's love drew you from the lofty heights and set you down beneath the depths and the [?] of the earth. Because you lowered yourself, the earth grew strong through your humility. Behold, those made of dust tell your story, weak though they are.

You descended from the heights, and behold, the depths are rich because of you. Make me rich too, so that I may proclaim your story within the depth. Mercy drew you to the lowest regions of the earth, our Lord, and therefore the dead spoke of you within their own boundaries. Who could have ascended to your lofty dwelling and spoken of you among the legions of flame? Who could have stepped among these hosts of Gabriel and proclaimed your story among the ranks of the heavenly beings? Who could have approached the awesome winged chariot and proclaimed your message [?] the trembling of the great heights? Who could have traveled the path of coals that cannot be touched, gone and seen, and returned to tell the earth your story? [?] which is between you and your Father—who could have stood there and opened his mouth [?] that are many for you? No one there proclaimed your story. You yourself came down to sinners, and now they sing to you with their tongues. In the depths of the dead, the mind examined you and raised its voice to cry out with trembling: “Great is your wonder, Son of God!” Thought saw you in the lowly assembly beneath the earth, and now, because of you, it raises praise to your Father’s lofty dwelling.

The understanding saw the hollows of the graves illuminated by you, and it too was illuminated, so that it might tell your story through its nearness to you. Here beside us, with us in our own land, you lived. Since the Father was pleased to bring you among us, now we speak of you. Even here we did not see you confined within boundaries, Lord of all boundaries, for you were with us and with your Father. Who can comprehend you? The entire way of the Son of God is beyond all limits, and whoever thinks he can set limits to it does not walk in it. His revelation is exalted, and unless faith sings of him in simple words, no mouth can recount his story. If someone approaches him through knowledge, he becomes bewildered; but if he seeks him through faith, he finds him. Knowledge failed, and all wisdom came to nothing, while his teaching shone forth through humble fishermen. The scribes were put to shame, and the interpreters became objects of contempt, because through uneducated men the good news took hold of the whole world. The wise boasted, but when they stirred themselves to speak about his coming, they fell away from the truth and became deluded. The philosophers were astonished and bewildered and became fools, because they saw uneducated men teaching wisdom. Those who only yesterday were holding fishing nets—

now the might of the world bows and bends down to listen to them! The earth inclines its ear to listen to the Galileans, and despises the scribes of learned Bero [?] and Greece. Needy men, without buildings or possessions— the owners of gold bow before them with their offerings! The commander is slain, yet his servants boast of victory. Through the slain one they took possession of the earth, so that it might dwell in his name. He chose vessels empty of knowledge for his own knowledge, so that he might send them out not with their own knowledge but with his. He commanded them to give up the possessions of the world, so that the whole world might be theirs while they remained poor. With these things of his own he enriched them and made them great, while nothing of their own remained with them. Yet his mighty deeds triumphed only through his death, and whoever is ashamed to acknowledge his death does not belong to him. Because Simon, the chosen one, said to him, “Far be it from you to die,” he called him Satan. Though he loved him, he showed him no favoritism. That disciple became the rock for the church he built, and out of love for him he gave him the keys of the heights and the depths.

Because he saw that his death displeased him, he rebuked him; and, as though in anger, he called the chief of the disciples Satan. If I had a love that pressed eagerly for instruction, I would now raise this question: why was this said? Why did he shortly afterward call that chosen apostle Satan, when he had even made him the foundation of the church? Love holds back so that he may incline his ear without argument; and if there is love, there is a word full of beauty. Let us now say why that disciple was insulted when our Savior called him Satan, as we have said. The hater of humanity envied Simon because he had become great, and he schemed to put a blemish on that beautiful man. He had seen that he was chosen, beautiful, pure, and full of light, exalted in his truth, and that his faith was full of beauty. He had heard that he received that revelation from the Father’s house, and that, as one entrusted with the mystery, he learned the name of the Only Begotten. He saw that he had received a great blessing from our Savior, and had become rich and gained royal power through blessings and revelations. He heard that the beautiful name of Rock had been given to him, and that he had become the foundation for the building of the royal house.

He had seen his Lord give him the keys of the whole treasury, so that he might command the heights and the depths with a master’s authority. He had heard that this decree had been issued concerning the apostle: that even in heaven he would have authority to loose and bind. He had seen that yesterday he was a fisherman, but today he reigned. He grew envious, burned with rage, and clapped his hands in bitterness. He had heard that the church, which had been laid waste, was being built, and that he and death were being driven away from it so that he could not enter it. The enemy learned that Sheol, his treasury, was being uprooted, and that the church of the firstborn was being built upon the disciple. He had heard that the barriers of Sheol were falling, being defeated, and coming to nothing, while the church was taking possession of the heights, the depths, and the whole world. He became aware that the road to Eden was being opened, and that a return was taking place, so that Adam might return to his inheritance. From the Son’s promises that tyrant learned that he would restore everything he had ruined, and then ascend. The evil one was distressed by these things he heard about Simon, and the corrupt one plotted against the apostle to destroy him. For he said, “I will batter the great foundation,

and look, that whole building he has seized in the heights will shake.” If the disciple slips a little, as though about to fall, the church trembles; for if it does not tremble, great is our downfall. If this man who became a rock should shift or tilt, the building standing on him also becomes unstable. I set a snare for Simon so that he would fall; and if he falls into it, look, I catch the whole flock of eagles that follow him. There are twelve of them, and if I seize one—that first one—all his companions come with him into darkness. If I seize its head, the gathering scatters; for if it gathers together, it wipes my tracks from every region. If I bind that commander of the apostolic company, the good news will retreat entirely and disappear from the regions. If Simon, the head of the disciples, stands firm in his truth, then downfall awaits me and Death, my dear companion. If the disciple persists in the beauty of that confession, the whole earth will learn from him and forget my teaching. If I do not snatch his keys by some scheme, he will bring out riches from the Father's house and mock me.

He enters and takes charge of the treasury of the Godhead, supplies the world with riches, and forgets me. All my images throughout the lands become a laughingstock, and the lofty horn of idolatry is broken. My celebrations, my festivals, and my assemblies disappear from the lands, and my priests wander about or are led to God. The whole sphere of the gods becomes a laughingstock, and the lofty idols I set up on earth fall to the ground. If Simon does not waver in his confession, I cannot stand my ground, and I must flee from his teaching. Satan felt great envy toward that disciple, and he set traps and hid snares for that faithful man. If the fool who went astray stirred up battle against his Lord, how much more did he threaten to harass the servant! He fought against God who is from God; how much more would he assail a human being in his insolence! He began with the Master and then came to the disciple, for he was scheming by every means to make error [?] reign. He raised darkness against the light to wage battle,

and held his ground as much as he could, so that he would not be exposed. The Evil One acted boldly and fought against our Savior; and as he lingered, he fell like lightning before the eyes of the angels. He trembled and became confused, and gave up his hold on victory. He recognized the Son—who he was and whose Son he was—and left him alone. He began to slink among the crowds of Jews, teaching the priests, scribes, and Sadducees ways to cause stumbling. He went in and lay hidden among those who reviled and showed partiality, so that he could delight in their blasphemies against the Faithful One. He stirred up trouble wherever our Lord performed miracles, so that, instead of praise, he might provoke disputes among those who saw them. He tried to claim for himself the signs our Lord performed: “It was Beelzebul,” he said, “who drove out demons, not the Only Son.” At one time he made the priests his companions; at another he brought rulers and officials into his company. He inflamed them with blasphemies and insults, to stir up disputes against the victorious one who had bound him in combat. But that sun proved stronger than the shadow, and wherever he went, he drove him fleeing from the roads. With rays of light he exposed him and laid him bare,

and made room for the light to take possession of the whole world. He watched all the mighty works our Lord performed, and stirred up trouble among the crowds, unsettling whoever would listen to him. He found an opening and once fell upon a disciple, and through greed corrupted his soul by its own free choice. He tore Judas away from that company of disciples, whispered and lied, and made him his companion through hateful deceit. He set the great trap of love of money for Judas, caught him, and brought him down into theft and hanging. If he had been able, he would have scattered all those who were gathered together, for he feared them from the beginning of their deeds. The great serpent bit the company of apostles on its heel, but it cut off that member and cast it to the ground. It bound and constricted it so that the gall would remain in one member, and the whole body was kept safe from corruption. Judas fell into the rope that cut him off from the disciples, and because his insides were full of gall, its violence burst him open [?]. Another member took his place among the disciples, and the body of the apostles remained without blemish.

It was not with Judas that the evil one began setting traps, but with the great one, the Lord of all lords. When he met with defeat in the terrible combat he had waged, he was left ashamed before the victorious one who had exposed his fraud. After this he barked at Simon, the head of the disciples, and one by one he probed all the good servants. He came down and found the one who carried the money bag unguarded. Inside the bag he set a trap for him and caught him there. He taught the chosen one theft, great deceit, and falsehood, and made him corrupt among [?] the disciples. Now listen: it was because of that stranger’s intrigues that Christ called Simon, the head of the disciples, Satan. He envied him and approached him to whisper to him, hoping, if he could, to cast him down from his greatness into a trap. He approached him with the cunning of his companion, the serpent, hoping to snatch the keys if he gave him an opening. As soon as he received that revelation from the Father and received and carried away a great blessing from the Son, he was appointed as the foundation of the Church, as one who was trustworthy, and the Son gave him the keys to manage his Father’s house.

Satan followed on that disciple’s heels, lying in wait for him to see whether he could find a way to put a blemish on him. Our Lord began to speak about his suffering and to reveal to his disciples the mystery of his crucifixion. Our Lord spoke about his killing and his suffering: when and how he would endure all these things at the hands of the Jews. Before it happened, he said what would happen, to teach them that he mounted the wood of the cross of his own free will. He told his apostles what would happen to him at the hands of those who would crucify him. On that occasion Satan approached to display his own work. He advised Simon, as a friend of the Son of God, to grieve deeply and, like a beloved companion, be stricken with distress. He could not set any other trap for him, because he was steadfast and would not exchange his love for his master for anything else. The chief of the disciples would not stoop to the love of money, nor would he steal or lie or turn away. He set a trap for him in the very friendship in which he stood firm, so that from love itself he might make a slippery place spring up on which Simon would come to harm. The demon of distress entered and stood before his mind,

and put on sorrow over the matter of the crucifixion. Simon became distressed like a close companion full of zeal, but that very distress within his soul belonged to Satan. He grieved like a friend at this news of suffering that he heard, and he became afraid and distressed for his master, like a close companion. The disciple became compassionate instead of steadfast, and began to give feeble advice to the Son of God. “No, my Lord! No, my Lord! Do not endure the sufferings of crucifixion. Let neither suffering nor death come near you in any form. Far be it from you to die or be mocked by the Jews! Far be it from you to suffer or be dishonored by those who crucify! No, not so! Let suffering not strike you, our Lord! You who have been holy from eternity, far be it from you to be insulted by troublemakers! Life and glory are fitting for you, for you are the Son of the Living One. Death is unfitting for you. Far be it from you to die, you who give life to the dead!” With this troubling advice born of feeble love, the chief of the disciples was rebuking him, telling him not to suffer. But the one who examines the heart saw his soul and who was disturbing it. As the one who knows everything, he knew where the words came from. In secret he examined the thought stirring in the apostle: the serpent had planted it, and it did not belong to that disciple himself.

Immediately he turned toward Simon, though he loved him, and, as though in anger, called him Satan, although he was an apostle. The feeble advice [?] that came from Satan, while the apostle himself, for his part, remained with our Savior. He called that distressing thought within Simon “Satan,” because it would not consent to the crucifixion. The serpent who served death to Adam among the trees was giving advice that the Son should not suffer on the cross. Knowing who had counseled the virgin, he rebuked his friend because of the enemy who was troubling him. Our Lord did not accept feeble counsel as Eve did, for he had come to heal the bite through his crucifixion. He was not persuaded by the disciple who loved him to abandon the cross, through which life is obtained for the world. Because he wanted to keep him from it, he called him Satan, for the death of the Son of God distressed Satan. “Go, Satan, and get behind me,” he told him. “Do not obstruct the road I have taken toward Golgotha. The Father sent me to be a sacrifice for sinners.

Why are you preventing the great sacrifice from being offered? Get out of my way, so that I may reach the death prepared for me, through which I will release the prisoners of Sheol from darkness. Come behind me, for the road leads straight toward suffering, and no one can stand against me and stop me. You are a stumbling block to me, for you want to obstruct the road to death. It cannot be blocked. Get behind me, Satan! I have only a short distance to go before I reach Golgotha. Who persuaded you to obstruct the road that is full of life? It was my will to be conceived in the womb, born in a manger, and baptized in the river. Is the cross to be held back, and Adam to live? Why should it be far from me to die and give life to the dead in Sheol? Look, they are waiting for me to enter and loosen their bonds. If you had kept me from conception, or from birth, or from the river, it would have been easy for you to keep me from Golgotha. The Father who sent me appointed a meeting for me in the depths of Sheol. Unless I go down and explore the abyss, I will not return. The Father's image has sunk into the mire, and now I am going down to draw it up in my own person. Unless I bring it up, I will not ascend.

The serpent had cast Adam from Paradise into the grave. That is why I have come: to enter and bring him out of destruction. If you tell me, ‘Far be it from you to suffer,’ then, according to what you say, far be it from the world to live! Is this what you are saying: that I should stay away from Golgotha, and the great image should remain in Sheol without being renewed? Is this your counsel: that I should abandon the cross and not ascend it, and Adam should waste away there in Sheol, where he is? If you keep me from death, you hate life, for unless I die, life cannot be obtained for Adam. The captives are imprisoned in the hollows of the graves, and now I am going to bring them back. Why are you keeping me from delivering them? The tyrants of Sheol have plundered my possessions. Get out of my way, so that I may go and recover my property, which thieves have stolen. The children of destruction have bound Adam in the realm of darkness. Let me enter and release those in chains, and then I will return. The serpent and Eve took counsel together and brought Adam down. Let your counsel be rejected, for if accepted, it resembles theirs.” Why should this be far from me, if I am to do a deed in Sheol and shatter the gates of death that bar it?

I will cut down the lofty barriers of the daughter of darkness, and demolish death’s fortress so that it can no longer be inhabited. I will devastate the pampered one who swallows generations, and uproot all her walls with the standard of my cross. I will be a guest among the dead for three days, and proclaim to Sheol’s prisoners that she must release them. I will roll in the dust of the dead and search in it for the beloved coin that bears our image, which had been corrupted. With the remedies of crucifixion I will repair the image that the crafty serpent corrupted among the trees. Why, Simon, do you say, ‘Far be it from you to do these things’? For if I do not die, as you say, all these things come to nothing. Your word stands against the mysteries of prophecy, for if I do not die, they will not be fulfilled as they were spoken. If they do not hang me on the wood before the people, Moses is proved false, for he saw life hanging on the wood. If they do not pierce my feet and hands, as you say, David will protest because he has been exposed as untruthful.

And if they do not give me vinegar and gall to drink, the mystery of prophecy comes to nothing, and you are accepted instead. If the people do not divide my clothes, as was sung, who will confirm that King David was a prophet? If I am not among the dead, as he prophesied, why did he cry out, ‘Look, he is among the dead,’ if I am not to die? If they do not lead me like a lamb to become a sacrifice, Isaiah too, who called me a lamb, is proved false. If I am not silent like a ewe before its shearer, is it not a great distress for the prophet that he has not been vindicated? If the marks of the nails are not seen in my hands, what shall I say to the prophet Zechariah when he asks? If the sun does not grow dark and shine again at the crucifixion, why was it said that there would be light at evening? If I am not in the heart of the earth for three days, the image of Jonah is erased from the revelations. If it is to be far from me to taste death, as you urge, then all the prophets are henceforth annulled, as you say. This plea that the path of crucifixion should be abandoned comes from Satan, who seeks to throw good things into confusion. You are a stumbling block to me on the road that leads toward suffering. Get behind me; I will go forward toward Golgotha.

Our Lord was looking toward that great salvation which he accomplished through his crucifixion when he called the apostle Satan. ‘Far be it from you to die’ was like saying, ‘Far be it from you to save.’ For this reason he rebuked him, rejected him, and treated him with great contempt. He looked and saw how many bonds he would loose through his death, and how many closed gates he would open for those imprisoned. And how fully he would pay the common debt on behalf of the generations, and how many hidden snares of the Accuser he would shatter. And how greatly he makes peace between those above and those below, and how completely he abolishes the hostility that the serpent introduced! And how many dead are raised through him when he dies, and how many prisoners see light when he descends to Sheol! He considered these things, and when it was said, “Far be it from him to die,” he rebuked his friend and cast him behind him in great anger. “You are a stumbling block to me if you say to me, ‘Far be it from you!’ For you are thinking not of the things of God but of human things. Because the Father revealed to you in his love that I am his Son, you think that it would be a disgrace for me to die. Because you know whose Son I am, death disturbs you. You say, ‘There is no possibility that the Son of the Immortal should die.’ You do not consider that, if I wish, it is easy for me to die,

and that, if I die, the life of my own being remains preserved within me. You are thinking in human terms when you observe that compulsion drives a human being to become dead. Even against his will, he is subject to death by the sentence passed upon him, and his appointed end brings him low and drags him into the dwelling of Sheol. His spirit departs, and he returns to his earth to become dust. He experiences decay, wastes away, and perishes upon the dust. Moths and worms tear him apart within their domains, and he dwindles to nothing there amid the darkness. His story is forgotten, and he no longer returns to his loved ones. He leaves his friends, and they are never again satisfied with his companionship. This is the human way that you are thinking of, but you do not consider God's way, in which I walk. Since you have learned that I am God, the Son of God, do you not consider that, if I die, my death is in keeping with who I am? When I die, the bars of Sheol will not hold me back, and death will not be able to look me in the face when I come out. I will not experience decay there among the departed, nor will death have the power to shut the door in my face. They will not say to me, ‘If you are dust, you must also return to it.’ Nor will devouring creatures and moths trample me as they usually do. I will not be overcome by destruction among the departed,

nor will death bind me in its pit as it does the rest. Sheol, the devourer, will not imprison me when I descend to it, nor will the worm sink its fang into me to destroy me. I will not disappear from my friends like a human being, nor will my relatives [?] say, ‘He is no more, for he has decayed.’ You have not considered that, if God approaches death, life is hidden within him, and even when he dies he will give life to the dead. You are thinking of human beings, O disciple, who die and perish, and whose remaining memory fades away. You have not considered what belongs to God: when he enters Sheol, it trembles and vomits up the dead it has swallowed.” You did not consider that when God descends to the grave, throngs of the dead come out from destruction to meet him. You are thinking of human beings, whose lives cease when they die, and who become dust inside their graves. You did not consider that when the Son of God enters Sheol, he tears it apart, empties it, and returns to his own place. You did not consider that if God consents to die, he does not experience decay there in Sheol like a human being. Look, you are thinking of human things, not God's things. The road is mine; if you look at it, regard it as mine.

For I told you that I both die and rise. Rejoice in the resurrection, and do not grieve over death. My road to the depths of Sheol runs through Golgotha, and it cannot be opened except through the sufferings of crucifixion. Wait here for me for three days until I come, for this is not a human departure, since I am coming back. I will go and hold a three-day vigil for the dead, and open for them the gates of Sheol that were shut. I have two stages to travel on the road of death, and I will return on the third. Do not grieve. It is easy for me to die and easy to live, and I have the authority to go and come whenever I wish. No one can hold me back. The gates of Sheol cannot be shut when I enter it. It collapses, and the dead imprisoned in it rise. For I can lay down my life if I wish, and whenever I want, I take it up again. I have the authority. It is not someone else who takes it from me when I die, for I willingly place it in the Father's hands. You did not consider this about God—that he has such power. Instead, look, you are considering the death of human beings. Through Simon's case, the Church learned from our Savior:

When the account of his death arises within her, she should not grieve. The death of the Son of God puts death to death, and his suffering also makes sufferings suffer, for whoever understands it. Sufferings suffered through him when he suffered on Golgotha, and death died through him when he died, but it did not hurt him. Through Simon, the chief of the disciples, he taught the Church to cherish the news of his killing whenever it is told. With rebuke and a reprimand full of anger, he drove fleshly thoughts out of the disciple. He rebuked Satan and drove him away from the Church, so that he would not sow in her a feeble way of thinking that fears to acknowledge the Son's death. He took the disciple himself away from Satan and brought him to his side, so that he might hear the news of the crucifixion without fear. The one who was shamed by being named withdrew, for he was an outsider, and took with him the feeble thoughts he had brought. Satan fled behind Jesus, while the disciple remained before the Son, taking refuge in his crucifixion. “Go, Satan,” was what was heard, not “Go, Simon.” The evil one went away, and the apostle remained to confess his Lord. The feeble counsels that came from Satan fled from Simon, and Peter remained, a rock within the building. The Son of God held fast to his friend through the rebuke he delivered.
And the enemy fled, so that he would not obstruct the Son’s way. He set his face toward suffering without hesitation. Blessed is he who, by his death, brought to life all those lying dead in Sheol.
Here ends the discourse on what our Lord said to Simon: “Get behind me, Satan.”
Another work by the same holy Mar Jacob. Homily 21. On Simon’s denial.

Turn my mind toward the hour of your trial, Son of God. Command me to speak about your humiliation as I grieve. My thoughts have entered the courtroom to tell of you. Grant me there to see the wonder of your humility. The mind pressed in among the crucifiers and stood gazing at you. Grant it to recount the story of your trial richly. The hidden, spiritual mind saw you before the judge and marveled at you, for there you stand calmly.

Into the place where even the disciples were afraid and deserted you, the word has entered to tell of the beauty of your humility. Where Simon Peter denied you, saying that he did not know you, there this lowly mouth seeks to acknowledge your trial. May your love, our Lord, clothe my mind with discernment, and may it speak lovingly through it about the story of your trial. Only through love can a mouth speak of you, for your own love drew even you to suffer for our sake. The great sign of the Father’s love is the slaying of his Son: he loved the world so much that he handed over his Only Begotten. See how much he loved us: he gave his Son to death and redeemed us. Let us therefore speak about our Savior with that same love. Love has great compelling power wherever it is found, for no power is stronger than it among those who possess it. Who could have compelled the Father to hand over his Son, except love, which is greater than everything, as it is written? In this way a person draws near to God, for in this same way he too drew near to us and became one of us. For who can love as he does? Or who can love the Son enough in return for his salvation?

Who entered into judgment with the Son and endured suffering? Love alone accompanied him as he was humbled. When the crucifiers armed themselves against him in murderous rage, his friends abandoned him. In his great love he stood in the struggle. The lambs had fled, and the Lord of the sheep remained alone, so that the sign of his love for his flock might be revealed. At the hour of slaughter, love came down there to the contest. Had it not been the Son’s love, it would not have triumphed over every other love. The outsiders fled, but the shepherd did not flee from his flock, so that through this the sheep might learn who loved them. Truth weighed the Son’s love against that of his disciples: the disciples’ love proved light, while the love of the Son of God weighed heavily. The chief of the disciples denied Christ, saying that he did not know him. Where, then, would you seek love except in the Son? Come, see Simon swearing and heaping up curses, raising his voice to say that he did not know the Son of God. Simon’s denial wove a crown for the Son’s love, for he alone endured sufferings on behalf of many. By denying him, the great apostle taught this: no love can equal the Son’s love. When he swore before many people that he did not know him, he painted a picture of Christ’s love, which is greater than all.

His very denial is also a powerful witness to his proclamation that the love of the Son of God has no equal. The faithful man denied him so that, through him, the Lord of truth might be believed: his love is greater even than the worlds and all created things. Peter proved light in the balance; who, then, could weigh heavily beside our Savior? This is clear: no love can compare with his. At the time of the trial, Simon went in to see his suffering, but he did not remain to carry the great burden with him. They seized the Son, and trembling overwhelmed the apostles; suffering and death drove them away from the Savior. Although Simon distinguished himself far more than his companions, he longed only to look on and see his trial. When the conflict rose against him, he turned his back, for no one except our Lord was equal to that battle. The disciple looked and saw his teacher standing there, surrounded by a band of accursed men who were insulting him. The master was being struck, and the servant could not speak. The teacher was on trial, and the chief of the disciples stood at a distance. Wolves surrounded the Lamb on every side, goading him toward slaughter amid great suffering. The sword was sharpened, and the spear stood poised against the Savior.

He drank suffering and endured terrors at the hands of many. Insult, abuse, and ridicule from the wicked surrounded him. He remained quiet while he was mocked, and the sons of the left struck him. The mighty one was imprisoned, and lowly men threatened to put him to death. The assembly raged, but he remained silent and did not speak. That disciple cried softly in sorrow, but fear of those who were to crucify him kept him from raising his voice. The sheep groaned for the shepherd who was being savaged, but feared to approach because of the wolves surrounding him. His soul was wasting away with sorrow for his teacher, but he could not weep where the people would see him. He put on a cheerful face, though his mind was troubled like the sea, to show them that he was a stranger to the Savior. He watched furtively, afraid that they might see him, waiting until the Son’s trial was finished before he went away. He held back his tears so that they would not flow in front of the outsiders, and they would not realize from his weeping that he belonged to him. He remained silent, though he loved him, and stood far away, though he was devoted to him. He could not show his love openly. He stifled his sobs so that they would not be heard as he cried out, and he too would be caught up in the death sentence along with the innocent one.

He cleverly mingled with those who would crucify him, so that on that pretext he could stay and watch his entire trial. He set aside his mourning and sat warming himself with the wicked, so that he could see the outcome and then leave the court. Although he had thoroughly deceived them in this way with all his stratagems, they recognized who he was, whom he belonged to, and where he came from. For they were saying, “You too, man, are one of them. Your very speech sounds strongly Galilean.” A storm rose against the faithful man, and he wavered. As though in the sea, he sank into denial among those who would crucify him. The scribes battered him far more fiercely than turbulent waves, and engulfed the boat in the raging storm of denial. The priests blew like tempests with their threats, and Simon became afraid and let himself sink. They were saying to him, “You too, man, are one of his followers.” At this, he quickly rushed into denial. He began swearing, “I do not know this man! Do not unjustly revile me over something I know nothing about. I came in here with the others to watch the trial, but I truly do not know the man himself.” He hid behind falsehood and protected himself, and the threatening fury that had risen to torment him subsided.

His soul had been covered in wrongdoing, so that he did not realize that it was a great crime to deny the Son by saying that he did not know him. Sin had entered and spread a veil over his mind, so that he could not see who our Lord was while he denied him. Delusion entered and took hold [?] throughout his soul, and as he swore, he did not think that he was lying. Falsehood had filled the place of truth within him, and as he uttered curses, he thought that he was not lying. He had utterly forgotten that Jesus was the Lord when he denied him, and he was even swearing truthfully that he did not know him. The eye of his soul had been blinded by terror, and he did not know who Jesus was while he denied him. He was blinded by the threats and could not see clearly. He reviled the Son without knowing who he was. He repeatedly swore that he did not know him, and it was true: at that moment he did not know him, because he had forgotten him. He feared being killed so much that he lost his understanding. He trembled before the crowd and set his face toward denial. Death terrified him, and he fled along the path of falsehood. In the terror of his heart he forgot the Son and stood there denying him.

Just as the storm had subsided around him and he was about to find relief, another wave rose bitterly against him. A woman among the crucifiers saw him and said to them, “This man too is certainly one of them.” When the crucifiers pressed Simon with threats, he again set his face to lie, just as before. He began swearing, just as he had already sworn, that he did not know him. He shook out the fold of his robe as though he had never seen Christ. A second wave rose against him and shook him again. Already submerged in falsehood, he sank still further. “Oh,” he said, “now I do not know this man! Since I have never seen him and am not acquainted with him, why this injustice?” “Judge fairly! Do not condemn me when I have done nothing wrong.” “I do not know who the man you are holding is. An occasion brought me here to come in and see. Why should I die?” “May I be cursed if I know him as you say! I have never seen him, so why should I suffer because of him?” Simon was sinking into the great abyss of falsehood.

The harder he struggled to climb out of it, the further down he went. The deep waters of denial surrounded that faithful man, and turbulent waves covered him during the Son’s trial. The true friend denied his friend, saying that he did not know him, for terrible danger confronted him there, and he forgot his love. The good servant saw his master being mocked, but he was afraid to reveal himself, lest he too be struck. The disciple trembled when he saw his master being mocked. He called down a curse on himself, saying that he was not even acquainted with him and did not know him. Simon, who had hated the world and followed the Son of God, openly denied him: “I do not know this man.” He had left parents, brothers, and fishing nets when he commanded him, and had followed him. But when danger arose, he denied him and fled. Terror entered and opened a breach in that fellowship. In place of love came denial, division, and disavowal. Just as he was about to prevail through his lie that he did not know him, eyewitnesses again accused him of being his disciple. The nimble man fell into three traps and became entangled. All three traps caught him as he trod on them. Both the first snare and the second bound him, and he was caught again in the third, just as in its companions. Falsehood closed around him and overwhelmed him.

He repeated it a second and a third time, calling down curses on himself and saying that he did not know him. He put on the armor of disavowal before the crucifiers, and opened his mouth to speak with oaths. For the third time, the faithful man denied him still more vehemently, calling down curses on himself: “I do not know who this man is.” The chosen one was sinking in the great sea of falsehood; the flood and the turbulent waves of denial covered him. His soul had been dyed in wrongdoing for a long time, until it took on the hateful color of injustice. Our Lord showed great love to the whole world, for no one loves as he loved humanity. Out of love he gave himself up even to death, for one who loves does not waver even in death. Our Lord alone was equal to that struggle. No one else joined him in his trial, because no one else was able. While Simon watched him from a distance, he denied him and swore curses. If he had come near and borne his trial, what would he have done? He watched the Son's humiliation from a distance and was terrified. If he himself had been humiliated, how afraid he would have been! The sound of mockery sent trembling through his limbs. How far he was from enduring mockery himself, if that were required!

He heard a threat and denied the Son, saying that he did not know him. If the nails and the spear had reached him, what would he have done? No one but our Lord was equal to these sufferings, and it was fitting for him himself to endure them all for everyone's sake. Simon denied him and repeatedly swore, “I do not know him.” With oaths he warded off the sufferings so that he would not have to bear them. When he had become wholly caught up in falsehood, our Lord looked at him. He came to his senses, and his heart was appalled at his transgression. The rooster crowed, and Simon remembered the Son's words. Anguish seized him over what he had done without realizing it. He saw that he had slipped from the height of apostleship and fallen into the great pit of falsehood. He despised himself because, in place of the love of discipleship, he had sunk to the hateful rank of falsehood. Understanding came in and sat over him like a judge, and he was scourged with thoughts as though with rods. He was ashamed of himself and needed no rebuke. He judged himself and condemned himself as guilty. Our Lord looked at him when his denial was complete, and without a sound, in silence, he wisely judged him. Our Lord's gaze was full of understanding and wisdom:

In silence, as though with words, it rebuked the chief of the disciples. He looked at Simon as though saying these things to him: “Why, Simon, do you deny me at the time of suffering? “O my disciple, where is the love of your apostleship? Chief of the disciples, why do you flee in the hour of danger? “When I pronounced a blessing on you all, you were first; and when I promised thrones, you were again at the head. “You never fled from me until today, O disciple. You abandoned me in danger; where, then, is your love for me? “When, Simon, did you not know me, except today? And where did you forget me, except here where I am being mocked?” When the waves of the sea bore me up, you ran toward me; but now that the scribes cover my face, you deny me. When I turned water into wine, you were near; but now that the priests have splashed me with spit, you are far away. When I multiplied bread in the wilderness, you were giving orders; but now that the people have prepared bitter things, you do not see me. When Elijah and Moses were on the mountain, you did not disown me; but because disgrace surrounds me here, you deny me. Your love is feeble if you change with the times,

for not even a trial turns someone who loves away. A true friend shows his love in a crisis; but you, the beloved and chief of friends, why do you deny me? Because disgrace and mockery have come upon me, you do not know me; and because sufferings surround me, you have utterly disowned me. In peace you followed me, but when war came, you abandoned me. And you even deny me, saying, “I do not know him at all.” The occasion gave you an opportunity to deny me, O faithful one! And love that falters amid changes is deficient. Because you saw me humbled among those who would crucify me, the moment swept you away, so that you too denied me and turned away from me. The Son's silence conveyed these things to Simon; and Peter himself despised himself for what had happened to him. Never say that Simon was destined to deny him because our Lord had foretold it just as it happened. It was not because our Lord said it that the faithful one denied him; rather, our Lord was looking ahead to this denial that would take place. He knew beforehand what would happen, before it happened; but that did not make Simon blameless when he denied him. If his denial had not truly been hateful, then his repentance would not have been beautiful either.

It was ugly of him to deny him, and beautiful of him when he repented. He truly sinned and truly repented, not merely in appearance. Therefore, when he denied him, he was a denier; and when he wept, he was truly repentant. It was not merely in appearance that he denied Christ, saying that he did not know him. He had sunk into a great, unfathomable falsehood. That is why he also wept sincerely: he saw himself in the great pit of denial. Denial took him out of the circle of apostles, and tears brought him back into the number of disciples. When he was calling down curses, he was a denier and not a disciple; but after he wept, he was a chosen apostle and not a sinner. While he denied him, he had no share in apostleship; and after he confessed him, there was no trace of denial in him. He denied the Son and became estranged from fellowship with him; that is why he was filled with bitterness and tears of sorrow. He saw that he had lost the great truth of discipleship, and he began to weep because he had become estranged from that greatness. The sin that had stood against his soul fled from him; his path grew bright, and he began to come to repentance. Denial finished its wicked work and departed from him, and remorse came in after it to instruct him like a teacher.

He began to judge himself discerningly and wisely brought accusations against himself. Woe to me! I have fallen from that height of love for the Son, and now I stand with the crucifiers in denial. It is a great crime—whom have I denied! I have hated my own life, and instead of being the chief of the apostles, I have become a denier. Why did they not bind me with him at his trial, so that I would not have denied him? Death with him would have been worth more to me than treasures. I ought to have suffered blows with him when he was being beaten, and when he was struck among the crucifiers, they should have struck me too. Where shall I go to seek the life I have lost? And whom shall I confess after denying the Son? Why did I not endure the pains of death for his sake and stand firm in declaring before everyone that I knew him? I ought not to have denied him, even if I had to die, for death with him is a good life without end. Instead of a disciple, I have become a denier. What shall I do? Instead of a companion who shared his bread, I have become a companion of the crucifiers. Among the apostles I was a brother, a leader, and the first; but among the crucifiers, one who hates his master and curses himself.

Let my ten companions weep bitterly over me, for truly great is the pain that has overtaken me today. It would have been better for me if I had fled as they fled. Because I did not flee, I became a denier instead of a fugitive. Let Thomas weep over the offense of his brother Simon when he hears that I denied the Son before many people. Let James wail, and with him Matthew and Bartholomew, at the news of the crime I committed today among the wicked. Come, John, learner of mysteries, weep over Simon, for like Caiaphas he denied the Son, saying that he did not know him. All my brothers, lament for me over what has happened to me! I was an apostle, and now I am mixed in with those who deny him. I denied the light, and now I stand amid darkness. I hated the day, and night has surrounded me on every side. I let go of life and took hold of death on the left side. What shall I do? Who will bring me over to the right? With these words Simon was deeply distressed, weeping with great sorrow over his offense. The great delusion had fled from his mind, and he sighed over what he had done, because it had happened. Perhaps he said: If only I could suffer with him,

and through my sufferings erase the written record of my denial! If only there were an opportunity at the trial for me to approach him and endure humiliation, mockery, and persecution with him! But who would grant me to receive the spittle from his face, and offer my cheeks to blows for his sake? Simon was driven this way and that. What could he do? He was afraid to approach, yet he was also distressed that he had gone far away. He could not go in and bear the Son’s sentence; and because he had denied him, he was ashamed and humbled, and he wept and wailed. He swore and lied, and lost out on both sides: he was like neither the disciples nor those who crucified him. He was no apostle, yet he did not agree with the murderers. He had fallen away from his companions, yet had not joined those who crucified him. To [?] remain quiet in denial was a great offense; yet when it came to going to the disciples, he despised himself.
