Through denial he had descended from that rank of perfection, yet to remain quietly in that sin was painful to him. He was accustomed to truth, and when he tasted falsehood, he wept and sighed: how bitter was the taste he had found! He stood in wrongdoing, while his soul clung to righteousness; and among all possible courses, he knew nothing to do but weep.

When distress had entered and engulfed him on every side, grace came and spread her wings over his torments. Come, Simon, and bring tears of repentance. Weep and do not stop; weeping is good for you today. Your great wound requires many tears, for this pain cannot be healed except by tears. Come, let us go to justice, who threatens you; with sighs I will appease her so that she listens to us. Take tears with you and bring them before her when you enter, and immediately all the fury of her severity will subside. Let your weeping rise like incense, and send up sighs instead of spices; then all anger against you will surely subside. Nothing but weeping can quench the fire of wrongdoing. Pour tears upon the flame that threatens you. See that you do not approach despair, for it is death. Take courage and ask for mercy, and you will be accepted. Great sorrow chastised Simon like a judge, and scourged him into walking the great road of repentance. His soul was illuminated by the grace that shone upon him, and he began crying out in great sorrow over his transgression.

I beg you, my Lord, do not let me be estranged from fellowship with you. Wrongdoing has driven me out; let the love of your kindness bring me in. Sin lay in ambush for me, threw me down, and shattered me without pity. You who are wise, bind up the wound inflicted on me. Waves of wrongdoing surrounded me on dry land to drown me. My Lord, draw me up from the floods, as you are accustomed to do. Look, you are enduring these sufferings for the wicked. Show your compassion first in me by forgiving me. Look, you stand in this trial on behalf of sinners. Give life first to me, a sinner, for I have asked you. I denied you, and now it is I who confess you. Accept my confession and erase the written record of my denial. Where could you demonstrate your compassion if not in me? For I have committed injustice more wickedly than anyone else. See, our Lord, a great chasm of wickedness has swallowed me. Give me your hand so that I may climb out of it and not perish in it. I have fallen into an abyss, and if you neglect me, I cannot climb out. My Lord, extend your mercies to me, so that they may draw me up. The evil one has caught me, and now he is choking me inside his snare. Break his snare yourself, so that I may escape torment.

An ulcer of denial has broken out in me, and now it is eating away at me. Good physician, apply your medicine to me so that I may be healed by it. The deceitful one encountered me and gave me denial to offer you. Now accept from me also the confession that I offer you. Good shepherd, go out in search of the sheep that has strayed. Do not leave me in the hands of the evil one who seeks my life. Simon was trembling with these stirrings of repentance, and he was bowed down amid thunderous sobs. He knelt on the threshold of the Son’s mercy, crying out, so that his persistence might open the door of the Judge’s house. Here is a mirror for anyone who needs forgiveness, so that he too may persist in petition—and see, he is forgiven! Simon’s denial became an occasion for repentance, so that its path might be revealed and made clear before many. Take an example from that chosen man when you plead, and cry out bitterly in sorrow over your transgression. Weep as he wept, and you will be accepted as he was accepted. Grieve sincerely, and see, you are truly forgiven! Look at Simon as he wept bitterly, for he keenly felt the pain of wrongdoing. He was filled with bitterness so that he might drive out the sin that had entered him,

because he did not want it to live beside him as a neighbor. He saw Gehenna roaring fiercely against him. He opened a flood of tears and inundated it, and it was extinguished before him. The evil one surrounded him with tightly packed ranks of denial. But he roused himself to weep, and with sobs he defeated his legions. The wise man saw the fire of wrongdoing heaped up within him, and from the top of his body he opened a channel to extinguish it. With the sound of weeping he silenced the thunder of denial, and with confession he paid off the debt recorded against his wrongdoing. He saw the filth of wrongdoing in his soul and was deeply distressed. He poured out pure water and wisely washed it away. Mud had come out of his mouth, and he had become smeared with it. He poured out tears from his eyes, bathed, and was cleansed. He transgressed like a fool, but turned back and made amends like a wise man, so that you too might learn how to make amends when you transgress. That discerning man’s eyes paid what his tongue had incurred, for he had authority over his bodily members to put them to work. He saw sin moving about within him to gain a foothold, and he drowned it in tears so that it would never return to his thoughts. He saw that the accursed devourer had fastened onto him and was swallowing him.

And he poured out salty water so that the devourer would be blinded. He washed his soul in the clear waters of repentance until it became white, fit to be a garment for the royal house. He lost his beauty and wept greatly as he searched for it. He found what was his, and then he turned away from festivities. Simon has given you abundant material, O penitent, so that he may open the door of mercy for you when you plead. It was also fitting that the Church should learn from Simon which door all penitents enter through. For who can build a house without a foundation? It is fitting for Simon to be first in everything. It is therefore fitting to imitate this rock in all the courses of masonry that the Church has on every side. He is the head of both the chosen and the faithful, and he himself has also been made first among penitents. He is perfect among the apostles, and his story is mingled with sinners, so that all the ranks within the Church may imitate him. There is an example in him for both the righteous and sinners, so that everyone looking at him may see him in a condition like their own. He has been made a mirror for both the perfect and penitents,

so that everyone within the Church may adorn themselves by his example. He was complete in truth and utterly complete in denial; complete when he sinned, and still more complete when he repented. He was eloquent in denial and like thunder in the voice of his confession. He was rich in tears and foremost in revelations. For he was the first to confess who the Son was and whose Son he was; and he himself was also the first to deny him, saying that he did not know him. He became the head and the first in repentance, and fittingly the Church, in all its diversity, is built upon him. For the son of carpenters who laid its foundations is wise; that is why he built it upon Simon from the beginning. The Church glories in repentance more than in anything else, for through it all its congregations become abundantly rich. If a prostitute presses to enter, and a robber too, who would open the door to them without repentance? For this reason the Church is built upon one who denied, so that all its courses of masonry might fit together without anxiety. Who could build himself upon John, whom sin or wrongdoing had never touched? The breast of fire honored him and carried him lovingly.

And who could imitate him without trembling? It is easy for you to look to Simon the chosen, who is full of hope: after he denied, he repented and was truly accepted. Through him you learn that repentance has power, until you reach the lofty rank of perfection. He was first, and after he sinned and truly repented, he did not descend a rank to become second or third. He ascended through tears and stood in his place unchanged, holding in his hand the keys, the title, and the authority. What he had lost through denial he regained through tears, so that everyone who comes to repentance might find hope. All the ranks within the Church rest upon him, and he is joined to and stands alongside both the high and the low. For there is no one above him in perfection, nor among sinners is there anyone below him, since he was a denier. When he confessed, he extended his revelation as far as the Father; and when he denied, he swore that he did not even know the Son. Through sin he descended to the very limit of denial, and through repentance he reached the rank of perfection. On one occasion he heard from our Lord, “You are Peter.”

On another occasion, he changed his words and called him Satan. At one moment the sea supported him, though he was a rock; and a little later the deep swallowed him because he doubted. In him are ranks both very high and low, so that all the orders within the Church may be arranged upon him. The perfect who are in the world can perhaps scarcely reach him, while sinners too are beside him through repentance. In him there is room for both the prostitute and the robber, for the righteous and sinners, all together. For he is the foundation, and all the courses of masonry are laid upon him, so that in every way the whole house may be completed upon him. Look at Simon and take your place upon his building, for whoever you are, you have a place in him if you wish. If you are righteous, let your faith resemble his; and if you are a sinner, emulate his tears and his repentance. If waves of wickedness surround you to drown you, cry out as he cried, “My Lord, help me!” and he will lift you up. If a great sin surrounds you like a flood, call to the Son, “My Lord, my Lord, lift me up!” and he will rescue you. If you are held captive by wickedness as powerful as denial,

weep like Simon, and through your sobs you will be forgiven. If you fall as he fell, rise as he did, for he is a mirror for you, and if you look into him, you will be adorned. The Son’s door is mercifully open to whoever seeks him. Blessed is he who called us to repentance, so that through it we might be forgiven. Here ends the discourse of Mar Jacob the Teacher on the denial of Simon Peter, chief of the apostles. From the discourse of Mar Jacob on repentance. On Exhortation
There was a wound in the soul of Simon, the chief of the disciples, for wickedness had ambushed him and brought him to ruin through denial. But when he sought refuge in repentance and brought tears, Christ bandaged his wound and restored his former beauty. Before he sinned, he had been made head of the disciples; and after he denied him, Christ restored his place through his repentance.

He did not demote him to fifth or third place, but raised him up and established him in his former rank. Before he denied him, he was the steward of the household. He denied him and went out; but when he repented, Christ brought him in and also gave him his flock to tend. He gave him back his keys, which he had lost when he denied him, and also entrusted him with lambs, sheep, and ewes. Just as his beauty was increased through repentance, Christ also increased his authority over the flocks he had found. The Son of God loved his flock and died for it, and he gave it to Simon, trusting him to guard it. This man is a disciple of repentance. Repentance brought him inside; without it, he would have gone away. He had denied his Lord, sworn an oath, and called down curses, saying that he did not know him. He grew angry and went out of the house, and there he went away. Repentance ran after him as he fled and turned him back to kneel at his Lord’s threshold. It taught him to bring tears instead of an offering, and he took them and brought them, as repentance had taught him to do. As soon as he came, Christ looked at him, and he became beautiful. Christ welcomed him into his company as though he had never denied him at all.

Afterward, he gave him the entire flock for which he had died, as to a friend who had never sinned. He made him an image and a mirror for those who repent, so that they might know the power of repentance. With the beauty that belongs to human nature before it sins, a person enters and stands in God’s house as soon as he repents. Even the angels rejoice over a sinner who repents, because the King’s image, which had been lost, has been found. Now, soul, take confidence and be certain that your beauty will be restored to you. Come to God. Just as it was restored to Simon, the head of the apostles, all the beauty of your nature will be restored to you. From a homily by Mar Jacob on the five talents that our Lord gave his servants. (Simon Peter.)
He uprooted and demolished the lofty temples of idolatry, and established the Church, building himself into it as the first stone.

He laid himself as a foundation for the bride of light, and built his fellow apostles into her walls as beloved courses of stone. He was in the foundation, and his companions in the footings, and the building rose. Christ came at the head of the corner and became its shelter. He placed the cross in its midst as a lampstand, and our Lord as its light; it has no need for the sun to shine in its neighborhood. He opened within it the spiritual womb of baptism, which conceives the dead, gives birth to the living, and presents them to the Father. He built an altar in her, the table of the King who is full of life, and on it he set the banquet of the body and blood. He broke the bread of life, mixed the bowls of wine, called the guests, and distributed the wealth his Lord had given him, putting it to profitable use.
By Mar Jacob. Homily 22. On the commemoration of the departed and on the breaking of bread. And on how the departed benefit from the offerings and alms given on their behalf.

If there were an ear that would listen lovingly, I would now be eager to speak with discernment. But if love does not listen to me, why am I speaking? For without love my words are devoid of benefit. Love of good things has grown cold among humanity, and teaching is not loved when it comes to light. Little by little the world has abandoned good customs and driven hope, love, and faith far from itself. The fear of the Lord, which is the source of all good things, has diminished today, and therefore discernment has ceased. Evil has gained dominion and taken possession of humanity,

and it gives goodness no room to act. People today have not merely abandoned almsgiving; they have also withheld the offerings for their departed. Of all vows, offerings, and tithes, this alone remained among humanity, and it too has been forgotten. This sacrifice remained for the world to be sanctified through it, but now people neglect it and do not honor it with discernment. In the bread and wine, which are the mystery of the body and blood, all sacrifices reached their spiritual fulfillment. Through it the people of earlier times were also brought near to God, and forgiveness came to those of later times from his Majesty. With bread and wine Melchizedek, the great priest, entered to minister before God in a symbolic manner. With this sacrifice, without foul odor or smoke, he served as priest, depicting a pattern of things to come. This man, who in his perfection became a priest forever, chose bread and wine from among all sacrifices to offer. As a spiritual man who discerns everything, he knew beforehand that only through this could the whole world receive forgiveness.

Although he had the example and patterns of Noah and Abel before him, he did not wish to bring the blood of animals to God. A spiritual impulse stirred in his soul, and he perceived that bread and wine alone were suitable to offer. These mysteries, through which the Church stands today, were already being used by Melchizedek back then. Moses himself, the great prophet who offered sacrifices, also pointed to this pure sacrifice—how beautiful it is! With the bread of the Presence, which was never absent from the table, he symbolically adorned all his sacrifices. Although there were very many sheep and oxen that he offered, he always honored the bread far above them all. He placed it on the table before the Lord, and the great prophet called it the bread of the Presence. This bread adorned all the sacrifices, for the great mystery of the holy body shone in it. If those of old carried it reverently in their hands, how much more fitting is it for those who came later to attend to it! And if the old covenant honored it so that she might be honored through it,

how much more should the new covenant strive to honor it! If, while it was bread, it was more honored than all sacrifices, now that it is the body, what sacrifice is as great as it? For those of old depicted symbols through their offerings and gave those who came later a clear view of the realities. It is not because the King's daughter received images from those of old that she breaks the bread of the mysteries today. In the upper room she saw her Lord breaking his body, and from him she learned to do every day as he had prescribed for her. It was not Melchizedek who taught the Church how to act. She looked to her Lord, and every day she does as he did. She did not receive her pattern from Moses, who was a human being; rather, Jesus, who was God, taught her the mystery. And see, she carefully guards it, honors it, and takes pride in it, for it is the great sacrifice through which the living and the dead are brought to perfection. Why, then, has this very great blessing become so small in the eyes of many today, and why is it not celebrated? People have despised the holy bread and do not bring it. What shall I say, and why, and where, or to whom?

Shall I remain silent rather than rebuke the discerning, or shall I speak lovingly to those who understand? You who listen to me, I speak to you lovingly. Receive it with love, for love also moves me to speak. Do not let the Lord's bread be absent from his table on your account, and pour out his holy wine every day in a spiritual way. Bring bread, wine, and love to the house of atonement, so that the priest may enter before the Majesty with remembrance of you. Moses inscribed the names of the tribes on topaz stones, so that the priest might bring their memorials into the Holy of Holies. You too, write down your own memorial and those of your departed on a list, and give it to the priest to present before God. Prepare a feast and invite your dead: they will come to the altar, which is the harbor and resting place of all spirits. You who love the deceased, show your love for him in this way, not by holding a great mourning that does him no good. Give his name and memorial to God along with your offering, and divine justice will not deprive your faith of its due. Place his memorial on the table in the house of atonement, with bread and wine, which are the mystery of the body and blood. I will now speak with discernment to the company of women,

if they will listen lovingly to me with the ears of the soul. Look, they go about among the graves to weep for the dead, and through their wailing they show their love for their departed ones. They abandon the church, its worship, and its sacred offerings, and go weeping among the graves for their loved ones. O faithful woman, seek your loved one in the holy temple, with God, in whose hands all spirits are placed. Do not call to the dead man in the grave, for he cannot hear you. He is not there; seek him here, in the house of forgiveness. Here all the souls of all the departed make their way, for this is the place, the harbor of life, where they find rest. Here their memorials and their names are recorded in the great book of the Godhead, in which everything is contained. The blood of the Crucified One sprinkled resurrection upon the souls, and his great power drew them to come to him. And since your departed one, woman, is truly here, why do you wander among the graves like a foolish woman? Your discernment has departed, or your faith is incomplete; habit has drawn you after these foolish things.

An impulse has carried you to the grave to speak with your departed one, and in your agitation you have multiplied senseless folly. If there were love for God in your soul, prayer would be born in your mouth instead of lamentation. Cease, miserable woman, from ignorant thinking, and ground your soul in the discernment of faith. Let your love for your loved one resemble true love, and commemorate him with offerings and prayers. Your dead loved one does not benefit from your weeping beside the grave, but your offering is good and helpful both to you and to him. Those tears that were poured out beside the grave—sprinkle them here in the church with discernment. Good deeds are not performed as they ought to be, while the world eagerly busies itself with empty things. The departed one is deprived of the offering that helps him, while they choose to call to him in the grave, although he cannot hear. The necessary things are not done with discernment, while things that are not fitting are carried out unjustly. Abel offered the firstborn of his flock and their fat,

and righteous Noah sacrificed clean animals from those that remained. Abraham gave three three-year-old animals among the sacrifices he offered, and Jacob gave the Godhead a tenth of everything he possessed. Discerning Lot surrendered his daughters for the sake of righteousness, and the great Moses commanded that all the firstborn be sacrificed. The Hebrews brought gold and silver for the tabernacle, and spun fine linen and fine garments, each according to his ability. Through sacrifices and vows, through tithes and good gifts, the righteous showed their discernment toward God. But today it has fallen to you to offer a piece of bread, and you have despised and neglected the discernment that helps you. Love has lost its savor, for people's faith has become cheap; and the soul has been darkened to discernment by the wickedness that has multiplied. The piece of bread that is the soul's sacrifice has been withheld, and no one brings it, as duty requires, to the place of atonement. The practice of good deeds has vanished from humanity, and people are eager only to serve evil. They are intent on dividing the dead person's estate,

but they are not accustomed to making an offering in his memory. They remember him neither from his own possessions nor from theirs. The wicked heirs have taken his property and forgotten their love for him. Like plunderers, they divided the fine clothes he owned and cast lots for his beautiful possessions. All plunderers peacefully divide the booty they have seized, but heirs do so with anger, quarrels, and disputes. Heirs, then, are worse than plunderers, for every day, in everything, they deny the love owed to the dead person. If the love of the Lord were in their minds, when they divided the estate they would make him a brother and an heir as well. They would reserve a share for him from his property when it was divided, so that it would provide for his commemoration and his offering after his death. But those who are far from righteousness and duty have divided and taken, defrauded and forgotten good deeds. Anyone who has divine love in his soul shows his love after a person's death by not forgetting him. Through commemorations, offerings, and prayers, he brings his case before God into the holy sanctuary.

That the dead benefit from the offerings made by the living seems to me not even to need questioning. But if someone is bold enough to question what is plain, it is easy for him to hear the truth from the teaching. Judas Maccabeus, that mighty warrior for righteousness, acted wisely and offered a sacrifice on behalf of the dead. The man's great faith accomplished its work, and his victory itself testified through his sacrifices how greatly they benefited. His battle against the Greeks openly proclaims that the dead benefited from that discerning man's offering. He was wise, a mighty warrior of God, a man of great faith, knowledgeable and full of zeal. He offered sacrifices on behalf of the dead and made atonement for them, so that the world might learn his beloved deed and imitate him. And if, while death was alive and ruling and wore a crown, sacrifices could make atonement for the dead within his dominion, now that he has been slain, his realm uprooted, and his crown taken away, who can any longer doubt the atonement of the dead? Judas was able to offer the blood of animals to the Lord,

and he appeased him on behalf of the dead and made atonement for them because they had been defiled. Today the Church makes atonement for the dead, not with perishable sacrifices, but with the blood of the Immortal One. And if that ordinary sacrifice of Judas made atonement, how much more will the great slaying of the Son of God cleanse everyone! On behalf of the souls of the dead, the priest enters and stands, and places the bread and wine of consecration on the table. There he recalls the death of Jesus and also his resurrection, and summons everyone who has departed to the sacrifice to receive forgiveness. He lovingly remembers all who set aside and brought a contribution, and celebrates the mystery in remembrance of their departed. He offers sacrifices on behalf of all the dead who have fallen asleep, and calls upon the Father, reminding him of his Son’s death. The Spirit moves in majesty, descends, and rests upon the offering; the mystery takes bodily form in the bread, and it becomes the body. By his hovering he makes the mixed wine into blood. From then on, the body and blood are the sacrifice that sanctifies everyone. Through this sacrifice the priest makes atonement for all the dead, for it has the power to conquer death and destroy its realm.

At the fragrance of life that flows from the great sacrifice, all souls gather and come to receive forgiveness. From the resurrection that the body of the Son of God brings forth, the dead draw life every day and receive forgiveness through it. Therefore, take care to commemorate their loved ones and to provide the offering that can bring forgiveness to your departed. And if someone says of a departed person that he does not receive forgiveness from the offering made by a living person and gains no benefit from it: “Others performed it while he was unaware of it. What benefit does it bring? A person benefits from his own deeds, not from those of his companions. The living person’s own choice is greater than his offering, for he makes it and he benefits from it, and not others. For when a living person makes an offering on behalf of a departed person, how can the departed benefit from it without taking part? What connection does this person’s righteousness have with that person’s? He himself set aside the gift and brought it, and he himself receives help, not the departed.” But I say in reply to anyone who says these things that it is the Church’s practice to grant forgiveness to someone who is unaware. The infant who is baptized without being aware of baptism—

has he received what is his, or has he perhaps not, as you claim? The Church grants forgiveness both to those who are unaware and to those who are aware, for faith raises the dead, without any doubt. She receives the infant from his parents when he is only a few days old, and baptizes him, grants him forgiveness, and sanctifies him while he is unaware. If the holy sacrament does not bring forgiveness to the dead, as you say— Nor does baptism benefit an infant who is unaware of it. Then all the Church’s sacraments are empty, and she labors in vain on behalf of the departed, seeking their forgiveness. Why does the priest say, “Pray for everyone who has departed”? And why does he baptize an infant who is unaware, and sanctify him? Believing parents bring an infant to baptism, and the Lord sees their faith and sanctifies him. He brings him into adoption as a son without his knowing it, and writes his name in the Church of the Firstborn while he is unaware. Likewise, the believing heirs of someone who has died and departed bring bread and wine in his name to the holy altar. The priest and the people pray for the departed, and the Lord forgives the dead person whom they commemorate. But if the dead person is not forgiven through the offering, neither has the infant entered among the children through baptism.

If a living person’s discernment benefits only the living person himself, then it is the parents who exercised discernment and had the child baptized who benefited. Where, then, is the faith that brings the dead to life and offers prayer on behalf of the departed so that they may be forgiven? It also brings infants down to baptism to sanctify them, and has the hope that whatever it asks will not be withheld. The hope of the King’s bride is firm and will not prove false. Her faith is beautiful and great, and cannot be faulted. Through glorious sacraments she serves her Lord spiritually, and the Watchers marvel in holiness at her service. This is the Church’s faith, O discerning ones: that she can make bread and wine into body and blood. She breaks bread and recognizes it as nothing other than the body. She mixes wine and affirms that what is in her bowl is blood. She calls out the names of all her dead over the offering, and joins them with herself in spiritual sacrifices. She gathers them to the banquet of the body and blood, and they delight with her spiritually in what she has prepared. O discerning ones who know the mysteries of faith, make offerings for your departed without doubt. Why have the customs that the Church taught her children diminished, become tasteless and insignificant among many, and ceased to be practiced?

For the loaf comes to the house of God to be offered in a contemptible, disdainful, and commonplace manner. There are many who have stopped altogether and no longer bring it. And there are those who, even when they bring it, do not bring it with discernment. A man sends his sacrifice to the house of God by the hands of his maidservant, as though it were a disgrace for him to bring his sacrifice to the Lord with his own hands. The lowly servants of his household, assigned to lesser tasks—these are the ones he orders to bring his sacrifice while he himself stays away. Why do you not bring your sacrifice with your own hands, O discerning one, like Abraham, who carried the calf to the angels? He and his wife were ready and stood attending to the service; he did not practice righteousness through the hands of others. Today human faith has dwindled; love has grown cold, and discernment and faith are held cheap. What rich man has brought a loaf to the house of God and carried it in his own hands as he brings it into the house of forgiveness? Either he does not bring it, or, if he does, he orders the lowly members of his household to bring his sacrifice while he himself stays away. Blessed is the widow who presents her sacrifice with her own hands,

and the bereaved woman who carries it and takes pride in it. She does not send the Lord a loaf as the rich man does. She offers it herself and cries out in sorrow that he may accept it from her. Like a priest, she brings her vowed gift before God, sorrowfully remembering her dead over her offering. She knows how to set aside sacrifices and bring them to the Lord—not the rich man who sends something to him as though to someone in need. The bereaved woman's offering is precious when it is presented, for tears, love, and faith are mingled in it. A loaf is in her hands, tears are in her eyes, and praise is in her mouth; and, like the offering, great is the excellence of her faith. For an offering is not accepted without love. Blessed is he who, in his love, sacrificed his Only Son for the sake of many.
Here ends the discourse on the loaves for the departed.
By the same holy Mar Jacob. Homily 23. 1. On the Holy Fast of Forty Days.

Let my words run to the gathering of your praise, Son of God, for all who can speak are obliged to praise you. Let my tongue raise its voice toward you in its songs, and through you let me sing to you aloud of the wonder concerning you. I will receive from you and turn to speak about you, so that on every occasion you may be praised by those who hear. Yours are voices, words, and tongues, mouths and minds, thoughts and reflections. Give me something of your own, for you have enough to give to whoever asks you; and receive abundant praise from your gift. Your glory is within you, and those who praise you add nothing to you. Though you need nothing, accept my words, Son of God. I opened my mouth to you, and you filled it, as you promised. Let your great story be spoken through it in a loud voice. I gave you my open mouth, an empty vessel, and in your grace you filled it with praise because of your love.

All who lack anything receive from your fullness. Let the needy man be filled through you and proclaim your gift. If you give speech to a donkey, who is praised: the donkey that speaks, or the giver of things hard to accomplish? The animal spoke with the diviner so that he might be rebuked. Astonishment was his, and praise was yours in every circumstance. An unfamiliar utterance came from the donkey in a great wonder; all the praise returned to you, while she gained nothing. Let me not, like it, be deprived of benefit. I am your image, my Lord; let what is yours benefit from communion with you. Let me be neither a donkey nor a flute for your word, but soil that yields choice fruit a hundredfold. The sweet music that comes from a flute does not benefit the flute itself. Grant that I may rejoice with those who feast on your songs. Even the donkey received speech, but without understanding. Grant me understanding, and fill me with love so that I may speak. Our Lord, grant me also listeners who cling to you and lovingly hunger for the word of life as they hunger for bread. Bread and water sustain bodily life, and the word of the Lord is the spiritual life of the soul. From eating bread come heaviness and sluggishness;

but the word of life grows wings for the soul so that it may fly. Let us eat in moderation and listen to the word without measure. Let us shorten our meals and prolong our studies of divine things. Abundant food darkens the soul, but the mind grows rich when it indulges in learning. In these days when the body is restrained from food, let instruction abound for the soul, so that it may be nourished by it. On the day when the great fast shines in the congregations, I will raise my voice in righteousness for those who listen to me. Today, when the mouth of indulgence is stopped and shut, let the ear open a door to the voice of instruction. On this day, when the stomach is empty and the soul is awake, speak, speak, O mouth, and benefit those who listen to you. In this month, when frivolity has been stripped of its power, the word is free to flourish abundantly. You do not always have sweet fruit to eat, for there is a season when the tree is deprived even of leaves. Nor do you find grapes in your vineyard every day. There is an appointed season for gathering all your crops. Nor are there stacks and sheaves in the field every day, for it is the proper month of the year that produces a heap of grain in the field.

If the body's crops follow their seasons, let the soul's harvest proceed diligently in its own season. In this season, when provisions for the soul are gathered, let everyone awaken and fill their baskets with every good thing. In this season, when the sick soul is healed, come, you who fast, to the physician's door and have your sores bandaged. Look, in these days a fair is being held for the Lord. Go out, merchants of the spirit, and grow rich through trade. In these days a marketplace has been established for righteousness, and look, it is sold for nothing to anyone who desires it. The Son of God has set out his kingdom at your doors. Give him pieces of bread and buy it, for he accepts them. Distribute alms to the poor and receive the kingdom. He wants to give; he is looking for an occasion to pour out his treasury. For stitched scraps and unwanted Babylonian garments, he will exchange a robe of glory with you, if you give them to him. Give him the shreds that have come off the edges of your rags, and he will give you a robe of glory filled with light. Give him the patches of clothing and the torn pieces that have fallen from your bedding, and receive for yourself a bed into which pain cannot enter. Give the needy some of the leftovers from your supper,

and go and enjoy yourself with Lazarus beside Abraham. Pour a cup of water for the thirsty, and receive as your reward an entire treasury filled with limitless wealth. Lovingly open the door of your house to the stranger, and all the doors of the kingdom will be opened to you. Fasting is beautiful when righteousness runs through it. Give it what belongs to it; do not estrange yourself from its fellowship. Give the hungry person whatever you have cut from your food, so that you do not become a miser rather than someone who fasts. What you have withheld from yourself, give to the person whose belly is hungry, so that through one fast you may gain two honors. If you are someone who fasts, honor the fast with two mouths: your own, which abstains, and the mouth of the person who eats from your provisions. Fast for God, give to the needy, and double your gains, for this is what righteousness asks of anyone who practices it. Purify yourself as you fast from food, and through almsgiving buy the kingdom of God's household. Let all the expenses that fasting has saved from your table be given during it to someone who lacks food. Do not keep for yourself whatever fasting has saved you. Instead, put it into the bellies of the hungry while you fast.

If you have not eaten it, but it is being kept for you, look, it is still yours! Your fast is undone, together with the expenses that have been saved for you. But if you give the hungry what fasting has saved, your fast is truly a fast, crowned with righteousness. At sowing time no one is reluctant to scatter his seed, for he knows that he gathers a harvest in proportion to what he sows. Sow alms and do not grow weary, you who fast, for you will reap a sheaf of glory in the new world. The needy are good soil: scatter your seeds in it, for its harvests in heaven never come to an end. There is soil that holds back the seeds sown in it: some it yields, but others it withholds, and they do not sprout in it. There are fields that rob their farmers of their seed, but the field of the poor never cheats the person who sows in it. All the seeds sown in it, in every form, it receives and keeps, and it eagerly bears fruit. Even if someone sows a cup of water, that too produces a crop. He gathers a sheaf and comes to a heap filled with blessings. Whatever you sow, you will reap abundantly. The seed is kept safe; do not doubt the harvests. The crops of all farmers face enemies every day: frost, heat, locusts, hail, and every kind of damage.

Even if the crop comes in and reaches the granary, there is still fear for it, for it faces floods and countless harmful mishaps. All the thieves, all the collectors, all the plunderers, all those who take their share—through them the harvest dwindles and wastes away. But when acts of charity are sown, there is no danger, and their harvests suffer neither loss nor damage. The harvest of righteousness is stored above in heaven, where heat, hail, and locusts have no power. It is in the lofty place where neither thieves nor collectors nor plunderers can diminish it in any way. The harvest of all who fast is kept safe in the Lord’s hand, and in that same hand all acts of charity are kept safe for those who perform them. In that right hand which weighed the mountains and measured the heights, the harvest of everyone who sows righteousness is kept safe. That small coin you give to the poor at the door—go and look for it in the Lord’s hand: there it is! Sow among the needy, and you will reap from God. Scatter here, and gather every good thing there. Carry your treasures away from the earth, which is full of danger, and place them in heaven, in a place protected from thieves. Look, workers stand at your door, ready to labor with you.

For a small wage, accomplish a great work through their hands. Hire the poor for the bread they eat, and they will prepare a lofty place for you in the world of light; put your treasure there. They build a great palace full of blessings, so that you may enter and dwell there, and there find all your treasures. They construct steps to the heights from your acts of charity, and by them you ascend to God without toil. They clear the path of life before your steps, so that you may travel to the bridal chamber of light without stumbling. They accompany you on the fearsome road, and at that great crossing they plead for your deliverance. They stand at the crossing that is full of fire and sprinkle the dew of the Fourth, whose image they are. They make a ship of water in the sea of fire, so that when you cross, the flame will not come near you. They open the bridegroom’s door before you knock, welcome you, and gladden you in the banquet hall. They also call Lazarus, who is their brother, and he comes to you in their company if you call him. They testify to your acts of charity among the angels, and because of them you are loved among the heavenly beings.

They stand and point you out, as though with a finger, saying, “This man provided for us in our need and did not grow weary of it.” Be their friend, so that they may welcome you into their dwellings, for they are the whole beauty of righteousness. Send everything you have with them to God, and go and find it at the King's gate, together with its profit. Store provisions for the journey with them before you depart, so that when you pass from this world to the next, you will lack nothing. Their companionship is good when you travel through fearful places; and if your possessions go with them, they will not be plundered. Whatever you leave behind of your possessions is lost to you. Snatch some of it away for yourself and give it to the poor man: he will keep it safe. As long as you do not give it away, what is in your hands is not yours. Once you lodge it with the poor man, it becomes yours. As long as what you have remains with you, you are not its owner. But if the poor man takes it from you, he keeps it safe for you. If you are wise, let everything you have become yours: send it ahead with the poor to God. If you long to acquire possessions, acquire them truly. Do not leave them behind here and become poor. Give the needy your entire load to carry,

so that when you go, you will find everything you acquired in the land of light. If you wish to be rich, be truly rich—not rich for a time, but for all time. Load your wealth onto the shoulders of all who are in need, and there, in the land of the living, you will find your entire treasure. Give, confident that whatever you give is yours. Send it away and sleep, confident that it will not be plundered. Assign wandering beggars the journey of carrying your wealth, and without charge they will carry it all with you to the kingdom. As long as your money lies in your purse, it belongs to someone else, not you. But if you distribute it, it is kept safe under God's seal. As long as you have gold in your house, you are anxious about thieves, bandits, and borrowers, and about oppressors, plunderers, judges, and rulers, lest they pick a quarrel with you on some pretext. But once you have given it away and all who are in need have been provided for through it, it has passed beyond danger and entered the kingdom, where it awaits you. No one there steals it from you or diminishes it, for the one with whom you deposited it guards it carefully for you. What you have given him does not merely earn interest: he has promised to return it to you a hundredfold.

Here he repays a hundredfold, and there with life without end, repaying the loans of anyone who does good deeds. You who fast, call the poor man and give him bread. Do not wait for him to come; go after him yourself and fill his stomach. Fields do not come looking for their farmers. The farmers themselves carry seed and go to the fields. You too must carry seed: go out to the fields that can speak and entrust it to them, and look forward to the harvest without anxiety. If a needy person comes to your house to ask something of you, you owe him payment for his footsteps, because he has made the journey for you. The mountain has spared you, for it was your duty to go to it. Now that it has come to you, double your gift and let it go. If a field could walk and come to the farmer, how he would rejoice over it and sow the seed it awaits! A poor man has come and stands at your door; do not let him be delayed. Give the field its seed and send it away, rejoicing as you do so. When a poor man knocks, do not tell him, “Our Lord provides.” These are empty words, bringing no reward to the one who says them. He wants to receive something, not to learn who provides for him. For he knows better than you who provides for him. Give him something; do not tell him, “The Lord provides.”

For the Lord provides for him through your gift, if you give to him. If you truly assure him that the Lord provides, give a gift and say those words, and they will not be a disgrace to you. But if you say them without giving, you are a liar, because the Provider has not, through your hands, fed the man whom you reassured. Bread is costly, but words are cheap for the one who speaks them. Give him bread; he is not asking you to let him hear a speech. His stomach is hungry, and he has come to fill it from your table. What good will hearing words do him if he receives nothing? The poor man did not seek you out as a teacher. Be quiet; do not teach. Give your gift, which silently bears witness to the Provider. If a farmer says to the field, “You have seed,” and keeps repeating to it, “You have, you have ten thousand seeds,” but does not sow seed in it, it is of no use, for neither a heap of grain nor crops come from words. So too, if you tell the poor man ten thousand times, “The Lord provides, the Lord provides,” but do not give him a gift and fill his stomach, your seed is wind, and it yields you no crops. Be silent, giver, and stretch out your hand to the poor man. While remaining silent, speak to him through your gift.

Do not preach to someone who is hungry, bent over, and trembling all over. Sustain him with bread so that he does not collapse while listening to you. If you have a gift to give, give it in silence. Your gift itself teaches about the Provider. But if you are poor, needy, and short of food, answer the poor man, “The Lord provides for both me and you.” If you have no gift, give him a word. But if you have something, give it silently and let him go on his way. You who fast, sow your alms with both hands, so that you may reap with both your right hand and your left. Today the earth readily receives seeds from you. Sow them in it abundantly, for they will all sprout and bring you joy. Look, hungry mouths are weary at your doors. Go out, you who fast; sustain the needy and receive the benefits. Weave a great crown of alms for your fast, so that it may shine in the kingdom with every good thing. A garment needs beautiful designs, and fasting needs abundant acts of charity. Like a skilled painter of the Spirit, Isaiah painted a portrait of fasting so that all creation might see its beauty. Because he saw that there are fasts that are not beautiful,

he portrayed this one in all its spiritual beauties. That lyre of prophecy understood that there is a person who fasts yet even angers God by his fasting. There is a person who fasts while puffed up and conceited with pride, and there is one who, while fasting, is resentful, agitated, and full of anger. There is one whose mouth is closed to food by fasting, yet he sees a needy person and does not relieve his distress. There is one who humbles himself by fasting and bows his neck, yet has no desire to share his bread with the poor. There is one who spreads sackcloth and ashes on his bed, yet a needy person cries out in distress and he shows him no mercy. Isaiah rebuked this kind of fasting, despised and scorned it, dishonored and abandoned it, rejected it and cast it down before those who fast. He painted a portrait of the chosen fast of righteousness, so that it might be known in the assemblies of all who fast. The wondrous prophet showed the world what fasting is, so that everyone might learn its divine distinctions. This is fasting: that you loosen the knots of injustice from yourself and cut the bonds of deceit from your mind. A knot of injustice is a knot tied by your own mind, while the judge is muzzled by greed and does not untie it.

The bond of deceit is also the wickedness of a heart that sets snares, deceives, and wrongs all its neighbors. You have a lawsuit that remains tangled, and the fast has arrived. Settle with your brother, even though he wrongs you, if you are fasting. Bring to an end the matters that injustice and oppression have delayed, and proceed along the path of righteousness: this is fasting. Let love of the Lord enter and resolve the tangled lawsuit, for this is a fine deed to carry out during the fast. Every matter in which greed has tied a quarrel—these are the knots of injustice. Untie them, you who fast. Every intention that seeks to ambush a brother in secret he calls a bond of deceit. Cut it, discerning one. From Isaiah came the command for those who fast: to loosen the knots and cut the bonds of deceit. Whatever is tangled, whatever is hidden, whatever is deceitful—cut it away and untie it, and fast before God with a pure heart. This prophet, the chamberlain of the Godhead, came out and showed you the way of fasting and its deeds. He teaches you to share your bread with the hungry during the fast, for this deed befits those who fast before God. From the Lord’s own mind he learned what he loves:

And he revealed it to people, so that everyone might learn his deeds. The Lord loves it when you let into your house a guest who has come from abroad, and the prophet revealed this to whoever listens to him. God desires that you cover the naked with clothing, and Isaiah, as one entrusted with his secret, revealed this before many. The one who is worshiped desires that no one neglect his own flesh and blood, and Isaiah sang of this will of the Godhead. The needy man lying at your doorstep is your own flesh and blood. Understand his needs from your own, fill his belly, and your fast will be great. His body is flesh, not flint, as he lies abandoned and naked. Cold and heat torment him, yet you have no pity. Mercy formed him too from the same lump from which it formed you. The clay is the same, and however great you become, he is one of your own kind. Why do you fast unless you show mercy to your neighbor? For this is the fast the Lord has chosen: that a person should show mercy. Take care not to shut the door of mercy in the faces of the poor, lest you become an accursed faster whose fast is a disgrace. Take care not to hate your brother in your heart while you fast, lest a foul smell from your fast reach the King. Take care not to curse someone who hates you while you fast, lest your curses make your fast stink and prevent it from being accepted. Your mouth fasts from food; let it also fast

from curses, insults, and mockery. And from boasting, ridicule, quarreling, and oaths. Be truthful in your yes and your no. Take care not to speak a word during the fast that breaks your fast and defiles you along with the dissolute, even while you are fasting. A word can defile the person who says it. Therefore guard your tongue, you who fast. Isaiah himself placed this among the safeguards of fasting: he commanded the person who fasts not to speak a word. Not all the words a person speaks are alike, and the speaker should not refrain from all of them. Praise and thanksgiving are words too, as are spiritual songs and the stirrings of prophecy. These words fill those who speak them with life, and no one who fasts should refrain from them altogether. Isaiah said not to speak a word during the fast, and it is understood what kind of speech ought to cease. Let no word of wrongdoing or envy be spoken, or of jealousy, slander, or quarreling. Let the mouth refrain from insults and mockery, and from every word that strays aside into darkness. A word can shut the door against someone who fasts,

and he may be rejected according to the divine rule. A word can cast its owner into Gehenna and throw the one who spoke it into everlasting burning. With a word from his mouth, Moses, the treasury of prophecy, provoked the Lord, although his deeds were good. The prophetess Miriam, the sister of Aaron the high priest, was clothed in leprosy because of a word her mouth spoke. And what shall I say about the robber on the right, who spoke a word and became an heir in the garden of blessings? Since every word the mouth speaks will come under judgment, who would not fear to speak needless words? Since a person is justified or condemned by his words, who would not weigh his word with trembling before speaking it? Since a person is defiled by his words even while fasting, why does he not tremble at speaking a word that is not good? Moses provoked the Lord, Miriam became leprous, and the robber entered: faults and virtues came through words alone, without deeds. From now on, then, you who fast, be afraid of your words, so that you do not surrender your mouth to sin while you are fasting. Do not enslave yourself to speaking of empty matters, nor recount people's deeds that are not good.

What compels you to pick at a sore that is not yours? Why do you dwell on your neighbor's affairs when he is far away? Your brother has sinned: why are you eager to recount his faults? He has a master; be wary of a servant who is not yours. David considered this a great virtue when he said, 'People's evil deeds have never passed my lips.' That lyre of prophecy spoke well: no one should recount the evil deeds of his fellow human beings. Do not let your mouth become a passageway for empty talk. What do you gain from insults against your companions? If someone sins in speech while fasting from bread, what has he gained? He has built up and torn down, and lost his reward. He fasted and became righteous, but then he spoke and spoiled his righteousness. His stomach is empty, yet he has broken his fast without realizing it. His fasting is good, but his foolish words are ugly. He has put incense and dung on his censer, and he is not accepted. You who fast, be afraid to speak a word, for it too can be deadly, and it is a great evil for anyone who falls into it. The mouth is free to offer praise, to sing, or to glorify God, or it may choose pure silence for itself. Everything that builds up, every encouragement, everything beneficial, every account from which its hearers benefit.

Give to the needy, visit the poor, support beggars, provide for orphans, and clothe the bodies of the naked. Invite the widow and fill her lap from your table; take the orphan with you and load his arms with your harvest. Keep silent rather than speak words full of your companions' sores, and guard your tongue from turning over needless matters. The fast has come upon you: prepare yourself for good deeds, and like a diligent worker, tear up the records of debt written against you. This is the season when the great gate stands open to all who fast. Rise, repentant one, and pay off your debts with your almsgiving. Let every sinner tend to his soul through righteousness. Blessed is he who gave us fasting to bandage our wounds.
The first homily on fasting is ended.
By the same author, Saint Mar Jacob. Homily 24. Second homily on the holy forty-day fast.

I have gathered the sweet fruits of fasting from instruction. Lord of Eden, accept my offering upon your table. Various forms of ascetic discipline have come to knowledge, and now she distributes them among her companions. Through you may they be set in order. Fasting has captivated the mind with love for it, so that it speaks about it. All my words are for your praise, Jesus, as I bow in worship. The season calls on me to speak rightly about it. May my speech be sweet incense in the place of atonement. The tongue has been stirred by fasting, which is the beauty of righteousness. Through you may it occupy itself with your praise. Give me your attention, you who love your own lives, so that I may bring before you a subject that is entirely life. We have been far too idle in seeking spiritual benefits. Let us run now, so that poverty does not overtake us. We have slept too long, leaving good deeds undone. Let us wake up now and open the door to good works.

We have been far too eager for excessive food. Let us fast today, so that our mind does not sink into dung. We have run too long with the body in pursuit of food. Let us now seek the life of the soul, so that we may gain it. We have been far too fond of gathering bodily things. Let us labor a little for spiritual things, [?] they can be found. We have taken much pleasure in food, which is all dung. Let us now labor a little in fasting; let it not be burdensome to us. Look, foods and delicacies are left to decay. Why are they pursued so diligently when they come to nothing? The belly has taken all the fruit of our efforts, and it has decayed within it. It is a Sheol that rots every deposit entrusted to it. Throughout the whole year we have given all our labor to the body. Let us now give the soul something with which to console itself. The body's delicacies have fermented and decayed and become dung. Let us now taste fasting, which never decays. If the body is the soul's partner, why does it oppress her and take for itself all the fruit of diligent effort? Warm clothing, fine bread, and pleasant wine; meat and oil and excessive delicacies.

O will, standing between the body and the soul, rise and show us that you distribute fairly. Two partners ask you for what they need. Distribute fairly, then, if you are just. You have given all your labor to the body for its food, while the soul is left without her share in the distribution. You have lavished every luxury and every indulgence on the body, every delicacy and every choice food. Delightful pleasures and constant rest throughout the year—but the soul is neglected, and although she is the body's partner, she is disregarded. You who distribute the shares and have given the body so much, what are you doing? Give the soul her own share, so that she too may live. All year you have deprived her, and she has gone without any gain. The fast is upon you: give the soul her provisions. For even now, when it is a month bare of crops, labor with the soul, whose work does not perish. At this time, when there are neither winepress workers nor reapers, support her as she labors in fasting, which enriches those who labor at it. Now, when the season is difficult for bodily labor, let us rouse the soul to perform good deeds. Now, when all the farmers have ceased their work, rise, you who repent, and gather the harvest of righteousness.

Come, O will, distribute the shares and treat the two siblings equally. As you have given to the body, give the soul what she needs. In summer both of them worked diligently in the field. Set aside the soul's share for her to receive from the harvest. Give the soul's share to the needy and to beggars, and feed the hungry, so that you may be fair when you distribute the shares. It is not right that the soul, who worked alongside her partner, should be deprived of the necessities she requires. She wishes to clothe the naked: carry this out with her. Cut back on the body's expenses and allow her to act. The soul longs for the body to refrain from its meals, so that through its fasting she may feed all who are needy from its provisions. O body, bend your shoulder and work alongside the soul, who seeks to preserve life for both you and herself. Place her yoke upon your neck and perform every good deed. Her labor is worthy, for none of what she strives for perishes. She does not seek to gather wealth for herself alone, for her diligent striving in good deeds is shared [?]. O soul, compel your partner to strive alongside you. Do not give him the leisure to sink into desires.

The teacher compels the child to learn what he needs. Because he loves him, he does not leave him unchecked, lest he suffer harm. Keep your pupil under control so that he does not stray from your teaching, lest, when he falls away from right conduct, he drag you down as well. Do not give the body comforts that are not good for it. Wear it down and bring it into subjection, for the more it labors, the more beauty it acquires. This is love: not to abandon it to desires. Give it labor, so that through discipline it may find life. Out of love for the child, the teacher disciplines him so that he may learn. He whips him because he loves him, so that he may become wise. But if he spares him and pampers him without teaching him, he treats him as an enemy would, even though he loves him. The child wants to eat and drink and play. If the teacher grants him his desire, he becomes a source of harm. The body wants to obtain rest and pleasures. Do not let it fulfill its desire, lest it perish. Give it fasting and withhold food from it, for hunger benefits and nourishes it more than bread. O body, incline your ear toward the woman who is your scribe; hear her good counsels and carry them out. Follow the soul, who loves beautiful deeds.

For if you obey her, your beauty will shine among the angels. Walk with her, for she loves to fly upward. Rise from the mud, for she wishes to dwell in heaven. Your dust is heavy, but if you give your hand to the soul, she can easily raise you from the dunghill to the royal palace. Your kind is clay, and if she obeys you and comes with you, you will decay into a rotten lump, both you and she. Have pity on the beauty of the pure soul, so that it does not perish. Labor with her in beautiful deeds, so that you may reign with her. If she gives you a fast to observe, do not be distressed. Accept it and rejoice, for great is the crown you will obtain through it. If she deprives you of foods, do not become gluttonous, for through her abstinence she has invited you to the King's table. If she wears you out with long vigils and prayers, wake up and labor, so that you may become a companion of the heavenly beings. Give her your hand in all the labors of righteousness, so that with her you may obtain every spiritual beauty. O will, through which soul and body receive their commands, you have authority over good deeds and evil deeds. Body and soul obey you in their conduct. Urge them on, so that they may practice beautiful deeds. Rise, O will, and command the forces like a king.

Body and soul obey you and do not resist you. If you are willing, the partners triumph in their deeds; but if you are negligent, the whole person slips into destruction. O you who fast, it is your will that guides you. Love victory, and you will find it on every occasion. While there is still time that offers an opportunity for righteousness, do good deeds, so that they may be stored up for you like treasures. It is up to you to love fasting and abstinence; but if you wish, you can acquire every kind of debauchery. It is easy for you to eat, and easy to fast if you wish. O you who fast, set your will on ascetic discipline, and see, it will become pleasant to you. Nature is pliable and lends itself to every kind of change. However much you constrain it, it has the strength to endure. It can even ascend to heaven if it practices righteousness; it can also easily descend into the abyss if it is not diligent. However much you demand of it, it has the ability to perform beautiful deeds; but if it grows lax, it dozes off and falls asleep amid ugly deeds. If you awaken him, look, he becomes a companion of the heavenly beings; but if you [?] him, he sleeps on the clay and [?] his dust. O you who fast, awaken yourself to righteousness, for you can practice righteousness as much as you wish.

Righteousness is very easy for someone who loves it: he gathers and collects it from small deeds. He offers a little bread to the hungry and satisfies him; he gives a little support to someone in need and helps him. Sometimes he has compassion on a poor person and gains righteousness through him; at another time he feels sorrow for a beggar and does not despise him. There are also times when he visits a sick person in need, and at no cost he satisfies that person's longing through his gift. He abstains a little, keeping himself from foods; and although he lacks nothing, he rejects wine and does not drink it. He keeps himself from oaths, and it is easy for him: he maintains this habit and becomes trustworthy without toil. He restrains his mouth from insulting his companions, and foul speech does not pass his lips. He binds his love to the doorway of God's house, and every day he asks the physician to drip mercy upon him. He greatly fears spiritual harm and seeks to benefit both in his hidden deeds and in his public ones. A small sin is a cause for mourning to him if he encounters it, and he flees from it as from a nest of snakes.

Every small benefit he finds, he seizes for himself, and when he acquires it, he rejoices as though it were something great. Someone who loves righteousness takes such care that he guards even the glance of his eye from harm. Through little things he gathers and builds up righteousness, until it becomes a lofty mountain rising above the earth. The bee, too, gathers little by little from plants and makes a sweet substance full of wonder. She does not grow weary of flying even among thorns and weeds and taking whatever serves her needs. Every day she labors to add to her gain each day, and little by little she provisions herself from droplets. She does not take from a great storehouse to fill her own storehouse, but gathers laboriously from the droplets of all the flowers. Today a little, another day less than a little—and through her diligence, what she has gathered becomes abundant. Righteousness, whose taste resembles a honeycomb, is gathered little by little from deeds. If weariness had seized the bee, so that she despised the thorns and would not settle on the weeds, and she became discouraged because her work involved toil,

and she scorned the honey because it was scattered over the heights, and she sought rest instead of the hardships of traveling from place to place, she would not have gathered the sweetness she has collected. A honeycomb is an image of righteousness, and whoever takes care gathers it like a bee. But if he despises little things when they arise, scorning one, neglecting another, and belittling another; And when a needy beggar meets him, he leaves him and passes on, and wearily passes by someone who is sick without visiting him; And if some business presses him, he swears without fear, and provided he is not lying, he does not consider it a sin to have sworn; And he cleverly breaks his fast on every pretext, and drinks wine for his friends’ sake—out of love, he says; And in his simplicity he has spoiled his observance of the fast, and has slept and rested, supposing himself to be without sin; And he neglects a small gain and does not seize it, while his love for the greater gain is cut off, and he does not seek it; Little by little, all righteousness slips away, and whoever is negligent in his deeds does not acquire it. He has not been diligent like the bee, which has stocked itself with little things, and now is praised for its great [?].

A person acquires righteousness through perseverance, but it flees from anyone who grows weary, and he cannot catch it. Look, you who fast: labor these days for righteousness, so that you may gather that sweetness which is full of life. The good news dawns, and those who have labored rejoice in their honors. Seek confidence before the dawning of the great day. Run through the fast like a diligent person seeking his life, so that when the resurrection reveals itself, you may be joyful. Fast for the Bridegroom, so that you may rejoice with him at his banquet, for he comes to honor those who fast with their crowns. On his great day, when confidence is required, how will you rejoice unless you have mourned with those who fast? At that festival which brightens the faces of all who are sorrowful, what benefit will you find, seeing that you are already cheerful? When every comfort is given to all who fast, what will you receive if you are already living in pleasure today? When rest comes in its proper turn to the one who has toiled, how will you rest with those who fast unless you have toiled? If the suffering of the Only Begotten does not cause you suffering, neither do you have a share in his joy to delight in it. The great day that comes to make all who fast forget:

What will it make you forget if fasting has not wearied you? When the good news gives the reward for observances, what will it give you unless you have kept them righteously? Give the fast the labors and exertions of righteousness, so that when you reach its end you may find a great crown. The crown of the fast is the resurrection of the Only Begotten, and unless you fast, you are a stranger to the crown as well. Fasting, keeping vigil, and prayers, together with almsgiving, enter as gifts for the Bridegroom when he rises from the dead. The fast is passing, and the resurrection of the Only Begotten is coming. What will you offer him unless you fast righteously? While the fast lasts, gather from it every kind of [?] for yourself, so that when the Bridegroom sees you on his day, he may rejoice to meet you. Like a bee, gather different kinds from your acts of charity, so that you may bring a honeycomb with you to the feast. Righteousness is a sweet flavor at the great feast. Let it go with you; otherwise the Bridegroom will not delight in you. When those who fast enter before him in their attire, each one carrying his vigil, his fasting, and his self-denial; when acts of charity shine like lights at his feast, what will you bring if your deeds leave you dark? When the angelic watchers surround his tomb in their white garments,

and the women disciples with their spices and perfumes; on the great morning when the faces of all who fast shine, be the first to claim your reward with confidence. Run swiftly toward the good news, like John, and see the resurrection without being scorned by justice. For the resurrection, put on a garment woven from acts of charity, so that you may be beautiful like the angels in their white garments. Work hard and prepare splendid clothes for yourself for the great feast: pure fasting and righteousness full of beauty. Who will grant you spiritual joy at the feast unless you have labored bodily during the fast? Rise and be diligent in prayers, in acts of charity, and in the observances that the fast requires of those who fast. Let everyone, according to his rank, guard himself against harm. The fast belongs to everyone; let everyone labor in good deeds. Let the shepherd fast for his flock and for himself, and through his prayers carry the burden of all the sheep. Let the [?] too close every breach through fasting, and carefully guard the sheep against robbers. Let the chaste members of the covenant pursue holiness, for without it no one can see the Lord.

Let the old man fast, whose span of years has contracted and grown short, so that he may please the Lord in what remains of his life. Let the child fast, for victory befits childhood, and let childhood recognize how easily it can fall. Let young men fast, for the impulse of youth is fierce. If fasting does not humble it, it forgets what benefits it. Wives, adorn yourselves with fasting, and through purity please God and your husbands. Fasting is beautiful for virgins and betrothed women, for it gave Esther the beauty to surpass the beautiful women. Let the widow who has buried her husband also love fasting, for it brings her near to God, so that he may be her husband. Let the orphan who has lost his father fast, pleading with the Father of orphans to supply what he lacks. Let the farmer fast for his field and for his soul, so that the harvest and his soul may be kept safe from harm. Fasting also helps the merchant traveling on the road, so that, along with his merchandise, he may gather every spiritual profit. Fasting also benefits the rich, so that through almsgiving they may gain friends who will welcome them into their dwellings. Fasting also befits the poor man whose stomach is hungry, so that he may willingly make that very hunger a fast for his God.

Let the solitary ascetics, the children of the kingdom, fast diligently, for the contest, the struggle, and the victory befit them. Let the sinner fast, whose debt is greater than his ability to pay, so that perhaps he may manage to pay off a little of his bill of debt. Let the righteous man fast to add beauty to his righteousness, for however high he climbs, there is another step toward the height above. Let the penitent fast, for this is a time that binds up the wounded; if he takes care, all his sores will be healed during it. During this fast, let virgins and holy people fast, for during it the Virgin’s Son fasted for our sake. Let married couples fast and win one another through righteous deeds; although their marriage bed is indeed pure, let them honor it. Even the adulterer, if he fasts, suffers no harm, for through fasting he beats down his passion and drives it away from himself. Nor would a prostitute lose anything if she fasted, for fasting can curb the shamelessness of dissolute women. Let all groups, in their ways of life and their ranks—everyone in his own station—honor fasting, which is full of benefits. Very dearly loved is the righteousness that comes from many people, and it has the power to obtain all its requests every day. Raindrops, taken one by one, are only drops; but when they gather, they become a torrent that cannot be crossed.

From many drops comes a great flood, and through the prayers of the whole people the fast becomes splendid. The bride of light, together with all her children, asks for mercy, so that prayer may abound from every mouth—and look, she has been heard! It is like drops, so to speak, coming from a rain cloud and becoming a torrent that cannot be crossed because of its greatness. Through many speaking mouths there is one song of praise; she asks and receives, and the Judge does not refuse her. Through all who fast, and in every measure, she observes the fast; through every mouth she calls abundantly upon her Lord. She gathers each person’s fast and makes one great fast, like a river gathered together from drops. Come, you who fast: gather and combine your individual portions, so that there may be a great fast in the assembly of the daughter of light. The bride’s beauty is the radiant fast of many people; her adornment, her vigil, and her prayers are like pieces of jewelry. The virgin of light keeps herself from food so that, at the end of the fast, she may eat the beloved Bridegroom. All flavors are contemptible, despised, and scorned in her eyes; unless she eats him, the daughter of daylight finds no relief. For this reason the pampered woman fasts and wears herself down,

so that when she eats him, she may be kept from wantonness. Through fasting the bride seeks to tear apart the beloved bridegroom; and look, peoples and worlds are invited to her, so that she may feed them. She fasts out of love for him and because she longs to eat of him. In her longing for the bridegroom whom she desires, she has forgotten bread. Where have you ever seen a bride who eats her bridegroom, or a virgin whose betrothed is set before her on the table? She longed, loved, fasted, hungered, approached, and ate. She delighted, grew fat, entered, and inherited the Father's treasure. During the fast she saw him fighting against the ruler. She fasted with him, and when he became a sacrifice, she broke him up for her children. She desired him in the wilderness because he was fighting on her behalf; and now she begs to eat and be filled with the beautiful one. Fasting is sweet to the Church, the betrothed of the Only-Begotten; at its completion she sees the bridegroom in great splendor. Look, those who fast await your feast, Son of God, so that you may bring your peace from your treasury to the four corners of the world. Accept our fast and establish your peace throughout our lands. Glory to the compassion that sent you to the earth, so that through you it might find peace.
The second discourse on fasting is finished.
By Saint Mar Jacob. Discourse 25. Third discourse on the holy forty-day fast.

Third discourse on the holy forty-day fast. Once again I undertake to speak about fasting. Make me worthy, my Master, to speak and benefit whoever hears me. A discourse stirs within me about the days that call for the race of righteousness. Grant that I may speak through you. My righteous Teacher, teach me a subject full of benefits, so that I may recount it to the Church, which you purified through your sacrifice. Look, teaching has dawned, ready to speak radiantly. Lovers of truth, give me your attention, so that we may delight you. Come, you who fast, let us recline at the King's table, and without bread let us feast spiritually today. Come, athletes who have entered the contest of righteousness. Let us now speak about the spectacles of fasting and what it is. Come, you who wear armor forged from acts of charity. Draw up your ranks for battle, for the devil has deployed his legions. Come, diligent ones who shoot the arrows of prayer. Press into battle, for demons threaten your fasts.

Look, the left side is drawn up in battle against the right. Run toward heaven; sweat in the contest for your victories. Fasting is accustomed to bring crowns of righteousness to those who love it and to enrich them with victories. It is accustomed to bind the enemy before those who fast, and in combat to humble the might of the ruler of the air. It is accustomed to bring forth the hidden mysteries of God's household and to reveal to the world, with great wonder, things concerning its Creator. Fasting can interpret dreams and untie knots; it can bring out all hidden things and proclaim them on the rooftops. It is easy for fasting to quench the power of fire and sprinkle dew from the flames upon those who fast. It has the power to teach animals to fast and to put a bridle in the fearsome mouths of lions. Through fasting Moses came to see the presence of the Most High and to speak with him of hidden mysteries from the thick darkness. On the mountain Moses ate fasting as though it were bread; through it he grew fat, became beautiful, and shone without food. He fasted from bread and reclined at God's table; he ate light, drank radiance, and gained beauty. He delighted in wine pressed from the thick clouds,

and took on the color of flame in a delightful form. Fasting prepared for him a banquet full of life, with food whose flavors never fail. The sight of the Lord filled that fasting man with satisfaction, and through his revelations he was nourished spiritually. Fasting brought him into the house of mysteries and showed him the citadel of the world as it was being built out of nothing.
