He was purified of heavy foods, and his mind became bright so that he could see hidden things openly. Food weighs down the soul's senses, so that it falls away from the hidden knowledge of divine mysteries. Any disciple who eats too much is no true learner, for his food makes his mind too sluggish to learn. Moses and Adam were two disciples of God: one fasted and learned, while the other, because he ate, lost his book. The disciple ate fruit in Eden at the wrong time, and for that reason he forgot what he had learned from God. His great teacher had strongly commanded him not to eat; because he ate, he received no further instruction. His eating dulled his mind and heart, and he had no opportunity to learn the law that would have given him life.

His soul was stopped up by the fruit he ate from the tree; it grew dark and blind to spiritual understanding. He ate and was torn away from that spiritual order; he could no longer learn, because he had become sluggish. The food he had greedily desired weighed heavily upon him. Because he took it in lust, it killed him, and he never digested it. But Moses, a descendant of Levi, entered to learn as well, and guarded himself against food so that it would not weigh him down. He recognized that Adam's master had expelled him because he ate, and he restrained his mouth from food so that he might be enlightened. With great understanding he examined fasting, which can teach the hidden mysteries and secrets of God's house. In his humility he learned fasting, through which the soul's eyes are opened so that it can gaze upon hidden things. He saw that Adam had been expelled from Paradise because he ate, and he fasted so that he might enter and see the tree of life in its beauty. He set fasting against the craving for that food, so that he might be enlightened and able to receive much. He emptied himself of rich foods so that he might grasp all the depths of divinity. Through fasting he shone like a lamp of great light,

until he could explore all the folds of God's creative power. For forty days he dwelt with God in fellowship, and without bread he delighted in waves of radiance. Fasting purified him until he became entirely light, so that he could go and see beyond the world and on this side of it. He disdained foods and rejected bodily tastes, so that he would not be hindered in his learning while meditating on it. He became a stranger to bread and water, because he knew that food darkens the mind and weighs down the soul. Through fasting Moses saw God and learned his mysteries, for if he had eaten, he would not have mastered that teaching. Scarcity of bread and abstinence from food made his mind a spacious receptacle, so that it could grasp more. He learned many hidden mysteries of divinity, and in his learning he forgot bread and did not eat. The disciple shone through taking little food, until he became entirely a countenance of great light. The teaching grew sweet, and because he had abstained from food, he became still freer, until he could see all hidden things. That head of the human race became mortal through eating, but Moses the prophet learned of God's creative power through fasting. Because Adam gave himself to gluttony, he was expelled from Paradise. 593 But when Moses fasted, he entered into God's thick cloud. The fasting man ascended the mountain of the Lord and there saw creation coming from nothing to become something. His soul's sight rose and surveyed hidden things. He learned them and brought their revelations to the world. Through a great fast the Hebrew acquired a great mind, with which to encompass created things, the worlds, and their arrangements. He became radiant and dwelt in God's thick cloud, and there God taught him all the folds of his creative power. On two tablets Moses' master wrote a book for him, because he knew that he was capable and could receive much. His teacher saw that he was fasting and wanted to learn, and he filled two tablets with treasures and gave them to him so that he might become rich. He gave him two, so that he might read from one and keep the other for the new covenant of his Son when it was revealed. On one tablet he wrote the Law and its observances, and he gave the Gospel another tablet on which it might be explained. One covenant was to be written on one tablet, and because there are two covenants, two tablets were needed. One for the Law, so that it might speak through it of events; one for the Gospel, so that it might be interpreted through it spiritually.

He gave him two, so that when the new covenant appeared in its time, no one would say, “Why have two covenants been established for us?” So that generations, ages, and the peoples of the earth would know that both the new things and the old things come from one. Through the two tablets, the great prophet understood that God had another time in which to speak. “At this time he has given teaching to the world through my hands; at another time he will teach the whole earth through his Son. A prophet like me will arise after me from among your brothers; he too will teach fasting to the earth, and it will be enlightened by him.” In Moses’ fast, this fast of our Lord was being glorified, and that number was being matched to this reckoning. For that same number of days the Son of God was tested. As he fasted, he preserved the honor of Moses in his fasting. Elijah too, who was a confidant of the Godhead, traveled the road for that same number of days through the fast he observed. Moses began the great fast, and our Lord brought it to completion; Elijah too ran between them to the mountain he reached. Both Elijah and the great Moses looked toward our Lord, and because of his fast they undertook fasting, so that they might resemble him. Through Moses’ fast, creation learned about its Lord:

How he made it, and how it came into being from nothing. Through Elijah’s fast, he drew forth revelation, and it gave him strength to remove kings and establish kings in their kingdoms. Through this fast of our Lord, demons are overthrown from their ranks, and rulers have their authority taken from them. The ruler of the air fell like lightning and was scattered; mercy supported fallen Adam, and he arose and fought. There was a spectacle, and the Son of God descended into the arena. In Adam’s place he took up his contest and fought it. He traveled the road that his Father’s prophets had prepared for him, so that the world might learn that he was no stranger to the one who begot him. Like Moses, he fasted forty days while being tested, and like Elijah he ran in the contests of righteousness. The servants fasted for the Lord’s sake, to portray him; but the Lord himself fasted and was tested for Adam’s sake. For Moses fasted, but did not help Adam at all; Elijah fasted, but the common debt was not paid. Nor did they fast for Adam’s sake so that he might be helped, but to show how his Lord would fast on his behalf. Through their fasts they painted an image of the Son’s fast, so that the earth might become aware of the news of his coming before he dawned upon it.

But when Adam’s Lord came and began his fast, the prophets rejoiced in him, because he had come to fulfill their revelations. Both the earlier prophets and those in between became his witnesses: he is the Lord who descended into the arena on behalf of his servant. He came down to renew the battle between Adam and the dragon, and for this reason he undertook a fast as he fought. Through fasting he repaid the debt of that eating which the serpent had introduced, so that in hand-to-hand combat he might free Adam from his debts. For the one who had eaten too soon, his Lord delayed eating, so that that gluttony might be replaced by self-discipline. The battle in the garden, among the trees, had ended in defeat; for this reason the fighting was renewed in the wilderness. That victorious one prolonged the battle for forty days, so that during them he might repay the belly’s debt as he fought. Concerning forty, I will now explain why this number is set down in Scripture, throughout all its books. Among the people, the Law commanded a woman who gives birth to a male child to bring, at forty days, the sacrifice that purifies her. Again, it commands a woman who gives birth to a female child to remain in her bleeding for forty days and another forty, and then to be purified. Moses himself, too, the treasury of books and revelations,

fasted for forty days and learned the mysteries of the Godhead. Elijah too, who bore the image of the Son of God, traveled for forty days, for he too was undergoing training symbolically. Without my listing many examples, recognize for yourself that this number is very prominent throughout all the books. For forty days the Son of God fasted and was tempted. If you listen with spiritual understanding, come and comprehend. Our Lord came down to win victory for this nature in battle, and on behalf of all of it he entered the contest, himself victorious. Now this nature has elements from which it is constituted: four that are equal but opposed in their forms. When this nature fell in battle against that accursed one, the elements became guilty by departing from that course of righteousness. For this reason he gave each element a course of ten days, and then he won victory in the athletic contest. Now this number, ten, is the limit, and beyond it you find no further number. For this reason he gave the element ten days—as much as to say, the whole course of righteousness. He repeated these ten four times, so that through them the whole nature might stand in righteousness.

Forty days provided a contest for the four that had fallen, so that they might stand triumphant in complete victory. For this purpose our Lord came down to battle, so that through him the whole nature, which had been guilty, might be acquitted. Because of this hidden mystery laid down in the Scriptures, these forty days were prominent among the readings. In the Gospel, however, a course of fifty days is laid out for us, and unless you run the fifty, you cannot run the forty. This mystery shows that through fasting the senses, as well as the elements, rise from the fall into which the serpent cast them. For the five senses, fifty days of righteousness; then the sin that conquered Adam’s household is conquered. Of the fifty, forty stand as days set apart, through which the four who were defeated among the trees gain victory. This is the mystery of this fast, full of victories. Rise, you diligent ones; run in the contest of righteousness. Lift your mind a little higher here, listener, for this discourse is no ordinary speech from an orator. The mysteries of fasting stir within me spiritually, and whoever listens in a bodily way does not hear me. For forty days he fasted and fought against the ruler,

and in the great battle he gave victory to the whole of human nature. Look, today the fast extends over fifty days for the Church, but forty of them are the days spent in the contest. If you read the Law spiritually, you will find the mystery of fifty clearly revealed in it. The fiftieth year is the year of weeks, a year of restoration, release, and consolation. In it all the lands that had been sold are restored, returning to their original owners to bring them joy. Poverty had forced them to sell, but at the release they became heirs to their inheritances. The fiftieth year restores villages to their possessors, and fields to their original owners who had given them up. Whoever lost his land through a sale and became estranged from it receives it back into his hands in the fiftieth year and cultivates it. Needy heirs who sold and abandoned their holdings return in the fiftieth year and stand within their boundaries. Here is the resurrection and that great day of the good news, which comes at fifty and was foreshadowed in the Law. On the fiftieth day, the heir rose from the grave in the garden and took back Eden, which the serpent had deceitfully bought from him.

On the fiftieth day our Lord comes to his lands, and that usurper who deceitfully bought what belonged to him loses it. After fifty days he shines upon the souls that had been sold like fields, and they return. The devil stirred up confusion and bought them; he led them astray and acquired them. After fifty they return to their master, so that he may inherit them. A year was spiritually represented by a day, for Ezekiel too then took a day for a year. In the fiftieth year there is restoration and release, and joy for the heirs who have regained their holdings. On the fiftieth day there is resurrection and consolation, and souls return to God so that he may inherit them. At the end of the fast, the Son’s resurrection is given to us, and like that fiftieth year, he restores those who were sold. All the souls that had been sold for nothing—he redeems them and restores them for nothing. Moses spoke to the Hebrews through these mysteries: in that year, the year of weeks, there was to be a release. Because of this great mystery of righteousness, he prescribed fifty, and called its conclusion a release.

The fast runs for fifty days, and at its conclusion the resurrection grants one pardon to all who are guilty. During these fifty days righteousness runs its course, and at their conclusion forgiveness arises to renew them. During fifty days there is sweat, struggle, and strenuous effort; after these come a great crown and victory. This fast rests upon these hidden mysteries. You who fast, do not slacken in your labors. During these days an image of righteousness is painted. Let everyone bring choice colors from their pigments. Because of these fifty days, Moses prescribed that the fiftieth year should be a year of restoration for the people. So that this human nature might become beautiful and righteous, a contest is held for forty days among the champions. They win in forty days, but they are not rewarded until fifty, for at the conclusion of fifty the Savior rises for the earth. You are desirable, O fast! Blessed is the one who gains victory through you, for all mysteries and all prefigurations are found in you. Forty belongs to you, and you possess fifty in abundance: a fierce contest, and at its conclusion a great crown.

You are great, O fast, and great is the mystery enacted in you, for through you every victory is given to all the champions. Through you the great prophet, a son of the Levites, became radiant, and in the splendor he wore he became a sun of flesh for the people. Through you he entered within, went in, and explored the depths of the Godhead; then he came out and proclaimed life to the world with great hope. Through you Elijah became beautiful and clear, and acquired wings; he flew and ascended to the place where death cannot enter. Through you our Savior threw down our enemy in combat, and at your conclusion he laid waste to Sheol for our sake. Fasting is armor, but if someone who is slack puts it on, he is hindered by it and does not win when he fights. Stand like determined fighters who have understood what fasting is, and run its course righteously, in keeping with the character of the fast. With faith, which is the mystery of good deeds; with love for humanity, which brings you near to God; With armor forged through prayers and almsgiving; with righteousness on the right and on the left; With humility, which offers its cheek to the one who strikes it; with pure love, which does not become angry with its neighbor; With gifts that go out from your doorstep to anyone in need, and with alms that fly from you to beggars;

By every means that lends a hand to good deeds, and in every course of action through which righteousness is practiced; In everything that the chosen fast requires of those who fast, run, you who fast, so that you may be able to save your soul. It is a great contest, and diligence is required in it. Toil in the struggle and look toward the crown that comes from righteousness. Do not grow slack, dozing a little and sleeping a little, and lose the harvest that gives the soul abundant life. This fast is an arena for athletic combat: whoever falls dies, and whoever does not fall wins the victory. You who fast, beware of the warrior who guards the air! There he stands, stripped for combat and eager to fight those who fast. Take Jesus with you, for no one wins except through him; through him you can subdue all the powers on high. Fasting is a weapon, and Jesus has given it to all who are victorious. Servants of the King, take up your armor in the bloody contest! This fast is the struggle in which a person stands firm even to the shedding of blood, to bring his life out of the battle. In this contest the soul kills or is killed; it conquers and stands, or is conquered and falls terribly.

This fast is appointed for the battle of righteousness, and no one can withdraw from the struggle. There is fasting, and there are those who fast, and there are distinctions. But this fast is unique for those who enter the contest. The Law gave the Israelites ten fasts in a single year, along with many observances. These fasts were prescribed for various reasons, in connection with deliverance and with the festivals throughout the year. This fast is unique and divine. It is something great, through which all human nature is renewed. The Son of God fasted to make the whole human race righteous, and his purpose is greater than all other purposes. For forty days he placed all human nature as though in a fiery furnace and forged it, so that what had been corrupted might become beautiful. Through his great fast he brought down the enemy’s strength and raised up the fallen, who had long lain overthrown. The debt of all is now being paid through the Son’s fast, and everyone is bound to labor with him for his own salvation. If the innocent one entered the contest on behalf of the guilty, how can anyone who is guilty rest from the struggle?

During this fast he fought three rounds against the strong one and humbled his pride in all three. Satan set three snares of three passions, and the Son of God broke all three. He arrayed love of food, love of glory, and desire for wealth in battle against the one who fasted and willingly went hungry. All these things through which Adam had incurred condemnation—he brought them all, to defeat the contestant through them. While the strong one stood alert and watched over his snares, the Watchful One broke them through his fasting and made him a laughingstock. He trampled down love of food through the hunger he endured, and love of glory was defeated by his humility. He trampled down desire for wealth through love of poverty, and in a single fast three passions were brought low. Through his fasting he gave instruction to monks on how to overcome the devil in their struggles. He reproved Adam: if he had chosen to fight, he would not have been defeated in the battle against desire and excess. He scorned the tyrant who brought him down to the arena, and he stood and fought. The mighty one was defeated, and the nature that had been condemned was victorious. The Son of God fought in the person of Adam,

and the victory that the Lord won he gave to his servant. For the debt that Eve incurred, the Virgin’s son paid her bond. Blessed is he through whose fasting those who fast were victorious in their struggles.
The third homily on fasting is finished.
By the same author, Saint Jacob. Homily 26. On Love. Son of God, who came in his love to renew all things,

give me your love, so that through it I may speak to those who hear me. Exalted one, who came down from his dwelling places to our wickedness, grant me to ascend to the realm of your love and recount its beauties. O you who in your love endured the sufferings of crucifixion, let your blood seethe within me, so that I may speak about your grace. Let my speech be stirred by the fervor of your love to proclaim your good news, so that I may tell your story abundantly among those on earth.

Come, beloved ones, whom the womb of baptism bore. Let us acquire love, for it is great wealth to whoever possesses it. You who became brothers of the Only Begotten through the waters, come, let us take delight with understanding in the account of love. Beloved children whom the Father raised on the blood of his Son, give me your attention, so that I may deliver the discourse on love with fervor. For every subject, when it is spoken of, has its own flavor, and the language of every discourse resembles the subject it concerns. Today I am moved to speak about love. It is a sweet dish; come, let us delight in its flavors. O discerning person who pursues beautiful things, capture love for yourself, for it is what brings you near to God. O teacher, advocate of the divine mysteries, speak with love; otherwise you cannot benefit anyone. O disciple whose ear is inclined toward discoveries, give me love and receive a word full of life. Let anyone who teaches without loving keep completely silent, for he labors in vain over a series of words that bring no benefit. And let anyone who does not listen with love close his ears, for the sounds and words he hears do him no good. Skilled teacher, who wishes to enrich those who hear him,

love much and speak little with your disciples. And you, learner, listen to a little speech with great love and become rich through it, for without love no one becomes rich. As soon as love enters the soul, its thoughts become radiant; the mind enters and stands in the realm of divine mysteries. Although good deeds are beautiful for those who do them, if they are done without love, they are not beautiful. Salt from the mortar makes foods pleasant; good deeds likewise need love, so that they may be done with it. Good deeds are arranged like limbs in a body, and love fills the place of the soul for the whole body. Fasting is beautiful, but if someone fasts without love, his mouth stinks, and there is no benefit in his abstinence. Prayer is beloved, but if love does not raise it up, its wing is weak, and it does not see the Most High in his dwelling. Righteousness is greatly beloved by the one who practices it. But if he does not love while practicing it—but if he does not love while practicing it, his labor is empty. Glorious is the crown of virginity and holiness, but if a holy person is empty of love, he is like an adulterer. Great is the reward of the one who breaks his bread for the hungry;

but if he breaks it for him without love, it brings no benefit. For a martyr to give his body to fire and burning, he needs love; then he receives a crown with the martyrs. Love surpasses prophecy and faith, for without it there is neither one who prophesies nor one who believes. From its actions you learn what love is, and its deeds testify to how beautiful it is. In love the Father handed over his Son for sinners, for without love this deed would not have happened. Love drew the Lord, and he came down from his dwellings. It mingled him with human beings, so that the Master might become a companion to his servants. Love brought the Son of God from his Father's house and made him human, and he endured the sufferings of crucifixion. Love confined him both within the womb and within the tomb—the Son of the Mighty One, by whose hidden command creation hangs. Through the Father's love, which had existed in him eternally, he lent his likeness to create humanity in the image of his Son. In that same love he created all creatures when he brought them into being, and in it he also handed over his only Son when he redeemed them. What king had the strength to do such a thing:

to hand over his son for a people in exile, to bring them back to their own land? For what rich man would it have been easy to scatter all his wealth among beggars out of love, and make them rich? Who would have given his son as a burnt offering, to become a sacrifice for servants who had fled from him, in order to bring them back? Who among the good would not have been afraid to give himself up, to taste death for the wicked and give them life? And what living person could have probed the depths of Sheol and bound himself in order to release the prisoners from darkness? Who among those on high would make the grave his dwelling and raise the dead to the lofty dwelling of the heavenly beings? Love brought the Son of God to do this deed: to taste death for human beings and give them life. For this reason love stands above the virtues, and all good qualities are placed beneath its heel. Righteousness and perfection stand below it, for no one can become perfect except through love. However righteous a person may become through righteous deeds, he needs love, and only then is he made complete in perfection.

It seems to me that the discourse about it that lies before me is difficult, and the subject I have undertaken weighs heavily on the listeners. No one listens to a discourse about love except with love. Where shall we seek it, or with whom shall we speak about it? Among us there are resentment, rage, and hardness of heart; envy, deceit, falsehood, and slander; Every kind of dispute, every kind of quarrel, every kind of conflict, every kind of strife, and every pretext for hateful speech. This one quarrels, that one is angry, and another is deceitful. Where is love, so that we may speak about it without confusion? If it were present, it would be good for us to speak about it. But since it is absent, the discourse about it is wronged and beaten down. Love can never be forced by anyone to become angry, for it loves both those who are near and those who are far away. Love cannot hate the person who hates it. It looks to its Lord, who endured the cross for everyone. Come, you who are angry! Come, be reconciled to the person who hates you, for anger will destroy your soul if it spends the night within it. For this reason the apostle commands those who listen to him: “Do not let the sun go down and find you still angry.”

Hurry, discerning person! Seek reconciliation while it is still day, for if anger spends the night within you, it does its work during the night. It darkens your soul, confuses it, and corrupts it. It pains the heart and gives rise to every kind of troubled thought. It lets the mind loose into disturbing, unpleasant dreams, and at night stirs up every kind of conflict within you through evil impulses. A dream brings your enemy and draws him up in battle against you, and all night long he humiliates and torments you. You felt a great need to keep away from him because you hated him, but a dream led him in and placed him inside your bedroom. You drove him away so that he would leave, but the night brought him back and entangled him with you. Anger slept within you, and disturbing dreams choked you. Visions sprang from that day's dealings, and all night long they brought your enemy to quarrel with you. Woe to you because of him! There he lies beside you on your bed, and while you sleep, he quarrels with you and strikes you. The anger that spent the night within you drew an image of the person you hated and set it before you in a dream, so that you would be tormented by it. If you hate him, be reconciled to him and be rid of him. Place love within yourself before you sleep, and then he will not trouble you.

Remove hostility from your soul while you are awake, and put love within it so that it may give birth to divine dreams. From the evening onward, bring peace into your mind, and you will find restful sleep all night long. Let the sun set and love rise over your mind; let the light of love overcome the night so that it does not grow dark for you. The night is dark, and anger is dark. If you surrender your soul to both, who will give you light or make you glad? The day has sunk away. Take love as your great sun; go in and illuminate your soul with it at night, away from evil. Look upon your enemy with love when you go to sleep, and your sleep will be pleasant, and you will be free of strife. All thoughts, good and evil, are seeds. The soul is the soil, and the will is like the farmer. If you sow evil thoughts in your soul in the evening, you will reap troubled dreams all night long. If you bury love within your soul when you go to sleep, a sweet fragrance will rise from your bed as you sleep. Anger thoroughly disturbs your soul when it enters it. Clear your soul of it and fill it with peace when you go to sleep. Paul, the physician who can readily bind up souls,

applied this dressing to the soul so that it might be healed by it. He commanded the angry person not to let the sun set on him, but to drive anger out of himself so that he would not go to sleep with it. Resentment in the soul is rust to the person who harbors it. If it spends the night within him, it takes hold like gangrene and corrupts him. For this reason he offered reconciliation to the angry person, so that anger would not fester within him at night if it remained there overnight. While it is still light, illuminate your soul, discerning person, so that when it grows dark you are not tormented by dejection and sorrow. What should you do to your enemy when he wrongs you? Love him and overcome him, for if you hate him, he overcomes you. As long as you hate him, he becomes a thorn within your mind and pricks you. Unless you love him, you have not driven him away. You are formed in the image of the Son, you who hate your brother. How will you resemble him unless you love the person who hates you? Jesus your master changed water into good wine. Do a new deed like his, and imitate him. Take your enemy and change him into a friend within your mind, so that, as at Cana, you may see all these new things within your soul. You call the Father on high “Our Father” in the place of atonement. Show that you have within you some likeness to the Only Begotten.

He made wine from water because he is the Son of God. Make peace from strife, and imitate him. Without grumbling, he offered his cheek to the person striking him. Yet at a word you are upset, agitated, and full of anger. For sinners he bore spit on his face and lashes on his back, and he endured it so that he might taste death in their place. While they hated him, the Son of God loved them; and while they crucified him, he offered himself for their lives. Come, tell me, angry man who hates his brother: what has he done to you that makes it hard for you to be reconciled to him? Has he wronged you? Look at God, who was also wronged. Has he insulted you? They insulted him too, and he endured it. Your brother has insulted you, abused you, and deceived you; you are still under obligation, for the Son of God endured the cross without hating. And after all this, unless you love him, you cannot say “Our Father,” if you are the brother of the Only Begotten. Forgive the one who has done wrong, run to him, and be reconciled to him, for the gospel prescribes this action to whoever listens to it. O disciple, unless you love the one who hates you, find yourself another teacher, for the crucified one will not be your teacher. If Jesus is your instructor, this is what he teaches:

That you should love your enemy and hold him dear. And if you do not obey him, your instructor is that serpent who, through his deceit, casts every kind of quarrel and division among the disciples. The world has had two teachers from the beginning, and the one does not teach their disciples as the other does. Through their teachings, the serpent and our Lord are the earth’s instructors: one kills his disciples, and the other gives his disciples life. The serpent teaches hardness of heart and envy, hatred of brothers, anger, and constant deceit; Great wrath, jealousy, rage, and turmoil; quarreling and resentment, along with disputes and evil divisions; Theft, falsehood, adultery, and division, along with strife and the shedding of blood. But Jesus teaches purity of heart and generosity, love for people, cheerfulness, and fellowship; Great peace, undisturbed harmony, pure love, integrity, uprightness, and humility; Also serenity, sincerity, faith, and righteousness, and that a person should love whoever hates him. Come, disciple, take one of these as your teacher, and do not stumble over his teaching if he is your teacher.

Choose your instructors and learn from him as he tells you, for you cannot obey them both. If your mind desires to become a disciple of the serpent, be angry—it suits you—and hate your brother even while he loves you. Be troubled, perverse, gloomy, and hateful toward people. Prepare ambushes, provoke quarrels, and stir up anger. Summon strife, cause uproar and turmoil, and unleash the sword; be bitter, like a disciple of the biting serpent. Does your brother love you? Hate him without cause—why are you idle? And if he hates you, hate him as he hates you, and scheme against him. Set a trap for him, dig a pit for him, and cast him into destruction. Devise evil things and heap abuse on him because he has wronged you. And if he comes to make peace with you, do not accept him, lest your master, the evil serpent, become angry with you. He teaches you not to be reconciled or appeased: “Let no one overcome you, so that you do not become one of the weak. Instead, repay the one who wronged you with grievous injuries. Do not forgive him, or he will despise you and laugh at you. Do him greater harm than he did to you, so that everyone will fear you and honor you.”

These are the things the serpent teaches his friends and disciples. Woe to anyone who listens to him and accepts him! After these things, come and hear what Jesus says to you, and become a disciple of the teaching of God's household. “Love the one who hates you, and turn your cheek to the one who strikes you. Surrender your life for your friend if it is demanded. Love your enemy indeed, if you are my disciple; and if he wrongs you seventy times seven, be reconciled to him. Endure insult, but do not insult the one who hates you. Be good even to the wicked who revile you. Forgive your brother all the wrongs he has done.” For this is what Jesus, your teacher, teaches, if you belong to him. Look at the cross, and look at the crown of thorns upon him, and immediately resentment and anger will die out in your mind. To reconcile the human race, who were at enmity, he endured blows and humiliation and made peace throughout the world. The teaching of the Son of God has been forgotten, and everyone runs against him through their deeds. The disciples have fled from the teacher of truth, and the commandment that teaches peace to those who obey it has been despised. Evil has grown so strong that a priest becomes angry, and the steward of the mysteries hates his brother and mocks him.

Should I be silent here, or speak while I tremble? Should I raise my voice, or close my mouth and cease teaching? The priest is salt and the reconciler of all who are at enmity. But if he becomes angry, who will reconcile him with his neighbor? No one puts salt into salt to give it flavor. And if it has become tasteless, what seasoning can restore it? If the seasoning has gone bad, who will salt it? For if it has become tasteless, all hope of its flavor is lost. Come, our salt, and bring your flavor to make us pleasant. Do not go bad yourself, for we look to you to be seasoned by you. Spread yourself among us, for we have become tasteless and confused. Strengthen our weakness, and add abundant flavor to our tastelessness. Everyone looks to your own flavor to be seasoned by you. But if your flavor is lost, there is weeping over your ruin. You are salt, priest. See that you do not become angry with your neighbor, lest outsiders say that the salt has become tasteless. You are the salt of the earth and the peace of the land, the light of the world and the stewards of God's households. Through you, the one who is angry with his neighbor is reconciled. Through you, the one who is upset with his spouse is appeased. From you the world learns to love those who hate it.

And from you it hears teaching full of life. You read aloud from the lofty pulpit of the Godhead: “Forgive your brother if he sins against you seventy times seven.” On your harps the good news of the Son of God sings words of love, teaching everyone to love those who hate them. From you the pure congregation of the church of the nations hears that no one should ever repay evil for evil. I have loved my enemy because of the reading you taught me. But if I see that you hate your brother, what am I to do? You teach me to love those who hate me, yet you are unwilling to be reconciled with your brother who is angry. You have frightened me by saying that unless I forgive, he will not forgive me. Yet you are unwilling to let go of your anger against the one who sinned against you. If you neglect your duty, who will teach you? It is frightening for me to direct instruction toward you. When you read aloud, I learned from you about reconciliation: anyone who is angry is not accepted in the place of atonement. “Go, be reconciled, and then come and offer your gift,” is said to the one who is angry, so that once he is reconciled, he may readily come. The fragrance of incense without reconciliation is a foul smell.

And if someone who is angry carries a censer, he dishonors the sanctuary. The soul’s love is the incense of the place of atonement, which the mind has gathered from the blessed roots of Eden. The choice spices that the priest brings into the Holy of Holies are thoughts that are clear and free from evil. The branched lampstand with its seven lights, whose radiance is strong, is the love of the Lord placed within a pure soul. The perfumed oil that anoints the priest when he is consecrated proclaims love, whose fragrance is sweeter than spices. The stones of Perfection and Light upon his breast are the choice fragrance and clear light of faith. When he anointed his hand, his foot, and his earlobe, it was to make known that he was a servant of the crucifixion. He was commanded to put salt in all the sacrifices, and it was made known that love serves in every sacrifice. The linen covering that the priest wears inside the sanctuary is love spread over his mind when he serves as priest. The multicolored garment he wears when he goes out to the people, to the congregation, shows that he mingles and associates lovingly with everyone.

Through the golden bells and the pomegranates on the apron, he stirs the priest to fear, to love, and to be watchful. The crown, the cap, and the ephod that he wears when he ministers are hope, love, and faith that cannot be torn apart. The priest’s crown proclaims the priest’s love to the people, for that love binds all virtues together for him. Through love a priest can enter God's presence; if he does not love, a layman who loves is better than he is. I do not dare offer instruction to a priest, lest I be put to shame for meddling in things higher than myself. No one lights a lamp while walking in the sunlight, for the sun itself lights every road for every traveler. Be silent, speaker, lest the sun be dishonored by you. Cover your mouth: the subject you have taken up is greater than you. You are the lowliest of people; what business have you speaking? You whose understanding is dark, what are you saying to one who is enlightened? Leave this subject, for there is no room for words concerning it. It is a lofty rank. Be silent, lowly one, and look at yourself. Turn your teaching toward the congregation; speak to it, for it is peaceful and simple. There is room for you there, and love that listens kindly.

It is not for you, man, to speak to the [?]. Leave the owners of the sheep alone; their affairs are guarded. Speak to the sheep, the little and innocent ones, for whose sake the Son of God endured the cross. Listen, innocent ones, bought with the blood of the Only Begotten: once again a discourse on love is being spoken to help you. Virtues cannot be acquired except through love. Let whoever is eager for spiritual gain run after it. Love one another as the body's members love those beside them, for the whole body has one head, the Lord Jesus. Anyone who is angry with his neighbor and will not be reconciled is like a limb cut off and cast away from the other members. Love is the soul. Anyone from whom love has departed is left a cold, rotting corpse and is not among the living. Who can reconcile a man who is angry with his neighbor, except love, which is the [?] of new life? Tell me now, what is the matter behind this anger? Among those who are angry with one another, who should press for reconciliation? There was a quarrel: one person was insulted, and the other insulted him. The one who was insulted should seek love; it is his duty.

The one who did wrong is devising ways to establish his own case. He is ashamed to come; go yourself to meet him and be reconciled to him. If a poor man is offended by a rich man, that rich man is obliged to plead for reconciliation. But when the poor man has done wrong, he becomes afraid and bewildered; he trembles and withdraws, and cannot devise a way to be reconciled. In every circumstance, it is fitting for the one who is free from blame to seek peace with his neighbor. Let the one who is superior, exalted, and honored lower himself to the lowly one and be reconciled to him in humility. At the beginning of the world there was a quarrel stirred up by the serpent, and from that time the Lord and Adam were estranged. Who was inferior, who was poor, and who had done wrong? And who went to meet the other to be reconciled to him? Adam did wrong. He showed contempt and acted insolently; he went astray and rebelled. He stole and transgressed; he snatched and ate; he grew angry and went out. After these things, the King's Son set out from his Father and came to reconcile the one who had become angry of his own free will. The honored one lowered himself to the lowly one, and the rich one sought reconciliation from the poor one. The owner of the garden came down to plead with the thief. He reconciled him and gave him the fruit of life to eat.

In his love, the good shepherd carried the sheep that had strayed. It had become angry and gone away, but he came and lifted it onto his shoulders. Tremble, you who are angry, and strive every day for reconciliation, for the Lord in his love reconciled us to himself when we had angered him. Let no one say, “So-and-so did wrong; let him come to me. I am better than he is. It would be a disgrace for me to go and seek reconciliation with him.” “He wronged me. Let him come and plead with me, and I will accept him, so that through his humiliation everyone may learn of his wrongdoing.” The Lord did not choose to treat Adam, who had sinned, in this way. Instead, he humbled himself and asked Adam to be reconciled to him. If the Lord had remained in his own place until today and had not come to meet him, Adam would still be angry with him. Since he knew that this would help, he humbled himself. He himself pleaded with the slave who had fled to be reconciled to him. The Most High came down in his compassion to those below. He reconciled them, led them, and brought them up to his own place to exalt them. The rich one made his way to the poor. He made peace, enriched them, and brought them up to the one who begot him. The mighty one made reconciliation with the weak. He honored them, redeemed them, and brought back those who were lost.

The master humbled himself before slaves, and the king before the lowly. God himself came down to reconcile human beings. You who are angry, look at your God and imitate him. Act wisely and make peace with your neighbor. Wash away your rage, resentment, and malice, and let love for the Lord dwell in your soul like a kingdom. Whoever is angry with his neighbor and does not love him hates the Lord and refuses to love his brother. For human beings are the image of the Godhead, and whoever honors the king's image loves the king. But if someone despises or insults his image, the king demands an accounting from those who despise it for the insult to his image. No one can love God while hating his brother or turning away from his neighbor. God is hidden, but your brother is near, and he is God's image. Honor the one who is far away through the one who is near. But if your heart hates your brother, who is visible and near, how will you love the Lord, who is hidden and far from you? Show through your brother the proof that there is love in your soul. Then declare that you love the Lord, who is high above you.

The king is far away, but his image is near. If you insult the image, the king becomes angry and demands an accounting for the insult. All the obligations you would lay upon God, show them toward your brother, and the Lord will settle your claims against him. Honor the image, cherish it, love it, and be reconciled to it; and the King, who has no need of your honor, will repay you for your pains. Love God and love your brother from your heart. Blessed is he who in his love reconciled the world with the one who begot him.
The discourse on love is finished.
By the same Saint Jacob. Discourse 27. On admonition.

A newborn needs a nursing mother to receive life from her, and creation needs the Creator to be sustained by him. If a mother abandons her infant when she has given birth to it, it would have been better for it never to have been born from her.

And if the Lord of the world had abandoned it after creating it, it would have been better for it never to have existed from the beginning. He does not abandon it, for a woman does not abandon her infant. Even if she forgets, he never forgets creation. If he had merely created it, he would only have been its Creator, and he would have had no other name but this. But because he carries it after creating it and also feeds it, he is called both the Mighty One and the Nourisher. Because his judgment is upright, he is just; and because he shows mercy, he is also called merciful. His judgment is just, and mercy accompanies it. He is full of zeal, and kindness is found in him. All his governance flows from grace, and all his work rests upon justice. He is not hindered by justice when he shows mercy, and when he exacts punishment, his grace does not reproach him. Both justice and grace befit him, and they help one another every day as they shine. He has mercy, and he has scourges; therefore he is both loved and feared by anyone full of discernment. Compassion is his, zeal is his, and love is his; and he has anger against anyone who turns away from justice.

Wherever he sees injustice taking place, he becomes zealous; and if humility meets him, he becomes gentle. For if he did not hate the wicked, he would not be just; and if he did not have mercy on the humble, he would not be kind. Just as he is just, he is also kind. His governance is upright and above reproach. Sometimes he sees injustice and remains patient; as though he had not seen it, injustice prospers, and he does not strike it down. And sometimes, as soon as evil occurs, he stirs up his burning anger against those who committed the evil that took place. One person pursues injustice all the days of his life, and neither censure nor discipline overtakes him. But if another even thinks of doing evil, justice arrives with her sword drawn to strike him down to destruction. In one place his servants suffer blows from the wicked, and they are not rescued, nor does he show zeal to avenge them. In another place, if one of the righteous is insulted, he sets about passing judgment on the offensive word. The people who fashioned the calf stoned righteous Hur, yet his case was not even brought forward to ask why they stoned him. And because Miriam spoke a word, she was clothed with leprosy:

Retribution for the word, but no condemnation for those who threw stones. Isaiah was sawn apart, and the Lord, his master, did not vindicate him; yet because righteous Lot was insulted, the land was burned. There was a place where he displayed his power inside the furnace and bound the fire so that the young men could tread it underfoot. In another place, a woman threatened one of his chosen ones, and he did not call to account the mouth that spoke insolently against the righteous man. The fire is bound, while Jezebel is free to insult, for sometimes he exacts retribution and sometimes he refrains from it. Anyone who sets out to investigate these things becomes bewildered: why does the whole course of events not follow one consistent pattern? Why is one person struck when he does wrong, but another is not? Why does he overlook one person but call another to account so severely? Molded clay, why do you speak insolently against the potter, telling him what he should or should not do? The wisdom of the Most High is set over the governance of the world, and through it all events run their course at their appointed times. By that knowledge which fashioned the sun and made the moon, the turbulent world is governed by God. Whether he exacts retribution or overlooks an offense, it is wisdom; yet because he is concerned that humanity should benefit, he is thought to be confused. He is not confused when he gives nourishment to the Watchers,

and to human beings their food within their territories. He was not at a loss in his work of creation when he gave light to the sun and provided the moon with its phases, names to the stars and a swift course to the heavenly hosts. They do not confuse him as they speed along their paths. He is not hindered when he spreads the sun’s rays and stretches daylight over the lands. It is no burden to him when he gives nourishment to the fish in the depths of the seas, a welcome supply to the inhabitants of the waters. It is not difficult for him to count the number of hairs, for without him not one falls to the ground. The grains of sand, the drops of rain, and the waves of the sea are all easily numbered by the Godhead. The weight of the earth and the great burden of the whole world—he stands bearing it without growing weary or being troubled. All creation receives life from him every day, everything in its own place, and providing for them is easy for him. The governance of the turbulent world is also administered by him, through that knowledge which directs these courses every day. Whether he exacts punishment or refrains from doing so, his purpose is one: to [?] human beings every day.

When the Most High sees injustice taking place and remains silent, do not think that he is neither jealous nor an avenger. And when he exacts punishment fiercely, do not suppose that anger compelled him and that he was stirred to punish the injustice he saw. He is the same both when he exacts punishment and when he refrains, for God does not change from what he is. And because he truly has two worlds, he refrains here so that he may execute judgment in the greater world. He assigned each of them a task through which things might be set right; and where he sees injustice, he immediately executes judgment. He settles the matter so that the world may recognize that judgment exists. And where he refrains when evil is committed, he teaches that God truly has another world. When the deeds of the people are punished here in our land, let the world learn that it belongs to God to execute judgment. And when someone openly commits injustice and he does not punish him, he shows that he is keeping him for that world, to judge him there. And when you suffer no blows, learn that judgment is reserved for the world beyond. Both are very necessary when they occur, for both bring benefit to the whole world. If all deeds were left unpunished,

who would affirm that there is a God who executes judgment? And if every evil committed here were punished, it would seem as though there were no other world. If everyone who did evil had his evil come back upon his own head, and everyone who did good received repayment for his goodness here, it would seem and appear to anyone considering it that judgment had already taken place and that there was no further judgment to come. But because some deeds are punished and others are held in reserve, the existence of another world and of the Lord of the world is established. When justice rises in judgment against a deed, it shows that there is a just one who punishes the unjust. And when he instead lets a deed pass and does not punish it, he confirms that he has a judgment in that other world. It is the same with his servants when they are persecuted: he rescues one, while he leaves another alone and does not rescue him. His providence is great, beautiful, and worthy of praise, both when he rescues and when he refrains from rescuing. Some he delivered even from fire and wild beasts, but others he allowed to burn and did not deliver. He rescued the three and left the seven without rescue, yet all ten belong to him. Why, then, was this? If he had delivered all his servants from afflictions,

the love of them all would have been far less worthy of praise. It would have been said that no one suffered blows for his sake, since he rescued everyone who came to suffer blows from being struck. That is why those who come for his sake come: they know that he rescues them from affliction. He does not let anyone suffer utterly for his sake; if he allowed them to be afflicted, they would not come. The glory of God's servants would have lost its savor for him if he had delivered and rescued them all from affliction. Outsiders would have said that he did not even exist: if he did exist, why had he neglected his loved ones? He would have been reproached for watching his servants being destroyed without ever delivering even one of them from affliction. That is why he delivered them where he wished, so that the world would realize that these servants have a Lord who possesses power. And that is why, here and there, he allowed them to endure afflictions, so that the world would see how steadfast his servants' love was. Where he allowed them to burn, their love was magnified; and where he chose to rescue them, he himself was shown victorious. For this reason he did not deliver all his servants, so that he would not be glorified alone when he was glorified.

He allowed them to die by the edge of the sword and in the mouths of wild beasts, so that they would receive glory for all they endured for his sake. For this reason he delivered some of them and let others suffer, so that he would be glorified and his servants would be glorified with him. When he delivers them, he takes all the glory for himself; when he does not deliver them, he wishes to glorify them along with himself. He has compassion on them and allows them to die for his sake, so that they may boldly claim their reward from him. And so that they too might be glorified, their love for him held fire, the knife, and wild beasts in contempt. And so the world would realize what servants God has: when necessity demands it, they approach death for his sake. And so his servants' love would be illustrious throughout the earth, and he would be glorified because of them by those who saw them. And so they would have the blessing that, because of their deeds, he who is worthy of glory and praise was glorified. For this reason, when he does not rescue from affliction, discerning people consider it as good of him as when he does rescue. Someone who lacks knowledge finds fault here and there: the world's governance is hateful in his eyes, and he even pretends to be wise. However wise he may be, he errs in his arrogance by supposing

that if he had authority over its governance, he would set it in order. Whenever he saw injustice taking place, he would put a stop to it; and whenever a wicked person acted insolently, he would strike him down. He would not allow a single righteous person to be struck on the cheek, and he would not let an unjust person raise his head. There is someone who goes mad and loses his reason in his conceit, and thinks that the affairs of the world are not good. And although it is proclaimed that no one should envy the wicked, he envies them and raises an outcry against the wicked. He even wishes that, if he could, he might bring down fire upon the wicked and the unjust and burn them up. You fool! You do not bear with them as God does. Why are you so agitated that you would take his governance away from him? He is patient with evildoers so that he may win them over. He is not a partner of the wicked, though he bears with them. And when it benefits the righteous for him not to deliver them, he adds beauty to their beauty through their afflictions. But because you are hasty, agitated, and full of pride, you find fault with the Ruler who is full of wisdom. And among the things that are in use in this evil world, you think of diminishing this one and adding to that one.

You devise schemes concerning wealth and poverty, to take from one person and give to another, if you can. You also say, “Why is this man weighed down with gold, while this other man lacks even his daily bread? Why is one man so rich that he even forgets God, while his fellow is so needy that he grumbles against the Creator? Why is one man occupied with counting his gold and cannot reach its end, while this other man dies of hunger in his need?” You who lack understanding, from whom God's governance is hidden, do not find fault with the Ruler who is full of goodness. It is good that he created wealth and poverty, and through either one he can give life to whoever endures. Through poverty, look: Lazarus is beside Abraham! And through wealth, look again: Abraham is in the kingdom! These two, one rich and one poor, now dwell as equals in one high and exalted place. The one's wealth did not make him proud or incline him [?] toward evil, nor did poverty keep the other from good deeds. That rich man's wealth became an occasion for good for him, for through it he gave relief to both the rich and the poor. And poverty became an occasion for good for the other man:

For he endured and was patient, and his struggle pleased the angels. Wealth and poverty are alike for whoever encounters them; in either condition he can do well, if he is discerning. The body has both a right hand and a left hand. One is weak and one is strong, yet it is one body. There is wealth in the world, and there is poverty in it, yet it is one world, like a single body that is not divided. Whoever asks, “Why was poverty created?” should therefore also ask, “Why was the left hand created?” Both the right hand and the left hand are useful to the body, and they help each other every day in their work. The strong hand does not reproach the weak one, nor does it ever think itself better than the other within the body. If the left hand takes up a task that is too hard for it, the right hand immediately runs to help. Both have one good purpose: that each should [?] the other lovingly every day. The body is a world containing wealth and poverty, and these are arranged to help one another. The rich man is appointed to have compassion on the poor man, to care for him and supply all his needs.

The poor man, in turn, is appointed to bow down and submit, to work without grumbling and provide relief in the households of the rich. For if poverty had not bent his neck, he would not have given himself to work in the households of the rich. He would have kicked against it if he had even a little strength, and would not have lowered his head to bow down like a poor man. Much work in the households of the rich would have lain idle, and their affairs would have been left unattended and undone. For this reason the Lord's wisdom created the poor, so that the rich might have relief in their affairs. Their need would compel them to go to the rich, to submit to them and attend to their affairs. Therefore the poor man too is obliged to submit, and the rich man is very much obliged to show compassion. It is also right for the poor man to be patient and bear illness and poverty without complaint. For the rich man, however, compassion toward the poor man is fitting, and he should supply all his needs. He must not be puffed up, boastful, or arrogant. He must not imagine that the poor man is not of his own kind. He must not grow proud or exalt himself over the poor. Rather, they are known to belong to one kind, and they are equal.

They are placed like the right and left hands in the body, by the one who fashioned the body and the world as he pleased. Look at the body: there is a member assigned to dishonor, yet among the members it is honored far more than its companions. O rich man, look: the poor man is a member of your own body. The Lord made him for your honor; take care of him. He comes from your own earth, from your own clay; he is of your own kind. He belongs to your own body. Do not look at him as a stranger. Who sees a member of his own body naked and does not clothe it, or exposed and does not care for it and cover it? The poor man is weak and stands like the left hand in the body. O rich man, come near like the right hand and support him. Do not imagine that he had compassion on you and gave you much, but hates that man and therefore created him poor. He gave you wealth; he did not add a member to your body. Whatever is outside you is not your own. The Creator is upright, and his creation is above reproach. Favoritism is far from him in all his dealings. He made human beings equal in their limbs and their forms, and the whole body is alike in rich and poor. He made them equal in the womb and in the grave, in birth and death, and one cannot be distinguished from the other.

The rich and the poor have one nature; and when the artist skillfully drew their forms, he gave human beings the necessities equally; but of things that are not necessary, he gave more to one and less to another. He gave light and life equally to every body, and did not favor the rich man in what he gave him. Again, he equally provided the air that gives life to human beings: there is only one kind for both rich and poor. The very air that the king breathes and lives by is also breathed by the beggar, without any difference. The sunlight that shines in the citadel of kings is the very same light that shines, unchanged, in the homes of the poor. Wind, breeze, rain, dew, and all the air are the same for rich and poor. Look at the distribution made by the just distributor, and be afraid to find fault with him who is high and exalted above blame. Human nature is equal in his eyes, and he made his creation equal when he created it. He gave it equally everything necessary for it to live. Life, light, air, speech, pleasure, the shape of the body, and its physical structure—all without distinction. O you who grumble about the distributions, saying they are not good:

learn from them and through them, and see how good they are! Look at the artist: when he sketched human forms, he showed no partiality, but apportioned them fairly. When he fashioned the poor and the rich, he adorned them with the same pigment and the same likeness. Here you are, grumbling about wealth, which is nothing, while you pay no attention to the body, which is something and which he made equal. The fool envies the sumptuous bedding on that rich man's bed, as though the one who distributes were unjust. He does not consider that he apportioned sleep fairly, rather than bedding, which is nothing to its owner. It is not bedding that gives the body rest, but sleep, and this he gave to both rich and poor. He went even further and gave the poor man more, so that he might rest on his meager bedding. Sleep belongs to the body, but bedding is not part of the body. In what belongs to the body, he did not allow anyone an advantage over his fellows. The rich man is worn out by concern for gold and possessions; his sleep flees, and wakefulness wears down [?] his body. That bedding does not make up for his lack of sleep, and he gains nothing from it, however abundant it is.

If he had arranged for one person to sleep and another not to sleep, he would have been unjust, and the latter would have been wronged by the distribution. But if sleep, which gives the body rest, is equal, then a high bed brings neither gain nor loss. What use are the clothes piled up in the houses of the rich, when human nature cannot bear them as it desires? If we add one more garment to the body, it will not accept it: it weighs upon it, and it even throws it off and will not bear it. Even if someone has ten thousand garments, the body wants only one—the body for which fig leaves were enough when it was exposed. However many there are beyond one, they are superfluous, for the body asks you for only one garment. Yet greed doubles and stores up the surplus that the body cannot bear, piling it into chests. Look, the poor are naked in the streets like animals, while moths settle in chests and gnaw away in the houses of the rich. But God did not create the rich this way, to be greedy and miserly and refrain from doing good. Rather, they should be compassionate and merciful, supplying everything the poor lack.

They should give clothing to anyone stripped bare, and coverings from their chests to the naked. The rich man who possesses gold should know that he has been made a steward to provide for his fellow servants. He should be afraid, knowing that he must also give an account of everything he acquired and how he provided for his fellow servants. If he shows no mercy, he will find no mercy there, as the words spoken by Abraham testify. If he alone has enjoyed his good things, he will need a drop of water, and they will not give it to him. For this reason, too, it is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for mercy will be shown to them.” It is everyone's duty to show mercy to their own flesh and blood. Whoever shows no mercy must suffer at the hands of justice. “Do not neglect your own flesh and blood,” the Lord said. He reminded you how you were formed, lest you forget that the other person is of your own kind. Your body is not gold while his is clay; rather, both you and he are molded clay. That poor man lying abandoned and naked is of your own kind. Turn aside and show mercy to your own flesh and blood, and then go on your way. Adam, the father of us all, begot him and begot you too.

You are brothers. Rich man, have compassion on your brother! See how God gave him a body like yours; his features and his limbs are also the same as yours. Look, he resembles you, and it is clear that he is your brother. You are told not to neglect your own flesh and blood. He is no stranger for you to neglect; he is your neighbor. And it is written that you should love your neighbor as yourself. If you have no compassion on someone of your own kind when he is brought low, honor your Lord's image as a discerning person should. If you have no desire to show mercy to the poor, honor the image of God, the image of that majesty. And if you have forgotten the book of Moses, who will teach you? Look to the new mother, baptism, and do not go astray. Look, the poor man has put on Christ just as you have, and through the waters you are brothers of the Only Begotten. Either do not neglect your own flesh and blood, as it is written, or honor him because he is the image of the Great One. Or, because he has put on baptism and is your brother, care for his needs so that justice does not accuse you. Look, you are arranged like limbs in the body of the world, both the rich and the poor, and it is one body.

O rich man, acquire compassion in this world; and you, poor man, take care not to grumble against the Creator. Praised is the Creator, who made wealth and poverty! From the rich and from the poor, praise belongs to him.

By Mar Jacob. Homily 28. On Repentance.
The sight of the world is full of deceit for anyone who looks at it.

I will look at you, my Lord, for you are full of beauty for anyone who looks at you. The world is dark, and its road is tangled with stumbling blocks. In your light, our Lord, I will travel with you to your Father's dwelling. The world is a dream, and whoever goes astray in it finds regret. Awaken us, my Lord, for you are the dawn that awakens those sunk in sleep. The world's road is entirely full of pits and snares. Be our road, radiant Son, and let us walk in you. Throughout the world's regions are deceit and favoritism. Sin is its harbor, and its trade is nothing but losses. Among its rulers is bribery, and among its judges, theft.

In its marketplaces is injustice, and in its assemblies, favoritism. Its peace deceives, its love chokes, and its beauty leads astray. It is entirely bitter and full of woes for anyone who loves it. At its watchposts stand demons, the children of darkness. They set snares and hide traps for anyone who travels through it. The demons have covered the path of truth with their rags, so that no one may see the snare and turn aside to avoid falling into it. Free will, however, has grown idle and fallen asleep, neglecting good deeds. Look, injustice is awake, and all creation is choked by it. Everyone stretches his foot into the snare and falls into it himself. For the snare does not run after and catch the person who falls into it. The evil one certainly entices and certainly causes confusion, for he cannot overcome free will by force. He conceals his snares, but anyone who wishes can see them, turn aside, pass by, and mock the hidden snare. For not everyone takes care to look for the snare. If he wished, he could pass it by without its harming him. The demons spread great deception over the roads, and everyone can recognize it as deception if he wishes. Who does not know that death comes at the end of life, and that the day of his end is like a stone slab above his head? Who does not know that the world is a dream and a shadow,

and that it passes away and does not accompany those who love it? Who does not know that the world's road leads to the grave? A little later or a little sooner—there he is! Who does not know that even if he acquires tens of thousands of talents, they give him nothing to take with him when he enters the grave? Who does not know that even if he becomes as rich as the day, his wealth stays here behind him when he dies? Who does not know that even if he gives all his gold, no bribe is accepted from him when his end comes? Who does not know that a virgin is better than a prostitute, and chastity better than the enticements of adultery? Who does not hate a drunkard when he sees him, and flee far from his company while mocking him? Who loves someone who is quarrelsome, contentious, and disorderly, who despises the elderly and is not restrained by those worthy of respect? Who does not hate deceit and theft, which are never good, even for those who practice them? So the devil's traps are plainly visible, yet a person looks at them and stretches out his foot to fall into them. Gold is loved, though a person knows that it will not accompany him, and possessions too, though he sees that they pass away. Though he hates sexual immorality, he does not let go of it,

and he craves wine while rebuking someone who gets drunk. Human nature is upright, and its creation is very beautiful; good deeds are fitting for it to perform. Human nature hates evil deeds when they are committed, yet while hating them, it practices them lovingly. Who would not weep over free will, seeing how far it has fallen? It loves goodness, yet commits every kind of evil each day. Though God desires goodness and gives a reward, and the very nature implanted in a person also helps him, and goodness itself is beautiful and praised by those who see it, no one wants to do good, even though he loves it. Though everyone hates evil and condemns it, and God too hates it and takes no pleasure in it, and human nature itself also hates it, since it was not created within it, despite all this, evil is practiced diligently. When God created human nature, it was beautiful; whatever ugliness is in it now does not come from him. When God had made it, he saw it, and behold, it was very beautiful. The serpent introduced these blemishes into free will. Because the Creator did not place sin in human nature, it is despised and feels remorse whenever it sins each day. Ugly desire entered from outside into what was beautiful:

She disturbs him, so that he loses his former beauty. For this reason, when sin corrupts the soul, she suffers and is ashamed, and the sin she has committed displeases her. Although the soul is not forced to sin, she grieves over her evil deeds as though force had driven her. Although she would not have sinned if she had so wished, she is bitter about it. Whom can she blame but herself for all her wrongdoing? The tyrant Pharaoh took Sarah away from Abraham—the proud king took her from an exile wandering in the land. The king’s table was not as pleasing to that freeborn woman as the little bread she had left in Abraham’s house. The discerning woman lay on the king’s lofty bed, but sleep there brought her no pleasure because of her husband. She had bound her love to that exile and had not forgotten him, even while the king’s delicacies were laid out on her table. Pharaoh’s wealth was contemptible in her eyes, and she grieved amid it. She longed to leave and return to Abraham. O soul, whom the evil one has led away from God, let no bread shared with him please you, for he is a murderer. Return to God as Sarah returned to Abram. He is your portion; do not put your trust in the deceiver.

Sarah went unwillingly to Pharaoh’s house. Great is your disgrace, for you have willingly submitted to slavery! Remember, O soul, his great image imprinted upon you, and the salvation he accomplished for you through his Only Begotten. He united you with himself and enrolled you under his name, and now you belong to him. Who is this who has settled beside your ear and taken you captive away from him? The world disturbed you with its enticements and led you toward its pleasures. Now it has bound you with its comforts as with harsh shackles. Like the table of the king of Egypt, the evil world is spread out and filled with temporal delights that never run out. That table brought no pleasure to Sarah, the free woman. Look at her, O soul, and let the evil world bring you no pleasure. Remember God as Sarah remembered Abram, and return to him as she returned to her husband. Look, the Egyptians are guarding the gates so that they will not let you return to the righteous one who watches and waits for you. The demons grieve if you return to God. Grieve them with your repentance, O soul full of beauty. It is good for you, O soul, to live with God, and not with the world, which is full of death for anyone who looks to it.

The evil Pharaoh wants to take you away from God. Take care not to ruin your union, so full of beauty. O daughter of Sarah, return like Sarah to the righteous one. Do not defile yourself with the wicked one who seeks your soul. On the day you leave Pharaoh’s house, the heavenly watchers rejoice, while the Egyptians sit mourning over your deliverance. They led you to the house of Ham and unjustly handed you over to the Egyptians. You became lowly in the dwelling of slaves who enticed you and led you away. Flee from the world, O soul who loves beautiful things! Flee from Pharaoh, O free woman who was carried away from her husband! Do not trust the Egyptian who unsettles you with splendid clothes and choice foods. Do not let the world deceive you: it withers like a flower. Its beauty is a dream. Look to God, who does not change. Break off your dealings with the Egyptians, for they are liars. Do not let the filthy demons lead you astray with desirable things. How sweet Pharaoh’s bread is to you, that you eat it! Remember God, and come like Sarah to Abraham. O soul, free and full of beauty and without blemish, bride of the King and great image of the Godhead! O creature exalted above other creatures by the beauty upon her, daughter of the shining ones, whom the Great One chose and in whom he traced his image!

Beloved image of the Great One, exalted above other images, who has ruined these beauties that dwell within you? Sin encountered me, entangled me, bit me, and stripped away my lovely features. It filled me with blemishes, and my once-beloved beauties faded. Pharaoh carried me away from God, whom I love. He enticed me and imprisoned me under his tyranny, and now he mocks me. Sin breathed like a viper upon the radiance of my face. Now I am ugly and dark, because I have done wrong. Satan assailed me, a freeborn woman, like the Egyptian. He separated me from God and carried me away to mock me. Now fierce demons, children of darkness, guard me like Egyptians, so that I cannot return to God. The world has bound me and imprisoned me in wicked dealings. Who will bring me out of the darkness in which I dwell? I have sinned and been broken; I have done wrong and stand ashamed. Who will bind my wounds, and who will tell me that I can be healed? The beauty with which I was created has been ruined by the wrongdoing of my hands. If I return in my ugliness, who will open the door to me? They will not let me enter the land from which I departed and see the bridegroom, who greatly loves beautiful things. Come, O soul who has practiced wrongdoing in the evil world!

Return to God, and he will restore to you the wealth you have lost. Abraham too received Sarah when she was defiled. She was made holy through him, and he united her to himself in purity. Pharaoh sent her away with defilement upon her limbs, but as soon as she came to Abraham, he made her pure. He neither reproached nor rebuked that freeborn woman. Instead, he rejoiced in her, and she lived with him in a pure union. The Lord also rejoices in you and desires you to return to him. He will receive you, make you holy, and cleanse you. Come out! Leave the defilement in which you lie prostrate. The Holy One does not recoil from cleansing you in himself. Just as Sarah was made holy after passing through defilement, Abram’s Lord will make you holy through union with him. O repentant soul, come, enter God's presence through repentance, which opens the door and unties knots. Come out! Leave the palace of that wicked one, and immediately the Lord, your master, will open the door to welcome you. He stretches out his arms, welcomes you, and cherishes you. He even rejoices over you as though you had never done wrong. He does not reproach you for having sinned or accuse you. Instead, he rejoices because you have returned, and he loves you. You hold back from leaving, but he does not hold back from welcoming you,

for he is ready to come out to meet you when you return. Do not delay turning to repentance, then, since you are confident that the door of the one who welcomes you is open. Even Pharaoh has no power to keep you with him: as soon as you wish to leave him, he cannot hold you. Why does he despise you? Because, although he does not hold you, here you are with him; and if you wish to leave, he does not compel you to stay. Look, the one who makes the unclean holy stands waiting for you. He carries hyssop for sprinkling his blood, to cleanse you with it. If you turn back to him, he unites you with himself; and when he has united you with himself, because of him you are holy in him. For an unbelieving woman is made holy through a believing man. How much more will she be made holy through the Lord of holy things, if she joins herself to him! Through repentance the soul enters God's presence, joins herself to him, and becomes one with him in one spirit.
