And just as Sarah was welcomed when she came from Pharaoh's house, so the soul is welcomed by God, the Lord of Abram. Only come! The one who welcomes you is standing there, full of compassion, and his door is open to anyone who comes. O soul whom the world has taken captive through its desires, flee from the world, Pharaoh's house, which is full of wrongdoing.

Do not take pleasure in the company of Egyptian women. Abandon those foreign desires. Do not let Pharaoh's house, full of good things, lead you astray—the world with its evil comforts that do not last. Better fire and sword with God, if they come upon you, than pleasures and splendid gifts with Satan. In her pain the sick soul says, “Who will give me those beauties in which I was clothed before I sinned? Even if God, who is merciful, welcomes me, who can restore to me the beauties I have lost? My beautiful nature, once radiant as the day, has grown dark and dim. Who will give it light so that it becomes beautiful again? Even if, in his compassion, I am forgiven my sins, who will restore me to the rank from which I fell? If he merely forgives me all the sins I have committed, that is a very great thing. Why should I hope for anything more? But that beauty which belonged to my created nature before I sinned—where shall I see it now, after I have lost it?” Come, soul, image of the King that has lost its beauty! Look, your beauty is in your Lord’s hands, and it is kept safe for you. As soon as you come, he will give it to you just as you left it. He has cared for it and kept it safe for you, so that it may be restored to you.

The Lord, your master, does not treat a wound like a physician, for a physician leaves a scar on the body when he heals it. Even when he troubles the body with bandages, medicinal herbs, and mixtures, so that there may be no scar on it at all, a scar remains, whether small or large, because a physician cannot make the body as it was before. Sick soul, if you show God your wound, when he treats it he will leave no scar on your body. He does not, like a physician, cut flesh from the limbs, leaving a scar where the flesh has been removed. He applies something from his own body to the wounds, and when he heals the sore, he makes it level with the rest of the body. When a wound is deep enough to become a fistula, he weaves his body into it; it is restored and becomes a beautiful body. He does not mix medicinal herbs, whether hot or cold, and make medicine for the wounds to treat them. In his love he tears his own body and places it on the injuries—a new deed that no one but he has done. Where have you ever seen a physician who puts his own body on wounds, except our Lord, who cares for the injured and treats them?

All physicians take blood from the body, but this physician pours his own blood into the wounds. What physician readily pours his own blood into sores, except Christ, who opened his side and treated us with his blood? Others take, but he gives, for he readily gives his blood so that all creation may be healed by it. He applies his body to the sores and pours his blood into the wounds, and no scar of wrongdoing can ever be detected in the soul. Forgiveness from God brings a new creation into being, and the soul, in its beauty, sees his face as far as it is able. He leaves no scar at all in the wound he treats, so that when he heals it, the place where the wound was cannot be recognized. All the beauty belonging to its nature is restored to it, so that the Lord may say, “Look, it is very beautiful,” as he said before. Through repentance he renews his creation by forgiveness, and he leaves no scar of wrongdoing in it to make it ugly. He treats the wound as God, not as a physician, for God creates, and it is easy for him. That very beauty which he gave to nature when he created it, he grants it through repentance when he forgives it. If he were to leave a scar, it would be a disgrace to the one who bears it.

If he leaves a scar in the soul when he treats it, he himself is reproached for having healed the wound while its blemish remains. It would be said either that he was unable to do it, or that it was malice that made him heal the wound but leave the blemish. Stumblings and words are drawn from the merciful, blameless knowledge of the one worthy of praise. There was a wound in the soul of Simon, the chief of the disciples, because evil had lain in wait for him and brought him to ruin through denial. When he took refuge in repentance and brought tears, Christ bandaged his wound and gave him back his former beauty. Before he sinned, he had been made head of the disciples; and after he denied, Christ gave him back his place through repentance. He did not demote him to fifth or third place, but raised him up and established him in his former rank. Before he denied, he was steward of the household. He denied and went out; when he returned, Christ brought him in and, moreover, gave him his flock to shepherd. He gave him his keys, which he had lost when he denied, and also added lambs, sheep, and ewes. Just as his beauty was increased through repentance, Christ also increased his authority over the flocks he had acquired.

The Son of God loved his flock and died for it, and he gave it to Simon, whom he trusted to guard it. This man is a disciple of repentance: it was repentance that brought him back in, and without it he would have remained outside. He had denied his Lord, sworn, and called down a curse, saying that he did not know him. He became angry, went out of the house, and went away. Repentance ran after him as he fled, turned him back, and brought him to kneel at his Lord’s threshold. It taught him to bring tears instead of offerings, and he took them and brought them, as repentance had taught him. As soon as he came, Christ looked at him, and he became beautiful. Christ received him into his company as though he had never denied him at all. After this, he gave him the whole flock for which he had died, as to a friend who had never sinned. He made him an image and a mirror for those who repent, so that they might know the power of repentance. With the beauty that human nature possesses before it sins, a person enters and stands in God’s house as soon as he repents. Even the angels rejoice over a sinner who repents,

because the King’s image, which had been lost, has been found. Now, soul, take courage and be assured that your beauty will be restored to you. Come to God. Just as it was restored to Simon, the chief of the apostles, all the beauty of your nature will be restored to you. Just as Sarah was sanctified from defilement through her husband, Abram’s Lord will also sanctify you from your evil deeds. Pharaoh had broken apart the union of Abraham’s household, and in his tyranny had torn a limb from the chaste body. The Evil One has likewise taken you and torn you away from God; he has estranged you and separated you from communion with that Majesty. But Sarah returned, and the limb too came back to its place; the body that had troubled that Egyptian was restored. So you too, if you turn toward God, he will establish you in himself and unite you with his greatness. The rift that the Evil One made between you and God will cease to exist, as though it had never existed and never would. Sarah was not considered an adulteress in Abraham’s household: she went away and returned, and was a free woman, as though she had never gone away. As soon as she returned, she was not even regarded as having gone away. 662. For fellowship with the righteous man made her pure. Simon too, after he had denied him, was accepted as soon as he returned and shed tears, as though he had never denied him. You too, O soul, if you turn toward God, he will be with you as though you had never sinned at all. After pure Sarah had been in the wicked man’s house, and he who was far from God had been joined to her, and she had lived under his name in uncleanness and great disgrace, and had been separated from Abraham, the righteous man, and Pharaoh’s servants had required her to follow the customs of Egyptian women, and the Egyptian himself had treated her however he wished, and, that is to say, she had gone up to his bed with him like an Egyptian woman—and behold, she was about to be lost to God and to Abraham— she returned to Abraham, and what had been ruined was restored, as though these things that had happened among the Egyptians had never happened. The righteous man received his wife without complaint. He rejoiced that she had returned and dismissed the things that had been reported. God too, after she returned from Pharaoh’s house, gave her Isaac through Abraham, the righteous man. The Lord showed that Sarah was clean from defilement through the son he gave her, who was the heir and the child of the promise. And perhaps Sarah is a likeness and an image of the soul,

and for this reason she went away, and for this reason she returned to Abraham: to be an example for the soul that turns back from evil, showing that as soon as it turns toward God, he receives it. He forgives it, cleanses it, and sanctifies it; and it stands clothed in all the beauties established within it. Even the assurances and promises that God has for perfection, he gives to repentance. He withholds none of the promises from it, just as he withheld nothing from Sarah, who came out of uncleanness. Take courage, O soul that has fallen away from God! Rise and come to him who is crucified and stands waiting for you. All day long his hands are stretched out in crucifixion, and he is looking toward you, so that you may go with him to his Father’s dwelling. Amid his sufferings he cried aloud on the cross, so that you might come out of the house of the unclean Pharaoh who took you captive. Answer him, O soul, for look, he bears a burden for your sake. Say, “Yes, my Lord, I will go with you wherever you go.” Renounce Pharaoh, his delicacies, his table, and his choice foods, which are full of death.

Renounce the world and despise its wealth and its pleasures, its possessions, its fame, its glory, and its power. Renounce palaces if they are far from fellowship with you, and fortresses if they are not rich in your cross. Take possession of me, you who redeemed me. My captor took me captive after you let me go. Come in and bring me out of Pharaoh’s house, so that I may be with you. Do not expect me to come to you, for I am weak. Come to me yourself and take me away from the unclean one who captured me. Soul whom the world has corrupted with its pleasures, turn back and speak boldly to the Lord, your master: “The Egyptian captured me, ruined my freedom, and destroyed my purity. I have lived among the wicked in the uncleanness of wrongdoing. “Mine is the blame, for if I had not consented, I would not have been led away. His is the disgrace, for he dared to take captive from you the freedom that was mine. “Rebuke me and bring me out of the uncleanness in which I live. Hand him over and bind him, because he dared to attack your possession. “For me, [?] all that I saw among the wicked; and put him to shame as his [?] is led away from him. “Unite me with you, so that I may be made holy in you and belong to you. Cast him into destruction, to become food for the flame. “Comforts have sunk me into the sleep of wrongdoing upon his bed. Wake me yourself and lead me to you, so that I may be with you.

“Sin has held me back, and I cannot come to you. Come and take what is yours; do not let me perish after you have found me. “Work your will in me, so that I may will, and unite my will with yours. Thwart the tyrant’s will, so that he may not rejoice over me. “I incurred guilt because I sinned; I was ashamed because I went astray; I died because I consented. Through you may I become wise; through you may the shame on my face be forgotten. “The fragrance of life wafts from you, my King and Savior. Come and bring me out of the foulness in which I live. “The smell of death has blown into my face from the Egyptian. Let your name be oil of myrrh for me, so that I may be refreshed by you. “The world’s night has darkened my paths and multiplied my stumbling. Come, Christ, the daylight; lead me, so that I may be with you. “A snare confronted me, and I fell into it because I wanted to fall. Come, break the snare and rescue the soul that is being strangled in it. “The evil one has obstructed my good paths with his traps, and now I am walking on the path of wrongdoing. Bring me to you. “Restore me to yourself, my Lord, as Sarah was restored to Abram, so that I may be made holy in you and belong to you, here and hereafter. “Glory to you, my Lord! How greatly your compassion has loved me, that you should create me in mercy, guide me in mercy, and take possession of me in mercy.
“By that mercy with which you called me from the beginning, by that same mercy forgive my sins and have mercy on me.”
The end of the homily on repentance.
Spoken by the blessed Mar Jacob, the teacher. By the same Saint Mar Jacob. Homily 29. On repentance and admonition.

The great road of repentance is very easy, and milestones of peace stand in rows along it for those who travel on it. Who would not become righteous like the prostitute by walking on this way? She ran and entered the presence of the Forgiver, and was not held back. Who plundered, acted unjustly, and did wrong like the robber? Yet when he set his face toward the goal, he took up the race eagerly. He was bound to the cross, but his way to the kingdom lay open, for all difficulties are easy for repentance. He was fastened with nails, yet the journey he had undertaken did not stop.

For repentance is not crippled, not even by shackles. These examples are set like a mirror before anyone who falls, so that, seeing them, he may be stirred to rise from his fall. Let him take courage: if she found life in Christ, to what sinner will he not open the door if he pleads with him? The tax collector is near; who is far from God except the one who has stopped on his way in despair? The Law opened a way for the righteous, but it is very hard: they walk on it, yet are not justified by the Law. But through grace our Lord became a way for the world, so that even sinners are justified through him without the Law. He made himself available to tax collectors, so that they might come to repentance, and to prostitutes, so that they might approach him without being held back. Our Lord poured out mercy on those who were very wicked, for healing was fitting for them, since they were weak. Wickedness had spread like a disease throughout the whole world, and our Lord came down like a visiting physician to heal them. Because the world could not come to God, the Son of God carried it to bring it near to his Father. He became a way for the weary and carried them, and through him those too weak to walk were able to come.

This is the way that moved by itself and carried the dead to bring them across to the land of life. The way picked up those without feet to make them run; they would not have traveled had it not brought them near. For if he had not become a way full of wonder, prostitutes would not have run along it toward the Holy One. If our Lord had not enabled the tax collector to walk and come, he would have remained crippled by wickedness and would not have approached righteousness. So let us not grow weary; let us travel the way of repentance, for our Lord himself carries anyone who comes to him. Who would not come to this path full of good things? It brings you near, so that you may complete your journey without growing weary. The world's way had ceased to carry travelers, and even the righteous could scarcely travel along it toward God. Sinners never came along it at all, for under the Law even the righteous scarcely find life. But our Lord came and stretched himself out before sinners, becoming a way for them to walk on without the Law. And from then on, day after day, this way is never blocked. For who can cut off a way that travels along with its travelers? Come, then, sinners, and walk on this road.

For it was not Moses who opened it, but the Son of God. You who are weary with sins, walk with the tax collector who travels on it. You who are worn down by wrongdoing, look: the prostitute is accompanying you. Has wickedness bound you? The road is open, along with the robber. The excuse has been removed; do not neglect the journey. No one forces you to undertake the race alongside good people. It is full of wicked people who walk on it without being rebuked. Do not yourself give up good deeds altogether, lest you become worse even than the wicked who perform them. Look at the prostitute and weep with her over your offenses. But if you scorn this, I do not know what to compare you to. Ask for the kingdom like the robber, and it will be given to you. But if you are negligent, you are not a robber but a [?]. Imitate the tax collector and distribute a little of your possessions. If you do not repent even with these people, who is like you? Are you really more corrupt than the prostitute who repented? Or are you much more grasping than the tax collector who was justified? Are you worse than the robber in the deeds of your hands? How far, then, does your measure reach, if this is what you are like? If you are worse than the tax collector, the prostitute, and the robber, man, denial alone remains for you to practice.

High is the measure to which we have raised you, if you are a denier! You resemble Simon; repent like him too, and you will be accepted. Simon's denial is a mirror for you, if you wish to build yourself on that rock through repentance. Set your building on the foundation, if you are discerning. For who bears the weight of the house but Simon? Unless you have laid the courses of your dwelling on that rock, you are outside the house. Where will the master of the house look for you? Simon also wept bitterly for this reason: so that whoever sins might imitate him in repentance. Without repentance, the church has no place with God, for it is built upon repentance, and through it the church has stood from the beginning. The church glories in repentance, for it is her hope. Through it she catches people and brings them to God. It is the great net that the Son of God cast into the world: even if it gathers in the dead, they plainly become alive. See this wonder in the gospel: through repentance, even a prostitute fills the place of virgins. Simon, who was placed in the church as a foundation, had denied him, so that anyone who wishes to build himself upon him should not be afraid. Look at what the knowledge of the Son of God has done:

whom he first appointed as mediator between himself and the church. The one who had sunk to denial stood beside sinners as a companion, to lead them to the Faithful One. He descended through denial and took his stand on the left side, and stirred that whole side to come over to the right. Because he had denied, he was counted among sinners, to show them how to turn back to God. When his denial was confirmed and he was about to perish, the wise man wept and shattered the ranks of the left side. He denied and stood firm, as though he belonged to that side; but while they were leading him, he turned his hand around and led them. He became a companion of the wicked when he denied, and taught them that they could become good through repentance. He dug a baptismal font there among the wicked and filled it with tears, so that they might watch him as he was forgiven. In his own person he showed the work of repentance, so that everyone who sins might imitate him in every way. He wept bitterly over his transgression, and his weeping was enough to restore him to the rank of apostle. Sin lay upon him like a lion, biting him; but he hurled drops of tears at it and drove it away, so that it would not ravage him.

Sin kindled a flame and set it burning within him; but he sprinkled water, entered the blaze, trampled it down, and passed through. A sore broke out on him, and he sat bandaging it before sinners, so that they might watch him and bandage their own transgressions. The brave man was struck by the arrow of wickedness and grew faint from pain; and as he wailed, he pulled [?] out of his armor. He was a warrior who became an example to the wounded, showing what someone struck between the battle lines should do. Through weeping he pulled out the arrow that had struck him while he fought; and he bandaged the wound itself with tears and relieved its pain. He became a mirror into which all sinners might look and beautifully adorn themselves. Look, it is wisely made for this purpose: that through repentance you may become beautiful every day, if you become tarnished. God placed steps of love one above another, so that the world might climb them toward him and reach him. He was on high, while our dust lay upon its ashes; and through the means he arranged, he raised us up to be with him. Through the Son’s birth he made the earth a well-trodden path as he descended, so that it might be easy to ascend along it toward the one who sent him. Between the world and the Father, the Son stood as mediator.

And he appointed Simon, in turn, as mediator between himself and the Church. He made the ascent a well-trodden path, so that no one would stumble while traveling along it, by the steps he arranged when he descended to humanity. At the beginning of the road stands the denier, and now he calls to you: “Come, let us travel through repentance toward God.” When you follow him, you find him weeping [?]; and when you draw near, you find him a great apostle. On that journey he brings you closer, in turn, to see the Son; and he appears to you as a human being full of sufferings. And when you join him as a companion to walk with him, you discover that he too is God, like the one who begot him. Little by little you have climbed, O sinner, from the depths, so that you may be with God on high. Because Simon denied, he can speak confidently to sinners and encourage them concerning the forgiveness that comes from God. Again, it is written that our Lord, because he was tempted, helps those who are tempted when they call upon him in their distress. The sinner takes courage when he walks with the one who denied and learns from him about the practice of repentance. He is strengthened again when he sees Christ crucified, bearing iniquity and enduring sufferings for the wicked.

The Merciful One arranged easy steps for weak people, so that they would not stumble as they ascend to repentance. He made a persecutor an apostle to sinners, so that in his own person he might demonstrate the work of repentance. Again, he set the one who denied as the foundation of the house, so that all who repent might build their buildings upon him. Simon denied, Saul persecuted, and our Lord was crucified—all these things happened so that the wicked would come to repentance. Look at the proclaimers of good news: one who denied and one who persecuted! Who would be afraid to walk with these men toward God? The Son, the mediator, also endured sufferings for your sake and took your great iniquity upon himself so that you might be forgiven. The Teacher of life wisely caught the world, and he placed in the Gospel ways suited to repentance. He placed the one who denied among the ranks of the wicked, so that he might lead them as companions and come to weep before the Majesty. Simon's weeping is a great resource among those who repent, so that the sound of his sobs may awaken them to repentance. It is as though Simon were saying these things to sinners: There is hope for the wicked person who turns away from his hateful deeds.

Once iniquity bit me too, threw me down, and broke me. I gave tears as payment to the physician, and he came and bandaged me. I became one who denied and scorned the Son before those who crucified him. What sin in the whole world is greater than this? I am your fellow. Come, plead for forgiveness! Follow my example, for mercy had compassion on me in my own suffering. Weep as I wept, and you will be forgiven as I was forgiven. Cry out with sobbing, and your offenses will quickly pass away. At one time the snare of wickedness caught me too, but through repentance mercy broke it, and I escaped. Sin struck me and uprooted me from my foundations. I shed tears and wept over myself, for I had been shaken. I too suffered this pain that afflicts you, and as soon as I wept, I found relief from distress. I had fallen into this sickness of evil passions, and if weeping had not come to my aid, I would not have risen. Listen to me, my companions; I will show you what I did. I wept bitterly, and little by little I was healed. With my weeping, the sin that was killing me fled. I gave tears and received mercy from the Merciful One.

Do this, and you will be healed as I was healed. I have experienced it myself; do not doubt forgiveness. Simon's weeping says these things to sinners, to stir them with encouragement to shed tears. While the wicked were careless and absorbed in their sins, Peter wailed and urged them to repent. They were sunk in despair as though asleep, and he cast the sound of weeping over them to awaken them. He began a refrain for all sinners to repeat after him, for at its conclusion there is great hope for whoever sings it. The chief of the disciples wrote a new book with his tears and lovingly gave it to sinners to study. He said, “Read here until you learn righteousness. Evening and morning, practice repentance with tears.” When sin pierces the soul, pull it out with weeping, for it does not come out except through bitter tears. See, he laid a firm foundation for the repentant and taught them how to build themselves up. Simon's weeping accomplished a great work in the Church. Indeed, from the beginning there had never been another as great as it.

Through those tears that Peter shed in his repentance, he left the Church a great example to imitate. Who knew what to do when he sinned? And who was certain that when he wept he would receive help? Who can paint the king's image without models, or the greatness of the hidden soul without an example? Sin had marred it, and who would have known how it could be repaired if Simon had not wept and taught about its restoration? He is no ordinary man; let no one despise his teaching. Through himself, not through someone else, he teaches you what to do. Once the soul has been cleansed in the waters of baptism, there is no other sacrifice to make atonement for it except tears. The Son of God died to sin only once, and he does not die again. Offer something yourself if you sin. Another sacrifice will not be given for your salvation. Give something of your own that can atone for your wrongdoing. Be a courageous priest for yourself, like Abraham, and sacrifice your voice, like his only son, in the place of atonement. Sprinkle your soul with blood flowing abundantly—with tears, which become a sacrifice without defilement.

Make atonement for [?] yourself through your soul's suffering as you weep. Do not summon your Lord again to insult and abuse. Today let us weep bitterly over our evil deeds. We have driven goodness away from us with our rebuffs long enough. Today let us love repentance, which has its reward. We have worked at wrongdoing under contract long enough. We have saved righteousness for a tomorrow that is not near, while we have given the whole of today to wrongdoing to make use of it. Sin is close at hand, while righteousness is outside the gate. “I will sin here,” he says, “and be made righteous over there.” Look how often we say, “Tomorrow,” yet we have not kept our promise. Every day we promise repentance, and still it remains far away. We readily promise every good deed, but every day we carry out evil with vigor. Day after day we set a time for repentance, but our tomorrow never comes for us to benefit from it. We have driven good deeds away from us along with the passing days, so that the whole span of life passes without repentance. Where is that promise today which was made yesterday: “I will wait until tomorrow, when I will turn away from evil deeds”? Get up and do your work! Enough of making false promises!

Sin stands against you. Get up and fight your killer! Do not give all your days to wickedness. Set aside time for righteousness while you still have control. We sinned yesterday; let us weep today over our offenses. Let us not make sin our rule and give ourselves free rein. We have grown old in wickedness; let us become children through repentance, for only someone who is like a child enters the kingdom. Our Lord took a child in his arms to show how beautiful creation is in its proper order to someone who preserves it. Look at the apostles, to whom he showed the child, saying, “Become like this one, for this is the goal of perfection.” My Lord, how can an old man become a child when he has spent most of his days in emptiness? “There is something added to the created nature of anyone who has sinned,” he says. “He himself has added something of his own to the way he was made.” As long as a person's nature is preserved as it was created, he is always a child. But if he sins, he grows old in wickedness and falls into decay. Let the soul turn back and, through repentance, tear out of its makeup these structures that it built when it went astray. Take the trouble yourself and remove the excess things that have entered your being,

and give me only a pure nature, just as I created you. Do not try to make yourself righteous with anything of your own, not even a little. Keep your nature for me spotless and very beautiful. But if something extra has entered into the way you were made, it is no use to me. Let it be removed through repentance. “Turn yourself back,” he says, “and become a child, just as I created you, so that you may be an heir in the kingdom, as I called you to be.” Examine what there is in you that is your own [?], and throw it away. Leave what is mine unchanged, and you are a child of my kingdom. Uproot from your soul whatever sin has built there. My creation is beautiful; do not throw it into confusion with desires. “Therefore, turn yourself back,” he says, “and become a child, for that is the goal of perfection and righteousness.” See what a repentant person can do if he makes an effort: even if he is old, he can make himself a child again. Denial entered and made the chief of the disciples old, but through repentance he turned himself back into a child. He saw the sin that weighed upon him like old age, and as he wailed, he shook it off, for it displeased him. The soul is skillful, and her understanding rises above created things. She has the power to act in whatever direction she inclines.

When she turns to building good things, she uproots the foundations of wickedness to remove it from her dwelling. She enters her own being as though entering a great house, and sees that it is disordered and full of the refuse of desires. Wickedness lies there in a great mass, having entered from the evil one, and other sins are arranged there like stumbling blocks. It is full of evils, and its doorway is blocked with foul things. There is no room for goodness to enter from any side. Through repentance the soul is enlightened to see these things, and she sets herself to the toil of carrying away the full weight of all these evils. But when she sees that this task is beyond her strength, she calls upon mercy to help her in her work. She begins to drag wickedness out of her house, and with tears she hires compassion to work alongside her. She undertakes to sweep away the sins that have entered her since her childhood, and discerningly sprinkles herself with the water of her eyes. She sweeps sins out of her chamber like thorns, and boils with weeping to burn them up with its heat. Wisely she casts a fire of water upon them, to set them ablaze with a smokeless burning. Simon weeps: who would not wail if he is a sinner?

The robber entered: who would not take courage if he is repentant? The robber too became a child through that confession, and then attained the position of an heir in that kingdom. With a single word he moved all the mountains of wickedness that he had built, for his faith was strong. Mercy helped him accomplish this great deed, and if you desire it, mercy will come to help you too. Only begin, and compassion will immediately walk with you. Take the initiative, and your helper will not delay. You yourself are holding back from calling at the door of repentance. Glory to mercy, which is so joyful toward those who repent!
The discourse on repentance is finished.
